en: In the spring of the third year of the Chongzhen era, Master Tiantong composed the *Lüeshuo Yuanqi* (Brief Explanation of the Origins) to refute delusions and provide salvation. At that time, Han Yue sent me a copy of the *Wuzongyuan*. I set it aside and did not read it, further saying:
Regarding the single character "Mu" (Eye): I fear it may not transcend the path of the Sixth Patriarch and result merely in followers of the school of intellectual understanding;
thus, I cannot help but expose this. These are the words of this old monk that go against the grain, intended for Han Yue to recognize his error.
In the spring of the sixth year, Qingshan sent a letter to Han Yue which said: "Since the time of Avidyā (Wei-yin), when there were no forms, the One-Circle became a thousand."
The Buddha is the patriarch of ten thousand Buddhas. Linji’s “Profound Essentials” (Xuanyao) serves to reveal the secrets of the seven Buddhas and successive patriarchs;
as for that "single wooden wedge" (jian yijue tou), it is like the drool of a wild fox, and I, this old monk, set it aside as well. I simply say: give each of you one blow.
The reason for restoring Qing Shan was also because I hoped Han Yue would change his course.

Subsequently, upon seeing the *General Exposition* (Pushe) by Dingmu and the refutations by Layman Liu, I surmised they were all secretly commissioned by Han Yue; thus, I examined the *Origins of the Five Schools* (Wuzongyuan).

Only then did I realize that the "One" and "Zero" were already contained within the *Origins of the Five Schools*, which is why the *Three Records* (Sanlu) state what they do. Now, Tanji has recklessly composed the *Five Schools*...
I am deeply distressed by the calamity of Han Yue’s secret instructions, from which we can find no rest. How could this old monk bear to sit idly by and watch?
It is because Han Yue did not take his own realization as the core principle for directly pointing out all people, but instead sought out painters to depict the origins of the Seven Buddhas;
yet, since there is no record of the existence of Vipaśyin Buddha (Viyunwang Fo), he had no basis for his evidence.

10. [The character] ○ is the progenitor of the thousand Buddhas and ten thousand Buddhas. Furthermore, it is said that each of the five houses emerged from one aspect of this ○, yet only Linji is considered the orthodox.

Consequently, people falsely identify such categories as the "Three Mysteries" and "Three Essentials" as the core teachings, and they forcibly cite instances such as the "three strikes" and "three shakes" to align with them.
Is this not the great intent of the Buddha-dharma transmitted from the ancestors? How could it be...?
It has not been confounded or extinguished by Han Yue. Furthermore, he falsely claims to have long since mounted the power of his vows, as it is said of old:

"When the Dharma perishes, [Maitreya] will surely return. Tanji also claimed that since the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye had been submerged for a long time, there must surely be a Great Being who has mounted the power of his vows to arise and rescue it. These are both mere dreams, enchanting the children of the household. Now...
Although those individuals have all already passed away, I, this old monk, fear that other descendants of their lineages will still fall into this same pitfall,
deceiving one another in succession, so that students of future generations will forget the recognition of the "One" (the One-Character) and fail to attain self-awakening.

This constitutes the sin of extinguishing the Buddhas, extinguishing the Patriarchs, and extinguishing the life-force of wisdom. Since the time of Han Yue, I, this old monk, have sat by and watched without saving them;

this, too, is my own sin. Therefore, I cannot help but briefly summarize the essential points to refute those who act out of delusion while claiming to save others, precisely in order to provide true salvation.
Long ago, Yangshan drew a perfect circle and rubbed it away with his foot. Zifu Bao Chan...
When the Master saw Minister Chen Cao approaching, he drew a circle. Cao said, "I, your disciple, have come in such a manner that I am already at a disadvantage;
you further draw a circle. Fuyou added a dot in the center. Cao said, "I took you for the master of a South Sea merchant ship.
Fuyou then returned to his quarters and closed the door. "What kind of face is this? This old monk only wishes—"
The world and future generations take the ancients as their models; be careful not to fall into the trap of Han Yue.
Only then will you understand that Bodhidharma’s coming from the West was solely for the purpose of seeking a person who would not be deluded.

You will also see that this old monk did not initially compete with Han Yue and his ilk for victory or defeat, but only sought to clarify the great intent of the Buddha-dharma, so that every person may [awaken] for themselves.
Merely to certify one's own realization.
Written on the day of the Winter Solstice in the Wuyin year of the Chongzhen era by the old monk Yuanwu.

A Brief Explanation for Dispelling Delusions and Saving [Sentient Beings] by the Venerable Tiantong,
Compiled by Attendant Zhenqi, Scroll One:
The Seven Buddhas.
▲The verse of Vipaśyin Buddha says: The body arises from within the signless, Just like various forms produced by illusion.
The mind-consciousness of the illusory person is originally non-existent; Both sin and merit are empty, having no place of abiding.
▲ The verse of Śikhin Buddha says: The arising of all wholesome dharmas is fundamentally an illusion; The creation of all unwholesome karmas is likewise an illusion.
The body is like a mass of foam; the mind is like the wind. From illusion they emerge, without root and without substantial nature.
▲The verse of Vipaśyin Buddha says: "Relying on the four great elements, a body is formed; The mind is originally without birth, arising only due to objects.
If the external object is absent, the mind is likewise non-existent; Sin and merit are like illusions—they arise and then perish."
▲The verse of Krakucchanda Buddha says: To see that the body has no reality is the Buddha-body; to realize that the mind is like an illusion is the Buddha-illusion.
When one realizes that the nature of both body and mind is empty, how can such a person differ from the Buddha?
▲The verse of Kāśyapa Buddha says: "The Buddha does not perceive a body to know he is the Buddha; if there were truly a knowing apart from this, there would be no Buddha.
The wise are able to know that the nature of offenses is empty; they remain serene and unafraid of birth and death."
▲The verse of Kāśyapa Buddha says: "The nature of all sentient beings is pure; from the beginning, there is neither birth nor extinction.
This very body and mind are born of illusion; within this illusory transformation, there is neither sin nor merit."
The Master read Tanji’s *Wuzong jiu* (Rescue of the Five Schools) and critiqued it, saying: "The so-called 'school tenets' are the Dharma-eye transmitted from antiquity.
Our ancestor Linji, at the outset, said to Puhua and Ke Fu: 'I wish to establish the Huangbo school tenets here.
When Puhua asked, 'What did you say three days ago? Linji struck him. Three..."
Later, Ke-fu asked the Master, "Why did you strike Puhua the other day? Linji also struck him.
This was the establishment of Linji’s fundamental doctrine: to strike immediately upon being questioned.
Finally, he declared, "Who will know that my Treasury of the True Dharma Eye shall perish at the hands of a blind donkey? He never, apart from San-sheng, had anything else to transmit.

This is what is called the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye. Although Yangshan received from Danyuan the ninety-seven kinds of circular diagrams (*yuánxiàng*), he never heard it said that these circular diagrams constituted the fundamental tenet. Yet at the end, he said only: "One, two, three, two, child!
Leveling your eyes and looking up again—two mouths with no tongues. This is my fundamental tenet. Furthermore, how could it be [merely] about one and two?
"Outside of you two or three disciples, is there some other so-called 'fundamental tenet' (*zongzhi*)?
You have arbitrarily fabricated a circle (○) as the ancestor of the thousand Buddhas and ten thousand Buddhas, claiming it to be the fundamental tenet; this began with Han Yue.

Do not even mention Tan Ji—though he composed ten volumes of the *Wujiongjiu* (Rescuing the Five Schools), even if his fabrications were to fill the void of space, they could never rescue Han Yue from his arbitrary fabrication."

Regarding the sin of [distorting] the fundamental tenet: if you still do not believe this, please look at the lineage from Śākyamuni down to Tiantong—sixty-eight people in total—who were essentially one person.
Who could compare to Han Yue, who devised a particularly eccentric scheme and painted a "circle" (○) as the fundamental tenet?
According to his letter to Qing Shan, he wrote: "Ever since the era of Vipaśyin was formless, the 'one circle' (一○) has been..."

The progenitor of the thousand Buddhas and ten thousand Buddhas; thus, the Seven Buddhas [expressed this] through the "double-headed single knot" and the interlacing of the four dharmas, forging them into the unadorned secret seal (*mudrā*).
Kāśyapa transmitted it for twenty-eight generations, none of whom failed to transmit the Dharma-seal to the mind.
An old monk wrote in his critique: "The Seven Buddhas possessed only verses; I have never seen the 'double-headed single knot,' nor have I heard of it."
Śākyamuni possesses four dharmas that intersect, which together form the number ten (10). This constitutes the "Unwritten Secret Seal" (mujun mimm-in).
Now, as for the transmission of twenty-eight generations by Kāśyapa: since these four dharmas intersect, how can it be said that this is the "Unwritten Secret Seal"?
Master T'an-gi’s discourse, in refuting the arguments of the aforementioned [opponent], is entirely what is called "letting the words distort the meaning"; he is misrepresenting the ancients.
The Master [Zongmi] employs four methods of cross-referencing in his discourse; this merely harms the intent of the unadorned, esoteric seal (*amudra*).

Little does he realize that in offensive debate, there are both direct blows and indirect strikes. His *Pibushu* (Book on Dispelling Doubts) claims that the Seven Buddhas possessed only verses and that no "double-headed" or "single-knot" seals have been seen;
furthermore, he has never heard that Śākyamuni employed four methods of cross-referencing to compose a single work.
The circle (○) represents the Unwritten Secret Seal (*mudrā*). That the Kāśyapa lineage was transmitted through twenty-eight generations is stated according to the facts;
this is the primary meaning. Since the four dharmas are interwoven, how could it be called the "Unwritten Secret Seal"?
To briefly point out the contradiction within his own words is the secondary meaning. [The author] has repeatedly emphasized the circle as the unifying principle.

Regarding "verbal expression" (yanquan): verbal expression enters into the circle (○). Compared to the hexagram lines, the *Hun* and *Xici* commentaries, this is precisely what is meant by "using the old monk’s words to harm the old monk’s meaning.
According to the old monk, who cares whether there is verbal expression or not? It simply constitutes this single circle (○).
This is exactly where Han Yue’s fundamental error lies. The verse of Krakucchanda Buddha says: "Seeing the body..."

That which lacks substantiality is the Buddha-body; realizing that the mind is like an illusion is the Buddha-illusion. When one realizes that the nature of body and mind is empty, how does such a person differ from the Buddha?
Is this not the meaning that for the enlightened person, there is no difference from the Buddha, and that outside of man there is no separate Buddha?
Although the verses of the Seven Buddhas and the successive Patriarchs differ in their explicitness or obscurity, none of them has established a single [separate entity].
Regarding the claim that the "One Circle" (○) is the progenitor of the thousand Buddhas and ten thousand Buddhas:

since it has already been stated that the "Majestic Sound" (Vaiśvānara) is formless, if this "One Circle" is the progenitor of the thousand Buddhas and ten thousand Buddhas, then before these thousand Buddhas and ten thousand Buddhas had appeared, who was there to certify for Han Yue that this "One Circle" was the progenitor of the thousand Buddhas and ten thousand Buddhas? There was no one.

To claim that Yuezheng considers this "one circle" (一○) to be the progenitor of the thousand Buddhas and ten thousand Buddhas is for Han Yue himself to recklessly assert that this "one circle" is the progenitor of the thousand Buddhas and ten thousand Buddhas. Is this not groundless and delusory talk?
Therefore, I, the old monk, rely on the purport of the gāthās of the Seven Buddhas to prove the error of Han Yue’s "one circle. Tanji then said: "The Buddha-dharma..."
There is no place to put his mouth. Why not look to Layman Pang? When he first visited Shitou, he asked, "Who is it that does not take the myriad dharmas as a companion?
Shitou covered his mouth with his hand, and the Layman suddenly attained realization.
On another day, Shitou saw him and asked, "After you have seen this old monk, how do you conduct your daily affairs?
The scholar said, "If one asks about daily affairs, there is no place to open one's mouth. He then presented a verse to clarify the meaning of having no place to open one's mouth, saying:
"Daily affairs are no different; Only I am naturally in harmony with them. At every turn, there is neither grasping nor rejecting."
"Appearing and disappearing everywhere, who would designate 'Zhang' or 'Guai'? Who would label them 'Zhu' or 'Zi'? Mountains and hills are utterly free from a speck of dust;
spiritual powers and wondrous functions consist in carrying water and hauling firewood. As the ancients said, "I only fear that it is not the Buddha;
do not worry that the Buddha cannot understand speech. Yet, Tanji claimed there is no place to set one's teeth regarding the Buddha-dharma, borrowing the hexagrams of Fu Xi [to illustrate this].
Zeng Han-yueh 10: Although there are no written characters, they are fully endowed with the principles of heaven, earth, and the myriad things. Please consider Master Pang’s verse:
"At every turn and in every place, the crimson and purple robes fill the hills and mountains. Is this not the full endowment of the principles of heaven, earth, and the myriad things?
According to the first two lines, one abandons Master Pang and severs the principle that there is no heaven, earth, or myriad phenomena apart from oneself.
Thus, when Master Pang asked, "Who is it that does not take the myriad dharmas as a companion? Shitou covered his mouth with his hand;
this was merely to reveal the nature of Master Pang himself. How could he have ever shown the "one circle" (○) as the patriarch of Master Pang?
Later, when the Master [Zhaozhou] went to attend Mazu, he also asked: "Who is the person who does not take 'no-dharma' as a companion?
Mazu said, "When you can swallow up all the waters of the West River in a single gulp, I will tell you. At these words, the Master attained realization.
Suddenly grasping the profound essence, there is a verse that says: "Having sons, they do not marry; having daughters, they do not wed.
The whole family sits in a circle together, discussing the discourse on non-arising. It can be seen that Shitou, Mazu, and Pang Gong all took the person of the moment as the profound essence;
they never regarded the single circle (○) as the unadorned secret seal. Now, Tanji himself has not yet...
If you have already awakened, how can you distinguish between shallow and deep awakenings? You falsely claim that after the *Huazang* [Sūtra], this seal gradually vanished.
But were Shitou, Mazu, and Pang Gong also born after the *Huazang*?
Furthermore, since you equate Fu Xi’s drawing of the hexagrams with the single circle (○), let us ask further: did the hexagram-drawings precede Fu Xi?
If the hexagram lines existed first, they could not have been drawn by Fu Xi, because Fu Xi did not yet exist.
If Fu Xi existed first, how could it be that he was not fully acquainted with the principles of heaven, earth, and the myriad things, and instead relied merely upon the hexagram lines?
Since the hexagram lines cannot be relied upon in isolation, the pairing of "one" and "ten" becomes utterly meaningless.
This old monk takes Fuxi as the root and trunk, and the hexagram images as the branches and leaves. This is precisely what Yongjia meant when he said:
"Directly cutting off the source is the seal of the Buddhas; plucking leaves and seeking branches is not for me.

Thus, he did not employ the single staff as a mere staff, but used it to point directly to one's own self-realization. This clearly demonstrates that there is nothing else apart from the person, and nothing else at all.

This is the principle. Thus it is said: "The realms of boundless lands are not separated from one another by even a hair’s breadth; the ten ages of past and present do not depart from this very moment of thought. This accords with Mazu’s words to Pang Gong: "When you can swallow up the waters of the West River in a single gulp, I will tell you. This is the same as when Linji first arrived at Zhenzhou and addressed Puhua: [...the text continues... The above is the meaning of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. It is also the meaning of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*’s "Entering the Dharma Realm Chapter," which states: "The lands of the ten directions are all contained within a single pore; the Buddhas of the three periods of time are all encompassed within a single thought. It is also the meaning of the *Śūraṅgama Samādhi Sūtra*, which says: "The Tathāgata’s body is equal to empty space; it pervades the ten directions and is without obstruction. It is also the meaning of the *Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, which says: "All dharmas are the Buddha-nature; there is no dharma that is not the Buddha-nature. It is also the meaning of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, which says: "The three periods of time are not separate from the present moment. It is also the meaning of the *Awakening of Faith*, which says: "The nature of the mind is originally pure and eternally unchanging; it is neither born nor extinguished, neither increasing nor decreasing, and is equal to empty space. It is also the meaning of the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, which says: "The mind is the Buddha; the Buddha is the mind. It is also the meaning of the *Diamond Sūtra*, which says: "In the past, future, and present, all Buddhas rely on the perfection of wisdom to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. It is also the meaning of the *Lotus Sūtra*, which says: "The three vehicles are but expedient means; the One Vehicle is the true teaching. It is also the meaning of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, which says: "All sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature. It is also the meaning of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, which says: "The Buddha-way is not difficult; only fear of birth and death is difficult. It is also the meaning of the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, which says: "The Dharma is non-dual; it is neither existent nor non-existent. It is also the meaning of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Śāstra*, which says: "All dharmas are empty and quiescent; they are like illusions and dreams. It is also the meaning of the *Yogācārabhūmi Śāstra*, which says: "The storehouse consciousness is the root of all dharmas. It is also the meaning of the *Abhidharmakośa Śāstra*, which says: "The five aggregates, twelve bases, and eighteen elements are all empty. It is also the meaning of the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*, which says: "All dharmas are devoid of self-nature; they arise through dependent origination. It is also the meaning of the *Mahāyāna-samparigraha Śāstra*, which says: "The three natures are all empty; they are but the manifestations of the mind. It is also the meaning of the *Dharmadhātu-prakṛti-asambheda Sūtra*, which says: "The nature of the Dharma-realm is without differentiation; it is the same throughout the ten directions. It is also the meaning of the *Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra*, which says: "Within the bodies of all sentient beings, there exists the Tathāgata-garbha, pure and stainless. It is also the meaning of the *Ratnagotravibhāga*, which says: "The Buddha-nature is eternal, blissful, self, and pure. It is also the meaning of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra*, which says: "The Buddha is the father of the world; the Dharma is the mother of the world. It is also the meaning of the *Gaṇḍavyūha Sūtra*, which says: "The Bodhisattva’s practice is inexhaustible; it is like the ocean, vast and deep. It is also the meaning of the *Amitābha Sūtra*, which says: "If a person hears the name of Amitābha Buddha and, with a sincere heart, desires to be born in his land, they shall be born there. It is also the meaning of the *Karuṇāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, which says: "The Bodhisattva’s great compassion is impartial; it saves all sentient beings without exception. It is also the meaning of the *Bodhicaryāvatāra*, which says: "One should generate the aspiration for enlightenment; one should practice the six perfections. It is also the meaning of the *Śikṣāsamuccaya*, which says: "One should observe the precepts purely; one should cultivate the roots of goodness. It is also the meaning of the *Vinayapiṭaka*, which says: "One should respect the Teacher and the Sangha; one should uphold the Dharma and the Vinaya. It is also the meaning of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, which says: "The five aggregates are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self. It is also the meaning of the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya Sūtra*, which says: "Form is emptiness; emptiness is form. It is also the meaning of the *Ugraparipṛcchā Sūtra*, which says: "A Bodhisattva should dwell in the forest; they should practice the ascetic virtues. It is also the meaning of the *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra*, which says: "A lay follower should observe the five precepts; they should cultivate the ten wholesome paths of action. It is also the meaning of the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra*, which says: "The Bodhisattva traverses the ten stages; they perfect the ten paramitas. It is also the meaning of the *Akṣayamati-paripṛcchā Sūtra*, which says: "Wisdom is inexhaustible; it is the mother of all Buddhas. It is also the meaning of the *Gandavyūha Sūtra*, which says: "The Bodhisattva’s vows are vast; they reach to the limits of space. It is also the meaning of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, which says: "The Land of Ultimate Bliss is adorned with the seven treasures; its inhabitants enjoy immeasurable bliss. It is also the meaning of the *Lalitavistara Sūtra*, which says: "The Buddha’s appearance in the world is rare; it occurs only once in a hundred eons. It is also the meaning of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, which says: "The Dharma-body is omnipresent; it is the source of all phenomena. It is also the meaning of the *Mahāmegha Sūtra*, which says: "The clouds of Dharma rain down the rain of the Dharma; they moisten the seeds of the roots of goodness. It is also the meaning of the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra*, which says: "All dharmas are ultimately empty; they are beyond conceptualization. It is also the meaning of the *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*, which says: "The Bodhisattva’s giving is without attachment; they give away their head, eyes, and marrow. It is also the meaning of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, which says: "The Buddha appears in the world for the sake of the one vehicle; he does not preach the three vehicles. It is also the meaning of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, which says: "The Buddha-nature is the eternal, blissful, self, and pure; it is the ultimate refuge. It is also the meaning of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, which says: "The mind is like a magician; it creates all phenomena. It is also the meaning of the *Śrīmālādevī Siṃhanāda Sūtra*, which says: "The Tathāgata-garbha is the storehouse of all dharmas; it is the seed of all Buddhas. It is also the meaning of the *Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra*, which says
Huikeng said to Puhua, "I wish to establish the school of Huangbo here; you two shall assist me.

He sent the two of them down with the words, "Be careful! Once he had established the school, three days later, Puhua came back up and asked, "What did you say three days ago? Linji struck him. Three days after that...
Ke-fu followed Linji’s lead and asked, "What was the meaning of striking Puhua the day before yesterday? Linji struck him as well.
Could there possibly be some other school or principle to establish apart from Puhua and Ke-fu?
Yet Tan-ji claims that when these two men received the instruction and went up to ask, they not only failed to understand Puhua and Ke-fu, but they also insulted Linji. This is why [he says so].

They lack the eye of discernment. Furthermore, they claim that after Linji’s "three segments and two blows," he clarified [the teaching] through the "four categorical selections" (si liao jian), whereby the fundamental tenets such as the "profound and the essential" (xuan yao) and "guest and host" (bin zhu) were established.

It is evident that Han Yue and Tan Ji are merely lost in their own confusion; instead of recognizing their own heads, they point to Linji’s "three segments and two blows" and the "categorical selections" as the profound and the essential.
To take the names and characteristics of "guest and host" or "illumination and function" as one's primary aim is precisely the state where karmic consciousness is vast and茫然 (mángmáng);

how could such a person understand the great intent of the Buddha-dharma? Because they do not understand the great intent of the Buddha-dharma, they merely coordinate names and characteristics to establish the numerical categories of the "three segments" and "two blows.
Whenever there are three, they are cited as the root of the Three Mysteries and Three Essentials.
This refers to such acts as the three strikes and three shakes. Regarding the verse on Baizhang breaking the soy sauce jar, it says:

"The pestle was struck; the tradition passed down through three jars of sauce. This is the same as Xinghua’s presentation of incense, which also counts by threes. Thus, they have been transmitted to one another in succession.
To bewitch later generations with such views is to deserve three heavy blows of the staff.

Han Yue surely never heard of the principle of "two blows" or "four blows," so how could Tan Ji dare claim there were "two strikes"? To even call this "striking" is already like chasing after a clod of earth;
how much more so to take the "three segments" and "two strikes" as a fixed formula and attempt to clarify them through the "Four Selections"?
Nanyuan asked Fengxue, "You speak of the 'Four Kinds of Selection. What dharma do you select?
Fengxue replied, "When ordinary speech does not stagnate in ordinary sentiment, one immediately falls into the conceptual understanding of the sages; this is a great malady for students.

The former sages took pity on them and provided skillful means, like using one wedge to extract another. Thus, when a monk asked Linji, "What is it to take away the person but not the environment? Linji—
It is said: "The warm sun brings forth life, spreading a carpet of brocade; the infant’s hanging hair is white as silk.

As for saying that the infant’s hanging hair is white as silk—what emotional understanding could there be? It merely points to the fundamental substance of the person, which is no different from insentient things.
Yet people do not awaken; they mistakenly think it is a denial of the person, as if the person were entirely non-existent. A monk asked:
"What is 'seizing the object but not seizing the person'? Jue said, "The imperial decree has been issued and reached all under heaven;

the general is beyond the frontier, where smoke and dust have ceased. This is based on the meaning of seizing the person while leaving the object intact. A monk asked, "What is 'seizing both the person and the object'?
Jue said, "Communication is cut off between Bing and Fen; one dwells alone in a single region. This means that there is no passage of news or correspondence.
Thus, there are no others and no external objects; I alone am supreme. A monk asked, "What is it like when both person and environment are not wrested away?
Linji replied, "The King ascends the jeweled throne; the village elder sings his song. This means that the King and the village elder each find their own fulfillment;
they do not borrow from one another nor are they wrested away, but rather each enjoys their own experience. Miaoxi answered a monk’s question regarding the four kinds of selection (*si liaojian*).
The student asked, "I do not know whether what Linji spoke was the same as or different from what the Master [Miaoxi] has answered.
Miaoxi said, "A dog that bites on a piece of dung is no good dog; how much less so those of Tanzhi and Jigong, who take names and appearances as their fundamental principle?
Furthermore, Huangbo’s reception of Linji did not exceed three blows of the heavy staff, yet Linji established [the school]."
If it were so, would this not be the hexagram of the three blows? This is precisely because Tanji has not yet awakened from his dream;
he requires the three blows to realize the Three Mysteries and the Three Essentials. It is not merely a single stroke;

therefore, by means of the Qian hexagram with its three lines—not just one—he seeks to prove that my single blow of the staff is "one-piece head-hard Chan," and that [Tanji] is clinging to a single stroke.
This is to dry you up! You fail to realize that this old monk has clearly stated: "A single blow is not used as a single blow.
When has he ever debated "one" or "three" with Han Yue? Have you not seen how Confucius, having studied the *Yi* for many years, said in his *Xici*:
"The Way it represents undergoes frequent shifts; it cannot be treated as a fixed standard"? How could he have ever relied on the hexagram lines?

This is because the method of "dying" has arrived. Based on this, it is evident that Tan Ji did not understand *qian* (the Creative). For the reason that *qian* is so called is simply because it is the fundamental substance of the person.
Thus, the *Yi Jing* says: "The noble person is ever-active throughout the day," and it further says: [The noble person is active in the morning and active in the evening.]
"The noble person, accordingly, exerts themselves with ceaseless vigor. How could this mean merely relying on the three lines to constitute Qian? Guifeng said:
"Supreme, auspicious, penetrating, and correct—these are the virtues of Qian. Constant, blissful, self, and pure—these are the virtues of the Buddha.

Thus, Qian is the Buddha, and the Buddha is the human being; they are non-dual and without distinction. Does this not further prove that the One Circle (the *yuan* or *bindu*) is the source of the thousand Buddhas and ten thousand sages?"
The Buddha’s patriarchs were particularly free from groundless and false assertions. Furthermore, Han Yue cited the verses of the Seven Buddhas, saying:
"The formless body and mind are both existence and non-existence; existence and non-existence are both severed, like reeds intertwined in secret.
A clap of thunder cannot reach to cover both ears; the dream is broken, and the moon in the distant sky is solitary. He also produced this [seal] image, which is what is called "not to be existent."

There is nothing. As for those who find "neither being nor non-being" unacceptable, they are all like the *Tuan* and *Xici* appendices of the *I Ching*, which clarify the principle of the single circle (the *yuan*).
If one does not know that the single circle itself is already mistaken, what further can be said regarding the appended words?

Have you not seen how the Old Monk previously cited Yangshan’s statement that [all things] do not go beyond the Samādhi of Hiding the Body? He used his foot to wipe away this symbol of the circle (☲), overturning what preceded it.
Regarding the case of the "hidden body": now Han Yue has produced this sign; I, the old monk, reach out my hand to pluck it away and destroy it.

Tell me, is this the same as Yangshan’s [act], or is it different? Formerly, Danyuan presented the ninety-seven kinds of circular signs (*yuanxiang*) transmitted by National Teacher Huizhong to Yangshan. Later, when Yangshan ascended the hall to test him, Danyuan drew a woman.
I bow. What is the intended meaning here? When National Teacher Zhong transmitted the *yuanxiang* (perfect circle) to Tan Yuan, he instructed him, saying:
"In the south there is a śrāmaṇera who will greatly propagate this teaching. This was precisely for Yangshan to look at it and then immediately burn it away.
How could the *yuanxiang* ever have been taken as the fundamental tenet? Furthermore, how could Han Yue’s drawing of it be anything other than [a case of] using poison?

This is merely a verse for plastering walls concerning the Seven Buddhas. As for the line, "The dream is severed, and the moon in the distant sky is solitary," it is no more than similar to Zhao Qingxian’s verse on hearing thunder:
"Sitting silently in the public hall, leaning idly against the desk; the source of the mind is unmoving, as still as water.
It culminates in the words, "A single clap of thunder opens the crown of the head, awakening that which belongs to one's own self from before."
Thus, [the views of] Han Yue and [mine] cannot be characterized as being or non-being; such false assertions regarding being and non-being are worlds apart from the truth.
Indeed, because Han Yue derived his understanding from the *Dharma-transmission Gāthā*, he excavated a four-line doctrine and consequently fell into various errors.
Therefore, in my refutation, I cited the monk’s question to Mazu: "Transcending the four lines and severing the hundred negations—I ask the Master for a direct [instruction]."
To point to the meaning of the Westward Journey is precisely to clarify that there is no fourfold formula within the meaning of the Westward Journey.
If there were a separate fourfold formula apart from the meaning of the Westward Journey, how could one avoid the rebuke of being a heretic outside the scriptures?

Yet you, on the contrary, claim that this old monk merely explains the meaning according to the text, attempting to dissolve everything with the single word "no. Please look at what the World-Honored One entrusted:
The Dharma verse says: "Dharma is fundamentally no-dharma; no-dharma is also dharma. Now, when entrusting no-dharma, how has dharma ever been dharma?
This is precisely the fundamental Dharma of every person, which is originally devoid of names and characteristics.
Therefore, this old monk said that the World-Honored One used the word "no" to dissolve names and characteristics; how could there ever have been four dharmas intersecting? Furthermore...
Baizhang said: "The general intent of the teachings is that all consist of three successive phrases. You know only that there are three successive phrases;
why do you not look further at what lies beyond these three phrases? This is called a person who does not fall into any numerical categories."
What do you know? Even if you were to penetrate beyond the three phrases, you would still not have dreamed of the meaning of the Westward Journey.
Have you not seen how Yaoshan asked Yunyan, "What Dharma did Baizhang teach? Yunyan replied, "Sometimes he said, 'Go beyond the three phrases;
realize it within the six phrases. Yaoshan said, "Three thousand miles away, I am glad there is no connection."
Sheluo (涉) now maintains that the three [phrases] represent the profound intent of the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, and composed the *Origins of the Five Houses* (*Wuzongyuan*).

Zhitang Ji (潭吉) further maintained the three phrases to refute the Original Dharma, and composed the *Defense of the Five Houses* (*Wuzongjiu*). How could this be anything less than a total lack of connection, even at a distance of three thousand li?
It goes so far as to claim that the meaning of our teaching is like the three dots of the letter ∴, which Yantou took to be a rough approximation of the Gate of the Patriarchs.
Furthermore, why did he not look at Yantou? [Yantou] said, "Rest, rest. Because a monk requested him to provide an illustration, Yantou said:
"The meaning of my teaching is like the three dots of the character ∴. The first dot is placed toward the east; it opens the eyes of all bodhisattvas.
The second dot is placed toward the west; it strikes the life-root of all bodhisattvas. The third is placed upward..."

He then makes one descent, touching the crowns of the various Bodhisattvas. Although there are three points according to the ritual, in essence, the crown, the eyes, and the life-faculty are merely parts of a single Bodhisattva’s body.
Therefore, it says below: "It simply clarifies the grasping of the fundamental principle; fundamentally, there is no substantial dharma.
If you say that there is a dharma or a matter above this, you are truly making a hollow noise; you are muddling yourself up and binding yourself in a snare."
The ancients called this "the tethering stake for donkeys. If one were to bestow actual Dharma upon others, even the earth itself could not contain it;
how much more so in the case of Han-yueh, Tan-hsiu, and Chih-ji, who categorized various circular signs and various triads of dharmas as the formal methods of the Buddhas and Patriarchs?
This is truly a fabrication and a false teaching that destroys and extinguishes the fundamental宗旨 (zongzhi/principle). Therefore, this old monk cannot help but feel deep pain over it.

In opening this up, I shall follow the pivot of the upper gate and explain it point by point; I truly fear incurring the offense of the Buddhas and Patriarchs and will surely be reviled by those with clear eyes in future generations, but I could not help myself at this time.
Śākyamuni Buddha’s clan was Kṣatriya. His father was King Śuddhodana; his mother was Māyā.
Since the beginning of the world and the first opening of Jambudvīpa, the Kṣatriyas have been kings for generations.

Having practiced the path through successive kalpas, the Buddha received a prediction from Dīpaṃkara Buddha that he would become a Buddha in this kalpa. Subsequently, during the era of Kāśyapa Buddha, he perfected the stage of a Bodhisattva.
The Way: He was reborn above in the Tuṣita Heaven as the Great Being named Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
When the time for his manifestation had arrived, he descended into the womb of Māyā on the eighth day of the fourth month in the twenty-fourth year of King Zhao of the Zhou dynasty, a Jia-Yin year.
Born from the right side of Māyā, at the moment of his birth he emitted the radiance of great wisdom, illuminating the worlds of the ten directions.

From the earth there emerged golden lotus flowers, which spontaneously cradled his two feet. With one hand pointing toward heaven and the other pointing toward the earth, he walked seven steps and looked around the four quarters, declaring:
"In all that is above heaven and below heaven, I alone am the most honored."

The *Wujia jiuzhuan* records that when the World-Honored One was first born, he pointed one finger toward heaven and one finger toward the earth, walked seven steps, and looked around in the four directions, saying: "Above heaven and below heaven, I alone am honored. Yunmen said:
"Had I seen him at that time, I would have struck him dead with a single blow of my staff and fed him to a dog, just to ensure peace throughout the world. Yunmen.
Fengyue said: "Although Yunmen possessed a plan to settle the chaos, he lacked the way to emerge from it himself.
I, this old monk, say that this Yunfeng [statement] is based on the principle of the World-Honored One’s 'I alone am honored. I fear people will misunderstand Yunmen’s words;
[Yunmen] did not recognize that one blow would strike him dead and feed him to a dog, which was intended only to bring peace to the world."
This is a direct pointing to the time when each person is uniquely honored; therefore, these two phrases were uttered.
When Yunmen met the World-Honored One, it was as if there were the intention to manifest a separate body beneath the staff, and there was also a path for one’s own emergence.

It is this. An old monk once composed a verse on it: "As soon as one emerges from the womb, the whole body is manifest; pointing to heaven and pointing to earth, one proclaims it for the sake of others.
It leads countless deluded men and women, so that nowhere in heaven or among men can they hide.

How could you possibly be like this—accusing the World-Honored One of a crime by folding and curling yourselves into a five-colored ball? Ten-thousand-jun of fragrant bait has fallen upon the tip of the line.
"Gautama’s intention lies in the profound depths. Could a lame turtle and a blind tortoise have merely stumbled upon the hook?
The World-Honored One clearly declared: 'Above heaven and below heaven, I alone am honored.
When has there ever been a five-colored ball or a ten-thousand-jin bait to accompany this profound meaning? Now let me ask Tanji: Yunmen was a famous, one-legged master."
For what reason, then, did he say: "Strike him dead with a single blow and feed him to the dogs, so that all under heaven may enjoy peace"?
You, on the contrary, dare to claim that the lame tortoise and the blind turtle have merely climbed upon the hook. How could you possibly know the realm of the blind turtle?
Not perceiving any difference between the Buddha-body and one’s own body, one may for the first time claim to have realized the Way of Linji.

Who would have known that our Treasury of the True Dharma Eye was extinguished at the hands of that blind donkey? If so, how could the lame tortoise and the blind turtle possibly exist outside the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye?
To save the Middle Way, he preached the Dharma for forty-nine years, all in order to provide provisional guidance and protection according to the capacities of beings.

The old monk, however, speaks of guiding according to the capacity of the occasion. Thus it is said: "Furthermore, by means of diverse skillful expedients (*upāya*), one assists in manifesting the primary meaning (*paramārtha*).
It can be seen that these diverse skillful expedients are none other than the opening and revealing of the primary meaning.

This refers to what is called the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appearing in the world solely for the sake of the one great causal condition. If, instead, one were to provide protection through suppression according to the occasion...
If the ultimate truth were not revealed, then when did the World-Honored One wait until the moment of holding up the flower for Kāśyapa to break into a smile?

As for saying that by holding up a single flower, one perfectly realizes the vast and great Dharma of our own minds—once you speak of "vast and great," it has already become limited. The original face of our own being is all-pervading...

The present manifests all within the sands of the world-realms, yet they are gathered and contained within a single minute speck of dust. Furthermore, the extremely small is identical to the great, as boundaries are forgotten and severed;
the extremely great is identical to the small, as its limits and surfaces cannot be seen. How could there be anything vast enough to be described?
Han Yue recognized only the single flower being held up and was already mistaken from the start. Why not look at this old monk’s verse, which says: "The World-Honored One, in his entire being..."
"Wind and flow. Kāśyapa was showing off his entire person. At that time, among the hundreds of thousands of devas and humans, they saw only the picking up of the flower and the smile.
This truly embodies what the ancients called "the intent to pull out nails and extract wedges.

How could it be like you lot, who merely "push against a mooring stake and rock the oars," claiming "perfect realization is vast and great"—a mere speculative talk that falsely accuses the World-Honored One of being at fault? Furthermore, as for "spiritual..."
At the assembly on Vulture Peak, the World-Honored One held up a flower to show the multitude. Only the monk Kāñcanamuni broke into a smile.
The World-Honored One said, "I possess the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, the wondrous mind of Nirvāṇa, the true mark which is markless; I entrust it to Mahākāśyapa.
Vimalakīrti said, "Contemplate the true mark of the body; contemplate the Buddha in the same way. Kakusandha Buddha said:

To see that the body is without substance is to see the Buddha-body; this is sufficient to know the World-Honored One. What is called the "true mark" (bhūtalakṣaṇa) is marklessness (alakṣaṇa); there is nothing else remaining outside the body. How could there be a single flower to be picked up and displayed? Who, then, is it that has fully realized the vastness of the mind-dharma?

Furthermore, regarding those who open their books and take a single blow of the staff as the "total presentation" (quan-ti) and the sole authority—claiming that anything else besides this is the teaching of demons—I, this old monk, say: [The text continues: "If one relies on such words, one will surely fall into the pit of views and attachments. To speak of 'one blow' is already dualistic; to speak of 'total presentation' is even more so. If you grasp at these words, you are like a dog chasing a clod of earth. If you do not grasp them, you are like a person standing in the middle of a great void. Therefore, the ancients said: 'When the staff is raised, the whole world is revealed; when the staff is lowered, the whole world is hidden. This is why it is said: 'The staff is the Buddha, the Buddha is the staff; the staff is the patriarch, the patriarch is the staff. Do not seek for anything further outside of this. If you can understand thus, you will see that the staff is originally not a staff, and the Buddha is originally not a Buddha. Only then will you be able to avoid falling into the pit of views and attachments."
"A single blow is not used as a single blow" directly points to the fundamental essence of every person, establishing it as the sole, supreme, and total presentation.
To manifest this essence while claiming there is something else apart from it is identical to the teaching of demons. As the World-Honored One said: "The body contains the ten directions."
The infinite void—how could there be a separate staff outside of the body?
As for what I call "the sole honor," it is like a Son of Heaven who is the sole honored one among the myriad nations.

What I call "the total presentation" is like all nations being within the sovereign transformation of the Son of Heaven; a single edict is issued and the world is solemnized, a single word is uttered...
The world responds accordingly; when one official is removed and another appointed, the world receives his grace, and the teachings and transformations of the world all converge upon him.

Therefore, he is called "Uniquely Honored" (Duzun). According to Tan Ji’s account, this deludes worldly people and gives rise to greedy and delusive thoughts, thereby harming the true purport of the Uniquely Honored. Furthermore, it says: "It is not [the case that] the world..."
Outside [the world], there is a separate, solitary Honored One; outside this solitary Honored One, there is a separate world.

This is because Tanji has not yet "raised his head to look beyond the heavens. Who is such a person as I? Therefore, it is said that it is not the case that outside the world there is a separate, solitary Honored One.
Furthermore, do you know that the body contains the infinite void of the ten directions? Again, it is said that the Dong lineage has five [houses].
Regarding the position: the position of the sovereign is held as the most honorable. Why does Master Tanji not look at Dongshan’s saying:

"Coming from the very center, there is a path within non-being that leads out of the dust; if one can simply avoid touching upon the current taboo, it is superior even to the talent of those who had their tongues cut off in a previous dynasty"?
Since it is said that "within non-existence there is a path leading out of the dust," how could this be like you, who claim that the entire world returns to him as the Sole Honored One?
Is there not a Sole Honored One outside of the world? Dongshan further said:
"Even if it were manifested at every turn and revealed in every object"—this is precisely the intent of Han Yue, who meant that when "a single flower" is plucked up, then every object...

This is the case in every instance. Therefore it is said: "The one who has perfectly realized the vastness of our mind-dharma" — why then did Dongshan say, "I call him only a person who has finished his business;
I never call him one who is noble"? One should know that the path of the noble is distinct in itself.
Based on this, how could what Han Yue calls the "vastness of the mind-dharma" be considered Dongshan’s?

"Does the position of the patriarchal master constitute the highest honor? Furthermore, it is said that Linji had four types of guest and host, regarding the 'host within the host' as the most precious.
If you were to speak thus before an old monk like me, you would not have a day's end of receiving blows. Why is this so?
It is because Tanji merely studies the theory that the 'host within the host' is the most precious; in reality, it is the 'host within the guest' [that is truly so]."
I have not yet even dreamed of it, let alone the Lord of Lords. Furthermore, you say that Yunmen has both "full presentation" and "half presentation," and that the full presentation is the ultimate.
To speak thus before an old monk like me would deserve to be struck out with a staff right then and there.
Why do you not look at what Yunmen said: "It reaches the point where heaven, earth, and the great world are without the slightest flaw"? This, moreover—
Han Yue’s “plucking out a single flower” expresses the vast intent of the Dharma of Perfect Realization.
Yet Yunmen considered this merely a "turning phrase. He held that not seeing a single color was only the "half-raising" of the teaching;
one must further know there is a time for the "full raising. Because Han Yue Tanji did not understand this timing, he unilaterally engaged in forced interpretations, creating confusion.

This deludes people; conversely, they cite from within the teachings the "Ocean-Seal Samādhi" (*sāgaramudrā-samādhi*), claiming that the myriad phenomena are all manifested simultaneously within the light of the ocean, which they call the "total presentation of the sole honored one.

However, the Ocean-Seal Samādhi appears in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, yet there is no instance therein where it is referred to as the "total presentation of the sole honored one. Is this not the work of Han Yue, Tan, and Ji?
Is this mere conjecture? According to this old monk, it can only be said that the ocean and the myriad phenomena reflect one another and appear simultaneously;
it cannot be said that one is exclusively predominant. Why is this? Because between the ocean and the myriad phenomena, there is neither a subject that reflects nor an object that is reflected.
The ancients said: "A wild goose flies across the vast sky; its shadow sinks into the cold water. The goose has no intention of leaving a trace, and the water has no mind to retain the shadow.

This is precisely what Tanji cited to prove that Han Yue’s heart-dharma was so vast as to erase the Buddha’s own teaching that "the body contains the infinite space of the ten directions; I alone am honored. Yet he failed to see this.
The Way: before leaving Tuṣita, he had already descended into the imperial palace; before emerging from his mother’s womb, his work of saving beings was already complete.

How could there be a "Sea-Seal Samādhi" (Sāgaramudrā-samādhi) apart from the Tathāgata, such that one must wait for the single act of holding up a flower to finally exhaust all that is above and below heaven?

Is this not the principle of the Sole Venerable One? When an old monk does not employ his single blow as a mere blow, but points directly at all people, he is the Sole Venerable One who fully upholds the Dharma for everyone—the Sole Venerable One who is uniquely venerable to each person.

Just as there is one single void, heaven, earth, sun, and moon, so too does every individual perceive their own void, heaven, earth, sun, and moon; yet there has never been one [who perceives them otherwise].
A person does not merely fill one void-like heaven and earth with the sun and moon; how could it stop at the people of ten thousand nations?

It extends even to the exhaustion of space and the pervasion of the Dharma-realm, where each is perfectly complete and each is uniquely honored, from the outset without distinction between self and other, nor the slightest increase or decrease.
Therefore, it is said that this Dharma is equal, without high or low. How could it wait for Heaven?

When all below have returned to it, only then does it become uniquely honored. If one must wait until the whole world has returned [to it] before it becomes uniquely honored, then for every single individual, when could there ever be a time of unique honor?
Therefore, when an old monk uses his single blow not as a single blow, this is what the ancients meant by using the sixteen-foot golden body as a single blade of grass. One.
A stalk of grass is used to manifest the sixteen-foot golden body; essence and function are one, and killing and enlivening are freely exercised.

This is truly not something that those like Han Yue and Tan Ji could ever understand. How, then, should we be surprised that they mistakenly identify a single blow as the "solitude" of the "lonely one"?
From the time of his birth, various miraculous manifestations occurred, and his departure from the city and renunciation of the world are fully described as set forth in the sūtras.
Initially, he studied the concentration of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) for three years under Ārāḍa Kālāma; realizing it was not the final goal, he abandoned it.

He then went to Udraka Rāmaputra and studied the concentration of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) for three years; realizing that too was not the final goal, he likewise abandoned it. Furthermore, he went to Mount Elephant Head (*Gajaśīrṣa*) together with other non-Buddhist practitioners...
On the Way, he subsisted on hemp and wheat for six years. The World-Honored One reflected to himself: "This asceticism is not the true liberation.
I shall accept food and thereafter attain Buddhahood. He then bathed in the Nairañjanā River;
the heavens caused the trees to lean down for him, and the World-Honored One grasped one to emerge. He accepted the milk-rice offered by the daughter of a cowherd and proceeded to the Piṇḍola tree.

Beneath the *pātra* tree, Śakra, Lord of Devas, manifested as a man and gathered auspicious grass to provide a seat for him. Auspicious clouds and propitious winds arose from the four quarters, fluttering about.

The celestial Māra thought, "The World-Honored One has perfected the Way; I must now suppress him. Leading his host, he created difficulties, manifesting all manner of terrifying and seductive scenes to the limit.
Yet the World-Honored One remained unperturbed and unmoving. He pressed the earth with his finger, and the great earth shook violently; the Māras were all thrown into disarray.
The servant then brought him down. Thus the Sūtra says: "By means of no-thought, no-mind, and no-receptive practice, he completely subdues all non-Buddhists.
Having first sequentially demonstrated false teachings and shown various skillful means, he aroused their divergent views and led them to Bodhi.
Then, on the evening of the seventh day of the second month in the third year of King Mu’s reign, the year of Guiwei, he entered the Samādhi of Rightness. On the eighth...
When the sun rose and the morning star appeared, he attained great enlightenment and realized perfect awakening. He then sighed and said: "How marvelous!
All sentient beings possess the wisdom, virtues, and marks of a Tathāgata; yet because of their deluded thoughts and attachments, they are unable to realize it."
At that time he was thirty years old. Six years after his attainment of enlightenment, he returned to preach the Dharma for King Śuddhodana.
The king was greatly delighted and dispatched five hundred noble youths of his clan to follow him and renounce the household life.
When the World-Honored One was at the assembly on Vulture Peak, he held up a flower to show the multitude. At that time, the entire assembly remained silent;

only the Venerable Kāśyapa broke into a smile. The World-Honored One said, "I possess the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, the wondrous mind of Nirvāṇa, the subtle and profound Dharma-gate of the signless reality.
It does not rely on words and letters; it is a separate transmission outside of the teachings. I now entrust it to Mahākāśyapa."
Master Ye said:
"The picking up of the flower and the entrusting of the Dharma truly represent the source of the single school of direct pointing.
If this point is misunderstood, then a myriad of differences will arise from it; it must not degenerate into the conceptual paths of 'mind-nature' or 'self.'"
It thus flows into a state of muddled confusion, acting as a master over what is actually solid.
It is like the Heavenly Kings of the Five Directions, who each describe different colors when looking at a mani jewel, while the true pearl remains hidden.

This is precisely how Han Yue Tanji missed the point of the World-Honored One and misunderstood the "Plucking of the Flower" as the transmission of the Dharma; from this arose a thousand differences and ten thousand distinctions. Therefore, Han Yue...
The former [Tanhui] treats it as the vast path of meaning for mental dharmas; Tanji, however, reviles me as being such a "path of meaning.
Han Yue slanders the old monk as a "one-sided, rigid Chan practitioner," while Tanji likewise slanders the old monk as a "confused person who forcibly establishes a sovereign self.
Is this not like the Heavenly King looking at a pearl, each describing a different color, yet both raising their hands?
If that pearl were hidden, then according to the World-Honored One’s not regarding the *maṇi* as a pearl, it is proven that he certainly did not transmit the Dharma by holding up a flower.
If you claim that raising a hand constitutes the pearl, then apart from the World-Honored One, could there be any other pearl?
Therefore, this old monk relies solely on the World-Honored One as the source of the transmission of the Dharma, using him as proof for the old man [himself].
The Master [Yunmen] said, "Monks, the direct pointing to people is the very essence of our school.

In his *Jiuzhong* (Ninefold Commentary), he cited a "catch-all phrase"—a tethering stake for ten thousand kalpas—to prove his critique of the book, asserting that both the sentient and the insentient are clearly manifested as equal.

This constitutes the final phrase; it occurs precisely within the context of Chuanshi’s rebuke. Tanji failed to understand the meaning of Chuanshi’s words and thus fabricated this spurious correlation.
According to the account, as soon as Chuanshi saw Jiashan, he struck him immediately by asking, "Virtuous One, in which monastery do you reside?
This was what Chuanshi meant by the "silken thread suspended over green water," where the floating state determines existence or non-existence.
[Zhaozhou] intended this to test Jia Shan, but Jia Shan was not awakened; thus, he followed the words and gave rise to a conceptual interpretation, replying:

"If one dwells in a temple, one does not abide [in the truth]; if one abides [in the truth], one does not dwell in a temple. The Boatman then pursued him further, asking: "What is it that resembles 'not resembling'?"
Yet Jia Shan still did not know; he continued to follow along with the words, saying, "It is not the dharma before one's eyes.
Seeing that Jia Shan was merely a follower of mere words, Chuanzi asked, "Where did you learn this?
Jia Shan again followed along with the words, saying, "It is not where the ears or eyes can reach. Chuanzi saw that Jia Shan was repeatedly generating conceptual interpretations based on the words.
Therefore, Duan said: "A single phrase that hits the mark is nothing more than a tethering stake for ten thousand kalpas.

When I, this old monk, personally realized that the sentient and the insentient shine forth equally and clearly, with whom could there be any question or answer? This may indeed be called a phrase that hits the mark.
Is it not like a tethering stake for a donkey? Furthermore, I say that this old monk understands the "public case" (gong'an) of the Plucking of the Flower.
As for "Wei-yin" (Vipaśyin), it refers to the majestic countenance of all sentient beings; when one lifts the eyes, it is immediately clear. This is because understanding arises based on the Dharma.
This is according to Han Yue’s *The Origin of the Five Houses*, which states that he once saw an artist depicting the beginning of the Seven Buddhas, starting with Vipaśyin Buddha. Only...
Great Work, Number Ten. "Majesty" refers to that which is beyond form. "Sound" refers to that which is beyond voice. "King Majestic Sound" (Vaiśravaṇa) lies beyond both form and sound;
it has not yet appeared in written records and has no basis for verification. It is the supreme reality prior to the emergence of written characters.
The old monk says that Han Yue’s fundamental realization was not yet thorough, and therefore he did not see King Majestic Sound.
The Buddha. Why is this? "Majestic Sound" (Wei-yin) is none other than all Buddhas of the three periods of time;
it is the original nature of all sentient beings. It is evident at a glance, requiring neither deliberation nor verbal explanation.

This is precisely what was meant by the ancients when they said that one must know that the sentient and the insentient preach the Dharma without distinction. Therefore, at the assembly on Vulture Peak, the World-Honored One held up a flower and remained silent.
He looked upon the great assembly; a million beings, including gods and humans, were all at a loss as to what to do.
Only Mahākāśyapa broke his smile and laughed. The World-Honored One spoke where there was no speaking; Kāśyapa heard where there was no hearing. Is this not indeed the power of Ābhāsvara?

It is just like when the World-Honored One showed a mani jewel that reflects the colors of its surroundings and asked the Heavenly Kings of the Five Directions, "What color is this jewel? At that time—

The Heavenly Kings of the Five Directions each described the jewel as being of a different color. The World-Honored One concealed the jewel and again raised his hand, asking, "What color is this jewel?
The Heavenly Kings replied, "Your hand has no jewel; where could there be any color? The World-Honored One said, "How can you be so utterly deluded?
I was merely showing you a worldly jewel, yet you each insistently claimed it was blue, yellow, red, or white."

I showed them pearls, yet they remained entirely ignorant of them. At that time, the Heavenly Kings of the Five Directions all attained enlightenment upon seeing the World-Honored One raise his hand—a colorless color. This is precisely what we call a "monk of original color" within our own school.
Previously, I told Han Yue that his fundamental realization was not yet thorough; therefore, he did not see King Wei-yin.

The Buddha is this very thing. If a person attains silent resonance through stillness—just as the Heavenly Kings of the Five Directions perceived the World-Honored One’s hand as a pearl—they too can fully awaken to the Way on their own.
Having already awakened themselves, how could they falsely claim to be the progenitor of a thousand or ten thousand Buddhas? Yantou said: "If you say there is a dharma above..."
There is a matter. It deludes you and binds you. The ancients called it a "donkey-tethering stake.
If there were a real dharma to give to people, even earth could not contain it. Thus, Han Yue’s circle (○) is no different from the circle painted by Yangshan;
it too is a deluder, a binder, and a donkey-tethering stake. Therefore, Yang—

Mountan (Shan) immediately rubbed it away with his foot. How much more so for Han-yueh, who recklessly drew a circle (○), claiming it to be the ancestor of the thousand Buddhas and ten thousand Buddhas;
how could this old monk not rebuke and forbid him? Tan-ji further cites the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*:
"At that time, Ānanda and the great assembly each realized for themselves that the mind pervades the ten directions. They looked back toward their parents..."
The body of one born is like a single mote of dust; whether it exists or perishes, it is like a single bubble floating upon a vast, still ocean—arising and ceasing without a trace.
Each knows this for themselves, attaining the fundamental, wondrous mind that is eternally abiding and indestructible.

This refers to the teaching outside the scriptures discussed within this assembly of the Vaipulya Sūtras. If it were not thus, you would ultimately not have contemplated what you previously [attained] for yourself.
He cites the Sea-Seal Samādhi (*sāgaramudrā-samādhi*), wherein all the myriad phenomena are manifested simultaneously within the light of the ocean.

This serves as a total presentation of the Sole Honored One, proving that Han Yue’s mind-dharma is vast and great, precisely corresponding to each individual’s self-knowledge that the mind pervades the ten directions.
When one turns back to observe the body born of one’s parents, it is understood to be identical to a single mote of dust.
From this perspective, Tanji had not yet attained awakening himself, yet he relied solely upon Han Yue’s mind-dharma as his own awakening.
Han Yue had not yet attained awakening himself, yet he relied solely upon Da Zuo’s "one circle" (一○) as his own awakening.

This is precisely what is meant by "generating understanding based on the Dharma," which still falls within the realm of Māra. My old monk has awakened for himself, and my body is coextensive with the entirety of empty space and the pervasive Dharma-realm.

There is nothing that does not manifest universally. When has the body ever been like a mote of dust—sometimes existing, sometimes vanishing? If there were a separate mind that comes from pervading the ten directions, one could see it;
yet Han-yueh Tan-jih was at a loss, for he mistook the old monk’s own realized realm for something else.

Thus, he claimed it was the same as Yun-men’s “The vast heavens and earth have not a single hair’s breadth of affliction. This, too, is merely a turning phrase (a *zhuǎn-jù*). How could one know this?
Yunmen, for those who have not yet attained great awakening, points to their own realm and directs them back to themselves;

thus he says that heaven and earth, the great world, are without even a hair’s breadth of fault or affliction—this is merely a "turning phrase. This is precisely what Han Yue meant by the vastness of the mind-dharma.
Furthermore, Tanji’s claim that the myriad phenomena of the universe all manifest simultaneously within the light of the ocean reflects this same intent.
"Not seeing a single form" is merely the partial teaching (*banti*); one must further understand that there is a time for the complete teaching (*quanti*).
This is precisely what Yunmen anticipated when he spoke of Han Yue, Tanji, and others, who suffer from the ailment of not knowing the time for the complete teaching.
Regarding the "Root": Tanji cites the *Haiyin Samādhi* (Ocean-Seal Samādhi) and attempts to take Yunmen’s "Total Presentation" (*quántí*) as the ultimate realization.
To claim that Han Yue’s expansive mind-dharma represents the timing of the "Total Presentation" is precisely to contradict the intent of Yunmen’s Total Presentation.
As the ancients said: "Like a golden-winged bird cleaving the sea, it goes straight for the dragon to swallow; like a single blade entering directly, it takes [the prize]."
This is the head of the supreme teaching: a direct transmission outside the scriptures, uniquely transcendent, intended to uplift all four classes of living beings.
Therefore, this old monk relies solely on the single staff, yet does not employ it as a mere staff. Whenever anyone asks a question, I strike them immediately upon the head;
this is the moment of "total presentation. As the Ancient rightly said: "If you wish to know the meaning of Buddha-nature, you should observe the conditions of time and season. At that time—
If the proper time had arrived, it would have been like suddenly awakening from a dream or suddenly remembering what was forgotten. Now, Tanji does not understand the timing;

relying on the Haiyin Samādhi and the vast realization of Han Yue, he claims to verify Yunmen’s "total presentation," yet falsely asserts that my face-to-face guidance of people is merely a "stubborn one-sided Chan" and the deluded self-aggrandizement of a headstrong master.
When have you ever dreamed of the old monk’s state where the sentient and the insentient manifest radiantly and equally?
This is the truly equal and true Dharma-realm, where there is neither Buddha nor sentient being. A single body enters many bodies; many bodies enter a single body.
Throughout all of space and pervading the entire Dharma-realm, all who possess a body have their own bodily radiance, which mutually interpenetrates, reflects, and interlaces like jewels.
How could the net of jewels ever be fathomed through calculation or analogy? Yet, you instead slander it as a mere thing of the inner chambers, wishing to barge in upon the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
Why is it that those who claim to have grasped the "uppermost point" (xiàngshàng bābì) are so premature in their reckoning?
Regarding this talk of the uppermost point, among ten people of the present day, five or six are merely students of words. Thus, [Master] Tan...

Jixian previously took "himself" to be the path to the Dharma-meaning; furthermore, because Yunmen said he had reached the side of the Dharma-body, his own view still persisted, and he remained seated on the side of the Dharma-body—this is one point. Ultimately, he did not realize the Master’s subsequent words.
To let such a thing pass is unacceptable; for even having a mere "fragrance" [of attainment] is itself an illness. Miaoxi once said: "There is no need..."
This is a Zen assembly; it is not a meeting for practicing the Way, nor is it for deliberating on the "upward" direction.
This is the old fellow Yunmen speaking according to reality. In saying this, I am guilty of immeasurable transgression.
If you can discern this, I grant that you possess the eye of discernment; if you cannot discern it, then for now, remain within Yunmen’s tangle of vines.
"Consider this," said the old monk. "This is precisely Dahui. Seeing that people did not understand Yunmen’s meaning, he instructed them to investigate within Yunmen’s 'entanglements.
Fearing further that they would not understand, he said: 'Nowadays, those who study the substantial Dharma...'"
To pass through the *dharmakāya* is considered the ultimate; yet Yunmen regarded this as a sickness. Not knowing how to pass through it—how should one act?
When you reach this point, it is like a person drinking water: whether it is cold or warm, they know for themselves;
there is no need to ask another. To ask another would be a disaster. Yet, if one knows for oneself whether it is cold or warm, is that not one's own realization?
When I, this old monk, speak thus, I too am guilty of immeasurable transgressions; let Han Yue, Tan Ji, and others from all quarters freely examine and critique me.
Furthermore, as for the things within the inner chambers: when Layman Li Ao asked Yaoshan, "What are precept, concentration, and wisdom?
Yaoshan replied, "In my place, there are no such mundane furnishings. Li was unable to fathom the profound meaning.
Therefore it is said: "If the Prefect wishes to take responsibility for this matter, he must stand atop the highest mountain peak and walk upon the deepest ocean floor.
If one cannot relinquish the things of the inner chamber, there will be leakage.

This was Yaoshan pointing out to Layman Li that the inability to relinquish precepts, concentration, and wisdom constitutes the very things of the inner chamber. Standing upon the highest mountain peak—
Standing up, [Furong Daokai] said: "Walking at the bottom of the deepest sea—how could one escape the old monk’s ‘sentient’ and ‘insentient’? Are they not manifested radiantly as equal?
Furthermore, regarding the karmic conditions between Chuanzi and Jia Shan, Furong Kai took them up and said:

"The Dharma-body is subtle in principle and profound in expression; it suddenly transcends the afflictions of beginning and end. Gentlemen, do not think that there is a 'Dharma' existing apart from this illusory body."
"What is the body? Is this illusory body itself the Dharma-body? If you understand it in such a way, you are entirely relying on others to form your interpretations;
you are mired in confusion and duality, and your Dharma-eye has not yet attained clarity and penetration.
This is like the monk who asked Jia Shan, "What is the Dharma-body? He replied, "The Dharma-body is formless. [The monk asked again,] "What is the Dharma-eye? He replied, "The Dharma-eye..."
It is without flaw. Therefore, Wuye said: "When my teacher was still alive, if someone had suddenly asked me, 'What is the Dharma-body?
the sheep would simply lie down on dry ground. What is the Dharma-eye? The donkey would simply urinate where it is wet. Furthermore, if someone were to ask, "How is the Dharma-body?
[the answer would be] "Buying a hat to fit the head. How is the Dharma-eye? [The answer would be] "Buying a hat to fit the head."
Regarding the "Pit, Mound, and Hill" and the four turning phrases of Furong: how could they have ever escaped the old monk?

Sentient and insentient things manifest clearly and equally. Furthermore, it is said: "If one were to examine this closely, Jia Shan’s failure lies simply in his lack of clarity regarding the place of learning;
he is like a common, domestic object from within the inner chambers. This was Furong’s critique of Jia Shan, which [Jia Shan] was unable to [respond to].

They have abandoned the Dharma-body and the Dharma-eye—which are signless and flawless—causing their emotions to be sealed and their consciousness to be locked up like common household items found within a laywoman’s chamber. Yet, even so, they do not distinguish themselves from Jia Shan;

they merely learn to speak of the signlessness of the Dharma-body and the flawlessness of the Dharma-eye, while never having truly realized or personally accorded with them. Therefore, they must wait for the Boatman.
[Zhaozhou] pierced through [Furong’s words]. Furong then displayed his wit, saying:

"If this old monk did not manifest this directly before you, it would be difficult for those who have come after to know where to return. I exhort you all: do not seek the Truth; you must only cease your views.
If all views cease, the mirror of wisdom will be brilliantly clear, and there will be nothing else. Gentlemen, do you understand? After a long silence, he said: "The Pearl."
"Within it there is fire; you must believe this. Do not go to the heavens to ask about the sun.

If Old Monk had seen Fuyong speak thus, he would have struck him right on the head with a staff. Why? To spare Fuyong from further explaining that "there is fire within the pearl," which only muddles people.
This is just like the words, "Do not seek the Truth; simply let go of views," and so forth—how could they possibly be established [otherwise]?
When people ruin others, it is not a shallow matter; that is why this old monk does not speak of it much. Yet, if someone asks about the Dharma-body, I give them a blow right between the eyes.
If they ask about the Dharma-eye, I give them a blow right between the eyes. If they ask about what lies beyond the Dharma-body, I give them a blow right between the eyes.
If a student gives rise to divergent views regarding this, it has nothing at all to do with the old monk.
As for monastic affairs, I leave them entirely to Han Yue Tanji. His "one-piece head" of hard Zen is like the drool of a wild fox;
it is a muddled pretension of being a master. This does not concern me, the old monk.

If you were to come before me and speak in such a manner, I would strike you right at the head with a blow of the staff to sever and cure you. Only when all your various views are completely purified will you no longer [be so].
"To presume to act and speak thus is merely to engage in delusion and false discourse. Furthermore, Hong Juefan said:

"In the monasteries of today, it is the custom for masters and disciples to prohibit all intellectual understanding and to cast away all that is profound and subtle. They seek only direct questions and direct answers: if there is nothing, they must always say there is nothing;
if there is something, they must always say there is something. To deviate by even a hair’s breadth from this is called 'mad understanding.'"
If the Boatman had heard this, it would have been more than just a tethering stake for ten thousand kalpas.
Viewed from this perspective, it was not only a failure to awaken well; it was also a failure to doubt well.

One who doubts well must reflect upon the occasions when the thirty-three patriarchs transmitted the Dharma and the conditions through which they awakened to the Way; their words remain extant, and all can be investigated through reason.
This can be known through wisdom. From the Stonehead of Jiangxi downward, the various great masters responded to things through their dynamic functioning (*jīyòng*).
If one observes their dialogues, they are so vast and profound (*míngxìng*) that they make people nod off while sitting. Is their Way different from that of the Patriarchs?
If it were different, they would have succeeded to the Dharma; if it were not different, why are the words they speak so dissimilar? Thus we know that Linji’s greatness—
The Master said: "In general, when discussing the vehicle of the school (zongcheng), a single phrase contains the three mysteries (sanxuan), and each mystery contains the three essentials (sanyao).
That there are both mysteries and essentials is precisely to clarify this point. Those who do not understand point to it as merely the establishment of a formal gateway."

These expedient expressions are truly lamentable. That Han Yue and others now take the names of the "Three Mysteries" and "Three Essentials" to be substantial dharmas is because they rely on the words of Juefan while neglecting the speech of Linji. Why is this? Linji merely said:
"There is the provisional and the real; there is illumination and function. Yet Han Yue and his followers utterly disregard these words.
The "Pulse" (the core essence) must certainly possess the profound and the essential; how could this be anything other than relying on the words of Juefan?
