If you people wish to understand it, know that within a single phrase the three mysteries are complete, and within each mystery the three essentials are complete. Simply look at how Jia Shan questioned Chuanzi:
"You cast your line and throw your hook—what is your intention? The Master said: "The line hangs in the green water, poised between existence and non-existence."
Yunmen silently grasped the meaning and said, "This is what is meant by: 'The words carry the profound, yet there is no path; the tongue speaks, yet it does not speak.
Therefore, the boatman said, "I have fished through the waves of the river until at last I encountered the golden-scaled fish. Yunmen then covered his ears.
The boatman said, "So it is, so it is," and then he instructed him, saying, "From now on, you must ensure that where you hide your body, no trace remains."
Where there are no traces, do not hide your body. For thirty years I was at Yaoshan, and I did nothing but clarify this very matter.

If you recognize the "awakened model" as having some profound mystery or essential core as a substantial dharma, how could it be anything less than a tethering stake for a donkey for ten thousand kalpas?
When the World-Honored One arrived before the Stūpa of Many Sons, he summoned Mahākāśyapa, shared his seat with him, and enveloped him with his saṃghāṭī robe.
He then addressed him, saying: "I have secretly entrusted to you the Treasury of the Eye of the True Dharma; you must protect and uphold it.

Furthermore, I charge Ānanda to serve as your deputy in the transmission and transformation of the teaching, so that it shall not be severed. Then he spoke this verse: "The Dharma is fundamentally without dharma; The Way is fundamentally without way."
"Non-dharmas are also dharmas; now, at the time of entrusting non-dharma, how could dharma ever have been a dharma?
At that time, after the World-Honored One had spoken this verse, he further addressed Kāśyapa: "I shall take my gold-threaded *saṃghāṭī* robe and transmit it to you.

Pass it on to the one who occupies the seat of succession until the appearance of the Buddha Maitreya, so that it may not decay. Upon hearing the verse, Kāśyapa prostrated himself, bowing his head to the Buddha's feet.
He said, "Excellent, excellent! I shall follow your instructions, for I wish to respectfully obey the Buddha.
Jiu replied, "When the Sixth Patriarch entered the chamber at Huangmei, he likewise used his *kāṣāya* to enclose himself, so as to test his prior realization."

"Ultimately, one should give rise to the mind by dwelling nowhere. Upon these words, [the student] attained great enlightenment. Thereupon, [the Master] entrusted him with his robes and bowl. The former master said:
"The various threads of the *kāṣāya* clearly manifest the numerical categories of the Dharma; it is not a mere matter of convenience. Indeed, the *kāṣāya* ranges from one strip to twenty-five strips;
each strip consists of five [sections], and each [section] has four long and one short [strip], arranged in reverse order."
Intermingled, opening and closing, and undergoing transformation, these silently seal the vast and inherent essence of the mind within each of us.
Through their perfect fusion and sequential unfolding, without stagnating in any one-sidedness, one finally exhausts the mysteries of this mind and this Dharma.
It is not that there is some so-called "esoteric transmission" existing apart from the mind. As the Sixth Patriarch’s verse says: "Bodhi originally has no tree; the bright mirror..."
"Not a stand; originally there was not a single thing. Where could dust and grime gather?
Is this not a case of being stuck in a state of purity, such that one's realization of the mind-dharma remains incomplete?

If this verse were the ultimate teaching, then the accounts of "great penetration" occurring upon hearing a word during the three rounds of entering the room would not exist. Since such accounts do exist, the intent of the verse [is not final].
This is a partiality. Even if Master Lu were to appear once more, he would surely nod in agreement.
That people today fail to realize this and consequently claim that our former master fixed the essence of the school upon the robe—is this not an extreme form of deceiving the world?
This clearly reveals that Tanji was unwilling to reflect deeply and spoke empty, false words; he failed to consider that the *kāṣāya* is something produced by people.

Regarding the robes that are manufactured: if they were identical in essence to those that are inherently present, then the manufactured and the inherently present would mutually cancel each other out;

thus, the analogy and the dharma would not correspond. Furthermore, since the preceding section relied upon the threads of the robe to demonstrate the numerical categories of dharmas, it cannot be said to be arbitrary.
Later, he further said: "If the fundamental principle does not reside in the robe, is this not a case of inconsistency between earlier and later statements, resulting in self-contradiction?
Han Yue slandered the verse of the Sixth Patriarch, claiming it was the view of nihilistic heretics;

Tan Ji changed "stuck in purity" (*zhai zai jing chu*) to "not yet perfected in the mind-dharma" (*yu xin fa wei yuan*). However, the Dharma of the World-Honored One is fundamentally the Dharma of non-existence. No...
Phenomenon after phenomenon is also the Dharma. Now, at the time when I entrust the non-Dharma, how has phenomenon ever been a phenomenon?

Is it not also stagnating in the realm of purity, such that there remains something incomplete regarding the mind-Dharma? Furthermore, Kāśyapa’s verse says: "Phenomenon after phenomenon is the primordial Dharma."
There is neither dharma nor non-dharma. How could there be both dharma and non-dharma within a single dharma?
Since it is said that dharmas are originally dharmas, and there is neither dharma nor non-dharma, is this not the case that "originally there is not a single thing"?
Where, then, could dust and grime be stirred up? Han Yue Tan Ji, because he had not yet awakened to the original nature, spoke exclusively from outside the original nature.

This is the profound mystery of this mind and these dharmas. [The Master] instead rebuked the Sixth Patriarch’s verse on original nature, claiming it was stuck in a state of purity and had not yet dreamed of the ancients’ truth that is everywhere present.
"Everywhere is true; in every speck of dust is the person of original nature," as the Layman Pang said:
"In daily affairs there is no difference; only I myself am in harmony with them. At every turn there is neither grasping nor rejecting."
"Everywhere they vanish; Zhang Guai is gone. Who shall be the one to designate the 'purple' and the 'crimson'?

As for those for whom the mountains and hills are utterly free of a speck of dust—this is precisely the commentary on the Sixth Patriarch’s 'Originally there is not a single thing; where could dust and dirt cling?
Therefore, before Layman Lu has even emerged again, I, this old monk, shall decisively sever Han Yue Tanji from reaching the Buddhas and Patriarchs, along with all other people."
In the state where there is originally no differentiation, they falsely established the origins of the Five Schools and their exegeses.
Specifically, according to the *Tanji*, that which is the greatest among things is heaven and earth; that which is the most profound in principle is yin and yang.
The sages welcomed the sun and pushed the divining stalks, delineated the eight trigrams, examined the *Hetu*, and measured it with the armillary sphere.
By recording these in books of calendrical astronomy, one can then clearly perceive— as if pointing at them on the palm of one's hand— the movements and stillness of Heaven and Earth,
the courses and degrees of the sun and moon, the divisions of the stars and constellations, the cycles of Yin and Yang and the seasons of cold and heat,
the variations of intercalary months and the waxing and waning of the phases, and the hidden states of spirits and the netherworld. From this, we may observe the wisdom and foresight of the Sage.
You have surpassed others by a vast margin. Were ordinary men and women to follow this line of reasoning, how could they not only increase their own state of profound ignorance?
You may see for yourself that you have not yet realized the ground where all things are fundamentally non-different.

Why is this? Heaven and earth emerge from me; thus, they cannot be called the greatest of things. Yin and yang are manifested through me; [thus, they cannot be called the most fundamental of phenomena].

This may be called the most profound of principles: without a single stroke being applied, the Eight Trigrams manifest themselves; without the dragon-horse having been seen, the River Chart already appears.
It does not require the observation of the celestial sphere through the instruments of the *hūntiān* or its recording in the books of calendrical phenomena.

The movement and stillness of heaven and earth, the courses and degrees of the sun and moon, the divisions of the stars and constellations, the cycles of Yin and Yang and the seasons of cold and heat,
the variations of intercalary months, surplus days, and the waxing and waning of the phases, as well as the manifestations of ghosts and spirits in the dark realm—
all of these follow their respective seasonal signs and each attains its proper place. Thus, how could the wisdom and deliberation of the Sage ever possess even a hair’s breadth [of deviation]?

Beyond ordinary people—how could even a single man or woman have ever possessed the slightest trace of delusion? This is the realm where this old woodcutter has personally realized that the sentient and the insentient manifest equally and radiantly.
Based on this, the World-Honored One declared that the appearance of all Buddhas in the world is solely for the sake of the one great cause and condition;
the Seven Buddhas, the successive Patriarchs, and the Five Houses of Zen have all taken this as their foundation.
The fundamental principle of the uninterrupted continuity [of the Way] is as follows: Now, Tan Ji gazes broadly upon heaven and earth and observes deeply the Yin and Yang.

He calculates by welcoming the sun and pushing the divining stalks, measuring with the浑仪 (Hunyi, the armillary sphere) and recording it in the calendar books. This is comparable to [Fu Xi’s] drawing of the Eight Trigrams and examining the River Chart.
To regard this as something extraordinary about a sage is precisely what constitutes a state of "vague karmic consciousness" with no fundamental basis to rely upon.
How, then, can one not be surprised that he relies on Han Yue to fabricate and speak recklessly, slandering me, the old monk?

The First Patriarch of the Western Heaven, Venerable Mahākāśyapa, was a native of Magadha. His clan name was Brahmin;
his father was named Yinze (Drinking Marsh), and his mother was named Xiangzhi (Fragrant Arrival). In a past life, he was a goldsmith who encountered the parinirvāṇa of Vipaśyin Buddha.
The fourfold assembly erected a stūpa. A poor woman obtained a golden bead and earnestly requested a goldsmith to repair a missing portion of the golden face on the Buddha image within the stūpa.
Together they made a vow: "In every successive life, may we be husband and wife without other kin. By virtue of this causal connection, for ninety-one kalpas their bodies were entirely golden.
In this present world, she and the nun Suvarṇaprabhāsā (Purple-Gold Light) again became husband and wife. (Sanskrit: *Suvarṇaprabhāsā*)
Kāśyapa—here translated as "Drinking Light"—was so named because of the radiance of his body. However, both husband and wife lived in purity, free from worldly thoughts.
They subsequently left the household life and practiced the dhūta austerities. Then, a deity in the sky announced to them: "The Buddha has appeared in the world;
you should go and take him as your teacher. The Venerable One immediately hastened to pay homage to the World-Honored One at the Veṇuvana Monastery. The Buddha...

The Buddha said, "Welcome, Bhikṣu. His beard and hair fell away of their own accord. Among the assembly, the Buddha praised him as the foremost. Later, through the occasion of the plucking of a flower, he was entrusted with the Dharma.

At the time of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the Venerable was in the Piṇḍola Cave. With his purified divine eye, he saw that the World-Honored One was entering parinirvāṇa on the banks of the Hiraṇyavatī River. He immediately went to the twin trees and wailed in sorrowful longing.
When the Buddha revealed his two feet from the golden coffin, the Venerable addressed the bhikṣus: "The Buddha has already been cremated; the diamond-like relics are no longer ours."
"It is fitting that we should now convene a council of the Dharma-eye so that it shall not be severed. He then spoke a verse, saying: "Disciples of the Tathāgata, do not yet enter nirvāṇa.
Those who have attained supernatural powers (ṛddhi) should proceed to the council. Thereupon, all those who had attained supernatural powers gathered at the Piṇḍola Cave on Vulture Peak Mountain.
At that time, Ānanda was unable to join the assembly because his outflows (āsrava) were not yet exhausted. Later...
Having realized the fruit of Arhatship, he entered [the assembly]. The Venerable One addressed the multitude, saying: "This Bhikṣu Ānanda possesses great wisdom;
whatever Dharma he hears from the Buddha, it passes from one vessel to another like water, without any remainder. You should request him to compile the Sūtra Piṭaka.
The great assembly remained silent.
Once the council had concluded, the Venerable One reflected that he was advanced in years and should enter meditative absorption on Mount Kukkuṭapāda to await Maitreya.
He then summoned Ānanda and said, "I shall not remain much longer in this world; I now entrust the True Dharma to you."
Guard it well. Listen to my verse: "All phenomena are from the beginning the true Dharma; there is neither phenomenon nor non-phenomenon.
Why, within a single phenomenon, would there be both phenomenon and non-phenomenon?"
▲ The Second Patriarch, Venerable Ānanda, was a native of Rājagṛha. His clan name was Kṣatriya; his father was King Droṇodana, and he was the biological younger cousin of the Tathāgata.
He was profoundly learned and widely erudite, possessing unimpeded wisdom. The World-Honored One regarded him as foremost among those who possess *dhāraṇī*.
In Sanskrit he is called Ānanda; in Chinese this means "Joyous Celebration. He was so named because he was born on the day the Tathāgata attained enlightenment. Thus it is said.
One day he asked Mahākāśyapa, "Elder brother, besides the golden-threaded *kaṣāya* that the World-Honored One transmitted, what else did he transmit?
Kāśyapa called out, "Ānanda! Ānanda responded, "Yes? Kāśyapa said, "Throw down the banner-pole in front of the gate."
When the Venerable One was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he sat cross-legged in the middle of the Ganges River.
King Ajātaśatru and the King of Vaiśālī were both on the riverbank; they spoke verses to entreat him, saying, "Do not enter parinirvāṇa.
He replied with these verses: "O two kings, dwell well-composed; do not grieve in sorrowful longing. My nirvāṇa shall be in tranquility, for I am free from all states of existence. Furthermore...
He reflected: "If I were to go toward a single country, the other countries might dispute it; I should instead deliver all sentient beings with equanimity.
He then proceeded to the middle of the Ganges River to enter parinirvāṇa. At that time, the mountains, rivers, and great earth shook in six ways.
Five hundred rishis from the Snowy Mountains, beholding this auspicious omen, flew through the air and arrived. They prostrated at the Venerable One’s feet and said:
He said, "I shall bear witness to the Buddha-dharma for you, Venerable One. I pray that you will grant us great compassion and deliver us. The Venerable One accepted the request in silence.
He immediately transformed the Ganges River so that it became entirely golden ground. For the sake of the assembly of sages, he preached various Great Dharmas.
Then he thought, "The disciples I previously delivered should now assemble. In a brief moment, five hundred Arhats arrived from—
He descended from the sky. For the sake of the various seers (*ṛṣi*), he left the household life and received full ordination.
Within that assembly of seers, there were two arhats: one named Śāṇakavāsin and the other named Madhyāntika. The Venerable One, knowing them to be vessels for the Dharma, addressed them, saying:
"The Tathāgata entrusted the Eye of the True Dharma to Kāśyapa; Kāśyapa entered meditative absorption and entrusted it to me. I, now..."
As it was about to be extinguished, he entrusted it further to you. You must receive my teaching; listen now to these verses: "The Dharma originally entrusted exists;
once entrusted, it is said to be non-existent. Each must awaken for themselves; having awakened, there is neither existence nor non-existence.
Having spoken these verses, he further charged Śāṇakavāsin with the True Dharma Eye and commanded Madhyāntika to propagate it in the kingdom of Kaśmīra.
The *Dafayun* states:
The Third Patriarch, Venerable Śāṇakavāsin, was surnamed Viśākha. His father was Vanavāsin and his mother was Kauśeya;
he was a native of the kingdom of Mathurā. He remained in the womb for six years before being born. In Sanskrit he is called Śāṇakavāsin, which here [in Chinese] is translated as "Self-..."
"Ranfu" (然服) is the name for a nine-branched, exquisite grass found in the Western Regions. It appears when a sage descends to birth; when the Venerable One was born, this grass emerged.
Formerly, when the Tathāgata was traveling to convert beings, he reached the kingdom of Mathurā and saw a grove of green trees with lush branches and leaves.
He said to Ānanda: "This grove is named Uruvilvā. One hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, there will be one who..."
The name of the Bhikkhu was Śāṇakavāsin. Here he turned the sublime Wheel of Dharma. One hundred years later, Upagupta was born;
he left the household life, realized the Path, and received the Dharma-eye from the Venerable Ānanda. Arriving at this grove, he subsequently subdued two fire-dragons.
The dragons received the Three Refuges and offered him their land, upon which he established a Brahma-palace.
The Venerable One, having long since fulfilled his karmic conditions for transformation, contemplated who might be entrusted with the Dharma-transmission.
He soon found Upagupta in the kingdom of Ṭaki and took him as his attendant. He then asked Upagupta, "How old are you? He replied, "I am seventeen years old.

The Venerable One said, "Is it only your body that is seventeen, or is your nature also seventeen? He replied, "My teacher’s hair has turned white; is it because your hair is white that [your mind]... [is also old?]
Pāla said, "I am merely white-haired; my mind is not white. Guptaka said, "My body is seventeen years old, but my nature is not seventeen years old.
The Venerable One knew he was a vessel for the Dharma. Three years later, he finally shaved his head and conferred the full precepts upon him, entrusting him with the Eye of the Dharma.
The verse of dharma-transmission says: "Neither non-dharma nor mind, Neither no-mind nor no-dharma. Having spoken thus—
At the time when it is a mental dharma, this dharma is not a mental dharma.
The Fourth Patriarch, Venerable Upagupta, was a native of the country of Ṭhāṇā. His clan name was Śūdra; his father’s name was Kalyāṇabuddhi.
At seventeen he left the household life, and at twenty he realized the fruit [of Arhatship].

While the Venerable One was in the world teaching and guiding others, those who realized the fruit were most numerous. Whenever he ordained one person, he would place a tally-stick in a stone chamber.
That chamber was eighteen cubits in length and twelve cubits in width; it became filled with them until finally there was one remaining tall...
“Son, one named Gandharvasena has come to pay homage to the Venerable One and seeks to go forth. The Venerable One asked: ‘Do you go forth with your body, or do you go forth with your mind?
He replied: ‘I have come to go forth, not for the sake of body or mind. The Venerable One said: ‘If it is not for the sake of body or mind, then who is it that goes forth? He replied:
‘As for one who goes forth, because there is no self and no “mine,” and because there is no self and no “mine,” [it is thus].’”
The mind is neither born nor extinguished. That the mind is neither born nor extinguished is itself the tasting of the Way. All Buddhas have likewise tasted it. The mind has no form or appearance;

its essence is also thus. The Venerable One said: "You shall attain great enlightenment; the mind will naturally penetrate through to itself. You should rely upon the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha."

He caused the noble lineage to flourish and immediately ordained him, bestowing upon him the full precepts (*upasampadā*). He then addressed him, saying: "Your father dreamed of a golden sun when you were born;
you may therefore be named Tiṭṭhaka (Dīrgha). The Tathāgata has transmitted the treasury of the Great Dharma-Eye in successive order."
This has been transmitted down to me, and now I entrust it further to you. Listen to my verse: "The mind is itself the original mind; The original mind is not a dharma that exists.
If there were dharmas, there would be an original mind; But being neither mind nor dharma, it is the fundamental reality."
▲ The Venerable Diṭṭhagāma, the Fifth Patriarch, was a native of the kingdom of Magadha. His original name was Gandhamukha.
At the time of his birth, his father dreamed that a golden sun emerged from the house, its radiance illuminating heaven and earth; before it stood a great mountain, adorned with all manner of jewels.
A spring gushed forth from the summit of the mountain, flowing in torrents in all four directions. Later, he encountered the Venerable Kātyāyanīputra, who explained it for him, saying:
"The precious mountain is my own body; the gushing spring is the inexhaustibility of the Dharma. The sun rising from the house is the sign of your current entry into the Path.
Its illuminating of heaven and earth signifies that your wisdom is transcendent. Because of this, his name was changed to [Vasubandhu]. (Sanskrit)
"Kundopadhānīya" means "One Who Penetrates True Measure. Upon hearing this, the Venerable One leaped for joy and spoke in verse:
"The towering mountain of the seven treasures constantly wells forth the spring of wisdom; Transformed into the flavor of the true Dharma, it can deliver all who possess the karmic affinity.
Venerable Gupta also spoke in verse: "I transmit my Dharma to you; you shall manifest great wisdom. The golden sun rises from the house..."
He emerged, illuminating heaven and earth. When the Venerable One heard the verse, he performed a prostration and took it up for practice.
Later, he arrived in Central India. In that country, there were eight thousand great ṛṣis, with Mīḍhika at their head.

Hearing that the Venerable One had arrived, they led the assembly to pay him homage. They said to the Venerable One, "In the past, we were born together with you in the Brahma Heaven. I encountered Asita..."
"O Immortal, you have bestowed upon me the methods of the immortals. As your disciple, I have encountered the ten directions and practiced *dhyāna*.
Since then, our karmic destinies have followed divergent paths for six kalpas. The other said, "To be separated by such accumulated kalpas is indeed not in vain.
Now you may abandon the heterodox and return to the orthodox to enter the Buddha-vehicle. Mīḍhaka said, "In the past, the Immortal Asita bestowed a prophecy upon me, saying:"
"In six kalpas hence, you shall meet a fellow student and attain the fruit of outflowlessness (*anāsrava*). Is our meeting today not the result of past affinities?
I pray that the Master, in his compassion, will grant me liberation. Thereupon, [the Master] ordained him and had the noble ones confer the precepts upon him.

As for the rest of the assembly of seers, they initially gave rise to pride; the Venerable One then manifested great supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), whereupon they all resolved their minds on Bodhicitta.
At that time, upon leaving the household life, he addressed Mīchaka, saying: "In the past, the Tathāgata secretly entrusted the Great Dharma-Eye Treasury to Kāśyapa;
it was transmitted successively from one to another until it reached me. I now entrust it to you; you must protect and cherish it. He then spoke this verse:
"Thoroughly penetrating the mind of the fundamental Dharma, there is neither dharma nor non-dharma. Awakening is identical to non-awakening; it is the state of no-mind."
Nor is there any dharma.
▲ The Venerable Master Mīchaka, the Sixth Patriarch, was a native of Central India. Having transmitted the Dharma, he traveled through various regions to reach North India.
There, seeing auspicious golden clouds above the city walls, he sighed and said: "This is the breath of a person of the Way; it must surely..."

"There is a Great Being who shall be my successor. He then entered the city. In the midst of the marketplace, there was a man holding a vessel of wine who approached him and asked, "From where do you come, Master?
Where do you intend to go? The Patriarch said, "I come from my own mind; I intend to go nowhere.
The man asked, "Do you recognize what is in my hand? The Patriarch replied, "This is a vessel for contact that carries purity. The man said:
The Master asked, "Do you recognize me? The Patriarch replied, "I do not recognize you; if I were to recognize you, it would not be my true self.
He then said to him, "Try to state your own name and lineage, and I shall subsequently reveal your original cause. He answered with a verse: "Throughout immeasurable kalpas,"
As for his birth in this country: his original clan was Bharadvāja and his name was Vasu-mitra. His ancestor said:
"My teacher, Diṅnāga, stated that when the World-Honored One was formerly traveling through North India, he spoke to Ānanda, saying:
'In this country, three hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, there will be a holy man of the clan Bharadvāja named Vasumitra, who [will appear] among the patriarchs of dhyāna.'"

"You shall attain the seventh [stage]. The World-Honored One has prophesied for you that you should renounce the household life. He then set down his vessel, paid obeisance to his teacher, stood to one side, and said:
"I recall a past kalpa when I was a donor; I once offered a precious throne to a Tathāgata. That Buddha prophesied for me, saying:
'In the Dharma of Śākyamuni during the Bhadrakalpa, you shall propagate the supreme teaching. Now this accords with my teacher's words. I pray that you will grant me [the precepts]."
Dutuō (Duotuo) was immediately tonsured by his grandfather and subsequently received full ordination. His grandfather then told him: "The Treasury of the True Dharma Eye is now entrusted to you;
do not let it be severed. He then spoke this verse: "No mind can be attained; What is spoken cannot be called the Dharma.
If one realizes that the mind is no-mind, Only then does one understand the mind and its dharmas."
▲ The Seventh Patriarch, Venerable Vasumitra, was a native of Northern India. He used to wear pure robes while carrying vessels of wine, wandering through the streets and alleys;

sometimes he would chant or whistle, leading people to deem him mad. Upon meeting the Venerable Mīchaka, who proclaimed the Tathāgata’s past prophecies concerning him, he reflected on his former karmic conditions, cast aside his vessels, and left the household life. Having received the Dharma, he traveled to propagate the teachings as far as Kāmala.
In that country, Buddhist activities flourished extensively. Before the Dharma seat, there was suddenly a man of wisdom who declared, "My name is Buddhānandi;
I shall now debate the meaning of the Dharma with you, Master. The Patriarch said, "If you speak of 'meaning,' it is not the Way; if you speak of the 'Way,' it cannot be discussed as 'meaning.

If you intend to debate meaning, it will ultimately not be a discussion of the Way. Buddhānandi realized that the Master’s meaning was superior, and his heart was filled with reverence. He said, "I wish to seek [the Way]."
Daozhen was moistened by the flavor of the nectar of the Dharma. The Patriarch then granted him the tonsure and bestowed upon him full ordination.
He further addressed him, saying: "The Tathāgata’s Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, I now entrust to you; you must protect and uphold it. Thereupon he spoke this verse:
"The mind is identical to the realm of empty space; It reveals dharmas equal to empty space. When emptiness is realized, There is neither 'is' nor 'non-is'."
The Eighth Patriarch, Venerable Buddhanandi, was a native of the kingdom of Kāmarūpa. His secular surname was Gautama.

He possessed a fleshy protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*) upon his crown and was endowed with swift and unimpeded eloquence. Having received the Dharma from Venerable Vasumitra, he traveled through various lands to propagate the teachings until he arrived at the house of Viśāla in the kingdom of Ti-ga.
Observing a white light ascending from the roof of the residence, he said to his disciples, "There is a sage within this household."
His mouth uttered no words; he was a true vessel for the Mahāyāna. He did not walk upon the four crossroads, for he knew that contact with them was defiling.
When the elder came out to pay his respects, he asked what it was that [the Master] required. The Patriarch said, "I am seeking an attendant. The elder said, "I have a son named Buddhabhadra;
he is already fifty years old, yet his mouth has never spoken, and his feet have never trodden the ground. The Patriarch said, "If it is as you say..."
[The Master] said, "He is truly my disciple. When Puṇyamitra heard this, he rose immediately to prostrate himself and spoke a verse, saying:
"Parents are not my kin; who is the most intimate kin? The Buddhas are not my path; who is the supreme path? The Patriarch answered him in verse:
"What you say accords with the mind; parents cannot be compared to it. Your practice accords with the Path; [it is] the mind of all Buddhas."
"This is it. Seeking an external Buddha with form is not like you. To recognize your original mind, it is neither joined nor separate.
Upon hearing this verse, Vovada took seven steps. The Patriarch said, "This child encountered a Buddha in a past life; his compassionate vows are vast and great.
Fearing that his parents' affection would make him difficult to relinquish, he remained silent and did not walk. The elder then gave him up."
He caused [the master] to leave the household life. The Patriarch then conferred upon him full ordination and, entrusting the Dharma, spoke this verse: "Space has neither interior nor exterior;
the nature of the mind is likewise so. If one realizes space, one penetrates the principle of True Suchness."
▲ The Ninth Patriarch, Vajramitra, was a native of Ti-ga country. His secular surname was Viśrāvaṇa.
While traveling to transform beings in Central India, he encountered an elder named Gandhacchattra, who brought his son to pay him homage.

The elder said, "This child has been in the womb for sixty years (the *Zhengzong* edition reads sixteen). Once, a seer remarked that this boy’s physical characteristics were extraordinary; now he has met the Honored One."

[The Master] said, "You may leave [your home] and become a monk. The Patriarch then shaved his head. At the moment of the *karmavācanā* (formal ordination), auspicious light illuminated the seat, and thirty-seven *śarīra* relics appeared before them.
From then on, he practiced with such diligence that he forgot all fatigue. Before long, the Patriarch transmitted the Dharma to him, speaking this verse:
"The True Principle is originally nameless; To manifest the True Principle, one must respond to names. Having received the true and real Dharma, That which is not true..."
Not false. ▲ The Tenth Patriarch, Venerable Śrīkṣetra, was a native of Central India. His clan name is unknown. He remained in the womb for sixty years.
On the eve of his birth, his mother dreamed that a white elephant carrying a precious throne entered her chamber; upon the throne sat a bright pearl, and then he was born.

From birth, his divine radiance illuminated the chamber, and his body was imbued with a wondrous fragrance. Although he grew up eating grain-based food, he was entirely free from any waste or impurities.
His original name was Duṣprasaha (Difficult to Overcome). Later, while serving as an attendant to the Ninth Patriarch, he never slept;

it was said that his ribs never touched the mat, and thus he was titled the Venerable Pārśva (Flank Honored One). When he first arrived at the city of Pāṭaliputra, he rested beneath a tree and pointed to the ground with his right hand.
He addressed the assembly, saying, "This ground has turned golden; a sage shall enter this assembly. As soon as he had finished speaking, it immediately turned golden.
At that time, the elder’s son Pūrṇaśa stood before him with palms joined. The Patriarch asked him, "From where have you come?"
[The monk] said, "My mind does not go. The Patriarch asked, "Where do you dwell? He replied, "My mind does not stop.
The Patriarch asked, "Are you not settled? He replied, "All Buddhas are likewise so. The Patriarch said, "You are not the Buddhas. He replied, "The Buddhas are also not [the Buddhas].
The Patriarch then ordained him as a monk and conferred the full precepts. He then transmitted the Dharma to him, speaking this verse: "The true essence is naturally true; because it is true..."
The teaching is logical. One who has realized the true Dharma neither proceeds nor stops.
▲ The eleventh patriarch, the Venerable Punyayasas, was a native of the country of Pāṭaliputra. His secular surname was Gautama.

Having met the Venerable Upagupta, he was subsequently granted the Dharma. The Patriarch’s teachings spread to immeasurable beings, and those who attained the fruit numbered five hundred. Later, he arrived at Pāṭaliputra...
In the kingdom of Rājagṛha, there was an elder who came to attend the assembly. The Patriarch said to the multitude, "Do you recognize this person who has come?
The Buddha prophesied that the noble Mātr̥ceṭa shall succeed to my Dharma. Thereupon, Mātr̥ceṭa paid his respects and asked, "I wish to know the Buddha; which one is he?
The Patriarch replied, "If you wish to know the Buddha, it is that which does not know. He [Mātr̥ceṭa]—
Asvaghosa said, "Since you do not recognize the Buddha, how can you know that it is? The Patriarch said, "Since you do not recognize the Buddha, how can you know that it is not?

Asvaghosa said, "This is the meaning of the saw. The Patriarch said, "It is the meaning of being cut by the wood. The Patriarch asked, "What is the meaning of the saw? Asvaghosa replied, "I am leveled along with the Master.
Asvaghosa then asked, "What is the meaning of the wood? The Patriarch said, "You have been cut by me. At this, Asvaghosa was suddenly enlightened.
He attained awakening and subsequently sought ordination. The Patriarch said to the assembly, "This Great Being was formerly the King of Viśāli.
Because there was a class of people in his kingdom who were naked like horses, the king exercised his supernatural powers and manifested himself as silkworms to clothe them with silk.

Later, he was born in Central India; the 'horse-people' (those who had been naked) felt such deep longing for him that they neighed piteously, and thus he was named Aśvaghoṣa (Horse-Neigher). Thus it is said.
He came to bestow this prediction: "Six hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, Aśvaghoṣa shall appear in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī; he shall subdue the heterodox and deliver immeasurable beings.
Now is precisely that time. He then entrusted him with a verse of the Dharma: "Delusion and awakening are like concealment and manifestation; Light and darkness are not separate from one another.
Now I entrust you with the dharma of concealment and manifestation; It is neither one, nor is it two."
▲The Twelfth Patriarch, the Great Being Aśvaghoṣa, was a native of the kingdom of Vārāṇasī. He was also named Saṅgharakṣita;
because his cultivated and unconditioned merits were most preeminent, he was given this name.

Having received the Dharma from the Venerable Vasubandhu, he later turned the wondrous wheel of the Dharma in the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra. Suddenly, an old man fell prostrate before him. The Patriarch—
He said to the assembly, "This is no ordinary person; there shall surely be extraordinary signs. Having finished speaking, he vanished.
Suddenly, a golden man emerged from the earth, who then transformed into a woman. She pointed her right hand toward the Patriarch and spoke this verse:

"I prostrate to the Venerable Elder; You shall receive the prediction of the Tathāgata. Now, upon this very ground, You shall proclaim and disseminate the Ultimate Truth (Paramārtha). Having spoken the verse, she disappeared.
In an instant, they vanished. The Patriarch said, "A demon is about to come to contend with my strength.
After a short while, wind and rain arrived suddenly, and heaven and earth grew dark and murky. The Patriarch said, "The arrival of the demon is indeed certain; I shall eliminate him.

He then pointed into the air, and a great golden dragon appeared, manifesting its majestic spiritual power and shaking the mountains and peaks. The Patriarch remained solemn upon his seat, and the demonic disturbances subsided.
After seven days had passed, a small insect as large as a mayfly appeared, hiding beneath the Master’s seat.

The Master took it up with his hand and showed it to the assembly, saying, "This is a transformation produced by a māra, coming to eavesdrop on my Dharma. He released it to let it go, but the māra could not move.
The Master addressed him, saying, "If you simply take refuge in the Triple Gem, you shall immediately attain supernatural powers. Thereupon, he returned to his original form.
[He] prostrated and performed repentance. The Patriarch asked, "What is your name? How many followers do you have? He replied, "My name is Kāpimāra. I have three thousand followers.
The Patriarch said, "Exerting your supernatural powers to the full, what kind of transformations can you perform?
He replied, "I could transform a vast ocean; that would be a very minor feat. The Patriarch said, "Can you transform the ocean of nature (dharmatā-samudra)? He asked, "What is the ocean of nature?"
"I have never known this. The Patriarch then explained the ocean of nature (*dharmatā-samudra*) to him, saying: "Mountains, rivers, and the great earth are all established upon it;

the three samādhis and the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) are manifested through it. Upon hearing these words, Kāpimāra conceived faith and, together with three thousand followers, sought ordination.
The Patriarch then summoned five hundred arhats and conferred the full precepts (*upasaṃpadā*) upon them, further instructing them as follows:
He said: "The Tathāgata’s Great Dharma-Eye Treasury shall now be entrusted to you. Listen to these verses: 'Appearance and disappearance are the fundamental Dharma;
light and darkness have always been non-dual. Now I entrust this Dharma of realization; it is neither grasped nor abandoned.'"
▲ The Thirteenth Patriarch, Venerable Kāpimāra, was a native of the country of Pāṭaliputra. Initially, he was a non-Buddhist teacher with three thousand disciples;

he was well-versed in various heterodox doctrines. Later, he received the Dharma from the Venerable Aśvaghoṣa. Leading his disciples, he traveled to Western India, where there was a crown prince named Meghasvabhāva.
Admiring the Venerable’s reputation, the prince invited him to the palace to receive offerings. The Patriarch...
The Master said, "The Tathāgata has taught that a śramaṇa must not associate with kings, ministers, or powerful families.
The Prince said, "To the north of my kingdom’s capital there is a great mountain. On that mountain is a stone cave; may I practice dhyāna in seclusion there?
The Master replied, "So be it," and immediately entered that mountain. After traveling several li, he encountered a large python; the Master walked straight toward it.
He paid no heed. The serpent coiled itself around the Master’s body. The Master then conferred the Three Refuges upon it; having heard them, the serpent departed.
As the Master was about to reach a stone cave, an old man dressed in plain clothing came out, joined his palms in greeting, and paid his respects. The Master asked, "Where do you reside?
He replied, "In the past, I was once a bhikṣu who took great pleasure in solitude. There was a novice bhikṣu who..."
He came to request further instruction, but I was weary of answering him and gave rise to thoughts of resentment.

When my life ended, I fell into the body of a python and have dwelt within this cave for a thousand years. Having just encountered the Venerable One and been able to hear the Dharma of the Precepts, I have come to express my gratitude.
The Patriarch asked, "Are there any other inhabitants dwelling on this mountain? He replied, "Ten *li* from here, there is a great tree that provides shade."

There were five hundred great nāgas, and the king of trees there was named Nāgavṛkṣa (Dragon Tree). He had frequently preached the Dharma for the assembly of nāgas, and I too had heard and received it from him.
The Patriarch then went to that place with his disciples. Nāgavṛkṣa came out to meet him and said, "This deep mountain is secluded and solitary, a dwelling place for dragons and pythons.
Great Virtue, Most Honorable One, why have you deigned to trouble your divine feet? The Patriarch replied, "I am not a most honorable one; I have come to visit a worthy man. Nāga...
Nāgārjuna thought silently to himself: "Has this master attained the definitive nature and the eye of the clear Way? Is he a Great Sage who continues the True Vehicle? The Patriarch said:
"Though you speak with your mind, I already know it with my own. Simply prepare for the renunciation of the world; why worry that I am not a sage?
Having heard this, Nāgārjuna repented and apologized. The Patriarch immediately ordained him, along with five hundred dragon followers, and they all received full ordination.
[The Buddha said to] Kai: “I now entrust to you the Great Dharma-Eye Treasury of the Tathāgata. Listen attentively to these verses:
‘The dharma is neither hidden nor manifest; it is called the true limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi). To awaken to this dharma of hiding and manifesting is neither folly nor wisdom.’”
▲ The Fourteenth Patriarch, Venerable Nāgārjuna, was also known as Nāgasena. In his youth, he was able to recite the four Vedas;

as he grew, he became proficient in all arts. His eloquence was as brilliant as a deity. He left the household life and entered a stone cave to dwell among the dragon trees (nāga-druma), where he became the refuge for the assembly of dragons.
After meeting Venerable Māra and receiving the transmission of the Dharma, he traveled to South India. The people of that country were mostly...
The patriarch preached the Dharma for Xin Fuye. They said to one another, "Among people, those with meritorious karma are foremost in this world;
yet we speak in vain of 'Buddha-nature'—who can truly perceive it? The patriarch said, "If you wish to see Buddha-nature, you must first eliminate your pride.
They asked, "What is the size of Buddha-nature? The patriarch replied, "It is neither large nor small; neither broad nor narrow; it has neither merit nor retribution."

"Neither dying nor being born. Upon hearing this superior principle, they all returned to their original resolve. The Patriarch again manifested a body of sovereign mastery upon his seat, like the orb of the full moon;
yet the entire assembly heard only the sound of the Dharma and did not behold the Patriarch’s form.
Among the assembly was the son of an elder named Kanadeva, who asked the group, "Do you recognize this sign? The assembly replied, "It is something our eyes have never before seen."
[The assembly] looked on, unable to discern [what had occurred]. Deva said, "This is the Venerable One manifesting the essence and characteristics of the Buddha-nature to show us.
How do we know this? It is because through the formless samādhi, his form is like the full moon; the meaning of Buddha-nature is vast, empty, and luminous.
As soon as he finished speaking, the wheel-mark vanished, and he returned to his original seat, whereupon he spoke this verse: "The body manifests the circle..."
The lunar phases represent the essence of all Buddhas; their preaching of the Dharma has no fixed form, serving to distinguish that which is neither sound nor color.

When the assembly heard these verses, they suddenly realized non-arising and all vowed to leave the household life in pursuit of liberation. The Patriarch then shaved their hair and commanded the various sages to confer the full precepts upon them.
He composed the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*, and the *Dvādaśanikāya-śāstra*, transmitting them to the world. Later, he entrusted [the lineage]...

Dharma entrusted [the teaching] to Kanadeva. The verse of the transmission of the Dharma says: "In order to clarify the principles of manifestation and concealment, one then explains the logic of liberation;
regarding the Dharma, the mind does not realize it, being without anger and without joy."
▲ The Fifteenth Patriarch, Venerable Kanadeva, was a native of South India. His secular surname was Viśrāva.
Initially, he sought to cultivate meritorious deeds while also seeking to engage in debate. Later, he went to visit the Great Being Nāgārjuna.

As he approached the gate, Nāgārjuna, recognizing him as a man of wisdom, first sent an attendant to place a bowl filled with water before his seat. Upon seeing this, the Venerable [Kanadeva] immediately...
He cast a single needle into it and advanced; they joyfully reached a state of accord. After he had received the Dharma, he went to the kingdom of Kapilavastu.
There was an elder there named Brahmā Śuddhodana, who gave up his second son, Rāhulabhadra, to follow the teacher and renounce the household life.
The Patriarch said, "In the past, the Tathāgata prophesied that this son would become a great teacher during the second five-hundred-year period.
Our meeting today is surely in accord with our past causes. He then shaved his hair.
Upon arriving at the city of Pāṭaliputra, he heard that various non-Buddhists intended to obstruct the Buddha-dharma.

After reflecting on this for some time, the Patriarch took up a long banner and entered into their assembly. They asked the Patriarch, "Why do you not come forward? The Patriarch replied, "Why do you not fall back?"

The other said, "You seem like a lowly person. The Patriarch said, "You seem like a noble person. The other said, "What Dharma do you understand? The Patriarch said, "You do not understand anything at all.
The other said, "I wish to attain Buddhahood. The Patriarch said, "I have certainly attained Buddhahood. The other said, "It is not fitting for you to attain it.
The Patriarch said, "Originally I say that I have attained it; you truly have not attained it. The other said, "Since you have not attained it, how..."

"Why do you say you have not attained it? The Patriarch replied, "Because you still possess the notion of 'self,' you have not attained it. Since I am without the notion of 'self' or 'mine,' I naturally attain it.
When his arguments were thus defeated, the monk asked the Patriarch, "What is your name? The Patriarch replied, "My name is Kanadeva.

Having previously heard of the Patriarch's reputation, the monk repented his errors and offered his thanks. At that time, those among the assembly who had been debating with one another ceased their questioning.

The Patriarch refuted him with unimpeded eloquence, whereupon he submitted and took refuge. He then informed his senior disciple, Rāhulabhadra, and entrusted him with the Eye of the Dharma, saying in verse:
"I have explained the principle of liberation for the sake of one who transmits the Dharma; In reality, there is no realization of the Dharma, Neither end nor beginning."
▲ The sixteenth patriarch, Venerable Rāhulabhadra, was a native of Kapilavastu. While traveling to convert beings, he arrived at the city of Śrāvastī.
There was a river there called Suvarṇodaka (Golden Water), whose flavor was exceptionally exquisite; in its midstream, the reflections of the five Buddhas appeared once more.
The Patriarch addressed the assembly, saying: "The source of this river is five hundred *li* away, where the holy one Saṃghanandin resides.
One thousand years after the Buddha’s passing, he shall succeed to the sacred position. Having spoken thus, he led the assembly of disciples upstream.
Upon reaching that place, they saw Saṃghanandin seated in meditative absorption. The Patriarch and the assembly waited for him for—

After twenty-one days, he finally arose from his concentration. The Patriarch asked him, "Is your mind concentrated, or is your body concentrated? Dashi replied, "Both my body and mind are concentrated.

The Patriarch said, "If both body and mind are concentrated, how can there be entering and exiting [of concentration]? Dashi replied, "Although there is entering and exiting, it does not lose the characteristic of concentration;
it is like gold in a well: the essence of the gold remains eternally still. The Patriarch said, "Whether the gold is in the well or whether the gold has been taken out..."
“Wells,” [the Master] said. “Gold has neither motion nor stillness. What is it that enters and exits? Daiten replied, “If you say gold has motion and stillness, what is it that enters and exits?

If you say gold enters and exits, then gold itself is neither motion nor stillness. The Master said, “If the gold is in the well, what is the gold that comes out? If the gold has come out of the well, what remains inside?
Daiten replied, “If the gold has come out of the well, what remains inside is not gold. If the gold is in the well, then what comes out is not gold.”
[Daowu] said, "This is not a thing. The Patriarch said, "This meaning is not so. Daiti said, "That meaning is not attached. The Patriarch said, "This meaning shall fall.
Daiti said, "That meaning is not established. The Patriarch said, "Since that meaning is not established, my meaning is established.
Daiti said, "Although my meaning is established, the Dharma is not mine. The Patriarch said, "My meaning is already established, for I have no self. Daiti said, "I..."
"Because there is no self. What further meaning does this establish? The Patriarch said, "Because I am without a self, your proposition is established.
Nandī asked, "Whom did you take as your teacher to attain this state of no-self? The Patriarch said, "My teacher was Kanadeva; through him, I realized this no-self. Nandī praised him with a verse:
"I bow my head to Teacher Kanadeva, from whom you, O Benevolent One, emerged. Because you, O Benevolent One, are without a self,"
"I wish to take you, O Benevolent One, as my teacher. The Elder replied with a verse: "Since I am already without a self, you must perceive my 'self.
If you would take me as your teacher, know that my 'self' is not a self. At these words, Nandika’s mind was suddenly enlightened, and he immediately sought ordination and liberation.
The Patriarch said, "Your mind is autonomous; it is not bound by me. He then conferred the verse of the Dharma-eye:
"In the Dharma, there is truly nothing realized; Neither grasped nor abandoned. The Dharma has no marks of existence or non-existence; How could it arise internally or externally?"
▲ The seventeenth patriarch, Venerable Saṃghanandin, was the son of King Ratnavyūha of Śrāvastī.
From birth he was able to speak and constantly praised the Buddha’s deeds. At the age of seven, he grew weary of worldly pleasures and addressed his parents with a verse, saying:
"I prostrate to my Greatly Compassionate Father; I pay homage to my flesh-and-blood Mother. I now wish to leave the household life; I pray you will have pity on me."
Out of compassion, his parents firmly tried to dissuade him. He consequently fasted for an entire day, until they finally permitted him to leave the household life and become a monk.
He was named Saṃghanandin. They further appointed the śramaṇa Śāṇakavāsin as his teacher. For nineteen years, he never once grew weary or indolent.
He would often reflect to himself: "I dwell in a royal palace; why have I left the household life? One night, a divine light descended upon him.
Seeing a path that was level and smooth, he walked on slowly without realizing it. After about ten *li*, he arrived before a great cliff where there was a stone cave;
he then dwelt in meditative stillness within it. When the father lost his son, he immediately banished Śrīlāta from the country and went abroad to search for him, but did not know his whereabouts.
Ten years passed, and after the Patriarch had attained the Dharma and received his prediction, he traveled to the country of Mathurā to propagate the teachings.

Suddenly, a cool breeze swept over the assembly, bringing such unprecedented joy and comfort to their bodies and minds that they were unaware of its cause. The Patriarch said, "This is the wind of the Way and its Virtue.
A sage shall soon appear in the world to continue the ancestral lamp. Having spoken, he used his supernatural power to lead the great multitude on a journey through mountains and valleys.
Within the time it takes to eat a meal, they arrived at the foot of a peak. Pointing to it, he said to the assembly, "On the summit of this peak—"
A purple cloud like a canopy appeared, for a sage dwelt therein. He then lingered with the great assembly for a long time.
Seeing a youth holding a round mirror at a mountain cottage, he went straight before the Patriarch. The Patriarch asked, "How old are you? He replied, "One hundred years."
The Patriarch said, "You are still young; why do you speak of a hundred years? The boy replied, "I do not understand principle; I am truly a hundred years old.
The Patriarch asked, "Are you skilled in the pivot [of the Way]? The boy replied, "The Buddha said: 'If a person lives for a hundred years, yet does not understand the pivot of all Buddhas.'"
"It is not as good as being born for a single day and attaining definitive understanding. The Patriarch asked, "What does that which is in your hand represent?
The youth replied, "The great perfect mirror of all Buddhas; inside and out, it is free from flaw or obscuration. Two people see it together; their mind's eye is identical to his.
When the youth’s parents heard these words, they immediately relinquished him to let him leave the household life. The Patriarch took him to his own place and conferred the full precepts upon him.
Having completed his ordination, he was named Gayashata. On another occasion, he heard the sound of wind blowing the temple bells.

His master asked him, "Is it the bells that ring, or is it the wind? He replied, "It is neither the wind nor the bells ringing; it is my own mind that rings. The master said, "And who is it that possesses this mind?
He replied, "Because both are utterly tranquil. The master said, "Excellent, excellent! Who else but you could succeed to my Way? Thereupon, he transmitted [the Dharma] to him.
The Verse of the Dharma-Eye says: "The ground of the mind is fundamentally without birth; the ground arises from conditions. The conditions and the seeds do not obstruct one another;
it is the same with flowers and fruits.
[Image] The Eighteenth Patriarch, Venerable Gayasata, was a native of the country of Mathura. His clan name was Udraka, and his father...
Devadatta’s mother was exceptionally holy; she once dreamed that a great deity held up a mirror, and consequently became pregnant. After seven days, she gave birth;

her body was as translucent as lapis lazuli, and though she never bathed, she remained naturally fragrant and pure. In her youth, she delighted in solitude and quietude, and her speech was unlike that of ordinary children.
While out walking with a mirror in hand, she encountered the Venerable Nandika and received ordination. Later, leading her disciples, she traveled to the Great Yuezhi kingdom.

In the kingdom, [Bodhidharma] saw that a certain Brahmin’s house emitted an extraordinary fragrance. The Patriarch intended to enter the house, but the master of the house, Kumāralata, asked, "What kind of assembly is this?
The Patriarch replied, "We are disciples of the Buddha. Upon hearing the name of the Buddha, Kumāralata’s heart and mind were struck with awe;
he immediately closed his door. After a long while, the Patriarch knocked on the gate. Kumāralata said, "There is no one in this house. The Patriarch replied:
When asked, "Who is there? Rāhula heard the voice and, recognizing it was someone extraordinary, hurriedly opened the door to welcome him.

The Patriarch said, "In the past, the World-Honored One prophesied: 'One thousand years after my parinirvāṇa, a Great Being shall appear in the kingdom of Mo-ti (Mūlasthāna) to propagate and flourish the profound transformation.
Now you have encountered me; you are destined for this auspicious era. Thereupon, Kumārajīva [Rāhula] awakened to his past lives.

Zhì (Jñāna) surrendered himself in faith and left the household life. Having received full ordination, he was given this verse of the transmission of the Dharma: "When there is a seed and the ground of the mind, Through causes and conditions, sprouts can emerge.
If there is no mutual obstruction regarding these conditions, Then what is born will not be born again."
▲ The nineteenth patriarch, Venerable Kumāralata, was the son of a Brahmin from the kingdom of Greater Yuezhi.
Later, he arrived at the kingdom of Central India, where there was a Mahāsattva named Jayata who asked him:

"The parents of my household have long placed their faith in the Triple Gem, yet they have frequently been afflicted by chronic illness; whatever they undertake never turns out as they wish. However, my neighbors..."
For a long time he has practiced the conduct of a *caṇḍāla*, yet his body has always been brave and robust, and his undertakings have been harmonious.
What good fortune is his, and what crime have I committed? His grandfather said: "Why should you doubt this? Furthermore, the retribution for good and evil occurs across three periods of time.

Ordinary people see only that the benevolent die young while the violent live long, or that the rebellious meet with auspiciousness while the righteous suffer misfortune; they then claim that cause and effect do not exist and that sin and merit are empty. Little do they realize..."
Influence follows along with it; there is not even the slightest discrepancy. Even if it passes through hundreds of thousands of myriads of kalpas, it will never be extinguished.
At that time, Śāṇakavāsin, having heard these words, was suddenly relieved of his doubts. The Patriarch said:

"Although you have already gained faith in the three karmas, you have not yet understood that karma arises from delusion, delusion exists based on consciousness, consciousness depends upon non-awakening, and non-awakening depends upon the mind. The mind is fundamentally pure."
It is pure; it is without arising or ceasing, without fabrication, without retribution, and without victory or defeat.
It is profoundly still and luminously aware. If you enter this Dharma-gate, you may be equal to all Buddhas. All that is good or evil, conditioned or unconditioned, is like a dream or an illusion.
Having received these words and grasped their essential meaning, Jayata immediately awakened his latent wisdom and earnestly sought ordination. Once he had been granted [the precepts]...
[The transmission] is complete. The Patriarch said to him, "The time for my entry into parinirvāṇa has now arrived. You shall succeed me in carrying forward the traces of my transformative work.

He then bestowed the verse of the Dharma-eye: "In the fundamental nature, there is originally no birth; It is spoken only in response to those who seek it. Since nothing at all can be attained within the Dharma, Why harbor doubts about what is already resolved?"
▲The twentieth patriarch, Venerable Śāṇakavāsa, was a native of Northern India. His wisdom was profound and vast, and his transformative teachings were immeasurable.
Later, he arrived at the city of Rājagṛha to propagate the sudden teaching (*tun-jiao*). There, the assembly of students valued debate above all else.

The leader among them was named Vasu-bandhu (translated as "Pervasive Practice"). He always ate but one meal a day, never lay down to sleep, and performed prostrations to the Buddha during the six periods of the day.
Pure and free from desire, he was a refuge for the multitude. When the Patriarch was about to convert him, he first asked the assembly:
"This ascetic Vasu-bandhu is able to cultivate the pure conduct; can he attain the Way of the Buddha? The assembly replied: "Our teacher is diligent in his practice; why [should there be any doubt]?"
"No," said the Patriarch. "Your teacher is far removed from the Way. Even if he were to practice asceticism for kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, it would all be the root of falsehood.
The assembly asked, "What virtues and conduct does the Venerable One possess that you should disparage our teacher? The Patriarch replied, "I do not seek the Way, nor am I inverted.
I do not prostrate to the Buddha, nor do I treat him with contempt. I do not sit in meditation, nor am I indolent."
"I am indolent; I do not eat but once a day, nor do I eat mixed foods. I know no contentment, yet I have no greed.
My mind harbors no expectations—this is what is called the Way. When Pūrvavideha heard this, he gave rise to untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) and joyfully praised him.
The Elder then said to the assembly, "Do you understand my words? It is because his resolve for the Way is so earnest that I act in this manner."
"If the strings are too tight, they will snap; therefore, I did not encourage him. I have caused him to abide in a state of peace and happiness and enter the wisdom of all Buddhas.
He then addressed Viśvāmitra, saying, "I have just rebuked and suppressed you before this assembly; are you not troubled in your heart? Viśvāmitra replied:

"I have heard various evil words; they were like the wind or an echo. How much more so now that I have obtained the hearing of the unsurpassed nectar—how could I instead give rise to feverish affliction?
I only pray that, out of great compassion, you will instruct me with the wondrous Way. The Patriarch said: "You have long planted many virtues and shall succeed to my lineage. Listen to my verse:
'In a single word, one accords with non-arising, identical to the nature of the Dharma-realm. If you can thus..."
This is the explanation. Having completed the thorough penetration of phenomena and principles.
▲ The twenty-first patriarch, Vairocana (婆修盤頭), was a native of Rājagṛha. At the age of fifteen, he took ordination under the arhat Prabhāsa.
Moved by his sincerity, the Bodhisattva Vibhākara conferred the precepts upon him. He traveled to propagate the teachings in China.
In the kingdom of Ti (Vṛji), there was a king named Nityavaśavartin. He had two sons: the elder was named Mahāla and the younger was named Maṇḍala.
The king asked his grandfather, "How does the local custom and climate of Rājagṛha differ from this? The grandfather replied, "In that place, three Buddhas have appeared in the world;
now, in your kingdom, O King, there are two masters who provide guidance. The king asked, "Who are these two masters? The grandfather replied, "The Buddha has prophesied [of them]."
In the second five-hundred-year period, there were two great beings of supernatural power who left the household life to succeed the sages.
One was the King’s second son, Maṇḍara; though my virtue is meager, I am also counted as one of them. Formerly, in the kingdom of Nādi, there was a malevolent elephant that caused harm;
from the time Maṇḍara was born until this present moment, thirty years have passed, and yet people still do not know the reason why the elephant ceased its depredations.
[The king] sighed. Just as the King was conversing with Nāga, a messenger suddenly reported that more than ten thousand elephants were pressing against the city walls.

The King was distressed by this, but Nāga said, "If Nāla comes out, the trouble will be resolved. The King then tested him by ordering Nāla to come out; Nāla accordingly went out through the southern gate of the city.
Facing the elephants, he stroked their bellies and let out a great roar; the city shook, and the herd of elephants fell prostrate. In a moment, they all fled and dispersed.

Only then did the people realize that the thirty years of peace had been due to Nāla. The King, filled with great reverence and faith, commanded Nāla to leave the household life according to his grandfather’s tradition.

His grandfather immediately conferred the full ordination upon him and gave him the verse of the transmission of the Dharma, saying: "The bubble and the illusion are equally unimpeded; how can one not..."
He attained realization. He penetrated the Dharma within it; it is neither of this age nor of antiquity.
△ The twenty-second patriarch, Venerable Mañjuśrī (Māṇava), was of the Kṣatriya caste. His father was formerly King Īśvara.

Having received the command of Venerable Paṇḍu, the patriarch subsequently left the household life. After transmitting the Dharma, he arrived in the country of Mo-chi (Mūlasthāna). He [met] Hegalena (Haklenāyana) and...
Baoyin welcomed the Patriarch to the royal palace to offer him sustenance. On another day, Helena asked the Patriarch, "By what karmic conditions have I been moved by this flock of cranes?
The Patriarch replied, "In the fourth kalpa, you were once a bhikṣu who was about to attend a gathering at the Dragon Palace.
Your disciples all wished to follow you, but you observed that among the five hundred followers, not a single one was worthy [to go]."
He was provided with exquisite offerings. At that time, his disciples said, "The Master once preached the Dharma, saying: 'Those who are equal regarding food are also equal regarding the Dharma.

Now, since this is not the case, what sanctity can there be? You then ordered him to attend the assembly; because he sat there and consumed the food indiscriminately, his retribution was rebirth as a bird species.
Because of the karmic affinity between teacher and disciple from former lives, they now follow one another. Helana asked, "By what skillful means can you cause him to understand?"

Tuo said, "I possess the unsurpassed Dharma-treasure, which is the Tathāgatagarbha. In the past, the World-Honored One entrusted it to Mahākāśyapa, and it was passed down through successive generations until it reached me.
I now entrust it to you; if you can transmit it without interruption, even those flocks of cranes shall be aided toward liberation.
Accept my instruction and listen to this verse: 'The mind turns according to the myriad objects; in the place where it turns, it is truly capable of [liberation].'"
"Profound! Following the stream, one recognizes one's nature; there is neither joy nor sorrow. When the flock of cranes heard this verse, they flew away with cries.
The twenty-third patriarch, Venerable Holarana, was a native of the country of Moji. His surname was Brahmin; his father was Qiansheng, and his mother was Jinguang.
Having prayed to the golden pillar of the Seven Buddhas for a son, she dreamed that atop Mount Sumeru there was a divine youth.

Holding a golden ring, he said, "I have come. At his birth, the heavens rained down flowers. At the age of twenty-two, he left the household life and dwelt in a forest for nine years, reciting the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
Moved by his devotion, a flock of cranes followed him. At thirty, he attained the Dharma and traveled to Central India to propagate the teachings.
There was one named Siṃha who took refuge in him and asked, "I wish to seek the Way; how should I apply my mind?"
The Patriarch said, "If you wish to seek the Way, do not apply your mind. He asked, "If there is no application of the mind, who performs the Buddha-work?
The Patriarch said, "If you have any application, it is not merit; if you have no action, that itself is Buddha-work.
As the Sūtra says, "Whatever merit I have performed, I have no sense of 'mine' regarding it. Upon hearing these words, Siṃha immediately entered the wisdom of the Buddha. At that time...
The Patriarch suddenly pointed toward the northeast and asked, "What kind of phenomenon is this? The Master replied, "I see a vapor like a white rainbow piercing through heaven and earth;
furthermore, there are five paths of black vapor stretching across its midst. The Patriarch asked, "What does this omen portend?"
[Daowu] said, "It cannot be known. Nanyue Zuxiu said, "Fifty years after my passing, a calamity shall arise in the kingdom of Northern India;
it will cling to your person. Once I have passed away, I now entrust the Dharma-eye to you. Guard and uphold it well. He then spoke this verse:
"When the nature of mind is recognized, It may be called inconceivable. When clearly understood, there is nothing to be attained."
When he attained [realization], he did not speak of his knowledge.
▲ The twenty-fourth patriarch, the Venerable Siṃhabhadra Bhikṣu, was a native of Central India. His family name was Brahmin.
Having attained the Dharma, he traveled abroad and arrived at the kingdom of Kaśmīra. There was a śramaṇa named Parika who had originally practiced the dhyāna-contemplations of the Hīnayāna. His...

There were five types of practitioners: those who practiced meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), those who possessed knowledge and vision (*jñānadarśana*), those who clung to signs (*nimitta*), those who abandoned signs, and those who remained silent.

The Venerable One, using his unimpeded eloquence (*apratihata-pratibhāna*), refuted them and led them back to the correct path. Once he had gathered the fivefold assembly, his fame spread far and wide.
As he was seeking a Dharma heir, he encountered an elder leading his son and asked the father, "This boy’s name is Sthavira; from the moment he was born..."
He clenched his left hand; he was twenty years old, yet he had never been able to open it. He requested that the Venerable One reveal its karmic cause from a previous life.
The Patriarch beheld him and immediately reached out his hand, saying, "Give me back my pearl. The boy suddenly opened his hand and presented the pearl. The assembly was all struck with wonder.
The Patriarch said, "In a former life, I was a monk named Basha. I once went to a vegetarian feast at the Western Sea."
The Master accepted the gift of pearls and returned them to him, saying, "Now return my pearls; this is but natural. The elder then caused him to leave the household life.
The Patriarch assembled the holy ones and conferred the full precepts upon him. Because of his previous karmic conditions, he was named Vasiṣṭha. The Patriarch then said to him:
My teacher had secretly made a prophetic prediction: that before long you would encounter hardship. The Tathāgata’s treasury of the true Dharma-eye is now to be entrusted to you;

you must protect it so that it may universally moisten all beings until the end of time. The verse says: When the correct teaching of knowledge and vision is given, both knowledge and vision are but the mind.
"When the mind is present, there is knowing and seeing; knowing and seeing are right here and now.

Having spoken this verse, the Patriarch secretly entrusted his saṃghāṭī robe to Suta, instructing him to go to another land to transform beings according to their capacities. Having received these instructions, Suta traveled directly to Southern India. The Patriarch said:
It was impossible to evade this calamity easily; he remained alone in Kaśmīra.

At that time, there were two non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) in his native land, one named Māmuta and the other named Durlabha, who had studied various magical arts and intended to plot a rebellion together, feigning the appearance of Śākya disciples.

He secretly entered the royal palace. King Milinda then proceeded to destroy the teachings of the Śākya. Taking up his sword, he went to where the Patriarch was and asked, "Has the Master attained the emptiness of the aggregates?

The Patriarch replied, "I have already attained the emptiness of the aggregates. The King asked, "Have you transcended birth and death? The Patriarch replied, "I have already transcended birth and death.
The King said, "Since you have transcended birth and death, you may give me your head. The Patriarch replied, "The body is not the self."
[The King replied: "There is. Why be afraid for one's head? The King immediately brandished his blade and severed the Venerable’s head;

white milk surged upward several feet high, and the King’s right arm also fell to the ground, where he died seven days later. Prince Prabhāśiras sighed, "Why did my father bring this calamity upon himself?
He then led the assembly in repentance. At that time, there was a rishi on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa who deeply understood the law of cause and effect.
It is said that Siṃha and Rāhula were both laymen in a former life; because Siṃha harbored jealousy toward Rāhula’s excellence in the Dharma, he secretly murdered him.
Now, the karmic retribution has come to fruition. The assembly subsequently constructed a stūpa at the site of this ancestral retribution.
▲ The twenty-fifth patriarch, Vasiṣṭha (Póshè斯多), was a native of Jibin (Kashmir). His clan was Brahmin; his father was named Jixing (Śānticaryā) and his mother Chang'anle (Nityasukhā).

Initially, his mother dreamed of obtaining a divine sword and subsequently became pregnant. Upon his birth, he held his left hand in a fist. He encountered the Venerable Siṃha (Shizi), who transmitted the Dharma to him.
Afterward, he traveled to Central India, where King Kaniṣka (Jiasheng) offered him ritual greetings and provisions. There was...
The non-Buddhist teacher, who held the doctrine of no-self, had previously been honored and respected by the king. He now came before the king to debate for the sake of victory.
The Patriarch, maintaining his own dignity, said to him, "I understand silent debate; it does not require verbal expression. The other asked, "Who will know who wins or loses?

The Patriarch replied, "We do not contend over victory or defeat; we seek only the truth of the meaning. The other asked, "What do you take to be the meaning? The Patriarch replied, "A mindless state."
[The monk] asked, "What is the meaning? The Patriarch said, "Since you have no mind, how can there be a meaning? The monk replied, "I speak of 'no-mind'; it should be called a non-meaning.
The Patriarch said, "You speak of 'no-mind,' which should be called a non-meaning; I speak of 'non-mind,' which is the true meaning and not a mere name."
The other said, "The meaning is not the name; who can discern the meaning? The Patriarch said, "Your name is not the meaning; what name is this name?
The other said, "It is called 'the nameless' for the purpose of discerning that which is not the meaning. The Patriarch said, "Since the name is not a name, the meaning is likewise not a meaning."
The "Discerning One" is his name. What, then, is it that he should discern? Thus, after fifty-nine rounds of debate back and forth, the non-Buddhists were silenced and submitted in faith.
At that moment, the Patriarch suddenly turned north, joined his palms, and sighed deeply, saying, "Today I have encountered my master, the Venerable Siṃha."
"How difficult! This is truly lamentable. He then took his leave of the king and traveled south. Upon reaching Southern India, he lived in seclusion within the mountain valleys.
King Devaśrī (Tian-de) welcomed him and offered him sustenance. The king’s second son, Ratnamitra (Ru-mi-duo), subsequently requested to leave the household life.

The Patriarch asked him, "If you wish to leave the household life, for what purpose do you do so? Ratnamitra replied, "If I leave the household life, I shall not pursue that purpose. The Patriarch said, "Not..."
"For what purpose? Maitreya replied, "Not for worldly affairs. The Patriarch asked, "Then for what purpose? Maitreya replied, "It shall be for the sake of Buddha-affairs.
The Patriarch said, "The Prince’s wisdom is as sublime as heaven; surely it is the descent of various sages. You must ordain him and let him leave the household life."
He attended his Master for six years. Later, he received full ordination (*upasampadā*) within the royal palace; at the moment of the *karmavācanā*, the earth shook violently.

Thereupon, the Master bestowed upon him the verse of the transmission of the Dharma: "The Sage speaks of knowledge and vision; Within the objective realm, there is neither right nor wrong. I have now realized true nature: There is neither the Path, nor is there principle."
▲ The twenty-sixth patriarch, Venerable Rāhulamitra, was of the Kṣatriya caste and a prince of South India.
After attaining the Dharma, he traveled to East India. Its king, Drḍha, followed the non-Buddhist teacher Dīrghanakha the Brāhmaṇa.

When the Patriarch arrived, the king asked, "For what purpose have you come, Master? He replied, "To deliver sentient beings. The king asked, "By what Dharma do you deliver them? He replied, "Each..."
Inferring by analogy with this, the Brahmin immediately manifested a great mountain atop the Patriarch’s head, its force pressing down as it descended.

The Patriarch pointed at it, and the mountain suddenly shifted onto the heads of the assembly. He then pressed his hand against the ground; the earth shook, and the five hundred non-Buddhists were all unable to remain standing.

The Brahmin was struck with fear and prostrated himself in repentance. The Patriarch again pressed his hand against the ground, and the earth became still. He pointed at the mountain, and the mountain [vanished].

[The place] was destroyed. On another day, the King prepared a great vegetarian feast and assembled various non-Buddhist practitioners (tīrthikas). He earnestly invited the Patriarch to attend the gathering.
Initially, the Patriarch was unwilling to go, but he knew that the site of the assembly was about to collapse; thus, he went. The King said, "Master, you consented to come?

The Patriarch replied, "I have not come for the sake of receiving offerings; I have come to save [the people] from death. This ground has already become a dragon's lair; it will collapse in a moment. The King was terrified and [acted] accordingly.
The assembly was like a high plateau; when they looked back at that place, it had already become a deep, secluded pool. The King’s reverence and faith increased further.
The Patriarch expounded the Dharma for him and said, "In this kingdom there shall be a sage who will succeed to my Dharma.
