Previously, in East India, there was the son of a Brahmin, twenty years of age, who had lost both parents in his youth and whose name and lineage were unknown. He sometimes called himself "Hāra" (Necklace), and so people subsequently named him Hāla.
He was called the Youth *Ratnavyuha*. While begging from door to door in the village lanes, someone asked him, "Why do you walk so hurriedly?
He immediately replied, "Why do you walk so slowly? When asked what his surname was, he said, "It is the same as yours. No one could fathom this.

One day, the King and the Patriarch were traveling together in a carriage. *Ratnavyuha* prostrated himself before them. The Patriarch asked, "Do you remember past events? *Ratnavyuha* replied, "I remember."
"In a past kalpa, we lived together as teacher and disciple. You expounded the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, while I expounded the profound *Sūtras*.
Today’s events are surely in accord with our past causes. The Patriarch looked at the King and said, "This is the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
Two others will appear hereafter: one shall transform South India, and one shall have his karmic affinity in China. After nine years, he shall return here."
Because of these past causes, he was named Prajñātara. The verse for the entrustment of the Dharma says:
"The treasury of the true nature of the mind has neither beginning nor end; responding to conditions to transform sentient beings, it is expediently called 'wisdom'."
▲ The twenty-seventh patriarch, Venerable Prajñātāra, was a native of East India.
After attaining the Dharma, he traveled to South India, where the king, named Gandhāra, honored and made offerings to him with the utmost reverence.
Prajñātāra’s realization surpassed that of his peers, and the king further bestowed upon him a priceless jewel. At that time, the king had three sons: Candravarman, Guṇavarman, and Bodhi.
Rāma was the youngest of the bodhisattvas. His grandfather, wishing to test what they had attained, took the pearl he had bestowed and asked the three princes:
"This pearl is perfectly round and luminous; is there anything that can equal it? Candracchāya and Guṇaprabha both replied, "This pearl is the most honored among the seven treasures;
certainly nothing surpasses it. Bodhi, however, said, "This is but a worldly treasure; it is not sufficient to be considered supreme. Among all treasures..."
Among these, the Jewel of the Dharma is supreme; yet this is but the light of the world and is not sufficient to be supreme. Among all lights, the light of wisdom is supreme;
yet this is but the illumination of the world and is not sufficient to be supreme. Among all illuminations, the illumination of the mind is supreme.
This radiance of the jewel cannot illuminate itself; it must rely upon the light of wisdom to discern it. Once it has been discerned by this, one then knows it to be such.
A jewel: once one knows it is a jewel, one then clarifies its value as a treasure. If one clarifies its value as a treasure, the treasure is not a treasure in itself;
if one discerns the jewel, the jewel is not a jewel in itself. That a jewel is not a jewel in itself means that it must rely upon the "jewel of wisdom" to discern the worldly jewel.
That a treasure is not a treasure in itself means that it must rely upon the "treasure of wisdom" to clarify the Dharma-treasure. Thus, when the teacher possesses the Way, his treasure is [revealed].
[The Master] manifested [himself]. "Sentient beings possess the Way; the jewel of the mind is likewise so. The Patriarch praised his discernment and wisdom, and then asked again:
"Among all things, what thing is without characteristics? He replied: "Among all things, that which does not arise is without characteristics.
He asked again: "Among all things, what thing is the highest? He replied: "Among all things, the self is the highest. He asked again: "Among all things..."

"What is the greatest? He replied, "Among all things, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is the greatest. The Patriarch knew he was a vessel for the Dharma, but as the time had not yet arrived, he remained silent and mingled with him.
When the incense reached King Yan, the entire assembly wailed and fainted. Bodhidhara alone entered meditative absorption before the coffin and emerged after seven days.
He then followed his grandfather to seek ordination. Once he had received full ordination, his grandfather told him:
"The Tathāgata entrusted the Eye of the True Dharma to Mahākāśyapa; in this manner it was passed down successively until it reached me. I now entrust it to you. Listen."

My verse says: "The mind-ground gives birth to all seeds; through conditions, the principle is further produced. When the fruit is full, Bodhi is perfected; when the flower blooms, the world arises. Jiuzhou replied:
"The various patriarchs of the Western Heaven were divinely enlightened from birth; they were all Mahāsattvas of the Dharma-body who manifested in the world to succeed to the lineage."
At that time, those who were transformed by his teaching numbered in the millions; yet, at the moment of transmission, it always came down to but a single person.

Although it is a fine thing to cite the praises of Master Tanji regarding the various patriarchs as *dharmakāya* mahāsattvas, it actually causes all people to give rise to thoughts of inferiority, leading them to fail to believe in the equal and true *dharmadhātu*, wherein there is neither Buddha nor sentient being.

Thus was the imperial decree. Therefore, the World-Honored One, having attained self-awakening, exclaimed: "How wondrous! To universally observe all sentient beings, they all possess the wisdom, virtue, and marks of the Tathāgata.
How could they ever be like a stagnant pond? It is said that the Eye-Treasury of the True Dharma is not easily penetrated, and the Precious Seal of the Buddhas and Patriarchs is not easily joined.
To single out one person as representative of all people is just as when the World-Honored One first [attained enlightenment].
At his birth, he pointed one hand toward heaven and the other toward earth, walked seven steps, and looked in the four directions, saying:
"In the heavens above and on the earth below, I alone am the most honored. Is this not a direct pointing to the original nature—the self that is uniquely honored by every person?
Later, at the Mahāprajāpatī’s Stūpa, he commanded Mahākāśyapa to share his seat and sit with him, [presenting him] with the *saṃghāṭī* robe...
Lei surrounded him and spoke a verse, saying: "The Dharma is fundamentally no-Dharma; no-Dharma is also Dharma.
Now, at the moment of bestowing no-Dharma, how has any dharma ever been a dharma? Is this not the fundamental Dharma that is neither above nor below heaven, wherein "I alone am honored"?
To save the Middle Way, the Sixth Patriarch entered the chamber of Huangmei, and likewise surrounded himself with his *kāṣāya*.
Therefore, Han Yue said: "The every thread of the *kāṣāya* clearly reveals the numerical categories of the Dharma; it is not a mere trifle. Furthermore, I ask you all:
Why did Ānanda ask Kāśyapa, "Aside from the transmission of the golden robe by the World-Honored One, what else was transmitted?"
Then Kāśyapa called out to Ānanda, who responded with an assent. Kāśyapa said, "Topple the banner-pole in front of the gate. What was the intent of this?
Thus, it is clear that those who take the *kāṣāya* as the transmission of the Dharma are merely chasing after clods of earth.
Kāśyapa spoke in verse: "The Dharma of each and every phenomenon is the primordial Dharma; There is no dharma, nor is there any non-dharma. Why, within a single phenomenon, Should there be a dharma?"
There is a non-dharma. Is this not the truth in every place? In every dust mote is the person of original nature;
therefore, is it not the case that one relies solely upon the person of original nature as the dharma of original nature? The verse by Ānanda says: "The dharma originally entrusted exists;

once entrusted, it is said to be non-existent. Each must awaken for themselves; having awakened, there is neither existence nor non-existence. Furthermore, this is not because my staff does not strike.
The single blow of the staff is used to point directly so that each person may awaken for themselves. Apart from self-awakening, there is not a single dharma to be given to others.
The third patriarch, Śaṇakavāsin, spoke this verse of the transmission of the Dharma: "Neither dharma nor mind; No mind and no dharma.
When speaking of this 'mind-dharma,' This dharma is not a mind-dharma. Since it is said that "this dharma is not a mind-dharma," [how can anything be transmitted?]
When has Han Yue ever separately explained a "mind-dharma" as being vast? The Fourth Patriarch Upagupta, explaining for the Fifth Patriarch Diptaka, said:
"The jewel mountain is my own body; the gushing spring is the inexhaustibility of the Dharma.
Is this not a clear statement that there is no dharma outside the body? Having heard this, the Fifth Patriarch composed a verse:
The towering mountain of the seven treasures constantly wells forth the spring of wisdom. Furthermore, how could wisdom arise separately from outside the body?

If one takes this very body as the dwelling, then the sun emerges from that dwelling to illuminate heaven and earth—is this not the World-Honored One himself, who is "the one honored alone above and below heaven"? Thus, the intent of the *Dharmapada-gāthā* is naturally [contained herein].

The primordial mind: the original mind is not a dharma; if there were dharmas, there would be an original mind. That which is neither mind nor original dharma—how could its essential meaning be different?
Furthermore, as the Fifth Patriarch said when entrusting [the Dharma] to Mīchaka: "Thoroughly penetrate the mind of the original dharma;
there is no dharma and no non-dharma. Awakening is the same as non-awakening; without mind, there is also no dharma. This is based on awakening.
Being equally unawakened, what else could this refer to but the person of original nature? Thus it is said: "There is no mind and there is no dharma.
Furthermore, how could there be a mind or dharma that is vast and great apart from the person of original nature? The Sixth Patriarch’s verse for bestowing upon Bāsumati says:
"There is no mind that can be attained; even to speak of it is not called a dharma. If one realizes that the mind is no-mind, only then does one understand the mind."

Regarding the mental factors (*citta-dharma*): if one realizes that the mind is not the mind, how could it be anything other than the person who is the original source? Therefore, it is said: "Only then does one understand the mind and its mental factors.

Furthermore, it is not that every single object (*dharmadhātu*) is entirely the person who is the original source; is this what constitutes the fundamental mental factor? The verse of the Dharma-transmission from the Seventh Patriarch says:
"The mind is identical to the realm of empty space; It manifests dharmas equal to empty space. When the realization of empty space is attained, There is no..."
This is neither dharma nor non-dharma. Is it not the case that the body contains the ten directions and the inexhaustible void?
Could there be any room for this dharma or non-dharma within it? The Eighth Patriarch, Buddhanandi, said: "The void has no interior or exterior; the nature of mind is likewise so.
If one realizes the void, one penetrates the principle of True Suchness (Tathatā). Furthermore, this is not what is called the 'True Buddha'."
Is the Dharmakāya indeed like empty space? The Ninth Patriarch, Puṇyamitra, entrusted it to the Venerable Pārśva, saying:
"Ultimate Truth is originally nameless; one should apply names to manifest that Truth. Having received this true Dharma, it is neither true nor false.
Is this not what the layman Vimalakīrti meant when he said, 'Contemplate the true mark of the body, and contemplate the Buddha in the same way'?"
The verse of entrustment by the Tenth Patriarch says: "The true essence is naturally true; because it is true, there is reason for its explanation.
Having realized the dharma of true truth, there is neither practice nor cessation. Furthermore, this is not what is meant by the Tathāgata coming or going, sitting or lying down.
Is this person one who does not understand the meaning of what I have taught? Thus spoke the Eleventh Patriarch, Pūrṇayaśas.

The verse says: Delusion and enlightenment are like concealment and manifestation; light and darkness are not separate from one another. Now I entrust this dharma of concealment and manifestation, which is neither one nor two.
Is it not the case that delusion and enlightenment belong to but a single person? The Twelfth Patriarch, Aśvaghoṣa, entrusted [the dharma] to Kāpimāla with this verse:
Concealment and manifestation are the fundamental dharma; Light and darkness have always been non-dual. Now I entrust this realization.
The Dharma is neither grasped nor rejected; furthermore, it is not something realized that remains identical to the state of being unawakened.
The Thirteenth Patriarch entrusted it to Nāgārjuna, saying: "This Dharma is neither hidden nor manifest; this is called the True Reality (bhūtakoṭi).

To awaken to this Dharma of concealment and manifestation is neither folly nor wisdom. Since he pointed out that the time of delusion is concealment and the time of awakening is manifestation, concealment and manifestation are merely—
As for this one person, what wisdom or folly could there possibly be? The fourteenth patriarch’s verse says:
"To clarify the principle of concealment and manifestation, I shall now explain the logic of liberation. Regarding the Dharma, the mind does not realize it; there is neither anger nor joy.

Since both delusion and awakening are nothing other than the fundamental Dharma, one is liberated right where one is. Why rely on realization to falsely distinguish between anger and joy? Now, Han Yue—
He manifested his sovereign body to others like the full moon disk to certify the "One-Ten" (the ten patriarchs), serving as the progenitor of the thousand and ten-thousand Buddhas.
Why, then, did he himself recite the verses on the transmission of the Dharma (*dharmaparyāya-gāthā*) exactly as described above, yet fail to mention the mark of the full moon disk?
To rescue the Middle Way, one who possesses intelligence and sagely wisdom is not hindered from being a sage or a worthy; however, I have never heard of such a thing [as a lack of this mark].
The old farmer who brought Your Majesty to the heights of Yao and Shun—does the old monk not himself occupy the very role of Shun plowing Mount Li?
Furthermore, the Buddhas and World-Honored Ones appear in this world solely for the sake of the one great cause and condition.
As Nāgārjuna said: "It is to clarify the principle of concealment and manifestation that the truth of liberation is taught. All sentient beings...

Beings are deluded by themselves, concealed by themselves, and not liberated by themselves. Only through the opening and revealing instruction of the Buddhas do they begin to awaken and manifest themselves.
Yet, from the very beginning, the Buddhas have never added any separate dharma to the portion of the sentient beings.
This is precisely what Kambala meant when he said, "Neither foolish nor wise. How can one allow the two characters for "cleverness" to act as a thief?
To falsely accuse the World-Honored One and yet claim he is the "Omniscient One" (Sarvajña);

and further to say that the patriarchs of India preached the Dharma like surging clouds or bursting rivers, such that masters like Aśvaghoṣa, Mātṛceṭa, and Nāgārjuna each authored over a hundred fascicles of treatises—how could these be dismissed as merely "collateral branches" on account of their intelligence? This is precisely what [the critics] have failed to understand.
Though possessing the potential for intelligence, he lacks the substance of realization; he is merely one who pleads his own case and makes his own confession.

Furthermore, regarding the Dharma taught by Han Yue, he takes "One Zero" (0) as the progenitor of the thousand and ten thousand Buddhas, yet Tan Ji extols it as unfathomable, placing him on equal footing with Aśvaghoṣa and Nāgārjuna.
How does this differ from a beggar claiming to be an emperor? It is nothing more than that.

Take for example Aśvaghoṣa, Nāgārjuna, and others, each of whom authored over a hundred fascicles of treatises; when did they ever claim that the "one" (一) was the progenitor of a thousand or ten thousand Buddhas?
Furthermore, how could they have employed such various strange names and anomalous signs as "the four dharmas intersecting," "the double-headed," or "the single-knot"?
To now falsely accuse Aśvaghoṣa and Nāgārjuna with the two characters "cleverness" (聰明) is already to lose the "one."
"A single eye. Now, is your cleverness not what Yongjia called "the cleverness of external paths, which lacks true wisdom"?
Furthermore, to say that I, the old monk, am like yourself on the basis of our shared "top-of-the-head" perspective is also a false accusation against me.
Why? Because when I look upon all the people in the great earth, how have I ever seen even one person who is not like themselves?
"Indeed! Dingmu’s *A Single Article on Proclaiming the True Dharma* is a work that has been excessively contrived," the old monk said.
This was by way of admonition and exhortation, so that [Dingmu] would not tread the path of Han Yue’s past errors.

It is precisely because you were fortunate enough to have been under the forge of the former master that you have reached this day; thus, the old monk speaks of what was right before and what is wrong after, yet it is not [a matter of personal bias].
As for the person named Dingmu, he was not Han Yue. If one’s Dharma-eye were not fixed, one would follow Han Yue into delusion;
how then could one correctly affirm what is right and negate what is wrong? Furthermore, as the verse of the Dharma-transmission from the Fifteenth Patriarch, Kanadeva, says:
"I have addressed the person who transmits the Dharma, explaining the principle of liberation; yet regarding the Dharma, there is truly nothing realized."
There is neither end nor beginning. Is this not because the person themselves is taken as the fundamental dharma? Since there is originally no beginning or end, how could there be any "realization"?
This is precisely what is called being a transmitter of the Dharma. The sixteenth patriarch, Rāhulata, spoke in verse:
In the reality of dharmas, there is truly nothing to be realized; one neither grasps nor abandons them. Dharmas possess neither the mark of existence nor non-existence;
how, then, could they arise internally or externally? Is this not precisely what Pang Gong meant when he said: "At every turn there is neither grasping nor abandoning;

at every place there is no 'Zhang Guai' (the errant one). It is only I who am naturally in harmony"? To save the Middle Way is like the golden man who emerges from the well; it is like the principle of the saw that cuts through wood.

The patriarchs’ methods of examination were mostly like this. Later generations fail to discern their words and instead defile the patriarchs with superficial views such as "the original face" or "the host.
When I asked Tanji, "To what is the 'original face' of the patriarchs and yourselves similar? Furthermore, what else [is there]?"
How could such a thing be defiled? It is just as when Aśvaghoṣa asked the eleventh patriarch, “What is the meaning of ‘wood’?
The patriarch replied, “You have been understood by me. He pointed directly at Aśvaghoṣa alone; thus, Aśvaghoṣa attained sudden enlightenment.
I have often said that there are those who clarify the direct pointing through words and phrases—this is precisely of that kind.
Yet Tanji conversely claims that what is realized can be sought through the understanding of the "host" (zhǔgōng).
He even cites an ancient master who said, "Knowing this kind of matter, cast it aside. Tanji is then asked:
toward which side would you cast the original face, the host? Furthermore, what do you point to as yourself? And yet—
"Apply some effort! How much of your original face do you have? How much of the true master? How much of your own self?
[The student] says, "I cast it aside. [The Master] says, "You cling to it. Since there is still grasping and rejecting existing within your breast, how can this be your future face?
Having abandoned the original face, what else do you point to as body, speech, and mind?
"Is it pure? The old monk replies, "I take only the original face as the host. Then, throughout the entire world, there is no second person.

Why wait until one has climbed to the mountain peak or reached the bottom of the sea to know the vastness of the universe and the depth of the blue ocean, only then to take a single step that overturns the four great oceans and a single blow that knocks them over?"
"Is it Mount Sumeru? This old monk does not employ my staff as a staff; I use it to provide for myself and to exhaust you to the point of utter weariness.
What more is there left to scatter? Is there any idle talk that can reach the house or be recognized by people?
Furthermore, there is the verse of the seventeenth patriarch, Saṃghanandin: "The ground of the mind is originally without birth; because of the ground, [it] follows..."
Regarding dependent origination: the conditions and seeds do not obstruct one another, and the same applies to flowers and fruits.

Since it is said that the "mind-ground" is fundamentally non-arising, is this not precisely based on the fundamental state as being non-arising? Yet, Tanji claims that the image of a child holding a mirror while wandering out was used to symbolize the perfect wisdom of all Buddhas;
that this traditional illustration has been shown from of old and cannot be denied. Thus, according to the path of the child...
The Buddha is a great, perfect mirror, without flaw or obscuration within or without. If two people could both see it, their eyes and minds would be identical;
thus, everyone would be able to see one another. Why wait until holding a perfect mirror before seeing each other?

The ancients feared that those who chase after mere fragments in the future would fall into error by fixating on the very act of holding the mirror. Therefore, they said: "Bring me the broken mirror! and gave it to them.
"You have seen me, indeed. In years past, I once raised the ancient saying, 'The bright moon hangs in the sky,' and asked Han Yue, 'Just as when the moon has fallen, how do you see one another?
Han Yue then immediately left the Dharma hall, and I likewise descended from my seat;
for this reason, I transmitted to him the lineage whisk. I truly rejoiced in his solitary liberation and lack of dependence."
This refers to when Qianfeng raised the dialogue: "If you raise one, you must not raise two. [Zhaozhou] took up his staff and departed;

he was unable to reach ultimate liberation in solitude, and thus it is said he could only be considered a "side-branch. If you do not believe this, try examining the Dharma-transmission verses of the seventeenth patriarch:
which single phrase or single character accords with Perfect Mirror and Perfect Wisdom? It is exactly like a dragon.
The transmission of the Dharma through the trees has never taken the full moon disc as the signless samādhi;

yet Han Yue arbitrarily established the single circle (一○) as the progenitor of the thousand Buddhas and ten thousand Buddhas. Who would believe that this is not a contradiction? Furthermore, it was clearly stated: [text omitted].
Both persons see it together; their eyes and minds are identical. How can you say that at the time when the "dark and yellow" [the world] has not yet manifested, one cannot see by means of seeing?
Yongjia said: "The great trichiliocosm is a bubble in the sea; all sages and worthies are like a flash of lightning.
Why do you not look at the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, which says: "The body contains the infinite space of the ten directions"?
Furthermore, how could there be a separate great trichiliocosm outside of the body?

Moreover, since you refer to "all sages and worthies," is this not a contradiction of your own words, as it implies that no distinction is established between the holy and the ordinary? Furthermore, he cites the *Prajñāpāramitā*:
"All Buddhas, as well as the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* dharma of all Buddhas, all arise from this."
The sutra states: "An old monk asked Tanji, 'Does the Buddha come first, or does the sutra come first?
If the sutra comes first, then you may indeed say that all Buddhas and all Buddha-dharmas emerge from this sutra. Furthermore, the sutra says:

The Patriarch said: "If you are now unchanging, how can you be called the true mark? That which has already changed and passed away is likewise so [in its nature]. He replied: "Unchanging must exist;

"True. "Among existence and non-existence, what is called the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa)? Śālavatī, whose mind knew the holy master, understood intuitively and penetrated deeply;

The *Liji* says: "Today marks the completion of the Path at Mount Ao. Therefore, while residing there, he gave this instruction:
"The entire earth is this gate of liberation; though one pulls it by the hand, one cannot enter. At that time, a monk came forward and said, "I do not dare to blame the Master.
Another monk said, "What is the use of entering? Feng then struck him, saying, "Do you all dare say 'Snow'?"
Is Feng a madman for striking? Again he said: "The entire earth is the single eye of the śramaṇa;
where, then, do you all void your excrement? He also said: "The entire earth is the whole body of the śramaṇa;
do you all dare to say that this is the drool of a wild fox? If so, then as for Han Yue’s own [understanding]—
Externally, there are four distinct methods that intersect, forming double-headed and single-knotted patterns.

To take "One" as the progenitor of the thousand Buddhas and ten thousand Buddhas, and to hold such categories as the Three Mysteries and Three Essentials as one's fundamental principle—this is precisely to grasp with a mind that seeks attainment and to cling to dharmas that are attained, falsely claiming not to be hungry. One is far removed from the satiation of Xuefeng. [This is] a rescue.
The *Zhong* (Record) further states: "He performed three prostrations and stood in his place. At that time, [Huike] was among the four people present.
The recorder claimed that the First Patriarch specifically looked toward Huike to transmit the Dharma-eye, intending to signify that he had obtained the marrow;

it was not that there was any deeper significance in the character "looked" (*gu*). The author of the *Bishu* (Exposition of the Book) followed this by taking the two characters "silently looked" (*mo gu*) and interpreting them as such.

[The author of the] Commentary and Notes [replies]: "On the contrary, you laugh at the Three Peaks for having intellectual understanding," and so forth. This is still a slander against this old monk from the previous chapter;
it serves as a footnote to show that you share the same intent as those who cling to intellectual understanding. Now, let me ask Tanji:

if there were no profound meaning in the word "regard" (顧), why did the four men standing together all receive the transmission of the Dharma-eye? Please look at what the Patriarch said regarding the transmission of the Dharma: "You..."

One should propagate [the truth] and not disparage those who have not yet awakened; with a single thought, one may turn the faculty [of the mind] and immediately become identical to what was originally attained.

Yet now, Han Yue does not rely on the principle that everyone has this original attainment to instruct all people, but instead falsely fabricates a "one-circle" (○) as the ancestor of the thousand Buddhas and ten thousand Buddhas, and further drills out various strange names such as the "four dharmas interlaced," the "double-headed single-knot," and so forth.

Because their characteristics are different, this old monk does not decline to act as a follower of the school of intellectual understanding (*jiejie*), merely to correct the false knowledge and false interpretations of Han Yue. How could he not know that he is acting out of intellectual understanding?
Using a halberd to stop a halberd, using a wedge to extract a wedge—this old monk acts thus for you with such earnest, grandmotherly concern. Do you all understand?
▲The Second Patriarch, Great Master Huike, was a native of Wulao and the son of Lady Ji.

His father, Ji, having long prayed for offspring without success, one night beheld a miraculous light illuminating his chamber. Consequently, his mother conceived, and thus he was named Guang (Light) upon his birth.

In his youth, he was transcendent. He read extensively through all the recorded classics and was particularly skilled at discussing the teachings of Laozi and Zhuangzi. Later, upon encountering the Buddha-vehicle, he ultimately abandoned them all.

He went forth as a monk under the Chan Master Baojing and studied the doctrines of both the Mahayana and Hinayana. At the age of thirty-three, he returned to Mount Xiangshan, where he sat in quiet meditation all day long.
After another eight years, while in a state of profound stillness, he suddenly beheld a divine being who said to him: "You shall..."

"I wish to receive the fruit; you should go south. The next day, he woke up with a headache as piercing as needles. As he was about to treat it, he suddenly heard a voice from the air saying, "This is a transformation of the bones.
He went to see Jing and told him what had happened. Jing examined him and saw that his cranial bone (*mūrdhāsthi*) was towering and prominent.
Because five peaks rose majestically from it, and because of its divine wonders, it was renamed Shenguang (Divine Light). He spoke privately to his Master, saying, "Your marks are auspicious;
yet the spirits have directed you to the south. There, at Shaolin, dwells the Great Being Bodhidharma; he will surely be your teacher. The Master then proceeded to Shaoshi.
When he had received the Dharma and reached the Northern Qi dynasty, in the second year of the Tianping era, there was a layman over forty years of age.

10. Without disclosing his name or lineage, he came to pay his respects and asked the Patriarch, "I, your disciple, am afflicted by a wind-ailment; I pray that you, O Upādhyāya, will perform a repentance for my transgressions.
The Patriarch said, "Bring forth your transgression, and I shall repent it for you. After a long silence, the layman said, "I have searched for my transgression, but it is utterly unattainable.
The Patriarch said, "I have finished repenting for your transgressions. You should dwell in accordance with the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha. The layman said, "Now I see the Upādhyāya..."
"Furthermore, I already know what the Sangha is, but I do not yet understand what is called the Buddha-dharma. The Patriarch said, "This mind is the Buddha;

this mind is the Dharma. Dharma and Buddha are non-dual; the Jewel of the Sangha is likewise so. The scholar said, "Only today have I come to know that the nature of transgression does not reside within."
"It is not in the external, nor is it in the interval between. As his mind is thus, so too are the Buddha-dharma and I without duality.
The Patriarch held him in high esteem and immediately shaved his head, saying, "He is my treasure; he should be named Sengcan. This was on the eighteenth day of the third month of that year.

He received full ordination at Guangfu Temple. From that time on, his illness gradually improved. He attended the Master for two years, after which the Master finally entrusted him with his legacy, conferring upon him the robe and the Dharma.
He spoke in verse: "The ground of conditions exists from the beginning; From this ground, flowers grow from seeds. Originally there were no seeds;
Thus, flowers have never been born. He further said: "Having received my teaching, you should dwell in the deep mountains; you must not yet go forth to propagate the Dharma."
When there shall be national calamity, that which Prajñātāra predicted in his prophetic declaration—"Though auspicious within the heart, it shall be ominous without"—is precisely this.
I too have karmic debts from past lives; I shall now go to repay them. You must carefully contemplate the holy prophecy and avoid falling into the hardships of the world.
Having perfected his departure and his conduct, he waited for the opportune time to transmit the Dharma.

The Patriarch then traveled to the capital of Ye to guide and transform the fourfold assembly; they took refuge in him for thirty-four years, after which he concealed his brilliance and blended into the common crowd.
Regarding the manner of his transformative conduct: he would enter wine shops, pass through butcher stalls, practice street talk, or follow after common laborers.
If someone were to ask him, "Master, you are a man of the Way; why do you act like this? the Patriarch would say, "I am merely disciplining my own mind; what concern is it of yours?"
▲The Third Patriarch, the Great Being Sengcan, was a man of unknown origin. As a layman, he visited the Second Patriarch, whereupon he received ordination and the transmission of the Dharma.
Later, he lived in seclusion on Mount Wangong in Shu and frequented Mount Sikong in Taichou County.
During the persecution of the Dharma under the Northern Zhou dynasty, the Patriarch deeply concealed his identity and had no fixed dwelling for more than ten years; no one was able to recognize him.
In the twelfth year of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, there was a novice monk named Daoxin, fourteen years of age, who came to pay his respects to the Patriarch, saying:
"I pray that the Master will show compassion and grant me the Dharma-gate of liberation. The Patriarch asked: "Who has bound you? He replied:
"No one has bound me. The Patriarch said: "Why then do you seek liberation? At these words, Daoxin attained great enlightenment. He served the Patriarch with diligence for nine years. Afterwards...
He received the precepts in Jizhou and served his master with exceptional diligence. Nanyue repeatedly tested him with profound and subtle mysteries;

knowing that his karmic conditions were ripe, he entrusted him with the robe and the dharma verse, saying: "Though the seed of a flower depends on the earth, it is from the earth that the flower grows from the seed. Yet, if no one sows the seed,"
When the ground of flowers is exhausted, there is no birth.
The Third Patriarch’s *Inscription on Faith* contains nearly a thousand words; its essentials state: "The Ultimate Way is not difficult;
it only dislikes discrimination. Simply do not harbor hatred or attachment, and you will be transparently clear. A difference of even a hair's breadth, and heaven and earth..."
They are vastly separated. If you wish for them to manifest before you, do not harbor thoughts of compliance or resistance.

You must understand that the thousand wonders and hundred oddities of Linji and Deshan did nothing more than drive students to exhaust their intellects; this accords perfectly with these few words. Those who study the scholastic doctrines explain it thus:
"The Ultimate Way is fundamentally neither difficult nor easy; simply not making discriminations is it. It is, for example, like...

In painting a dragon, the head, horns, fangs, and eyes are all rendered with exact likeness; yet it cannot bring down rain. Thus, a difference of a mere hair’s breadth results in a world as vast as heaven and earth.
Without the fundamental principle (zongzhi), how could one distinguish between them? Based on Tanji’s judgment, this is how it must be understood.
This is the height of perversion; the offense committed against the former sages is no small matter. This old monk relies solely on Linji’s own words:
he rejected the teachings of the Tripiṭaka and reviled all the "little children," seeking people amidst both the adverse and the favorable.

Is this not because when the person of original nature manifests before one, one perceives neither the favorable nor the adverse, but sees everything as simply people? Therefore, it is said: "Seeking among the adverse..."
In examining this according to the *Zhongfeng lu*, Tanji conversely claims that Linji’s myriad wonders and eccentricities do nothing more than drive students to exhaust their intellects and minds;

how could this be anything other than a state of delusion? Furthermore, how could he know that when the person's own face is manifest before them, there is no functioning of intellect or mind? And when there is no functioning of intellect or mind, then—
This constitutes the Ultimate Way. Why is this so? Because from the very beginning, the Ultimate Way has never possessed mind or intellect;
it is simply the One Person alone. When there is difficulty and ease, there are two. Once there are two, there is discrimination. Once there is discrimination, there is attachment and aversion.
With discrimination, attachment, and aversion, there arises a difference as slight as a hair’s breadth, yet vast as the distance between heaven and earth—indeed, one's true face no longer appears.
First: All favorable and adverse objects are struck down as two stakes; from this, a thousand wonders and a hundred marvels arise.
One is thus far removed from the Ultimate Way (*zhìdào*). As for me, the old monk, I say that the "Ultimate Way" is simply another name for the "Ultimate Person" (*zhìrén*);
it is not that there is a separate Ultimate Way existing apart from the person. Therefore, Zhaozhou cited: "The Ultimate Way is without difficulty; it only dislikes discrimination."
Discernment: simply do not harbor likes or dislikes; let it be transparently clear. To say, "The old monk does not dwell within clarity," is this not Zhaozhou’s own realization of the ultimate Way?
However, what is called the "Ultimate Man" (the Perfected One) does not exist apart from humanity, nor is there some other ultimate place elsewhere.
Thus, Deshan said: "If one were to discuss this matter, it would be such that the Buddhas of the three periods of time have no [words for it]."
It hangs upon the wall. Furthermore, there is another person who laughs loudly, "Ha ha! If you can recognize this person, your study of the Way will be complete.
How could there be a Most Honored One or a Supreme Way existing apart from ordinary people? Linji sought people only amidst the conditions of adversity and favor;
therefore he said: "For twelve years, I have sought a trace of karmic nature even as small as a mustard seed, and I have found none."
It can be understood. Furthermore, how could there be thousands of wonders and hundreds of anomalies apart from human beings?
Hanyue regarded Linji as his true master solely because of those thousands of wonders and hundreds of anomalies. I ask you, Tanji: consider the student;
when a student possesses thousands of wonders and hundreds of anomalies, is it merely a matter of a hair’s breadth of difference, or is it a case of being worlds apart? Moreover—
The original face of a person cannot be traced, nor can it be painted. Consider this analogy: suppose one were to paint a dragon;
if every feature—the head, horns, tusks, and eyes—is exactly like the real thing, yet it cannot produce rain, would it truly be a dragon?

If it were indeed a true dragon, with every feature—the head, horns, tusks, and eyes—exactly like the real thing, then even when it does not produce rain, what difference would there be in its being a dragon?
How can there be such a vast disparity? This old monk takes the person themselves as the fundamental principle.
Therefore, whether it rains or not, the dragon manifests before one; whether things go smoothly or against one’s will, the person manifests before one.
From the very beginning, there has never been a second person. If you seek even a hair’s breadth of difference, it is as far apart as heaven and earth.
It is utterly unattainable.
▲ The Fourth Patriarch, Grand Master Daoxin, was surnamed Sima. His family had resided in Henei for generations, later migrating to Guangji County in Qizhou.

From birth he was transcendent and extraordinary; from childhood he admired the school of emptiness, and his mastery of the various gates of liberation was as if it were the result of past habituation.
Having succeeded to his patriarchal legacy, he restrained his mind and did not sleep; for sixty years, his side never touched the mat.
One day, while traveling to Huangmei County, he encountered a young boy on the road whose physical features were remarkably refined and extraordinary compared to ordinary children.
The Patriarch asked, "What is your surname? The boy replied, "I have a surname, but it is not an ordinary surname. The Patriarch asked, "What is it? The boy replied, "It is the Buddha’s surname."
The Patriarch asked, "Do you have no surname? He replied, "Because my nature is empty, I have none.

The Patriarch silently recognized him as a vessel for the Dharma and immediately instructed an attendant to go to his mother’s place to request that she allow him to leave the household life. Because of past karmic conditions, the mother showed no sign of reluctance;

he was thus ordained as her disciple. Eventually, the Dharma was entrusted to him and the robe was passed on. The verse says: "The seed of the flower has the nature of birth; because of the ground, the flower [arises]."
Life after life, the great conditions merge with one's nature; thus, that which should arise does not arise.
The Fifth Patriarch, Master Hongren, was a native of Huangmei in Qizhou. Previously, he was known as the "Pine-Planter" on Mount Poutou.
He once requested of the Fourth Patriarch, saying, "May I hear the Way of the Dharma? The Patriarch replied, "You have already..."
The old man said, "If I were to hear of someone capable of widely converting others, and if they were to come here again, I could still wait for you.
He then went to the water's edge and saw a woman washing clothes. He bowed to her and asked, "May I stay the night? The woman replied, "I have parents and brothers;
you may go ask them. He said, "Very well, I shall do so immediately. The woman nodded her head in agreement, and he turned his staff and departed.
The woman, surnamed Zhou, was the younger daughter of her family. Upon her marriage, she conceived immediately. Her parents detested her greatly and cast her out.

Having nowhere else to go, she worked daily as a hired spinner in the village and stayed at night beneath a public shelter. Later, she gave birth to a son; because they considered him an ill omen, they abandoned him.
He was thrown into a turbid harbor. When he was seen there the next day, he was swimming upstream; his physical appearance was bright and clear. Greatly astonished, [the people] lifted him up.
As a young child, he followed his mother in begging for food, and the villagers called him "The Child Without a Surname. He encountered a wise man who sighed and said, "This boy lacks seven marks;
he will not equal the Tathāgata. Later, he met Master Xìn and attained the Dharma, succeeding him in his transformation of others.
At Mount Pótóu, during the Xiánhéng era, there was a layman surnamed Lú named Huínéng who came from Xīnzhōu to pay his respects. The Patriarch asked him:
"Where have you come from? Lu said, "From Lingnan. The Patriarch asked, "What do you seek? Lu said, "I seek only to become a Buddha.
The Patriarch said, "People of Lingnan have no Buddha-nature; how can you become a Buddha? Lu said, "People may be from the north or the south, but how could this be true of the Buddha-nature?
The Patriarch ordered him to join the assembly in manual labor. Lu said, "The nature of my disciple has always given rise to wisdom; it does not..."

"Free from self-nature is itself the field of merit. I do not yet know what task the Master intends for me to perform. The Patriarch said, "This rustic fellow has a very sharp root-nature; go to the fodder shed.
Lu bowed at his feet and withdrew, then entered the millhouse and applied himself to labor with the pestle and mortar, working day and night without rest for eight months.
The Patriarch, knowing that the time for the transmission had arrived, addressed the assembly, saying: "The True Dharma..."
"This is difficult to understand; it cannot be merely memorized. I declare that its preservation shall be your responsibility. Each of you, according to your own inclination, compose a verse.
If your words and meaning correspond in harmony with mine, then both the robe and the Dharma shall be entrusted to you. At that time, there were over seven hundred monks in the assembly.

Among them was the Elder Shenxiu, whose learning encompassed both Buddhist and secular classics, and whom the multitude revered and looked up to. They all unanimously acclaimed him, saying, "If it were not for the Venerable Xiuxiu, who else could it be?"
"I dare to accept this. Hearing the widespread acclaim of the assembly, Shenxiu did not reflect further; he then inscribed a verse upon the wall of the corridor, saying:
"The body is the Bodhi tree; the mind is a stand for a bright mirror. At all times, diligently wipe and polish it; do not let it gather dust.
When the Patriarch was walking about and suddenly saw this verse, he knew it was composed by Shenxiu. He then praised it, saying: "Later..."

Those who practice in reliance upon this will likewise attain the supreme fruit. While Lu was at the mill, he suddenly heard someone reciting a verse and asked, "Fellow student, what chapter or passage is this?
His fellow student replied, "You do not know. The Master is seeking a Dharma heir and has ordered each of us to compose a verse expressing our realization.
This is the one composed by the Venerable Xiu; the Master has praised it with deep admiration and will surely transmit the Dharma and pass on the robe."
Yeluo asked, "What is this verse like? His fellow student recited it for him. After a long while, Yeluo said, "It is beautiful indeed, yet it is not fully realized.
The fellow student rebuked him, saying, "How could a common person know such things? Do not utter such mad words! Yeluo replied, "If you do not believe me, I wish to compose a verse in response.
The fellow student did not answer, but merely looked at one another and laughed. That night, Yeluo went to him in secret and told him.
A young attendant led him down to the corridor. Lu himself held a candle and requested Zhang Riyong, the Vice Prefect, to stand beside the verse by Xiu and transcribe it as follows:
"Bodhi originally has no tree; The bright mirror is likewise not a stand. From the beginning there has been nothing at all; Where, then, could dust and grime settle?
Later, when the Patriarch saw this verse, he asked, "Who wrote this? They have not yet seen their own nature."
When the assembly heard the Patriarch’s words, they paid them no heed. When night fell, the Patriarch went secretly to the rice-hulling shed and asked, "Is the rice white yet?

Lu replied, "It is white, but it has not yet been sifted. The Patriarch struck the pestle three times with his staff; Lu immediately struck the drum three times and entered the hall. He addressed the assembly, saying:
"The appearance of all Buddhas in the world is for the sake of one great matter. Therefore, according to the capacities of beings—whether large or small—they are led [to enlightenment]."
He guided them, and thus there arose the essential tenets of the Ten Stages, the Three Vehicles, and the Sudden and Gradual teachings, which were established as the gates of instruction.
Nevertheless, he entrusted the unsurpassed, subtle, secret, perfectly luminous, and true *dharmācārya-locanakośa* (Treasury of the Eye of the True Dharma) to the preeminent Venerable Mahākāśyapa.
It was transmitted successively through twenty-eight generations until it reached Bodhidharma, who arrived in this land and encountered the Great Master Ke (Huineng).
This lineage has been transmitted down to the present day. I now entrust to you this Dharma-treasure and the robe passed down from my predecessor;
guard them well and ensure that they are never interrupted. Listen to my verse: "When sentient beings come to sow seeds, The fruit arises again according to the ground."

"Since insentient things have no seeds, they likewise lack nature and do not arise. Having received [the transmission] with bowed knees, Lu asked about the Dharma; once he had received it, he asked, "To whom shall the robe be given?
The Patriarch said, "In the past, when Bodhidharma first arrived, people did not yet believe him. Therefore, he transmitted the robe to manifest that he had attained the Dharma.
Now that faith has matured, the robe is merely a source of contention. It shall stop with your person; it will not be transmitted further."

▲The Sixth Patriarch, Master Huineng, was surnamed Lu. His father was Xingtao and his mother was Lady Li. She conceived after experiencing a miraculous dream, and upon awakening, a wondrous fragrance filled the chamber.
She carried the child for six years before giving birth; at that time, rays of light soared into the sky. At dawn, there was a monk.

He came and said to the Patriarch’s father, “This son may be named Huineng. The father asked, “What does this mean? The monk replied, “‘Hui’ means to use the Dharma to bring relief and salvation to sentient beings;
‘Neng’ means being able to perform the work of a Buddha. Having finished speaking, he was lost to sight. The Patriarch did not drink breast milk;
at night, a divine being would come and bathe him with sweet dew. At the age of three, his father passed away, and his mother lived as a widow in the household.

He was extremely poor. From his youth, he gathered firewood and sold it to support his mother. One day, while carrying firewood through the marketplace, he heard a guest reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* until reaching the passage:
"One should give rise to the mind without abiding anywhere. He experienced a profound realization and asked the guest, "What teaching is this?
The guest replied, "This is the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Master Wuzu Ren of Dongshan at Huangmei constantly..."
He instructed his son to recite this sutra. Upon hearing these words, the Patriarch was suddenly stirred to seek the Dharma through renunciation.

He then requested from a guest that provisions for his mother’s annual needs be prepared, whereupon he took leave of her and traveled directly to Shaozhou. There he met the man of noble conduct, Liu Zhilüe.

They became friends. The nun Wujinzang was the paternal aunt of Zhiyue. She had previously read the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, and when the Master briefly listened to it, he immediately explained its meaning to her.
The nun then took up the scroll and asked about the characters. The Patriarch said, "I do not recognize the characters, but I ask for the meaning.
The nun said, "If you do not even recognize the characters, how can you comprehend the meaning? The Patriarch replied, "The Buddhas..."
"This wondrous principle is not concerned with words and letters. The nun was struck with wonder and informed the elders of her village, requesting that he reside at Baolin Temple.

If, outside of this fundamental dharma, one were to posit a separate "O" as the ancestor of the thousand Buddhas and ten thousand Buddhas, further drilling out all manner of strange names and extraordinary marks—how could such a thing be considered "returning to the old"?
▲ Chan Master Xiyun of Huangbo in Hongzhou was a successor of Baizhang and a native of Min. He left home at the age of youth at Mount Huangbo in his own prefecture.
A protrusion on his forehead rose like a pearl; his speech was clear and resonant, and his disposition was profound and serene.
Later, while traveling to Tiantai, he encountered a monk with whom he conversed and laughed as if they were old acquaintances. Upon looking closely, he saw that the other’s gaze pierced through him.

They set out together. Upon reaching a mountain stream, the water had suddenly risen in a flood. [Daoyi] cast aside his hat, planted his staff, and stopped. The monk urged the Master to cross with him.
The Master said, "If you wish to cross, brother, cross yourself. The monk immediately lifted his robes and stepped into the waves as if walking on level ground. Looking back, he said:
"Cross over! Cross over! The Master said, "Tsk! You self-satisfied fellow! Had I known earlier, I would have cut off your shin.
The monk sighed and said, "Truly a vessel for the Mahāyāna Dharma; I am not his equal. Having spoken, he vanished. He then went to the capital of Luoyang to beg for alms.
As he was chanting, the sound of his alms bowl was heard. An old woman emerged from between the thorny gates and said, "You are truly insatiable.

The Master replied, "You have not yet given anything; why do you reproach me for being insatiable? The woman smiled and closed the gate. The Master marveled at this and stepped forward to converse with her.
Having dispensed much medicine, the Master took his leave and departed after a short while. The old woman told him, "You should go to Nanchang to see Master Ma.
Upon arriving in Nanchang, Master Ma had already passed away. He then proceeded to Shimen to pay respects at the stupa.
At that time, Chan Master Baizhang was dwelling in a hut beside the stupa; he went there to visit Baizhang. Baizhang asked, "Majestic and dignified, from what direction have you come? The Master—
The Master said, "Majestic and imposing! You have come from Lingnan. Baizhang said, "Majestic and imposing—what business do you have?
The Master said, "Majestic and imposing—I have no other business," and he immediately prostrated himself. Baizhang asked, "How does one point to the ancestral vehicle (zongcheng) of the past masters?
After a long silence, Baizhang said, "One must not allow future generations to sever this lineage. The Master said, "I had thought..."
"You are a person of substance. He then rose and entered the abbot's quarters. The Master followed him in and said, "I have come specifically for this purpose.
The Abbot replied, "If that is so, you must not let me down hereafter. One day, the Abbot brought up the story of Mazu’s shout during the second interview;
the Master then attained his realization.
One day, Zhang asked, "Where have you come from, Master? The Master replied, "I have come from gathering mushrooms at the foot of Mount Daxiong.
Zhang said, "Did you see any tigers? The Master then let out a tiger's roar. Zhang raised his axe and made a gesture as if to strike; the Master immediately struck him.
Baizhang gave him a blow. Baizhang laughed heartily and returned to the hall, where he said: "At the foot of Mount Daxiong there is a great beast;
all of you must watch out for it. Today, this old fellow Baizhang has been personally caught by its mouth."
One day he ascended the hall. As the assembly gathered like clouds, he said, "What do you all seek?
He then drove them away with his staff, yet the assembly would not disperse. The Master sat back down and said, "You people are all nothing but those who eat dregs of wine.
To travel on pilgrimage in such a manner is to become a laughingstock to others; you go only where there are eight hundred or a thousand people."
One must not seek after such bustling clamor. When I was traveling as a wandering monk, I once encountered a man beneath the roots of a grassy thicket;
I then drove a single spike through the crown of his head to see what would happen. Had he been able to feel pain or sensation, I could have filled a cloth bag with rice and provided for him.
But since everyone nowadays is just like you—so easygoing—where else would there be such matters as we face today?
Since you all call yourselves wandering monks (*caryā*), you ought to apply some measure of spirit. Do you know that within the Great Tang there are no Zen masters?
At that time, a monk asked: "All the venerable elders of the various quarters have gathered here; for what purpose do they provide instruction and transformation?"
He then said, "There is no Zen master. The Master replied, "I do not say there is no Zen; it is simply that there is no teacher. He saved the Middle Way.
Three times asked, three times struck—throughout ancient and modern times, Huangbo alone has done this. Furthermore, he only received Linji for a single occasion;

had he used it again, those who merely mimic his appearance would have arisen like swarms of bees. How much more so if one were to ask a thousand times and receive a thousand blows, or ten thousand times...
Question: "Has it been struck ten thousand times and yet remained without wear today? In the past, Dahui said:

"The spark from striking flint, the flash of lightning—these have led countless people to dabble in their karmic consciousness. To understand as soon as they hear it mentioned—is this not the great den of the Buddha-dharma?
Yuanwu involuntarily stuck out his tongue and said: "Do not concern yourself with him. I have attained realization through it."

This is the deadline. If you do not achieve realization and verification, I shall by no means let you pass. Alas! This single word "realization" can only be authenticated through the fundamental principle (zongzhi).
Otherwise, gold and brass will be mixed together; who would dare to distinguish them?

As for me, an old monk, based on Linji’s three questions and three blows, I would administer a thousand questions and a thousand blows, ten thousand questions and ten thousand blows—what flaw could there be in that? Furthermore, regarding Linji...
Since it is thus, one should strike until the end of the future, not merely for today alone. Why?
Precisely because the aim is for every person to realize and witness [the truth]. Now, as for this word "realization," only the essential principle (zongzhi) can verify it.
Yet, the old monk says that the two words "essential principle" have long since been confused with counterfeit gold and brass. Who...
This serves as proof. Tanzhi further cited the saying, "It is not that there is no Chan; it is simply that there is no teacher," and offered this defense:
"In the time of Mahamati, the Chan school was at its peak, and even in various quarters there were such discussions. How much more so now, when the tradition has grown thin and faded?

I am preoccupied with saving the Five Houses from calamity and the cycle of birth and death; I have no leisure to dwell on such matters, fearing only for the sake of hundreds of thousands of generations."
"It is truly lamentable that there is no longer a Yangziyun. As for Tanji, he merely dabbles with karmic consciousness while attempting to save the Five Houses.
Old monk, I have no concern for whether you can deliberate or not; I shall beat you until there is no end to it.
Why? Have you not seen Huangbo say: 'When this old man was traveling as a pilgrim, if I encountered someone beneath a patch of grass roots...'"
Then he struck him with a single blow from the crown of his head. If one could perceive his pain and itching, one might fill a cloth bag with rice to offer to him.
This old monk says: "The old fellow Huangbo was also a mixture of gold and brass;
there will be no end to his days of eating blows. Have you not seen Baizhang say: "Today my nose does not ache either"? This too is correct.
I strike out directly. Let the world and future generations judge it for themselves; let those with clear eyes verify and observe it.
