Chan Master Linji Yixuan of Jingzhou succeeded Huangbo. He was the son of the Xing family of Nanhua in Caozhou.

From his youth, he possessed the aspiration to transcend the mundane world. Upon shaving his head and receiving full ordination, he immediately came to admire the Chan school. Initially, he was among the assembly at Huangbo’s monastery.
His practice was singularly pure. At that time, Muzhou served as the First Seat (the head monk).

He asked, "How long have you been here, Senior Monk? The Master replied, "Three years. Muzhou said, "Have you ever questioned him [the Abbot]? The Master replied, "I have never questioned him; I do not know what to ask.
Muzhou said, "Why not ask the Abbot, 'What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma'?"
The Master then departed. Before the sound of his question had even faded, Baizhang struck him. The Master came back down. Mazu asked, "How was your inquiry?
The Master said, "Before I had even finished asking my question, the Master struck me; I do not understand. Mazu said, "Just go and ask again.
The Master asked once more, and Baizhang struck him again. This happened three times; having been struck three times for three inquiries, the Master reported this to Mazu.

The monk said, "I have long since received your encouragement and have repeatedly been granted the staff by you, Master, as I inquired about the Dharma. I have only regretted that due to my karmic hindrances, I have not grasped the profound meaning.
I shall now take my leave. Baizhang said, "If you are going, you must first bid farewell to the Abbot before you depart. The monk bowed and withdrew.
Zhaozhou first went to Huangbo’s place and said, “The monk who engaged in dialogue, though he is but a youth, is truly extraordinary.
When he comes to take his leave, use skillful means to receive him; in the future, he will become a great tree whose shade will shelter all people under heaven.”
The Master was about to take his leave of Huangbo. Huangbo said, "There is no need for you to go elsewhere;
simply go to Tancheng in Gaoyang to visit Dayu. He will surely explain it for you. When the Master arrived at Dayu’s place, Dayu asked, "Where have you come from?
The Master replied, "I have come from Huangbo. Dayu asked, "What words did Huangbo speak? The Master said, "Three times I asked him about the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma."
He was beaten three times, yet he did not know whether he had committed an offense or not. Yunju said, "Huangbo’s compassionate heart is so earnest;
for your sake, he has brought you to utter exhaustion, yet you come here again to ask whether you have committed an offense or not.
At these words, the Master attained great enlightenment and said, "So it turns out that Huangbo’s Buddha-dharma is not very much. Yunju grabbed him and said, "You bed-wetting boy!"
“Devil! Just now you were asking whether there was an offense or not; now you say, ‘Huangbo’s Buddha-dharma is nothing more than this.
What principle have you seen? Speak quickly, speak quickly! The Master struck Daoyu three times under the ribs.
Dafu said, "Your teacher Huangbo is no concern of mine. The Master took his leave of Dayu and returned to Huangbo.
Upon seeing him, Huangbo asked, "This fellow comes and goes; when will he ever have an end to it? The Master replied, "It is only because of your grandmotherly concern.
Having finished the formal greetings, he stood in attendance. Huangbo asked, "Where have you been? The Master said, "Yesterday I received the Master’s [instruction]."
The Master’s compassionate instruction was to go consult Dayu. Baizhang asked, “What words did Dayu say? The Master recounted the previous conversation.
Baizhang said, “That old fellow Dayu is too talkative; wait until he comes back and give him a thorough beating. The Master said, “Why wait for him to come?”
[The Master] struck him immediately and followed it with a slap. Huangbo said, "This madman has come here to pull at a tiger's whiskers.
The Master then shouted. Huangbo called to his attendant and said, "Escort this madman to the meditation hall."
Later, the Master resided at Linji in Zhenzhou, where disciples gathered like clouds.
One day, he said to the two senior monks Puhua and Ke Fu, "I wish to establish the school of Huangbo here; you two should try to refute me.
The two took their leave and went downstairs. Three days later, Puhua came back up and asked, "What did the Master say three days ago?"
The Master struck him. Three days later, Ke Fu came up and asked, "Why did you strike Puhua yesterday?
The Master struck him again as well.

That evening, he gave a small lecture (xiaocan), saying: "Sometimes one takes away the person but not the environment; sometimes one takes away the environment but not the person. There was... [text fragment].
At times, both person and environment are taken away; at other times, neither person nor environment is taken away. Ke Fu asked, "What is 'taking away the person but not taking away the environment'?
The Master said, "The warm sun brings forth life, spreading a carpet of brocade; the infant’s hair hangs down, white as silk.
Fu asked, "What is 'taking away the environment but not taking away the person'? The Master said, "The Imperial decree has been issued and reaches all under heaven; the General..."
"Beyond the frontier, smoke and dust are extinguished. Fufu asked, "What is meant by 'both the person and the environment are taken away'?

The Master said, "In Bing and Fen, communications are cut off; one dwells alone in a single region. Fufu asked, "What is meant by 'neither the person nor the environment is taken away'? The Master said, "The King ascends the precious throne."
The village elder sang and chanted, signifying that he had understood the meaning beneath the words.
Jiufu said, "Linji’s application of the Dharma was like Guliang splitting Mount Hua or Nüwa smelting stones to patch the heavens;
nothing solid remained unbroken, and no trace remained unsevered. Yet later generations were startled and alarmed, regarding it as wild, eccentric, and preposterous."
Examining these words, they are indeed true. Furthermore, it is said that the spirit is subtle and wondrous, beyond the reach of comprehension and not to be fathomed by one's own intellect.
How could one know that the power of non-deception is inherently complete? It is simply that students, seeing a precipice before them, do not advance.
The old monk cites Puhua’s saying: "Linji was but a little fellow. Xuefeng said: "Linji was much like a thief who steals in broad daylight.
Look at these ancients; there is an eye within their words. Who can compare to Tanji, who tears open the flowers to patch the heavens?
Regarding such extraordinary expressions as "the ten suns shining together," [you] falsely accuse Linji.

Furthermore, you claim that he was an outstanding person of transcendent caliber who, in a state where there was not much of the Buddha-dharma, had "ten thousand households all seeing through. This is something one encounters every morning and evening.
Yet, you fail to consider that Linji himself said: "If someone with a transcendent understanding comes here, I, this mountain monk, will manifest my entire being for them."
If one does not pass through the various capacities of the faculties, who would engage you in debate over a thousand gates and ten thousand doors?
By the time you wait for dawn or dusk to encounter it, the arrow has already passed beyond Silla.

Therefore, when Guishan asked Yangshan, "At that time, did Linji obtain the power of Dayu, or did he obtain the power of Huangbo? Yangshan replied, "Not only could he ride upon the tiger's head, he also knew how to seize its tail."
Hugui: Is this not precisely Linji riding the tiger, seizing the tiger? Han Yue’s verse says:
"The tip of the horn bursts forth as the essential pivot within the mystery; the true masters of ten thousand ages value what they inherit.

How could there be a separate mystery and pivot outside of Linji, one that surpasses the old monk’s single blow which functions as nothing other than that very blow—this total embodiment of functioning? Han.
Since Yue did not understand Linji’s Way, he falsely claimed that his own total manifestation of function here was the true teaching;
is this not the height of shamelessness? Furthermore, in the *Jiuzhong* (Nine Rescues), it says:

"At that time, while Linji was at Huangbo’s place receiving blows, he could only cause all the grasses and trees throughout the great earth to simultaneously emit a great radiance. 帝 (Di) [is the seal].
Even Śakra and Brahmā could not exhaustively praise him. It is a pity that he was struck across the face by the Great Foolish Old Lady;
he could not avoid falling flat on his face upon level ground. Now, the venerable elders of all quarters say that Linji awakened to the principle of being struck by the staff or touched by the whisk.
But tell me, did Linji actually consent to this? It is just like the thirtieth day of the twelfth lunar month—
When the day comes and the light of the eyes falls to the ground, one does not know pain when sawn apart or hewn with axes;
nor does one know joy when gold is rubbed upon the body or incense is applied. At such a time as this, where would you place that which is struck by the tip of this staff?
This clearly shows that Danji contradicts his own words; his earlier and later statements do not correspond. Since...
Regarding Linji at that time: when he received blows from Huangbo, he was only able to cause the grasses and trees of the entire earth to simultaneously emit a great radiance.
It is further said that various quarters have misjudged Linji, claiming he merely realized the principle of being struck by the staff.
When the thirtieth day of the twelfth month arrives, one will not know the pain of being sawn apart and hewn with axes. [The text here ends abruptly.]
"One who does not know joy when smeared with incense" refers to that which is struck by the tip of the staff. Where would you place it?
I ask you, Master Tanji, and you elders of all quarters: Which one among you has realized the principle of "knowing pain and knowing joy" as Linji did?
You have merely mistaken the place where the staff strikes for the place where one knows pain and knows joy. It is just like this.
As for what was said: "What fault is there in realizing the principle of being struck by the staff?
If the fault lay in the two characters "principle" (*dào-lǐ*), then Xinghua should not have said, "I realized the principle of my late teacher Linji receiving the staff from Huangbo.
If the fault lay in the two characters "struck" (*fù-zháo*), then Linji should not have said himself, "I [received it] twice..."
For ten years, while at the place of my late teacher Huangbo, I asked three times about the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma;
on each occasion, I received a blow from his staff. It was as if he had merely brushed me with a stalk of mugwort. An old monk dares to say:
where the staff strikes, the grasses and trees of the entire world, along with Śakra and Brahmā, all simultaneously radiate light—there is nothing more to it.

This is attained through the oral praise that eliminates movement. Only then can one speak of the old monk’s face, which shines forth equally in both the sentient and the insentient atop Mount T’ung-kuan.
Only then can one speak of the principle of Linji’s receiving blows from Huangbo at that time.
Furthermore, it says: "Muzhou offered three pieces of advice regarding the inquiry, yet Huangbo struck him three times. Since this was not...
He attained enlightenment. Furthermore, he pointed [Linji] toward Great Fool (Dayu), where the three elders’ subtle and profound forging was truly revealed;

the very foundation of Linji’s establishment of the school’s tenets lies entirely therein. People today know only of Huangbo’s three questions and three beatings, and thus rely on the single staff as the ultimate principle.
Without the hand of a master carver from Ying, how could ten thousand blows ever bring a person to life? I, this old monk, furthermore—
I see that Tanji merely speaks of it in the abstract without attaining realization; he points others toward Dayu, yet has not realized it himself.
Therefore, he cannot explain the reason why Linji attained realization. This old monk, unable to restrain my impatience, shall bluntly reveal it for you:
it is like a person spitting in a dream, who then encounters pleasant or unpleasant scenes and consequently experiences joy, sorrow, grief, or anger.
When one is in such a state of anger, fear, and other emotions, and is suddenly struck by another, one awakens in an instant;

all dream-visions and mental projections vanish without remainder. This is why, at that time, Linji struck Daoyu in the ribs with his fist and slapped Huangbo across the face—what else could this be but the functioning of the total embodiment? It is just like planting...
"Next, the pines. Huangbo said, "In the deep mountains, what is the purpose of planting so many pines? Linji said, "First, to provide the mountain gate with a scenic setting;
second, to serve as a landmark for future generations. Having said this, he struck the ground three times with his mattock.
Huangbo said, "Even though it is so, you have already received thirty blows from me. Linji struck again.
"Earth, three; below. Huh! Huh! Huangbo said, "My school has reached you; it shall flourish greatly in the world.

He wrote in his book that one must strike with the mattock straight through to the bottom, establishing this as a banner for future generations. This is precisely based on Linji’s own personal practice;
it is simply because [the matter] does not reside within Huangbo’s own sphere. The old monk uses a single, most coarse blow to strike straight through to the bottom, the whole body [of reality].
It is the sword that kills, the blade that gives life. Has Tan Ji ever seen it in a dream?
You people merely manage to debate the fundamental tenets and all imitate Ke Fu by chanting the verses on the Four Selections. I, this old monk, am not like that. According to Linji’s teaching:
"Sometimes I take away the person but do not take away the environment"—to such a one, I too would give him a blow with my staff. There is...
At times, the realm is taken away but not the person; he gives him another blow. At times, both person and realm are taken away;
he gives him another blow. At times, neither person nor realm is taken away; he gives him another blow.
Tell me, is this the "Sword that Kills" or the "Sword that Brings Life"?
A monk asked, "What are the true Buddha, the true Dharma, and the true Path? We beg the Master for instruction. The Master said, "The Buddha is the purity of the mind;
the Dharma is the luminosity of the mind; the Path is the pure light that is unimpeded everywhere.
These three are one; they are all empty names without substantial reality. If you would truly be a man of the Path, let not your mind be interrupted from moment to moment."
Severance. Since Master Bodhidharma came from the Western Land, he sought only a person who would not be deluded by others.
Later, upon meeting the Second Patriarch, he was enlightened in a single word; only then did he realize that all his previous efforts had been in vain.
My own realization today is no different from that of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. If you can attain realization within the first phrase, you are fit to be a teacher to the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
If one realizes it in the second phrase, one is fit to serve as a teacher for devas and humans. If one realizes it in the third phrase, one cannot even save oneself.
A monk then asked, "What is the first phrase? The Master said, "The seal of the three essentials opens; the vermilion dot is narrow.
Before there is time for deliberation, host and guest are distinguished. [The monk] asked, "What is the second phrase? The Master said, "Subtle understanding..."
How could it be permitted that Asanga should question [Vasubandhu]? How could he compete with the "cutting-off-the-stream" faculty? [A monk] asked, "What is the third phrase?
The Master said, "Just look at the puppeteer on the stage; all the pulling and manipulating depend entirely upon the person inside."
Jiufu said: "Master Fengxue told Nan yuan, 'If ordinary speech does not remain stuck in ordinary sentiment, it immediately falls into the view of the sages;
this is a great malady among students. The former sages took pity on them and provided expedient means, like using one wedge to extract another.
Caoshan had four prohibitions, which he stated as: 'Do not travel the path where the mind dwells; do not don the garment of original nature; what need is there to be thus? "

One must strictly avoid [this] before the illness has arisen. These four illnesses are all seen by the Sages; thus the ancients established various medicinal teachings to treat them according to the specific ailment.
It is permissible to remove the medicine only after the illness has departed. Indeed, while the medicine may be removed, the physician may not be removed.
The "physician" refers to the Sage, who established these teachings in anticipation of those in future generations throughout the world.

This is a sickness. To desire to extinguish the fundamental tenets is to eliminate the physician. Moreover, the malady of the current disorder of the lineage is currently raging within the monastic forests (*saṃghārāma*).
Teachers have their heads shattered and foreheads split open, yet they cannot restrain it; they are struck and return the blow, yet they cannot discern right from wrong;
peddlers of the Dharma fill the roads, yet they cannot stop them—and instead, they are busily occupied with [erasing]... the brush.
To make the destruction of the fundamental principle one's primary task is like having a household full of illnesses yet scolding the physician and rejecting the medicine;

how could this possibly be the intent of the Buddhas' and Patriarchs' entrustment? Luoshan said: "The phrase within the meaning; the meaning within the phrase; the meaning does not abide within the phrase."
The meaning does not abide within the phrase; the meaning and the phrase do not belong to the same category. How should one understand this? He also said:
"The meaning can eradicate the phrase, and the phrase can eradicate the meaning. When meaning and phrase race against one another, this is what is truly fearsome.
Yantou said: "As soon as it is thus, it is no longer thus. Thus, the phrase is eradicated, and the non-phrase is also eradicated. Naturally, there is bare exposure."
It revolves and turns like a mass of flaming fire; what place is there to approach it?
Now, taking the single blow through to the end as the dharma-method is to be certain and unchanging.

Taking the moment of entering and exiting through the face-gate as the "eye" of the staff is to bring the mind to rest within this phrase. Thus, both the sentient and the insentient are made manifest.
However, these [preceding] phrases are presented as the final words; they represent the noble vision and the true Dharma in which one may find refuge and dwell.
They cannot be compared to a great mass of fire. Some have mistakenly grasped the meaning of the "mass of fire" and attempted to explain it with a single blow of the staff.
How could such an approach possibly be discerning? Indeed, those among people today who employ the staff and the shout are truly numerous. For...

The protagonist is Bangyan (棒眼). He himself wrote a commentary on this book, which may indeed be called detailed. Even a person of extreme dullness can grasp its meaning entirely upon a single reading.

Now, as for Kāśyapa hearing it directly from the Buddha and Bodhidharma arriving specifically for its sake—what is there particularly noble about that, such that it has been venerated down to the present day?
Furthermore, Chan Master Deshan Xuanjian rebuked [the notion of] substantial dharmas.
This is truly profound. Yet there is the first phrase. As for the other schools—Yunmen, Guiyang, Caodong, and Fayan—it goes without saying.
If their fundamental tenets were merely substantial dharmas, then these venerable masters would have established them themselves and immediately rebuked them.
To become insane and lose one's mind to such an extent is not the way. An ancient worthy said: "One need only clearly grasp the fundamental principle;
fundamentally, there is no substantial dharma. Thus, the fundamental principle is the forge for refining substantial dharmas. Why, then, should one have any doubt?
Tangji borrowed the "Four Prohibitions" of Caoshan to deceive this old monk.

He failed to consider that if such obscure talk of Caoshan had reached my presence, I would have struck him straight away so that he would have no way to ascend to heaven and no door to enter the earth—not letting him go at all.
Furthermore, since you have cited Luoshan’s principle that "the meaning does not abide within the phrase, and the phrase does not abide within the meaning," [you must understand it thus].
To eradicate the phrase within the mind; to eradicate the mind within the phrase. Yantou eradicates both the phrase and that which is not the phrase.
Furthermore, Chan Master Jian of Daode Mountain was one who most severely rebuked the existence of "real dharmas," yet he spoke of a "first phrase.
Is this not a contradiction of his own words? In the past, when I raised my staff and said to Han Yue, "Raise one..."
"One must not raise two; to let one point pass is to fall into the second. Throwing down his staff, he said, "The old monk has already fallen into the second.
As for the first, how can it even be raised? Han Yue failed to realize this and instead seized the staff and left.
Thus, the old monk had the words, "I can only act as a peripheral departure," yet Tan Ji still does not know shame and instead cites De...
Master Shanjian had "the first phrase. Is this not, in fact, a case of turning it back upon the old monk?
To cite one and not two, to let pass one move—does this not fall into the second? As for the other schools—Cloud Gate (Yunmen), Muiyang (Weiyang), Caoxi (Caodong), and Fayen—it goes without saying;
what is meant is that all five houses take the first phrase as their fundamental principle.
The essential point is this: furthermore, it is not that I am merely verifying the old monk’s realization. "This one fact alone is real; the other two are not true.
You people must truly reach the stage where the old monk’s state—both sentient and insentient—is radiantly and equally manifest.

There, you will naturally be in a state of bare exposure and seamless turning. At such a time, even the phrase "this" is eradicated, and even the phrase "not this" is eradicated; there is nothing left within the mind.
The phrase halts; within the phrase, the meaning does not halt. A single blow is not used as a single blow; killing and enlivening are entirely free.
What place is there for anything to approach? To call it "a mass of flames" is already superfluous speech.
Can you call it "sacred"? Can you perceive it? Can you call it a "real dharma"? You further claim that if the fundamental principle were the real dharma, then...
The elders stand up and rebuke themselves: "One who is insane and has lost their mind would not go to such extremes;

this is precisely your own insanity and loss of mind. Your words contradict themselves. Why? If you take the first statement as your fundamental tenet, how could there ever be various names and characteristics?
Yet you still cling to various names and characteristics as your fundamental tenet. How [can this be]?
I have previously relied upon the first phrase. Although it is said that there is fundamentally no real dharma, who would believe it?
According to Linji himself, "First of all, do not grasp at what this mountain monk says. Why? Because his words lack any basis; for a time, he has been painting pictures on empty space.

Jiure said: "In the past, when the *Bai shu* prohibited [the term], it stated that 'host and guest' refers to 'you and I.

Recently, he has further explained that 'your shout and my shout,' or 'shouting for the ox and shouting for the horse,' are also clearly cases of host and guest. Thus, at first he was complacent in his ignorance;
recently, he has forcibly taken what he does not know to be knowledge. From beginning to end, his arguments are contradictory and inconsistent, showing no regard for the truth."
In later generations—alas! How painful it is! I never thought that the Way of Linji would come to such a state.
Many years ago, when I was replying to a letter from the immortal layman Liu, Han Yue claimed that the simultaneous shouting in both halls is the "mother" of the four guest-host relationships.
He asserted that shouting simultaneously is the "guest of guests," while shouting simultaneously from the left and right is the "host of guests" and the "guest of host."

It is so. A simultaneous shout is the "Master within the Master. As for those two people currently facing each other in combat, every one of them understands a shout of a thousand or ten thousand catties;
yet, whether it be you shouting or me shouting, who knows that they have fallen into the state of being "guests within guests"?
It is no different from shouting "cow! or shouting "horse! Therefore, the old monk cited the Great Awakened One (Dajian Huineng) asking Xinghua:

"I have heard you say that after traveling south on pilgrimage, you did not encounter a single person with whom your staff could strike a chord regarding the understanding of the Buddha-dharma. On what principle do you speak thus? Xinghua then gave a shout.
Jue struck him. Huazhu shouted again. Jue struck him once more. On the following day, as Huazhu was passing by the Dharma Hall, Jue called out, "Head of the Monastery!
I have a direct doubt regarding those two shouts you made yesterday. Huazhu shouted again. Jue struck him yet again.
Hua shouted again. Jue struck him once more. Hua said, "I learned a 'guest-host' phrase from my elder brother, the Third Sage, but I have been completely defeated by you, elder brother.
I pray that you will grant me a dharma-gate of peace and happiness. Jue said, "You blind fellow!
You come here to surrender your defeat. Take off your patched robe; I shall give you a thorough beating!"
Sudden. Under Xinghua’s words, he realized the principle by which the late Master Linji received the staff at Huangbo’s place.
If Han Yue were to realize the principle of Linji receiving the staff, he would understand Xinghua’s point of awakening;
if he understood Xinghua’s point of awakening, he would see the fundamental intent of this humble monk. Thus it is:
"You drink, I drink; you drink the ox, you drink the horse. Herein, guest and host are clearly distinct.
How could there be a "guest within the guest" such that one's name would fall [into error]? Only Han Yue treats "shouting" as shouting and "striking" as striking;

thus his karmic consciousness is vast and茫然 (vastly bewildered), with no fundamental basis to rely upon. Furthermore, how can one blame him for being unable to provide a clear analysis, and instead merely covering it over and suppressing it?

This was likely done to mislead Han Yue, who failed to rely on Linji’s instruction that the distinction between guest and host is the true essence, but instead rolled around exclusively within the "shout" to confuse later generations. This old monk writes this letter...
Entrusting this to Han Yue and entrusting it to Layman Liu. Since Han Yue has also sent a letter, I have again written in response, saying:
"When I, the old monk, ask you, Han Yue: 'Try to leave me aside and point directly to your own present state; apart from that, point out another guest and host for me to see.
You should know that when you question me, the old monk, you are the guest, and my answering and pointing back is the host."
"You are yourself the host. Furthermore, when you were twice summoned to the hall for examination, you were the guest and the old monk was the host;
the old monk was not your equal. You have merely used the "host and guest" dynamic of Linji as a pretext to deceive the common people.
These two accounts have both been carved into a single volume and circulated in the world, with their respective precedents and sequels distinguished within it.
Tang Ji then took what was later and placed it before what was earlier, saying: "In years past, the Old Monk forbade Han Yue, saying:
'Host and guest' refers to you and me. He then took what was earlier and placed it after what was later, recently explaining again:
'Your shout, my shout—shouting at the ox, shouting at the horse—these too are clearly host and guest. Although the Old Monk’s statements occurred at two different times, in reality..."
There is no place where the beginning and end contradict one another. One [aspect] is taken as the prohibition; one is taken as the liberation.
Yet you shift what comes before to what follows, and shift what comes after to what precedes. I do not know what kind of mental activity this Tanji possesses.
Setting aside for a moment the matter of before and after, I, the old monk, simply ask Tanji: if you eliminate the "you" and "I" of every person, then what else would you point to?
How could host and guest be clearly distinguished? If you cannot point them out, do not confuse the fundamental principle. Why is this so?
If Han Yue, Tan Ji, and others were to depart from the "you" and "I" of all people and speak of host and guest separately, they would fall into the calculations of the empty externalists.
Furthermore, according to their own defense, they claim that Sudhana went directly into the great multi-storied pavilion and emerged from samādhi...
Rising up, he suddenly dropped his cloth bag and cast away all the profound and subtle insights he had previously attained, leaving no trace of a single dharma.
Only then did he realize the original face of Sudhana. Yet, are not the ox-heads and horse-heads also his original face?
Since it is said that he cast away all the profound and subtle insights he had previously attained...
Cast it away! Why did Hanyue and the others not, beneath this old monk’s staff, lose their satchels?

Why did they not cut off the ten directions and leave not a single dharma remaining, casting away everything they had previously clung to—the Three Mysteries and Three Essentials, as well as all the guest-host phrases they had learned—casting them all away to the bottom?
It is just like Huayan Puzi, who raised the dialogue on the Four Guests and Hosts. First:
He made one sweeping gesture. After a long silence, he said: "If it were Tao Yuanming, he would have knit his brows and departed immediately.

He then asked Tanji, "What is the meaning of this? Furthermore, Linji himself stated that what the mountain monk has cited here is entirely for the purpose of discerning demons and selecting the extraordinary;
knowing what is heterodox and what is correct, the establishment of the four guests and hosts is specifically for the sake of discerning demons and selecting the extraordinary.
"The demon palaces and the Buddha lands of Tánjì appear simultaneously before me. One may enter the Buddha-land, but one cannot enter the demons.
Such confused talk—without knowing where it began—was met by Linji, who opened his mouth and said:
"Those who study the Way must be extremely careful. You all fail to follow this at all, and instead slander me, the old monk, saying: 'At first...'"
Thus they settle for ignorance; yet when close at hand, they forcibly claim what they do not know to be knowledge.
Their beginning and end are contradictory and inconsistent, showing no regard for future generations. Alas, how painful! I never thought that the Way of Linji would come to such a state.
When I, this old monk, read to this point, I dare not add further annotations, but I too sigh deeply and say: "Alas, how painful!"
I did not expect the Way of Linji to reach such a state.
He addressed the assembly: "Sometimes I first illumine and then act; sometimes I first act and then illumine; sometimes illumination and action occur simultaneously;

sometimes illumination and action do not occur simultaneously. When I first illumine and then act, there are those who are present; when I first act and then illumine, there are those who are present."

The Dharma consists of illumination and function occurring simultaneously. It drives the plowman’s ox; it snatches food from the hungry man; it beats the bone to extract the marrow; it applies needles and awls with piercing force.
When illumination and function differ, there are questions and answers; there are guest and host established; water and mud are blended together; responding to capacities and engaging with beings.
If one is a person of transcendent capacity, before the words have even been raised, they would immediately spring up and go. Even so—
"A mere trifle. He ascended the hall and said: "Upon this lump of red flesh, there is a true person of no station who constantly enters and exits through the gate of your faces.
Those of you who have not yet verified this, look! Look! At that time, a monk came forward and asked, "What is the true person of no station? The Master stepped down.

[The Master] took hold of a monk at his meditation seat and said, "Speak! Speak! The monk hesitated. The Master pushed him away and said, "The true person of no station—what kind of dried piece of dung is that?
He then returned to the abbot's quarters.

Jiù said: "The former master said, 'One must wait for the mind to die before submitting it to execution. One must urgently employ the illumination of the former [mirror] to first capture and then remove its bonds;
briefly employ the lamp of the latter [lamp] to truly illuminate the true tiger of function. It is like a divine physician who scrapes the bone to treat an ailment:
he must see the disease before he applies the blade. If one were to fixate on a single prescription and recklessly apply the needle,"
To "separate" [from attachments] is to add yet another layer of illness. An ancient worthy said: "As soon as there is something held as weighty, it immediately becomes a habitual trap.
Now, the habitual traps of students are manifold, yet the Master’s illumination and application are adapted to the moment. This has been so from the time of the ancient sages.

There are none who are not thus. It is like Jia-shan’s reception of Luo-pu, or Da-jue’s reception of Xing-hua—what are called "the death of the mind and its subsequent execution," or "capturing the subordinate and removing the bonds.

This is because the illness of these two masters lay in having a "single-stump hard Zen" as their sovereign; thus, as soon as they were questioned, they would shout, taking such behavior to be the Way of Chan.
It was simply this. Relying on the two great elders who confronted him with the mirror of the Dharma, he was left with no place to hide or escape;
only then did he beg for his life from me. Thus, with a single word, I cured his chronic ailment—this is what is meant by the phrase "briefly picking up the lamp used later.
He has already refuted this in his letter several times, yet now he attempts to justify himself again, seemingly thinking that it is not so.
"I do not know it. Or, knowing it, I do not practice it. If one says this, the world may be deceived;
but can the successive patriarchs of old be deceived? Can one's own mind be deceived? I say that Master Tiantong’s use of his mind would certainly not be like this.
It is likely that some who seek to cause trouble have borrowed his name to defile the Dharma-gate. As stated in the *Pibushu* (Book on Opening Up): "From..."

The explanation of the four illuminating functions (*zhào-yòng*) states: If persons do not conform to the Dharma, the Dharma is not established; if the Dharma does not rely on persons, it lacks a standard.

When the Dharma lacks a standard, its application has no point of reference; when persons are not established, illumination has no fixed pattern. Because one uses a person to illuminate another person, it is called "illumination."
To regulate people by means of the Dharma is called "function" (yòng). This [usage] follows Linji’s principle that “the person is subordinate and the Dharma is supreme.

Yet, you have given rise to an interpretation based on mere words and fabricated this explanation. Observing your intent, you take the person facing you as the "person" and treat a single, fixed blow as the "Dharma.
Is this not an error? Linji said: "First illumination, then function; there is a person."
To be present yet not be what is called a person—this is because there is a method that functions first and then illuminates. Yet this too is not what is called the method.
If one takes the person who stands in opposition as the person, and takes the single blow of the staff as the method, [one has fallen into a dualistic trap].
As for the statement that "both person and dharma are stripped away," how can it be explained? The former sages said: "It is better not to speak of breaking [the seal].
I have no choice but to provide a single thread of connection. The ultimate reach of Linji certainly does not lie here.
When I, this old monk, observe Tanji rescuing Han-yueh, I wait for his mind to die so that he may be executed; one must urgently employ the aforementioned illumination to first capture him.
Going downward, he releases his bonds; briefly selecting the lamp used later, it truly illuminates the authentic tiger.
Every sentence is Han-yueh’s; he first established a nest and a trap. You say he "scraped the bone to treat the disease," while I, the old monk, say he "dug sores into healthy flesh.

You say he "applied the knife upon seeing the ailment," while I, the old monk, say his eyesight is not at all clear. If you insist on adhering to one side [of this argument], [you will miss the point].
To needlessly apply needle and blade is precisely what is called "discussing the illness of Han Yue.

Why is this? One awaits the death of the mind before inflicting punishment; one first captures it and then binds it. It is not a matter of pre-designating a single method and needlessly adding to another's illness.
As the ancient masters said: "As soon as there is something held as important, it immediately becomes a habitual trap (ko-ju). How much more so when speaking of the habitual traps of practitioners!
"Not one. You have already lost one eye. Furthermore, how can you speak of the Master’s "illumination and function" (zhāoyòng) as being merely "opportunistic"?
Hanyue simply lacks an understanding of the times; therefore, he premeditatedly devised this scheme, claiming that from antiquity, no sage has ever been otherwise.
Is this not to compare oneself with others and falsely accuse the ancient sages? Have you not seen it said: "If you wish to know the Buddha-nature..."
Regarding this meaning, one must observe the conditions of time and season. When the time arrives, it is like suddenly awakening from a delusion, or suddenly remembering what was forgotten.
Therefore, I, an old monk, do not dare to have some separate dharma to falsely impose upon others. The staff and shouts are applied according to the occasion, leaving one vividly alive;
when has Han Yue ever established such a nest to pit later students into? Thus it is said.
The Old Monk struck Han Yue and said, "If you call this 'extremely coarse,' a single blow will send you into hell like a shot arrow.
He further said, "No matter how many skillful means you employ, the Old Monk will give you only an extremely coarse blow."
I strike you to the very end! To teach you that there is no path to heaven above and no door to the earth below;
that there is no place for you to hide and no place for you to escape. When your schemes are exhausted and your strength spent, your own face will be revealed;
only then will you know that this old monk’s single blow is most coarse—a blow with eyes in its head, never striking anywhere else. It was just as when Daqiao at that time—once [the blow fell].
Wuwei struck Xinghua all the way through to the end, yet Xinghua did not recognize where the blow fell; he sought instead another dharma-gate of peace and ease.
Therefore, Wuwei said directly: "You blind fellow! Coming here and exposing your defeat, take off your patched robe and receive a severe beating!
You all followed Xinghua’s lead by shouting "Ho! as soon as he asked a question, taking this to be the illness. In fact, the illness lies elsewhere.
To insist on being the master is like a head stuck in a wooden stake; it is certainly of no use.

The *Pibishu* (Refutation of the Letter) states that "illumination" (*zhào*) is so named because one uses a person to reflect upon a person, and "function" (*yòng*) is so named because one uses the Dharma to regulate a person.

Altogether, these do not go beyond what this old monk answered regarding the inner sanctum in response to Han Yue’s question: "Right now, where are you? This is precisely Linji’s "illumination and function occurring simultaneously."
To drive away the oxen of the plowman; to snatch the food from the mouths of the hungry; to beat the bones to extract the marrow;
to apply needles and awls with excruciating pain. Can you call this "a single peg"? Can you call this "a fixed and determined dharma"?
In short, it is the person who is the dharma, and there is no dharma apart from the person; there is no person apart from the dharma. If one does not [recognize] the person in relation to...
If one were a person, such a method of driving off the ox and seizing the food would likewise have no place to land. Why not look at Linji’s ascent to the hall:
"Upon this ball of red flesh, there is a true person of no station who constantly enters and exits through the gate of your face.
Those of you who have not yet verified this, look! Look! At that time, a monk stepped forward and asked, "What is the true person of no station?"
Ji descended from his meditation seat, seized the monk, and said, "Speak! Speak! The monk hesitated.
Ji pushed him away and said, "The 'true person of no station'—what kind of dried turd is that? He then returned to his quarters. Tell me, what kind of occasion was this?
It was just like when Ding Shangzuo seized Qinshan and said, "Tell me, how much difference is there between the 'true person of no station' and the 'non-true person of no station'?
Speak quickly! Speak quickly! He then seized all of you as well, saying: [The same].
Now tell me: what is the difference between one who is truly called a person and one who is not?
Speak quickly! Speak quickly! If you cannot speak, you shall be struck down by the "urine-in-bed" ghost-child!
In the eighth year of the Xiántóng era, the *dinghài* year, on the tenth day of the fourth month, as he was about to manifest his parinirvāṇa, he spoke this verse of transmitting the Dharma:
"Following the current without ceasing—ask how it is so? True illumination is boundless—explain it to others as such. Free from characteristics and free from name, no one receives it;
Once the 'hair-cutting blade' has been used, it must be sharpened immediately."
Jiū said: "The *Pìshū* (Book of Eradication) explains itself as following the current, flowing on and on without ceasing;
this is intended to mean that the 'Eye of the True Dharma' (*zhèngfǎyǎnzàng*) must not be extinguished. Yet you also say: 'The Eye of the True Dharma has already been extinguished by a blind donkey.
How can these preceding and following statements fail to look upon one another? This old monk, because of Hanyue, speaks of the single circle (○)."
The signs: guest and host roll on and on, straight entering the eyes of Śūla. This is what is meant by: "Following the current without ceasing, one asks how it is;
true illumination is boundless, so explain it to him. Free from signs and free from names, people do not receive it;
having used the 'blowing-off-hairs' sword, one must immediately polish it. Therefore, the old monk says: according to Han Yue’s explanation, this is truly laughable. Not so.

Seeing Linji say, "Who would have known that my Treasury of the True Dharma Eye was extinguished at the hands of that blind donkey?"—if even the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye was extinguished at the hands of a blind donkey, how much more so the various names and forms such as the "one circle," "host and guest," and "Śiva’s eye"?
These are left behind to harm future generations. This clearly shows that outside of Linji, there is no other Treasury of the True Dharma Eye.
The *Zhengfayan zang* (Treasury of the True Dharma Eye) may be transmitted; outside of the Three Sages, there is likewise no other Treasury of the True Dharma Eye to be received.
This is because Han Yue, in his refutation [of the *Zhengfayan zang*], posited a separate "circle" (*○*) outside of Han Yue himself.

His arguments regarding the rolling interaction between guest and host, and his direct entry into names and forms such as the "eye of Śiva," have brought harm to future generations. Now, Tanji has taken the two characters "shàng xiàng" (尚向) and changed them to "yǐ" (已).

Regarding these two characters, you do not consider the momentary nature of self and other. If even the practices currently prevailing in the world disregard the censure of others, how can you wonder at the *Linji Lu*?
It has never contained the phrase "seizing both person and dharma. You have fabricated this in your previous chapter to deceive and mislead me, have you not?
Furthermore, you say: "The school of Dongshan avoids language that is total or absolute; it does not wish to..."

[This constitutes] an offense. Why not look at what Dongshan said: "If one can simply avoid touching upon the current taboo names, that is superior to the talent of those who had their tongues cut off in a previous dynasty.
It is merely a matter of not touching upon taboos; how could there be no such thing as "the present"?
When Caoshan first visited Dongshan, Dongshan asked, "What is your name? Caoshan replied, "Benji (Original Quiescence). Dongshan asked, "And who is that? Caoshan replied, "He is not named."
Dongshan deeply esteemed Benji; however, he did not even grant him the name "Benji. How could there not be that other [name]?
You also said, "The pivot of the teaching values circumvention, for it does not wish to be defiled. Caoshan said: "Ordinary sentiment and the vision of sainthood..."
This golden chain is the profound path; one must directly engage in mutual interpenetration (*huìhù*).

This precisely points to the mutual interpenetration of all mundane and supramundane realms, as well as ordinary sentiments and sagely views, because these defile the body of the self. How could it ever have been taught that one should bring about mutual interpenetration by means of the body?
Chan Master Juefan Hong was one whom Han Yue relied upon as his Dharma-seal successor. His verse on "The Noble One’s Fall" states:
"Born into the family of an emperor, How could there be anything more noble? One naturally wears precious regalia; Looking at it, what cause for alarm or wonder?
According to the line "Naturally wearing precious regalia," he is completely enveloped [in it] yet remains unstained by it; how could there ever be any prohibition or restriction?
You and I, all of us, regarding this matter of our own fundamental allotment, know it exists yet do not grasp it.
You can see for yourselves that you have not yet awakened to your own fundamental allotment; instead, you treat it with surprise and wonder, failing to look upon it directly.

You harbor false notions that "you" and "I" are truly illuminating, calling it merely "true illumination," and never calling it "the Honored and Noble. Furthermore, since you speak of "looking back and seeing," is this not itself true illumination?
Furthermore, you cite the words of Shishuang: "Even if one has never ceased to maintain illumination, it is still the 'outer lineage' of the subject-rank.

To come forward and attempt to grasp true illumination is to remain unaware that from the moment we were born, there has been not even a hair’s breadth of separation between you and me; the numinous light shines alone and brilliantly.
True illumination is boundless; it does not rely upon the mundane or supramundane, nor upon ordinary sentiments or sage-like views, nor upon any names or characteristics.
It is just like a prince who, immediately upon birth, is able to succeed to the lineage—this is called "internal succession" and is termed the "royal lineage.

He is also called a "man of the Way without dependence," for he is utterly and uniquely liberated. He is also called the "true person of no station," entering and exiting through the gate of the face.
Therefore, Linji said: "Only the person who hears the Dharma and has no dependence is the mother of all Buddhas;
thus, the Buddha is born from non-dependence. Furthermore, in an ascending hall discourse, he said:

"Upon this ball of red flesh, there is a true person of no station who constantly enters and exits through the gate of your face. Those of you who have not yet realized it, look! Look! Now, since he says "look," [how shall one look?]
Look! Is this not the unique, true illumination? When Layman Li Ao asked Master Yaoshan, "What are precepts, concentration, and wisdom?
Yaoshan replied, "In my humble abode, we have no such idle furnishings. The layman did not fathom the profound meaning, so Yaoshan spoke again:
"If you, Governor, wish to maintain this matter, you must stand atop the highest peak of all mountains and within the deepest depths of the sea."
The "bottom-line practice" permeates the entire person; you must take responsibility for it yourself. You need not separately emphasize precepts, concentration, or wisdom.
To regard this as something belonging to the inner chambers that one cannot let go of is to allow it to leak into the very body.
When has it ever been pointed out that the Governor is an object of the inner chambers, or that he defiles the entire person? You are merely studying the ancients' talk of the "inner chambers."
"Household goods. When have you ever dreamed of household goods? What object are you pointing to?
By this, not only do you fail to understand Linji’s intent, but you also greatly defile Caoshan. Caoshan said: "Have you not seen Nanquan say..."

Even if you were to achieve tenfold perfection, you would still fall short of the One-Line Path (ekāntamārga) of the Old Master Wang. You must simply ensure that you and I are not separated by even a single thread;
what need is there to speak of eightfold or tenfold perfection? Therefore, Caoshan decisively stated: "This is a truly difficult matter."
Upon reaching this point, you must be thorough and meticulous; only then will you attain clarity and mastery.

Whether in heaven or hell, as a hungry ghost or an animal, you do not shift from your original state in any place; you are fundamentally the same person as before. It is simply that you do not travel the path you once did.
This is what Linji meant by "constantly entering and exiting through the gate of the face"—it means not shifting from one's state in any circumstance whatsoever.
How easy! Are you not the same person as before? Why do you not travel the path of old? It is simply because that old path does not enter or exit through the gateway of the face;
thus, the mind, intellect, and consciousness grasp at one thing and let go of another, shifting and changing at every turn.
Therefore, one cannot attain solitary liberation. If one were to attain solitary liberation, there would be no desire and no dependence.
If one awakens to this lack of dependence, even Buddhahood is unattainable; how could there be further stumps to guard, rabbits to wait for, or wedding garments to recognize?
Yunju Ying said: "If you move, you bury yourself ten feet deep; if you do not move, sprouts grow where you stand.
This means that if you move, you no longer rely on your former self and everything is shifted and changed, which is why you bury yourself ten feet deep.
If you do not move, you rely on your former self and nothing is shifted or changed anywhere, which is why sprouts grow where you stand. Now...
If you transform the "pond" (tan) into the "assembly" (hui), you will experience its utility while on the road;
if you do not so transform it, sprouts will grow right where you stand. To take these sprouts growing in situ as a sickness is to falsely accuse me, Erzhenzhao.

To remain within the "cave" (dong) is defilement. Why not look at the monk’s question to Dongshan: "Among the three bodies, which one preaches the Dharma? Dongshan said: "I am constantly doing so right here."
Is it not the case that you do not point to the place of non-movement? Since you already rely upon non-movement, when a sprout grows right there, what else would it depend upon?

Why then can you not achieve solitary liberation? Is it not like you all, who rely on Linji’s statement that "one phrase contains the three mysteries, and one mystery contains the three essentials," taking this as a substantial dharma? Now, I, the old monk, shall once again rely upon...
Asanga asked Mañjuśrī, "How many people are there in this assembly? Mañjuśrī replied, "Three times three before; three times three after. Asanga could not fathom this.
At that time, he sent the youth Maitreya to escort him out the door. Asanga asked, "Just now you said 'three times three before;
three times three after. How many people does that represent? The youth called out in a loud voice, "Venerable Sir! Asanga turned his head.
He assented. The youth asked, "How many people are there? He then questioned Tanji and others, "How do you understand this?
They instead claimed that Linji’s final instructions must not be misunderstood as referring to the realm of "you" and "I," nor to the person of no-abode who is unconstrained by words and letters.
He then asked Tanji, "If it is not within the realm of 'you' and 'I'..."
If you recognize it, then Linji’s final words at the moment of his passing would be placed in a position of utter uselessness.
Furthermore, for what purpose did he leave these words behind? Yunju Deng said: "It is like two mirrors facing each other;
their lights reflect one another, shining brightly without a trace of artifice. Is this not just as it is? Yet even so, people still call it a matter of reflections. I, the old monk, [say]:...
The Way. I shall wait for you all to shatter the mirror before I will meet you face-to-face.
He said again: "When the sun rises, its light illuminates the world; this clarity is one half. What is that other half? The old monk said:
"I shall wait for the sun to set before we meet. You say that people today have not yet recognized the gate of light and shadow."
To treat matters of the threshold as matters of the interior—how could that possibly work? This old monk truly does not recognize the affairs of the gateway of light and shadow;
there is simply this one old monk. If there were further affairs of the interior to be recognized, how could that possibly work?
Now, Tanji said to my late teacher: "The boundless true illumination is entirely the place of awakening. It is not...
It is merely that he resembles another; it is not that he lacks vision. Furthermore, let us ask Tanji and the others:
To what extent does Han-yue resemble him or not resemble him? Is there yet another true "other"?
For this reason, I, the old monk, rely solely on a most coarse staff to strike Han-yue through to the end, desiring that he may see that there is no second "other" to come.
It can take his place. As stated in the "Chapter on the Perfect Penetration of the Auditory Faculty": "First, within hearing, one enters the stream and loses the object.

This means that the sound which is heard is established by virtue of the consciousness that hears; if one does not become attached to the consciousness of the auditory faculty, then the sound that is the object of entry will naturally vanish.
Therefore, it says: "Entering the stream, one loses the object. To clarify this further, it repeats: [The text continues with the subsequent verses.]
Once that which enters has become still, the two characteristics of movement and stillness clearly cease to arise. As this gradually increases, both the hearing and that which is heard are exhausted.
This refers to the "entry" within the "rescue from the clouds," pointing specifically to the entry of the ear-faculty. Here, "entry" means the entry of awakening;

it signifies that when a student receives a blow [of the staff], they attain a point of awakening and merely enter the stream. Does this not further clarify that Tanji himself had not yet [attained this]?
Having realized the matter beneath the staff, you have intentionally spoken such nonsense; you even dare to falsely accuse Guanyin.

Even if you were to turn back from here and enter ever deeper, as long as you have not reached the source and bottom, it will still merely be a semblance. Old monk, let me ask you, Tanji: [What is it?]
