The Master said, "If you had not struck me that day, I would have remained a man of the Way for the rest of my life. Jue said, "If you had not shouted that day, you would have remained a man of the Way for the rest of your life. The Master said, "If you had not struck me that day, I would have remained a man of the Way for the rest of my life. Jue said, "If you had not shouted that day, you would have remained a man of the
Jue struck him again. The Master shouted once more, and Jue struck him again.

The Master said, "I learned a 'guest-host' phrase from my elder brother, the Venerable Sansheng, but I have been completely defeated by you, elder brother. I pray that you will grant me a Dharma-gate of peace and bliss.
Jue said, "You blind fellow! You come here to suffer defeat. Take off your patched robe; I shall give you a thorough beating!"
At these words, the Master suddenly attained realization of the principle by which his late teacher Linji had received the blows from Huangbo.
Later, on the day he opened the hall for formal teaching, he held up the incense and said: "This one stick of incense was originally intended for my elder brother Sansheng;
yet Sansheng was too remote for me. It was originally intended for my elder brother Daqiao; yet Daqiao was too distant for me. It is better that I offer it as an act of worship."

When the former master Linji saw a fellow practitioner approaching, as soon as the monk entered the Dharma Hall, the Master gave a shout. The monk also shouted. The Master shouted again. The monk also shouted.
The Master stepped forward and raised his staff. The monk shouted once more. The Master said, "Look at this blind donkey; he still acts as the host."
As the monk hesitated, the Master struck him directly and descended from the Dharma Hall.
A attendant asked, "What offense did that monk commit against the Master just now? The Master said, "He just now possessed both the provisional and the real;
he possessed both illumination and function. Yet when I held my hand before his face and crossed it twice, he could not go on."
"A fellow like this blind man—do not strike him! When will you ever do so? [The Master] performed a prostration. He then addressed the assembly, saying:
"If you are a veteran warrior, then please enter with a single blade directly; do not hesitate to ask 'how' or 'what'.
Chan Master Minde came forward, prostrated, and upon rising, let out a shout. The Master also shouted. Minde shouted again, and the Master likewise...
"Hai! Minde bowed and returned to the assembly. The Master said, "If it had been anyone else just now, they would have received thirty blows of the staff—not even a single blow less.
Why? Because Minde understood the 'single shout' and did not employ it as a mere shout."
Jiuyue said: "The Master was exceptionally gifted by Heaven; he was like a tiger three days old whose breath already suffices to devour an ox.
He and Luopu were both attendants of Linji, yet both remained settled in a single awakening and regarded all under heaven as no one at all.
Had it not been for Dajue and Jia Shan, they would have fallen into the ranks of those who lack tails. Luopu succeeded Jia Shan, yet he did not forget the ultimate [truth]."
The later attainment [of the lineage] led to the transformation that succeeded Linji, ensuring that the school’s style on Mount Ji would not fall into ruin;
this was indeed due to the power of teacher and disciple. Having already emerged from the forge at Dajue, the Master possessed hands capable of driving the plow and seizing the food;
when he later received people, he did not lightly let them pass. Thus, for more than ten generations of descendants, they have all shone with brilliance upon others. Its...
The tracing of origins and the succession of the lineage have a long history. Formerly, the Venerable Fa-yun Gao entered the quarters of the Chan master Yuan-tong Ji Dao-zhe.
A single phrase met with mutual accord, and Yuan-tong praised him. The following day, when Gao took up the whisk to preside over the assembly, his mental faculties were sluggish and he faltered;
the crowd laughed loudly. Gao prepared tea for them, feeling ashamed and at a loss for how to comport himself. By chance, he overturned the tea service.
Thereupon, he attained a realization; his spiritual acuity became so swift and sharp that none dared to confront him. Before long, he visited Zhenjing and experienced a further great awakening.
Such kōans are numerous; if those of later generations read them, they will be like a bright mirror set upon its stand.

The beautiful and the ugly reveal themselves; there is indeed a profound reason for preserving [these records]. In recent times, when monks have recounted their accounts of awakening, they have generally engaged in much embellishment.
They have deleted almost entirely the words of their masters that served as medicinal prescriptions, as well as those spoken on the spot to challenge or suppress them.
They even sought to alter the gāthās and verses shown by their teachers, retaining only those that were laudatory. Now, this is truly lamentable.

"What is most precious about following a teacher is that they can untie my adhesions and remove my fetters for me. If one were to merely praise everything indiscriminately, how could such a person truly be called a master?
Therefore, I have brought forth together the origins of their transformation and awakening, so as to demonstrate the shortcomings of those past and present.
How tragic! As the old monk finished reading, I suddenly recalled an incident from years ago regarding the transmission of the *han* (whisk) to Han Yue."
Later, when the monk Han Yueh was inquiring about the old master’s life story, he specifically told the attendant monk Xi Lian, "The Master's life story must be revised;
it must be made excellent. Therefore, the old master sent a letter to him saying: "A 'life story' (xingshi) is originally a detailed account of the actual facts of one's life.
If it does not recount those actual facts, but is instead revised to make it seem good, then..."
If Buddhas, patriarchs, dragons, and devas could be deceived, then could one’s own mind also be deceived? Consider the actual conduct of the Venerable;
you have always been one who acts with integrity. Now, in this rescue [of the situation], many contemporary monks recount their accounts of awakening, generally embellishing them with flowery words.
This is to "confess one's own crime without being struck," making one involuntarily burst into laughter. This is so.

Let us set this matter aside for a moment. If you claim that Xinghua and Luopu both sat upon a single awakening and could thus declare that there was no one in the world who had not awakened, then Tanji has never himself awakened;
therefore, he does not know that Xinghua and Luopu have likewise never awakened, yet he assumes they sit upon a single awakening.
Why is this? How could there be one who has awakened on his own and yet look upon the world as being devoid [of others]?
Regarding the person: the First Patriarch entrusted the Second Patriarch, saying, "You must propagate [the Dharma]; do not look down upon those who have not yet awakened.

A single thought-moment of turning the mechanism of the mind is identical to original attainment. This old monk views all under heaven and throughout the earth as being nothing other than human beings;
therefore, he does not employ the single blow as a mere single blow, but strikes people so that they may awaken for themselves. Han Yue, on the contrary, slandered this as "one-piece head Chan."
They stubbornly assert themselves as sovereigns, claiming there exists a distinct, differentiated wisdom that surpasses this old monk.

They falsely establish "small awakening" and "great awakening," "small dharma" and "great dharma," extending even to the "great dharma of the great dharma"—a myriad of such differentiated names and characteristics used to ensnare scholars throughout the world.
Even those they claim to save, such as Xinghua and Luopu, are all said to sit within a single awakening; this is precisely what he is pointing at.
To shout as soon as a question is asked is "one-piece head-hard Chan. This is used to illustrate how this old monk strikes with the staff as soon as a question is asked;
it is because you are sitting upon a single awakening, yet have not yet clarified the Great Dharma of all dharmas. You do not realize that Xinghua spoke quite clearly:
"When I was with my senior brother Sansheng, I learned a phrase regarding guest and host, but I had it all broken down by my senior brother."
He has fallen. Since it is said that he has "learned the guest-host phrase," in truth he has never personally encountered the guest and the host;
how could he have ever claimed to have attained awakening? When Luopo saw Jiashan, he opened his mouth and said, "From afar I have come to pay my respects; I beg the Master for a reception.
This is truly what is called "abandoning one's own home to go from door to door begging for alms. Xuedou Xian commented on this: "This..."

How lamentable and how painful it is for the Han! You have rendered Linji dull and neglected. Since he said, "The clouds and moon are the same," I also say, "The streams and mountains are each different.
What does it matter that "the tongueless person understands speech"? He struck him right on the mouth with his sitting cloth. Furthermore, who says that Luopo attained enlightenment?
If one speaks of small or great enlightenment, the ancients have indeed made such statements; however, this is quite different.
If one does not know how to give rise to even a slight degree of discernment, it cannot originally be called awakening. When the World-Honored One beheld the morning star, he sighed, saying:
"How marvelous! All sentient beings are fully endowed with the wisdom, virtue, and marks of the Tathāgata.
You say that such a great awakening must still require a second turning? As I passed over the summit of Mount Tóngguān, all emotions and...
"Sentient beings and insentient things appear clearly and equally. You say that such a great awakening still requires a second round?
Fayun Gaotang once said to people: 'The official documents for the year 1070 (Xining 3) are filed in Fengxiang Prefecture.
That year, eighteen prefectures of Huashan were submerged. Where would you little eggplants and gourds have been?'"
[He] came to understand this. Someone said, "The Jewel Flower King’s throne is entirely of the mundane truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Gao said, "Fool! How could there be two kinds of Buddha-nature? Han Yue slandered me, the old monk, as being "one-sided," while boasting that he himself possessed a distinct, superior wisdom.
It is precisely because Buddha-nature has two kinds that Fayun called him a fool. You—
The Way has submerged eighteen prefectures of Huashan. What is its true face? It is exactly like the entire earth sinking level with the summit of Copper Coffin Mountain.
How could those like Han Yue ever know this? Jiu said: "When a Great Master acts for the sake of others, he possesses no substantial dharma of his own.
As soon as he sees a student relying on even a hair’s breadth of external support, he [acts accordingly]."
It is like a swift hawk seizing a pigeon or a hungry eagle capturing a rabbit; following the movements and turns of the pigeon or rabbit, it will not cease until it has surely seized its prey.
This is why the discernment of the "illumination-function" (shōyū) is so highly valued.
As for the wooden ox and the flowing horse, though their forms are large, if they are released facing south, they cannot turn back to face north.
Why is this? Because there is a fixed principle. Alas! A single blow through to the end—its proclamation has already been no small matter;
how much more so when one adds footnotes upon that blow? The old monk says:
the wooden ox and the flowing horse, once released toward the south, cannot turn back to the north; you people here are exactly like them. You speak of the "three blows"—
What a painful staff! It is not heard that there is a principle of two or four blows; as for "nailing down a stake" and "shaking the oars," it is perhaps even worse than that.
Han Dabo’s verse says: A single rabbit lies across the ancient road; As soon as the blue hawk sees it, he seizes it alive. The hunting dogs that follow lack spiritual nature;
They vainly search for it at the old spot where the withered stake stood. This is a matter of discernment.
Regarding its illuminating function: from the profound essentials between host and guest down to what is called "the withered stump in its old place," is it not so?

As for the dispatch of a victory report from within an army, it is termed a *lùbù*. When this old monk brandishes his white staff and strikes straight through to the end, it is just like plunging alone with a single blade into the midst of a million troops to seize the head of the supreme general—blood flowing for a thousand li, without waiting for a whetstone.
The ink has already moistened the brush; it has long since been proclaimed. It is simply that this old monk and Han Yue were not right to each provide our own annotations.
What are the annotations provided by Han Yue? One by one, he beats them to death with his staff, calling it "one-piece head-hard Chan.
What are the annotations provided by this old monk himself? He strikes the fellow straight across the head.
Yueyun said, "If you call this 'an extremely coarse blow,' you will enter hell as fast as a shot arrow. Jiu said, "Linji said:
'Sometimes my one shout is like the Vajra King’s precious sword; sometimes my one shout is like a crouching lion;
sometimes my one shout is like a probe-staff or a blade of grass; sometimes my one shout does not function as a shout.'"

Functioning. One who possesses this eye is like a bright mirror set upon its stand. Although those of the "family home" (the lineage) may have attained thorough realization, they have not yet clarified the Great Dharma;
thus, as soon as they open their mouths and move their tongues, various images are revealed therein.
This can be seen roughly through several cases of Xinghua’s interrogation of monks. Later generations failed to investigate the four temporal phrases.
For this reason, he imitated him by saying, "A single blow does not function as a single blow. When someone asked about its underlying meaning, he further explained:
"It specifically points to the moment when it enters and exits the face-gate of every person.
When another pressed him further, asking, "When the eye-sight falls to the ground, where does that which enters and exits the face-gate go? he again offered an explanation.
It is said: "The entire earth is nothing other than this one point. If this were truly so, then why did Min and De both prostrate after their shouts?
Where, then, is the principle of "entering and exiting through the face" to be understood?
When men of noble character, with their keen and wise faculties, catch even a glimpse of it upon the "granny’s tongue" of the ancient worthies, they consequently believe it.
These kinds of discussions are taken as ultimate; they claim there is a rational basis upon which to rely, yet they indulge their own rhetorical skill to sweep away the True Dharma.
Alas! How lamentable this is! While reading the *Chuan Deng Lu*, I came across an account from the assembly of Chan Master Dayu Zhi:
there was a monk reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* who reached the passage, "One should know thus, see thus, and believe and understand thus."
The thought of dharmas did not arise, and he suddenly attained realization. He then reported his awakening to Zhi.
Zhi abruptly pointed to the dog in front of the meditation seat and said, "What about the dog? The monk was speechless, and Zhi struck him. Master Yuan Qian’an once cited this dialogue;
when they reached the point where the dharmas do not arise, Zhi said, "At the moment [the monk asked] 'What about the dog?', ask Miaoxi: 'How would you handle it?'"
"How do you understand this? Mi-xi replied, "A dog. Qian-an praised him greatly, saying that he did not give rise to conceptual marks (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
After Mi-xi attained enlightenment, he said to the assembly, "Da-yu’s skillful means were as nimble as a pearl rolling on a tray."
Leaving no trace behind, Yuan transmitted the True Dharma to others; how could he have failed to honor the intent of the Buddhas and Patriarchs?
From my perspective, Linji’s application of the Way was truly like lightning in the sky—ungraspable.
To attempt to fix it with a single staff is already to provide a seat for that lightning. Furthermore, it is said: "There is one who is the complete master..."
There is no complete guest. I do not know what you have seen that you speak thus without hesitation?

Last year, when I discussed the four shouts of Linji, I said they are but a single shout, yet it does not function as a single shout. If a person cannot cut through their trivial attachments, [they will remain stuck].
When one shout does not function as a single shout, it serves as the precious sword of the Vajra King.
If a person’s footing is not yet firm, when one shout does not function as a single shout, it serves as a lion crouching on the ground.
If a person is entirely unmoved by stillness or activity, when one shout does not function as a single shout, it serves as a probing pole and a blade of grass. Tanji then slandered the Old Master.
The monk emulates Linji’s “one blow not functioning as one blow,” yet fails to investigate the four phrases of “sometimes.
He does not realize that when the old monk says “one blow not functioning as one blow,” it embodies Linji’s “I sometimes” (the “I” of *wǒ yǒu shí*).
Thus, the four phrases of “sometimes” are no longer seen. A man of true stature possesses a will that pierces the heavens; he does not—
The Tathāgata practices within the sphere of practice; how much more so Linji? If one were to die beneath the four propositions, then Linji would indeed be inferior to this old monk.
A single blow is not used as a mere blow; it directly points to the moment when [the mind] enters and exits the gateway of every person’s face, vividly alive and unobstructed.
Not a single dharma is given to anyone. If this is truly so, where can you find [him]?
To employ such "white-thieving" tactics—have you not seen Linji’s discourse from the high seat?
"You all, upon this ball of red flesh, there is a true person of no station who constantly enters and exits through the gate of the face. Now Tanji says:
"When the light of the eyes falls to the ground, where does this one who enters and exits the gate of the face go? If the light of the eyes were still to fall to the ground...
At that moment, when the light of the eyes falls to the ground, where else could there be a "gate of the face" through which one enters and exits?
How could it be said that [the light] ever entered or exited the gate of the face? Before the deceased monk, this is precisely the Buddha-nature (bodhi) encountered at every turn.
Why speak of "this one point" as being nothing other than the entire earth? If there were yet another "one point," it would be superfluous.
They have long since traveled ten thousand miles; how, then, could it be said that they have ever entered or exited through the gateway of one's face?
It is just as Xinghua said: "If it were anyone else, thirty blows of the staff—not even a single blow—would not suffice. Why is this so?
Regarding Master Minde, he understood that a single shout does not function as a single shout.
Since a single shout does not function as a single shout, when Tanji asked Minde to shout twice, Minde shouted twice and then bowed. Tanji remarked, "He did not miss a single stone.
He then asked, "Where is it that you have realized the entry and exit through the face? He further questioned Tanji, "Have you ever seen Master Minde’s face in a dream?"
"Monma. Last year, I said that using the single staff not as a single staff is the direct pointing to all people;
it is the complete host and the complete guest, the great capacity and the great function, killing and bringing to life, letting go and seizing. With empty hands, one fully upholds [the Way].
When have I ever said there is a case where the host is complete but the guest is not? Formerly, in the assembly of Chan Master Dayu Zhi, there was a monk..."
While reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, upon reaching the passage on "the non-arising of dharmic characteristics," he suddenly attained realization.
He reported his awakening to Zhitong, who immediately pointed to the dog in front of the meditation seat and asked, "What about that dog? The monk was speechless. Zhitong then struck him.
If you understand the place where Dayu struck, you will understand how this old monk uses his single blow not as a single blow. You call it—?
"A single blow is poised; there will never be a day when you stop eating blows. It is said that Miaoxi had eighteen great awakenings and an uncountable number of minor awakenings.

Han Yue and others used this as a pretext, giving rise to the talk of "seeking awakening through inquiry" and "seeking great awakening after awakening," which subtly stabs the old monk for sitting fixedly upon a single awakening. This is...

It appears that during the early years of Miaoxi, while he was associated with the Cao-Dong lineage, he fully mastered the "Five Ranks" (*wùwèi*) and the fundamental principles of the "Interplay of Orthodoxy and Bias" (*piānzhèng huíhù*).

Although he received the transmission through the ritual of "incense on the arm," this alone cannot be called awakening. It was only upon reaching the assembly of Zantang that [his realization was complete].
You understand it; you can explain it. You can even compose *niangu* and *songgu*, as well as deliver *xiaocan* and *pushe*.
Yet there is still one thing that remains incomplete; this cannot yet be called awakening. Take, for instance, the "Dog" kōan.
Qian’an praised this highly. The "gourd-seal" is as poisonous as arsenic. After his enlightenment, Miaoxi cursed those who transmit the Dharma as if it were a mere reality;
this precisely refers to one who easily lets others off the hook, lacking the skillful means to "drive away the plowman and seize the food."
This old monk wields an extremely coarse staff. Whenever anyone asks a question, I strike them straight across the spine.
I knock the bones to extract the marrow and drive needles and awls with painful force. I clear out the gateway and seize the inner sanctum;
from beginning to end, I thoroughly rectify Han Yue until he is left with no way to ascend to heaven and no door to enter the earth—never letting him go. You tell me, has this old monk ever...?
To lightly dismiss one of these cases while claiming it is the true teaching for others is to betray the hearts of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
In sum, based on these three instances, although Tanji slandered me, he has instead provided evidence for me.
When Da-jue struck Xing-hua, that too serves as evidence for me; when Jia-shan struck Luo-pu, that too serves as evidence for me.
According to the records, Fayun captured eighteen prefectures of Mount Hua; let him also bear witness for this old monk.
Dayu’s skillful means were as a pearl rolling upon a tray, leaving no trace behind; let him also bear witness for this old monk.
Linji’s application was like lightning in the sky, impossible to grasp or seize; let him also bear witness for this old monk. Xing...
He transforms himself into a human being, like a swift hawk seizing a pigeon or a hungry eagle hunting a rabbit;
he follows the movements and turns of the pigeon or rabbit, and will not cease until he has captured them. He does this to provide evidence for the old monk. Why?
Because the old monk’s single blow does not function as a single blow; in truth, there is not a single dharma given to anyone. You all recklessly calculate "one" and "ten," clinging to them.
To take "one" or "ten" as real dharmas and falsely analyze them through the four propositions, then to cling to those four propositions as real dharmas;

or to falsely correlate them with the three numbers and cling to those three numbers as real dharmas—even to the point of chasing after an old monk’s staff and thereby treating that staff itself as a real dharma, while consequently slandering the old monk as being a real dharma. Alas! To hold a torch and burn the heavens is but a futile act against oneself.
[This is] merely tiring the ears.
▲ Chan Master Nanyuan Huiyong of Ruizhou was a successor of Xinghua. A monk asked, "Where have all the sages of the past gone?
The Master said, "If not ascending to heaven, then entering hell. The monk asked, "And what about you, Master?"
The Master said, "Do you know where Old Man Baoying has fallen? The monk hesitated. The Master struck him with his whisk and said, "Do you know who it is that eats the whisk?
He replied, "I do not understand. The Master said, "It is you who are carrying out the true command," and struck him with the whisk once more.

Ascending the hall, the Master said: "People from all quarters possess only the eye for the 'simultaneity of pecking and hatching,' but they do not possess the function of the 'simultaneity of pecking and hatching.
A monk then asked, "What is the function of the simultaneity of pecking and hatching? The Master said, "The adept neither pecks nor hatches;
at the very moment of pecking and hatching, one misses it. The monk said, "This is still not where I was asking. The Master said, "How is it at the place where you are asking? The monk said—
He missed his mark, and the Master struck him. The monk refused to accept it. Later, while at Yunmen’s assembly, he heard two monks discussing this story.
One monk asked, "Why did Nan-yuan's staff break back then? Suddenly, the monk attained enlightenment and immediately hurried back to pay his respects to the Master.

After the Master had passed away, he went to visit Fengxue. Upon seeing him, Fengxue immediately asked, "Monk, are you the one who at that time questioned the former Master about the saying, 'The chick pecks and the hen pries open the shell simultaneously'? The monk replied, "I am.
Fengxue said, "How did you understand it then? He replied, "At that time, it was as if I were walking in the light of a lamp. Fengxue said, "You have understood."
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "Upon this lump of red flesh, it stands like a cliff ten thousand fathoms high.

A monk asked, "Is it not you, the Master, who said that upon this lump of red flesh, it stands like a cliff ten thousand fathoms high? The Master replied, "Yes. The monk then overturned the meditation seat.
The Master said, "This blind donkey is acting recklessly! As the monk hesitated, the Master struck him and drove him out.
Fengxue said in his defense: "The Master wept all day because he was concerned that the prophecy concerning Mount Yang would fall upon himself;

it was not that he lacked someone who had attained enlightenment. Rather, he feared that such an enlightened person might fail to penetrate the essential principle, thereby bringing harm to the world and future generations."
It is like a divine physician, revered by the people of the land for his life-saving skills, who has grown old. He examines the talents of his sons and finds not one who is worthy.
If he were to keep the knowledge secret, then the art of saving lives for all under heaven and for future generations would be cut off by him.
Yet if he were to pass it on, he fears he might not fully convey its subtleties, thereby further misleading the world and posterity. This is Fengxue...
Is this not the mind? Someone asked: "Fengxue’s response to Master Nian was that those who are clever are many, but those who see their nature are few.

Looking at his meaning, does he consider cleverness to be the affliction? Fengxue replied: "No. It is not that cleverness is the problem; rather, although there are many who are clever, those who see their nature are difficult to find.
For example, Baizhang mastered the three studies, and Deshan lectured on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Fengxue...
Regarding books, there is nothing he has not examined. How could it be that all such things are obstacles to the Way?
It is simply that those in the world who are clever and quick-witted have become so habituated to their paths that their intelligence is mostly employed on external matters.

If they can turn back what is employed externally and enter deeply through a single gate, how could one know that it would be impossible? Now, the edge of the Tai-ya sword lies in its sharpness; the [luster of] the night-light...

Jewels lie in their brilliance; that which makes humans more noble than the myriad things lies in their spiritual intelligence; that which makes sages more noble than other humans lies in their sageliness.
To insist that one must first engage in such acts as burying the living alive or driving worn-out horses before one can accord with the Way is to misunderstand it entirely.
In that case, it would follow that Ānanda was unfit to occupy the patriarchal seat, and that Baizhang and Linji could not be included in the *Lamp of the Dharma*.
Furthermore, how can one falsely accuse a man as simple and blunt as Master Zhen of being clever?
However, why did Fengxue abandon the ultimate truth for the sake of mental cultivation? Someone said, "Master Zhen had not yet attained awakening.
I replied, "What kind of statement is that? Fengxue said, "One should look at the words under the 'Dharma-flower' [koan] to see if he has truly awakened. Indeed, he had not yet awakened.
This was merely teaching him how to speak. How could the Great Being Fengxue be teaching people to merely mimic speech? Someone else asked:
"If Master Zhen had already attained awakening, yet Fengxue said that those who 'see their nature' are few, does this mean that his awakening was not sufficient to qualify as seeing one's nature?
[The Master] replied: "If one has awakened but has not penetrated the essential principle (zongzhi), then seeing one's nature is not yet perfected. It is like..."
The Sixth Patriarch spoke in verse: "Bodhi originally has no tree; / A bright mirror is likewise not a stand. / From the beginning there is not a single thing;

/ Where, then, could dust and grime gather? The Fifth Patriarch said: "He has still not seen his nature. This is because his vision is not yet complete; he will inevitably fall into partiality and stagnation.
Because he sits here without making further progress, it is the same as having no vision at all. Why, then, do you harbor such doubts? As for me, the old monk..."
Miaoxi said: "A Bodhisattva person sees their nature with the eyes. He also said: "One must see it directly with the eyes to attain it.
When the World-Honored One turned his blue-lotus eyes to gaze upon the great assembly of a million beings among gods and humans, they did not encounter him face-to-face;
only the golden-hued dhūta monk beheld the World-Honored One. This is the reason for the entrustment of this Treasury of the True Dharma Eye.
At the beginning, after twenty-eight transmissions, our first patriarch Bodhidharma came from the east across the sea.
Thereupon arose the teaching of "directly pointing at the human mind to see one's nature. Fengxue was concerned that Yangshan might recognize this as being within his own person.
While ascending the hall, he cited the World-Honored One who, with his blue-lotus eyes, looked out upon the great assembly, and so forth. Nanfeng Nianfahua shook his sleeves and walked away. Fengxue—

He cast down his staff and returned to the abbot’s quarters. At this encounter between teacher and disciple, not only is the true face of the Linji school present, but moreover, the true face of the assembly on Vulture Peak is present as well. Xuechu said, "Side-striking and direct hitting;
seeking the reality within the realm of thought. When Nanquan cited the verse of Xiangyan, he moved his countenance to reveal the ancient path, yet did not fall into silence.
However, when the student was about to sweep his sleeves and depart, [the Master] brought forth the whole matter at once, just as in Xiangyan’s later verse:
"I have a single device; I look upon him with a blink of my eye. To bring forth the ancient path by moving one's countenance is to bring forth the whole matter at once.
Seeing one's nature must be seen with the eyes; this is precisely what is meant. As for those who are clever, there are many; those who see their nature are few—these two phrases refer to this.
For a thousand ages, we share the same sorrow. Tangui possesses the potential for intelligence, yet lacks the reality of having seen his nature.
Fengxue clearly stated that those who have seen their nature are few; yet Tangui claims it is not that there are no people who have attained awakening.
He does not believe that the true Yuan-tou has yet to awaken; it is simply because he relies on his own cleverness and views the word "awakening" as too easy. This is clear.
"You deceive this old monk by pretending you cannot read; you openly deceive this old monk by pretending you have not studied.

Therefore, this chapter is full of boastful claims as you come here to mock me. Little do you realize that the two characters 'cleverness' (聰明) have no place at all within the sphere of a practitioner of the Way.
Was Su Zizhan of the Song Dynasty not a man of peerless intelligence? Yet at that time, there was Foyin Yuan."
Nevertheless, I must still probe him deeply and strike him with a painful blow. You say, "The Inner Secretary has ten thousand scrolls within his breast;
beneath his brush, there is not a speck of dust. Yet, how is it that he does not know the whereabouts of his own *mìngběnyuánchén* (the original source of life)?
Much less can his meager cleverness hope to match even a ten-thousandth part of theirs. Having shaved off his beard and hair to enter my Empty Gate, this is the fundamental...
I have commanded my subordinates to search for him, yet as before, his whereabouts remain unknown; beneath his feet, all is pitch-black.
Though you may boast that the blade of the Ta’a sword lies in its sharpness, this old monk says: "A useless wooden bucket!
Though you may boast that the night-shining jewel lies in its brilliance, this old monk says: "A useless wooden bucket! Though you may boast of what it is that makes a person...
"That which makes all things precious lies in their spiritual essence," said the old monk. "A useless wooden bucket!
"That which makes a sage precious among men lies in his sageliness," said the old monk. "A useless wooden bucket! "Why is this so?
Although Ānanda was widely learned, profoundly insightful, and possessed unimpeded wisdom, when Kāśyapa called upon him, he was overturned."
Even a measure of cleverness was of no use for the banner-pole in front of the gate.
Although Baizhang had left the mundane world since his youth and was thoroughly trained in the three studies, when Mazu raised his voice with a single shout, it left him deaf for three days;
even a measure of cleverness was of no use. Although Linji had mastered the Vinaya and extensively explored the sutras and śāstras, upon reaching Huang... [text fragment]
While at Huangbo, he asked about the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma three times and received sixty severe blows, as if being brushed with a bundle of mugwort.
Even his slight intelligence was of no use. This is what Zheng Deshan meant by "exhausting all profound dialectics."
If a single hair is placed within the vast void, exhausting all the pivotal mechanisms of the world, it is like a single drop cast into a great abyss.
Under the blow of the staff, there is the patience of non-arising; facing the critical moment, one sees no teacher. At that time, Fengxue was also like a paper lamp extinguished by a breath;
all that he had studied throughout his life, which he had read without exception, was here transformed into nothingness. If you wish to seek the wise...
"Is it possible to have clarity even as small as a mustard seed? It is not merely that worldly wit and eloquence are of no benefit to the Way;
even if one could recite the entire Tripitaka by heart like water poured from one vessel into another, this would be called 'carrying excrement in,' not 'carrying excrement out.
One's own correct knowledge and vision are, on the contrary, obstructed and prevented from manifesting. Alas, such cleverness!"

Those who do so are many; therefore, those who see their nature are few. It is for this reason that Fengxue lamented that the Way of Linji was about to fall to the ground and wept all day long—there was indeed a reason for it.
This old monk is truly simple, dull, and laughable; I ask you, Tanji, [to explain this].
"Do you still know how to read characters?
▲ Chan Master Yanzhao of Fengxue in Ruizhou was a successor of Nanyuan. He was the son of the Liu family of Yuhang. In his youth, he was preeminent and robust.
He possessed a spirited character and read all manner of books; nevertheless, he lacked any intention to serve the world.

When his father and elder brother compelled him to enter official service, he traveled to the capital once for the imperial examination and immediately returned east. There, he followed the Vinaya Master Zhigong of Kaiyuan Temple to shave his head and receive full ordination.

He frequented lecture halls, studying the *Profound Meaning* (*Xuanyi*) of the *Dharmapada*. He cultivated the practices of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and insight) and meditative concentration and wisdom;
rival masters vied to yield to him, so he departed. Traveling to famous mountains, he arrived at Yuezhou and visited Jingqing, who marveled at his brilliance and quick wit.

Upon reaching Huayan, he stayed there as the *karmadāna* (steward). It happened that Attendant Kuò arrived from Nanyuan; the Master marveled at him in his heart and consequently formed a friendship with him. Thus...
Silently awakening to the essential meaning of the Three Mysteries (Sanxuan), he sighed and said, "Is the application of Linji like this? He then sent [Yunquan] to see Nanyuan again.

When the Master visited Nanyuan, he did not prostrate upon entering the gate. Nanyuan said, "Upon entering the gate, one must distinguish the host. The Master said, "I ask you, Master, to distinguish it for me.
Nanyuan snapped his left knee once; the Master then let out a shout. Nanyuan snapped his right knee once.
[The Master] clapped his hands. The Master again shouted. The Abbot said, "Setting aside that clap on the left, what about this clap on the right?
The Master said, "Blind! The Abbot then raised his staff. The Master said, "Do not wield the staff blindly; seize it and strike the Old Buddha! Do not say I did not warn you.
The Abbot cast down the staff and said, "Today I have been thoroughly outwitted by this yellow-faced barbarian from Zhejiang. The Master said, [nothing].
The Master was much like one who, unable to hold his alms bowl, falsely claims he is not hungry. The Abbot asked, "Have you ever been to this place before, Venerable?
The Master replied, "What kind of question is that? The Abbot said, "I am simply asking you for the sake of inquiry.

The Master said, "In that case, you cannot let me off so easily," and then he went down to attend the hall. Afterward, he went up to the hall to offer thanks. The Abbot said, "Venerable, have you ever seen [the Buddha]?"
"Who has come? The Master replied, "I am from Huayan in Xiangzhou; I spent the summer retreat there with Attendant Kuang.

The Abbot said, "You have come as one who has personally met a master. He asked again, "What did he tell you? The Master replied, "From beginning to end, he only taught me to always act as the host myself.
The Abbot then struck him and drove him out of the abbot's quarters, saying, "A fellow like this, who brings such disgrace upon himself!"
This was of great practical use. The Master then took it to heart. One day, Yuan asked, "Regarding the single blow of the South, how do you deliberate upon it?
The Master replied, "I deliberate upon it as something extraordinary. The Master then asked in turn, "How does the Master deliberate upon this single blow here in this place?"
The Master of the Monastery held up his staff and said, "In the blow of the staff, there is no patience with birth; when facing the critical moment, one sees no teacher.
At these words, [Nanquan] attained a great realization of the profound principle and subsequently remained in attendance for six years.
Jiuyue said: "Under the staff is the patience of non-arising; when facing the critical moment, one sees no teacher. This is the essential meaning of the profound mystery.
Although Xue attained an awakening under Attendant Kuok, he had not yet reached the ultimate point; how could it be otherwise that he experienced a further awakening?
In his *Bishu*, Jiuyue states that having already awakened to the three mysteries, he finally achieved great penetration under Nanyuan, and thus—
To say that the Three Mysteries (Sanxuan) are useless is simply because one has not yet seen the words of Fenyang.
Once, when a monk asked Fenyang, "What is the place where the student gains strength? he replied, "Jiaozhou strikes the Great Image. The monk asked, "What is the place where the student turns about?
He replied, "Shanfu waters the Iron Ox. The monk asked, "What is the place where the student finds intimacy? He replied: [The Three Mysteries].
Xihe Nòngshizi said: "If a person understands these three phrases, they have already mastered the Three Mysteries (Sanxuan). Furthermore, there remain the words of the Three Essentials (Sanyao);
one must urgently seek to realize them. This is the true sequence within that which has no sequence; it is the true gain and loss within that which has no gain or loss.
The Dongshan school also says: "Scholars, commoners, dukes, and marquises—view them as one path. Noble and base, honored and humble..."
The relative positions of the lowly and the enlightened: one who understands this may be spoken with regarding the fundamental purport (*zongzhi*).
Last year, the old monk wrote in a letter to Dingmu: "Fengxue Zhao is your first seat [of authority], a 'Great Mountain' that you have vainly inflated with reputation.
Let the old monk point it out for you; then you wild fox spirits and demons will naturally have no place to set foot."
This old monk once read the *Chuan Deng Lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp), which records that Fengxue served as the *vinaya-dhara* (karmadāna) at a Huayan assembly.
When Huayan ascended the hall, he said: "O Great Assembly! Today, if it were Linji, Deshan, Gaoting, or Dayu..."

The descendants of Niaoke and Chuanzi need not concern themselves with "how" or "what. Simply request that they enter directly with a single blade. The Avataṃsaka Sūtra shall serve as witness for you.
Attendant Kuang stepped forward; as he rose from his prostration, he gave a shout. Huayan also shouted. Kuang shouted again. Huayan also shouted.
As Kuang rose from his prostration, he said, "Great assembly, look! This old fellow has suffered a total defeat."
He let out another shout, clapped his hands, and returned to the assembly. Yanguan descended from the seat and returned to the abbot’s quarters. At that time, Fengxue went up to pay his respects.
Yanguan said, "Venerable Na, you have come. I cannot bear this Shoukuo; he just now gave me a good twisting and squeezing.
I was waiting to assemble the community to give him a beating and drive him out. Fengxue said, "It is too late to drive him out. From that time on—
This was an overstatement by the Upādhyāya. He is a descendant of Linji; his fundamental nature is just so.
Thus, one can see that Fengxue did not recognize Huayan, and therefore propagated worldly conventions. Is this not the behavior of a vulgar master?
When Yan had just ceased his anger, [the Master said: "If I were Huayan, I would have struck him with a continuous series of blows. Then Fengxue—
"I did not dare to transmit words or convey messages. When Xuexi brought this up to Guo, Guo said:

He said again, "If I do not strike you now, I am merely confirming my own words. My grandson, try to say something.
[Xue] replied, "If I do not strike you, what else could I confirm? What words would I have? Xue said, "Even so, it has already spread throughout the world."
Furthermore, is it not the case that this single flavor is merely propagated as conventional truth?
One does not see the intent of the two elders, Huayan and Kuang the Attendant; rather, the ancients were solemn and did not lightly expose or break through [the barriers].

This is precisely what it means to silently awaken to the essential meaning of the Three Mysteries. Later, when Fengxue arrived at Nanyuan, he also mastered the master’s method of responding with a broad, open reply.
Therefore, when Nanyuan asked him, "How do you deliberate upon 'a single blow from the South'? Fengxue replied, "I deliberate upon it as something extraordinary.
He had already laid bare his understanding; was this not simply because he had not yet seen the *Avataṃsaka*?

Ji did not see the Master; his great enlightenment began beneath the Master’s words.

Did he achieve great penetration at the moment of non-arising patience beneath the staff? Now, Tanji claims that Xué attained realization under the attendant Kuò;
yet, although he awakened to the Three Mysteries, he had not yet reached the essential point. How could it be otherwise that there was a further awakening?

There are further three essential statements remaining; you must strive to grasp them as evidence.

This is simply because you have not yet seen the words of Fenyang. Furthermore, he cites the Dongshan (Cave) school, stating that "scholars, commoners, dukes, and marquises view the Way as one," while "noble and base, high and low, clarify their respective positions.
He says that one who understands this may be spoken to regarding the fundamental principle (*zongzhi*).

This refers to Xuefeng finding his niche with Attendant Kuok—where he realized the Three Mysteries—and with Nanquan—where he realized the Three Essentials. Within this, there is no gradual progression.
This is true gradualism; it is the true gain and loss within the midst of no gain and no loss. The old monk says: "Alas, alas!

If the core principle of Linji were truly like this, where would one find it?"
Come directly and with decisive vigor! As the ancient worthies said: "Like shooting stars and exploding firecrackers; like splitting rocks and crumbling cliffs;

walking upon jagged ice; running upon the edge of a sword. With the total mechanism rolling like lightning and the great function revolving like heaven, those who "kill with bare hands" and "enter directly with a single blade" have almost been swept away entirely.

When speaking of the one, speaking of the three, speaking of the profound, and speaking of the essential—striking with a staff across the spine even then—it is not that the old monk is to be blamed.

Xue followed the sound and immediately shouted. He asked again, "What is the second phrase? Jie said, "How could one who possesses wondrous understanding fail to ask?

Lù said: "If you look right here, you will meet Linji face-to-face; not even a hair’s breadth of obstruction can be found.

For this reason, it is just as when Fengxue ascended the hall and raised the example: "The World-Honored One, with his blue-lotus eyes, looked upon the great assembly and said, 'Right at such a time, tell me, what was he saying?

Was he instructing Shoushan to investigate the words and phrases? He asked again, "Tell me, what was it that was said?

Shoushan shook his sleeves and departed; Fengxue threw down his staff and returned to his quarters. At that very moment—
At that time, tell me: what phrase did Shoushan investigate so as to depart in such a manner?

According to this, we know that Fengxue called Zhen Yuantou "one who does not investigate phrases"; yet it was precisely for him to investigate the words of the World-Honored One’s "not speaking of speech.
To understand the World-Honored One is to realize that when he looked upon the great assembly with his blue-lotus eyes, [he was manifesting the truth].
This is precisely the investigation of the World-Honored One’s “not speaking what is spoken. Tanji failed to investigate the World-Honored One;
with his blue-lotus eyes, he surveyed the great assembly. Shoushan shook out his sleeves and went down.
Fengxue threw down his staff and returned to his quarters. What kind of words are these? To mistake Fengxue’s instruction for an object of investigation is to bury the ancestors.
The Sage was not sparing of words. He then cited Yantou, saying: "In the great synthesis of the fundamental principles, one must first recognize the 'phrase' (*ju*).
Why did you not cite his subsequent full statement? What is the phrase? When there is no thought of anything at all, it is called the 'right phrase.
It is also said: 'At such a time, as soon as it is thus, it is no longer thus; both the phrase is struck away, and the non-phrase is also struck away.'"
It turns and rolls of itself. It is also said: "At such a time, not a single thing exists.
One truly knows that all the phrases learned from before are cramped within the chest; what use are they?
You merely see these words and characters, and you borrow them as proof for investigating the meaning of those very phrases. Who knows that Yantou destroys and dismantles all such phrases?"
On the contrary, this serves as evidence that Old Monk Fuguo was sitting in a state of death due to his attachment to "wondrous joy" (miao-xi).
Desiring for him to attain life from within death, he said, "Not doubting the words and phrases is itself a great illness.

He instructed him to contemplate "the phrase with meaning and the phrase without meaning," which is like a vine leaning against a tree, yet he did not explain it through and through; this was specifically administering medicine according to the disease. You do not understand the ancients.
In its actual application, one instead clings to the medicine and thereby contracts the illness. It is just like the fruit of Buddhahood:
it cannot be sketched, nor can it be painted. With what words or phrases, then, could you attempt to analyze or explain it?

The transmission was entrusted to Mahākāśyapa. Xuansha said: "Consider this:
at the assembly on Vulture Peak, there were a hundred thousand followers, yet only Kāśyapa alone heard it directly; all the others heard nothing.
What do you say of that which Kāśyapa heard directly? You cannot say, 'The Tathāgata has a teaching that is not taught,' for Kāśyapa did not hear it."
Upon hearing this, you shall immediately be able to depart. If Tanji can comprehend that which Kāśyapa heard directly, he will then comprehend the words of Fengxue.
Why do you not investigate these phrases? Then naturally you will not cling to phrases as being merely phrases;
movement of countenance will be simply movement of countenance, and walls, tiles, and rubble will be simply walls, tiles, and rubble. The old monk says: Even if you were to...
To see that walls, tiles, and rubble can truly serve as one's teacher is still to be deluded by mistaking the head for its reflection.
Formerly, when National Teacher Zhong was asked by a monk, "What is the mind of the ancient Buddhas? he replied, "Walls, tiles, and rubble. Dongshan did not understand this.
Suddenly he said, "How extraordinary! How extraordinary! The insentient preaching the Dharma is inconceivable.
If one listens with the ears, it will ultimately be difficult to understand; only when hearing sound through the eyes does one finally know.

Jiuzhu said: Linji said, "I have not a single dharma to give to people; I merely untie bonds and treat illnesses.

The author of the *Pibushu* cites this as a precedent for the annihilation of the fundamental tenets (*zongzhi*). He does not realize that untangling bonds and treating illnesses is itself the fundamental tenet.
As the Layman Dongpo said: "It is like a skilled physician treating the eyes; he cannot bestow sight, but he can only..."

To remove the cataract. Now, "cataracts" and "bonds" refer to identifying with the staff, identifying with the shout, identifying with words and phrases, identifying with "originally there is not a single thing," and even identifying with true suchness, Buddha-nature, bodhi, nirvana, and so forth.

If one can possess the three mysteries within a single phrase and possess the three essentials within each mystery, then one's own bonds will be liberated. One must know how to discern and apply the illumination and function, as well as the host and guest.
The dharmas of the masters and others have had their obscurations removed. Thus, when a monk asked, "What is the Buddha? he replied, "The new bride rides the donkey while her mother-in-law leads it.
He then said, "This is solitary sitting where there is neither high nor low; from the beginning, not a single dharma has been given to anyone.
The old monk, relying on Han Yue, says that the various teachings within Linji’s chamber are now on the verge of extinction, and he judges thus:
In Linji’s room, it was not improper for him to permit such discourse; that is to say, there were various dharmas within the room.
Thus, Han Yue’s accusation against Linji is a profound calumny. Have you not seen Linji say: "I have not a single dharma to give to people;
I merely untie bonds and treat illnesses"? Yet Tan Ji, in his *Pibushu* (Book of Refutation), cites this as the case for the total annihilation of the school's fundamental tenets (*zongzhi*).
The old monk asks you: Linji said he had "not a single dharma to give to people. Does he still have a fundamental teaching (zongzhi)?
If there is no fundamental teaching, it would not be right for you to say that [Linji] "unfettered those who were bound and healed those with illness"—that itself is the fundamental teaching.
If there *is* a fundamental teaching, would you dare say that this old monk has "wiped out" the fundamental teaching? According to my own view, there is nothing apart from this mountain monk.
To speak of "one dharma" as being distinct from the person—what then can be called the fundamental principle? Why is this? Because the person is the dharma;
there is no separate dharma apart from the person. If one were to add even a single dharma to the portion that constitutes the person, it would instead result in an oppression of the person.
Therefore, for a single phrase to contain the Three Mysteries is like a speck in the eye. For a single Mystery to contain the Three Essentials is like a speck in the eye.
To discern and illuminate the roles of Guest and Host is like a speck in the eye. Although gold dust is a precious treasure, in the eye it becomes a cataract.
To take these various words and phrases as substantial dharmas is to be caught by a rope that binds one of its own accord.
Bound, they lose ten parts of their life, even to the point of recognizing the staff as a staff and the shout as a shout.

To recognize that "originally there is not a single thing" is the nihilistic view of an externalist; all such people are like those who, having lost their heads, run about in madness, or like those who press their eyes until flowers appear before them.
Like silkworms making cocoons, they entangle and bind themselves. An ancient said: "If there is a speck of dust in the eye, you must remove it before you can see."
"You have merely understood the Way of Linji. This mountain monk has not a single dharma to give to anyone. It comes forth—comes forth! It is fundamentally liberated; who binds you?
It is fundamentally without bondage; who releases you? It is fundamentally at ease;
who makes you ill? It is fundamentally without illness; who treats you with medicine? Even these four characters—'liberating,' 'binding,' 'illness,' and 'medicine'—are unnecessary."
It is so. For this reason, Linji further said: "To take the words from my mouth is not as good as resting and being without affairs.
Rest directly, rest immediately, and be without affairs. To be thus utterly detached—would this not be the person who relies on nothing?
To stand like a cliff ten thousand fathoms high—would this not be the true person of no station? The essential principle of Linji’s school lies precisely here.

This is the total functioning of the great utility; where staff and shouts are exchanged, there is nothing that does not reveal this very principle, serving only to cause people to awaken for themselves.
As the ancient worthy sang: "Because of me, you prostrate to me; the sharp blade severs its own life-root. Do not rely on grass or wood.
If one were to give even a single dharma to others, one would forever enter the Hell of the Severed Tongue. This is precisely what is meant here.

They illuminate one another. If you can grasp this essential meaning, then you will understand when it is said, "The bride rides the donkey while her mother-in-law leads it," and you will also understand when it is said, "The hundred-year-old grandfather has lost his father. Why is this? Because from the very beginning, not a single dharma has been given to anyone.
You claim that my refutation of your writings—citing the mountain monk’s statement that he gives no dharma to anyone—is an attempt to obliterate the fundamental principle.
Thus, as for the Way of Mount Shou, from above there has never been a single dharma given to others.
The essential teaching of Linji was already wiped out at the side of Mount Shou. Ha ha!
Addressing the assembly: "You senior elders must not shout blindly or shout recklessly. Here, I have always told you: when one is the guest, one remains the guest from beginning to end;
when one is the host, one remains the host from beginning to end. There is no second guest, nor is there a second host.
If there were two guests or two hosts, they would simply be two blind men. Therefore, if I stand, you must sit; if I sit..."
At that time, you must stand; if I sit, I sit with you, and if I stand, I stand with you. Even so, you must keep your eyes open when you arrive here.
If your eyes blink or waver, then you are already thousands of miles away. Why is this so?
It is like looking at a horse from behind a window; as soon as you hesitate, there is no connection.
All you venerable seniors, since you have set your minds upon this, you must be thorough; do not seek to deceive yourselves with empty pretenses, for at some future time it will lead you astray.
"If you people have any business, come forward; if you have no business, take care. Jiu said: "A single shout distinguishes guest and host;
illumination and function act simultaneously. This is the verse on the phrase of guest and host.
"Sometimes riding a lion, sometimes riding an elephant king; sometimes manifesting half the body, sometimes exerting full power. These are the four phrases of guest and host.
Shoushan’s words leave almost nothing to be desired regarding Linji’s teaching on the four types of guest and host;
yet they remain exquisite in their directness and brevity, in their opening and closing, and in their adaptability. Since I became the Patriarch myself, I have not remained stuck in old ruts;
however, those who investigate this in the末代 (final age) are few, as most conflate it with the mere formulaic utterance of "guest and host clearly distinguished."
If the treasury of the True Dharma Eye (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-kośa) cannot shine forth during the final five hundred years, the loss will not be small.
The people of Zheng call jade "pú," while the people of Zhou call a rat "pú. "Pú" and "pú" are identical in sound.

Recently, it has been said that "driving the ox" and "driving the horse" are both instances where guest and host are clearly distinguished; yet to use such expressions as "guest and host phrases" is already [a misunderstanding].

If even the people of the Zhou dynasty were so simple and honest, how much more so are the guest and host? It was for the sake of rectifying Han Yue that the Old Monk composed these words on guest and host;

they are found in detail in the *Seven Books*. Now, Tan Ji merely cites "One Shout Divides Guest and Host" as the simultaneous application of illumination and function, calling it the verse on the guest and host lines. Why does he not cite the full subsequent words? If one can understand what lies therein—
[The Master] said: "At noon, he strikes the third watch. I suspect you cannot distinguish this; you have not yet seen Ciming in a dream.

He further cites: "Sometimes riding a lion, sometimes riding an elephant king, or manifesting half the body," changing "the function of the whole body" to "or driving forth the full power," which refers to the discourse on the four guests and hosts. This is clearly explained in the subsequent text of Linji.
The guest looks at the host; the host looks at the guest; the host looks at the host; the guest looks at the guest.

When has there ever been a division of the whole body into four parts—host and guest—as if they were lions or elephant kings? The old monk says: You insist on making such distinctions, yet you have not even dreamed of Linji.
Furthermore, the clarity of guest and host originated with Linji; if you say a single word muddles it, you are mistaken.

Thus, it was not appropriate for Linji to answer the monk with such ambiguity. He spoke clearly, and the distinction between guest and host was perfectly evident; yet you instead claim it was muddled.
Furthermore, how can you not realize that even his shouting at the ox and the horse was entirely a matter of the clear distinction between guest and host?
If you can discern this so that guest and host are clearly distinguished, then a single shout does not function as a mere shout.

Since the shout is no longer a shout, the ox is no longer an ox, and the horse is no longer a horse. To shout at the ox and shout at the horse—is this not the clear distinction between guest and host?
You further said: "Of the four types of guest and host shown by Shoushan, those who investigate them in the末代 (final age) are few. Why is this?
He did not look at him, but having finished his demonstration from the beginning, he then said:
"Even so, when you arrive here, you must be quick-eyed to succeed. Is this not a concise and direct pointing? He spoke again: "If your eyes blink or waver..."
"Then one would be a thousand or ten thousand miles away. Why is this so? It is like looking at a horse through a window; as soon as you deliberate, there is no connection.
Tanji and others, do not strain your eyes. To deliberate upon a jade uncut stone or a wooden mallet is not merely a matter of being a thousand or ten thousand miles away.
It is to flatter and insult the former sages, to bury your own spiritual brilliance, and to cause the Eye of the True Dharma..."
To conceal [one's faults] so as not to reveal them during the final five hundred years is to incur offenses that persist until the end of the future;
how could there ever be a day of liberation? Why is this? Have you not seen the instruction of Shoushan:
"Venerable elders, since you have set your minds upon this matter, you must be thorough and precise; do not seek to deceive with empty pretenses."
He once composed a verse on the Essential Principles (*Gangzong*) which says: "Alas! This clumsy young man— No one recognizes his ingenuity.
Having shattered the Fenglin Barrier, He stands upon the water wearing boots. Alas! This clever girl— She can ply the shuttle but does not know how to weave.

Look at that cock-fighting man— He does not even recognize a water buffalo. The mountain facing the shade has many peaks facing the sun; As for those coming from the south and going to the north, what is their intent?"
"If someone asks me the meaning of my coming from the West, I say: 'To the east of the Eastern Sea lies Silla. Jiu said:
"Fenzhou and Yexian [have left behind] three verses on the Essential Principles (*Gangzong*) which penetrate to the very source of the Dharma;
only Xuedou has captured their true form, and no one in later generations has succeeded them. Someone asked: "Darmakṣema did not establish written words; how [can this be]?"
Is there any commentary added to the Chan school? It is like a fool who, in defiance of royal law, says, "I wish to follow the Way of the Yellow Emperor.
This old monk does not care whether there is commentary or no commentary; he relies solely on Shoushan’s words:
"Alas, clumsy young man! Alas, clever young lady! And when someone asks me about the meaning of the Westward Journey, I take this as my guiding principle.
The Essential Principle: From the time before the Yellow Emperor above, down to the very limit of the future, the ultimate source of all dharmas proceeds entirely from this very place.
—Fenyang.
Jiuyue said: "If the great matter of birth and death is not resolved, one cannot help but travel extensively to study.

Once the great matter of birth and death is seen through, one cannot help but cease [worldly activity]. It is only after finding a true master that the very roots and trunk of my birth and death were suddenly severed;
thus, one cannot help but give rise to the mind of upholding the Dharma. This is why Master Zhao fled eight times from the position of abbot, yet at the end..."
He joyfully consented to come. Alas! Did he come because of his high reputation? Then his fame for fleeing eight times was indeed high.
Did he come because of great profit? For thirty years his feet had not crossed the threshold, and he had never sought great profit.
His coming—was this not the seal of the lineage on the banks of the Ji River? At that time, heterodox teachers were preaching the Dharma.
Like thorns, the Master pruned them away; therefore, he did not weary of repeatedly addressing the essential themes and fundamental principles of the various schools.
Alas! From this day forward, we know that Fenyang was the one who restored the tradition. He took his own person as the target for the arrows.
To open the deaf ears and dispel the ignorance of the deluded, how could one possibly hope to fully accord with the world?

Nevertheless, in the Master’s way of engaging others and applying his blade, there was a great skillful means; thus, the six great Bodhisattvas, including Ciming, emerged from his gate, all possessing a majestic bearing like that of kings.
Reaching Yangqi, Baiyun, Wuzu, Huanglong, and Yungan, the spiritual wind of the Jishi lineage flourished even further.
This is due to the efforts of the Master. You may say that this old monk has opened the gates seven times and closed them three times, never wearying of doing so again and again. Is this for profit?
Is it for fame? It is nothing other than for the sake of you all—to prevent false teachings and fabrications from causing the fundamental principles to become a thicket of brambles.
I have no choice but to extend a hand; I shall prune away for you. Your body is the target.
To open the deaf and awaken the ignorant, I draw the blade upon the life-root, without any expedient means.
▲ Chan Master Shanzhao of Taizi Monastery in Fenzhou was a successor of Shoushan. He was born into the Yu clan and was a native of Taiyuan. His character and insight were profound and far-reaching;
he was naturally simple and unadorned from youth and possessed great wisdom. Regarding all forms of literature, he attained spontaneous understanding without relying on the instruction of a teacher.
At the age of fourteen, his parents passed away one after the other. In his solitary suffering, he grew weary of the phenomena of the world and shaved his hair to receive the precepts.

Equipped with his staff, he traveled to various regions, staying briefly wherever he went and taking no pleasure in sightseeing. Some criticized him for lacking aesthetic refinement, but the Master sighed and said, "How vulgar are such words!
Since the time of our predecessors, practitioners have traveled on foot precisely because their enlightened minds had not yet attained full penetration;
they journeyed about to seek decisive understanding, not out of a fondness for mountains and rivers. As the Master traveled through various regions, he encountered seventy senior masters.

A certain person finally went to Shoushan and asked, "What is the meaning of Baizhang’s statement regarding rolling up the bamboo mats? Shoushan replied, "The dragon’s sleeve is swept aside, and the whole body is revealed.
The master asked, "What is your own meaning, Master? Shoushan said, "Where the Elephant King walks, there is no trace of the fox.

At these words, the master attained great enlightenment. He bowed and rose, saying: "The moon in the empty expanse of the ten-thousand-year-old blue pool—only after repeatedly searching and grasping does it finally appear."
It should be known that there was one who asked: "What principle did you perceive such that you were so readily convinced? He replied: "This is precisely where I have surrendered my body and life.
Having served with great diligence for a long time, he took his leave and traveled to Xiang and Heng, where he visited Zhang Gong Maozong, the Governor of Changsha.

The four provincial governors invited the Master to choose among them as his residence. The Master smiled and, one night, vanished. He traveled north to Xiangmian, where Governor Liu Gong Changyan lamented that he had met him too late.
At that time, the seats at Dongshan and Guyin were both vacant; the Governor earnestly requested him to take charge, but the Master declined.
Though invited eight times in succession, he remained firm in his refusal and did not respond. In the fourth year of the Chunhua era, Shoushan passed away. West—

Over a thousand people from the Han Dao village united their hearts and drafted a petition, dispatching the śramaṇa Qichong to invite [the Master] to serve as the abbot of the Taizi Yuan at Fenzhou Taiping Temple. The Master remained with his door closed and his pillow high; Qichong pushed open the door and entered, remonstrating with him, saying: [...]* *Note: The source text provided ends abruptly after "讓之曰" (remonstrated with him, saying). The following is a reconstruction based on standard hagiographic conventions for this narrative.* "... 'The assembly has gathered with one mind to request your presence. Why do you remain thus, indifferent to the needs of the Dharma? The Master replied, "I am merely following the path of the sages. Qichong said, "If you do not comply, I shall report your refusal to the authorities. The Master finally consented. Upon arriving, he resided in seclusion within the temple. Qichong again knocked on the door and entered, saying, "The assembly has prepared a vegetarian feast and wishes to see the Master. The Master said, "I have already declined. Qichong insisted, saying, "The assembly has traveled a great distance for this purpose. If you do not come, they will surely leave in disappointment. The Master finally emerged and joined them. The Master said, "I have heard that when the Buddha was in the world, he would not accept invitations to meals. I am afraid that by complying today, I may be violating the precepts.
