"The great matter of the Buddha-Dharma is at stake; the minor details of quiet withdrawal are of no concern. Fengxue feared that the prophecy would come true and that the fundamental tenets would perish.
Fortunately, there was my late teacher, but he has already passed away. You are one who possesses the strength to shoulder the Great Dharma of the Tathāgata;

at such a time as this, how can you wish to sleep peacefully? The Master started up in alarm, took Cōng’s hand, and said, "Had it not been for you, I would never have heard these words. He then urged him on.
He prepared his final arrangements and said, "I am going. Once he arrived, he sat in meditation upon a single mat for thirty years, never crossing the threshold of his room.
The monastics and laypeople of the world looked up to him with such veneration that they did not dare address him by name, collectively referring to him as "The Master of Fenzhou."
Ascending the hall, he addressed the assembly, saying: "Now, those who preach the Dharma must possess the Ten Wisdoms Identical with Reality.

If they do not possess these Ten Wisdoms Identical with Reality, they will fail to distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox, and will be unable to differentiate the monastic from the lay. They cannot serve as eyes for gods and humans to judge right from wrong.
It would be like a bird flying through the sky with broken wings, or an arrow shot at a target with a severed string; because the string is severed, the shot fails."
If it is not centered, the feathers will break and the arrow cannot fly through the void. When the string is taut and the feathers are firm, the arrow and the void both penetrate each other.
What is "the ten wisdoms being identical with reality"? I shall point this out for you all, venerable elders: first, identity of substance; second, identity of the Great Matter.

Third, sharing the same companionship; fourth, sharing the same true resolve; fifth, sharing the same universal pervasiveness; sixth, sharing the same fulfillment; seventh, sharing the same gains and losses;
eighth, sharing the same birth and death; ninth, sharing the same roar; tenth, sharing the same entry. It is further asked:
With what kind of person does one share the same entry? With whom does one share the same roar? What is this shared birth and death? What is this shared gain and loss?
Which one is the same in its full possession? What is it that is the same in its universal pervasion? Who possesses the same true resolve?
Who is able to participate as a fellow-student in this totality? Which one is the same in the Great Matter? What object is the same in its single substance? Is there anyone who can point it out?
To those who can point it out, I shall not withhold my compassion. If you cannot point it out, you have not yet attained the eye of study. You must discern this with all earnestness.
One must recognize right from wrong; the true face is present before you—it cannot be maintained for long.
Be careful. Jiu said: "Juefan replied to the Gentleman Wujin: 'The Ten Wisdoms Identical with Reality and the Three Mysteries share the same mechanism.
He then composed a verse, saying: 'The Ten Wisdoms Identical with Reality—the true face is complete; Among them, one wisdom is the root.'"
Yuan: "If a person wishes to see the Old Man of Fenyang, he must split the Three Mysteries into two sides. As for the meaning of "splitting," it is like adding the eyes to a painted dragon;
it cannot be communicated through words or discourse. The *Pibushu* states that since they have already been split, [the meaning is thus revealed].
"In future generations, there shall no longer be the Three Mysteries (sanxuan). What kind of talk is this? I have observed the venerable elders of recent times;
as soon as they open their mouths, they revile intellectual understanding (*zhijie*). Yet when one probes the depth of their realization, it should be like the lion king:
with a single roar, standing ten-thousand fathoms tall. Now, however, they are stubbornly convinced that the Three Mysteries can be used to split things apart. This is..."
"To take a lump of mud and fashion it into a drum to represent the Three Mysteries (san-xuan)—reading this, I could not help but burst into laughter.

The seventh letter cites Juefan’s verse to remind Han Yue that if one has already 'split open the Three Mysteries into two sides,' how can there be any such real dharmas as the Three Mysteries and Three Essentials? Tan Ji says that the meaning of 'splitting open' is beyond verbal discourse."
Regarding "penetration": can it be said that the Three Mysteries and Three Essentials alone constitute penetration?
Since they cannot be described as penetration, one must not take the Three Mysteries and Three Essentials to be substantial dharmas.
Based on this, how could you ever produce the meaning of Old Monk [Linji]’s realization that Juefan [Huihong] shattered? It was because a monk asked Linji about "guest" and...
Main sentence: He had always made his living on the basis of the host and guest. Just as he was about to answer the monk, he suddenly perceived it clearly within the very context of host and guest.
Only then did he realize that he had been misunderstanding host and guest all along.

By this analogy, he understood that the Three Mysteries and Three Essentials were provisional and not ultimate. Consequently, there arose the "fine examination" which is the mechanism for trapping the tiger.
This is precisely what is meant by the verse on "suddenly seeing the principles of the Three Mysteries and Three Essentials. Han Yue and others merely pursue dead lumps of earth;
they have searched through all the three dharmas of past and present, engaging in forced interpretations and artificial combinations to pass them down to one another.
Is this not to say they have been deceived by his tongue? If he truly recognized the Three Mysteries and Three Essentials as substantial dharmas, [he would not have acted thus].

Who would dare to write the two characters "split" (pò)? It is simply that he was not right to be so greatly alarmed and treat it as a minor marvel, saying, "I suddenly see the principle of the Three Mysteries and Three Essentials.
This has deceived all of you by no small measure. You, on the contrary, claim that by believing in the Three Mysteries one can "split" [them];
this is to take a lump of mud and a clay drum for the Three Mysteries. The Old Monk says: "The Three..."
"Xuan is precisely a mud ball or an earthen drum; it is simply that you cannot split it open.
If you can split it open, you will naturally stand forth in full majesty, alone revealed—without support and without reliance—just like this old monk letting out a roar of 'Zha ya!
and standing ten thousand fathoms high. If you cannot split it open, you will inevitably fall into making a nest within the Three Mysteries and Three Essentials."
He made a mortar. [The monk] was astonished, crying out, "How can an old monk like you open your mouth and immediately scold me? Do you think you understand?
"If you wish to fathom what I have realized and awakened to," he replied, "I guarantee that you will not find it even in a donkey's lifetime. It is solely the meaning of being split asunder.
If it were like painting the eyes on a dragon, it might indeed be something you could speak of. Why is this? Because with a single blow of the staff, I would strike him dead and give him to the dogs.
"Son, eat! Yunmen said this to bestow the "eye" upon the World-Honored One; yet here there is still a Patriarch.
"Bring him here and let me wash his feet," Xuedou said to bestow the "eye" upon Bodhidharma.
Today, I shall not only smash the Three Mysteries and Three Essentials into pieces, but will take them outright, tie them into a single bundle, and throw them onto a heap of refuse.
For my sake, Linji of seven hundred years ago has pointed out the radiance that shines upon heaven and earth.

Jiu said: "The Master also had another verse which says: 'The Three Mysteries and Three Essentials are difficult to distinguish; when one attains the meaning and forgets the words, the Way is easy to approach.
A single phrase clearly encompasses the myriad phenomena; on the Double-Ninth Festival, the chrysanthemums are fresh. There is yet another verse.
It is said: The first mystery: The Dharma-realm is vast and boundless; the myriad phenomena of the universe are all perfectly contained within the mirror.
The second mystery: The World-Honored One questioned Ānanda; the one of great learning answered according to the facts, responding to the capacity of the vessel with its squareness or roundness.
The third mystery: Directly appearing before the Ancient Sovereign, beyond the four propositions and the hundred negations. When Lü Zhi questioned Fenggan, he then said:
This is the verse on the Three Mysteries. What is the essential meaning of these Three Mysteries?
You must resolve this with absolute clarity; do not merely speculate in vain about the empty air, claiming, "I have personally attended upon the Master."
"Tell me! You are a liar who speaks empty falsehoods; the day will come when you shall be struck with an iron staff. He then wrote in rebuttal:

"The Three Mysteries and the Three Essentials are nothing more than the words spoken during a single occasion of Linji’s formal lecture. At that time, there were those who clung to these as the fundamental tenets;
therefore, Fenyang composed a verse to warn them, saying: 'The Three Mysteries and Three Essentials are difficult to distinguish... etc. Not so.

I do not know what sources you have consulted in the *Bishu* to arrive at this assertion. If the verse were identical to the admonition, it would be improper to divide them and treat the Three Mysteries (Sanxuan) separately in verse.
To prohibit such a thing yourself and yet violate it yourself—this suggests that Fenyang was either deluded or perverse.
Is it not so? For the most part, those who reject the scriptures, upon seeing even one or two phrases that resemble the words of the ancients, rely upon them as if they were Mount Tai;
yet when they encounter what they cannot understand, they attack it like a mortal enemy.

Since such resemblances are few while the unintelligible passages are many, it is inevitable that there will be internal contradictions from beginning to end. This is like the "Human and Heavenly Eye and Mind" (Ren Tian Ren Mu).
In the eighteenth question of the *Zaisi*, it is said: "Whenever a student composes and refutes words and phrases to conceal [the truth], they are all struck down by the teacher’s eye.
Why is this? It is simply because they have recognized [the truth]. The *Bishu* cites this as the basis for a single blow of the staff.
Yet one does not realize that recognizing [the truth] is something that cannot be achieved unless one possesses the talisman behind the elbow. Furthermore:
Now, it was merely one Fenyang who, when praising the Three Mysteries, dismissed them as "mad dogs," yet when posing the Eighteen Questions, relied upon them as his very support.

How could the ancients have known how to position themselves? If the praise of the Three Mysteries were incorrect, then Fenyang’s own realization would certainly be mistaken, and the Eighteen Questions would likewise be unworthy of regard. If the Eighteen Questions...
If this were the case, then the realization of Fenyang was originally correct, and his verses on the Three Mysteries (Sanxuan) would likewise be so.
Why then is there such inconsistency—first praising them and then reviling them?

Last year, when I wrote to Dingmu, I thought that Master Fenyang Shao must have already had people like you who were fixated on the Three Mysteries and Three Essentials (Sanyao); therefore, he composed those verses.
Jingyun said: "The Three Mysteries and Three Essentials are difficult to distinguish; when one attains the meaning, the Way is easy to approach.
A single phrase clearly encompasses the myriad phenomena—on the Double Ninth, the chrysanthemums are fresh.

Since it is said that words are forgotten, how could it be as you suggest—that those who have realized the Three Mysteries and Three Essentials from antiquity to the present must each point them out to others?

Regarding the "seal of approval" between teacher and disciple: today, Tanji revises this, stating that the "Three Mysteries and Three Essentials" were merely the words Linji spoke on a single occasion during his formal sermons (*shangtang*).
At that time, there were those who took them to be the core tenets of the school; therefore, Fenyang composed a verse as a warning, saying:
"The Three Mysteries and Three Essentials are difficult to distinguish... and so forth. These were merely for the occasion, and the subsequent text goes on to criticize [this view].
To act as a mad dog is entirely the fabrication of Tanji; this has been explained in detail in the "Discernment of Linji's Chapter.

Even in my own writings, I have already corrected those who rigidly cling to the Three Mysteries and Three Essentials (Sanxuan San'yao) as being the essential tenets (zongzhi) of that time—changing it to state that they were merely those who clung to them as such.
This is because the Three Mysteries and Three Essentials were originally established as provisional means; they are not the direct, ultimate lineage (zong) of Linji.
Your point is this: you are simply diminishing existence and augmenting non-existence; what loss does this cause for this old monk? It is merely the functioning of your own mind.

Furthermore, if you claim that a verse (*song*) is itself a warning (*jing*), then it would be improper to divide the verse into the "Three Mysteries" (*san xuan*); to establish such a rule yourself and then violate it yourself.

"Did you think that Fenyang was so ignorant and perverse as to reach such a state? The old monk laughed and said, "The 'jing' in 'jǐngwù' (to awaken) is a homophone for the 'jin' in 'jìnzhǐ' (to prohibit).
I cannot believe that Tanji’s ignorance and perversity have reached this point. Although Fenyang divided his verses into the Three Mysteries (*sanxuan*), he immediately added:
"This is the verse for the Three Mysteries; what, then, is the essential meaning of the Three Mysteries?"

You must reach a clear and decisive resolution. On that day, this old monk, relying on the principle of "attaining the meaning and forgetting the words," alerted you to the very summit of the matter, intending for you to realize the essential intent of the Three Mysteries and Three Essentials. You must not cling to the mere names and phrases of the Three Mysteries and Three Essentials;
this is exactly the same as the words of Fenyang, without any difference. Finally, Fenyang again gave this earnest instruction:
The warning says: Do not merely look into the void and give false interpretations, saying, "I have personally attended upon the Master, and he has explained it for me.
Such empty fabrications and deceptive speech will one day result in you being struck with an iron staff.
According to this principle, even one who has personally seen Fenyang is not permitted to take what another has said as his own realization; how much more so for Han Yue, who went to Linji?

For over seven hundred years, people have taken various names and phrases—such as "recognizing the profound essentials," "discerning and illuminating function," or "host and guest"—and treated them as substantial dharmas.
To then regard such empty, idle talk as the words of a true master is surely enough to make one laugh out loud.

Tang Ji again slandered the *Pibishu* (Book of Refutation). Whenever he encountered even one or two phrases from the ancients that resembled [his own views], he relied upon them as firmly as Mount Tai;
yet whenever he encountered what was unintelligible to him, he attacked it like a mortal enemy.

Because of Han Yue, the old monk has been forced to cite the famous sayings of the ancients, claiming they represent the essential meaning of the lineage, and thus I cannot help but quote an ancient master: [Insert relevant citation here] ...I cannot help but quote an ancient master.
Two words: "Using a wedge to extract a wedge. If it were within the scope of an old monk like me, I would simply rely on my own realization to point directly at all people;
upon whom else could I depend? Therefore, as for you who engage in such forced interpretations and artificial associations, this old monk does not care for the words of Buddhas or patriarchs;
I simply clear the way straight through to the end. Why is this? Because when a person of heterodox views speaks the True Dharma.
Even the True Dharma is itself perverse. You say, "I rely on an ancient monk. On which ancient person have you ever relied? On which ancient saying have you ever relied?

Furthermore, regarding the karmic conditions of the ancient worthies—from the summit of Mount Tóngguān (Copper Coffin Mountain) onward, where the sentient and the insentient were all clearly and equally manifest—they penetrated each and every point of their realization. How could there be anything further that is unintelligible? That which is not...
This is understandable. It is surely nothing more than a jumble of words that has never appeared in any recorded source and lacks any basis for verification.
As for works such as the *Qipie* and *Sanpie*, they are in fact intended to encourage the infant and cherish the child; thus, you yourselves are not even their enemies.
How much more so regarding the words of the ancients? For instance, the *Renzhan yuyan* (Human Eye and Celestial Eye) records the eighteen questions of Fenyang, concluding with:
"Whenever students present clever phrases and statements to cover over [the truth], they do so to test the master's eye.
Or they may present their intellectual views, acting as if they have heads and horns; each one is tested, and all are beaten down, simply because they are recognized for what they are face-to-face."
Whether disparaging or praising, the bright mirror stands upon its pedestal; what malevolent spirit could it possibly manifest?
What shape-shifting fox could conceal its true form? This old monk opened the book and brought [the text] forward precisely for the sake of direct, face-to-face encounter.
Therefore, a single blow is not used as a mere blow; it points directly to the true form of all things. Now, Tanji has deleted it.
The two characters "face-to-face" (dangmian) mean that only those who have recognized [the truth] can do so; it cannot be achieved unless one has the talisman behind the elbow.
Let me ask Tanji: do you have a face-to-face elbow? If you cannot recognize it face-to-face, what more can be said of the talisman behind the elbow?

You further said: "If the verses on the Three Mysteries (Sanxuan) are incorrect, then Master Fenyang’s realization was certainly not correct, and his Eighteen Questions are likewise unworthy of regard.

If the Eighteen Questions are correct, then Master Fenyang’s realization was fundamentally correct, and the verses on the Three Mysteries are also correct. I, this old monk, say: Master Fenyang was indeed correct; it is you who are not.
This is so. You further employ flowery words and clever speech to both restrain and transgress yourself, adding this to the portion of Fen-yang;
you praise him once and revile him once, adding this to the portion of this old monk. This old monk does not begrudge his own eyebrows as he shall explain it through for you.
Generally speaking, in the school of the Patriarchs, what is established is immediately swept away. Fen-yang has three secrets, which monks find difficult to discern. Furthermore—
He intended to ask how it was, but the staff struck him right on the head. At that time, a monk asked, "What are the three secrets?
The Master struck him immediately. The monk bowed. "Tell me," said Yangshan, "did that monk bow because he understood, or did he bow because he did not understand?
Fenyang then composed a verse for the occasion and further remarked: "Do not merely take such recorded words and phrases as your lifelong practice."
What benefit is there? According to this principle, even when establishing one's own three mysteries, one must still sweep it away oneself;
how much more so regarding Linji’s Three Mysteries—would he ever consent to establish them for you fools as you do, persisting in such a way? Therefore it is said:
"Fenyang is correct; you are not."
Li Hou, the Governor of Longdefu, had long been acquainted with the Master. He requested that the Master take charge of Chengtian Monastery, and messengers arrived three times;
yet the Master did not go. The messengers were punished for their failure, and upon their return, they said, "We must have the Master go with us;

otherwise, we shall face death. The Master replied, "I am old and infirm, and have already decided not to leave the mountain. If you insist on going, I shall simply follow behind you; why must we travel together? The messengers...

The Master said, "If you agree, you may choose whether to go first or last. The Master then ordered food to be prepared and his travel gear to be readied, announcing to the assembly, "I, the old monk, am departing.
Who can follow me? One monk stepped forward and said, "I can follow you. The Master asked, "How many li do you travel in a day?
He replied, "Fifty li. The Master said, "You cannot follow me. Another monk stepped forward and said, "I..."
They traveled seventy *li* in a single day. The Master said, "You cannot follow me either. The attendant came forward and said, "I can follow; wherever you go, I shall arrive.
The Master replied, "Then you can indeed follow this old monk. He then looked back at his messenger and said, "I shall go on ahead," whereupon he set down his chopsticks and passed away.
The attendant immediately passed away standing by his side. He had lived for seventy years.
There are eight [categories]. He sat [in meditation] for fifty-six summers.
Jiuzhi said: "Guan Ying, Lord Teng, Fan Kuai, and others rose from the regions of Feng and Pei during the reign of Emperor Gao of Han.

They besieged cities and plundered lands, gradually advancing according to their merits until the House of Han possessed the empire. Yet the positions of these several men did not exceed that of enfeoffed marquis."

As for Han Xin, upon a single meeting he was granted the authority of a supreme general; this is an instance of conferring rank before merit. Now, those who presumptuously occupy high positions while their achievements fail to match, rarely escape extermination. Likewise, once great deeds have been accomplished, those who become slightly self-conceited and boastful also rarely escape extermination. *Śūraṃgama Sūtra*... [text continues]... [text continues]... It is said: "In principle, there must be sudden enlightenment; in practice, there is gradual cultivation. Changsha said:

"When one's merit has not yet equaled that of the various sages, the three vehicles and ten stages are comparable to Guan Ying and Lord Teng. When merit surpasses enlightenment, the 'ordinary person with the great mind' transcends the school and exceeds the standard;
this is comparable to Han Xin. When enlightenment surpasses merit, it is the merit of no-merit. On this basis, I [say]: [Note: The final sentence is left open as the source text ends abruptly.]
Observing the realization and conduct of Fenyang, was he not one who received direct transmission as a supreme general yet did not boast of his achievements or take credit for his victories?

According to the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*: "In principle, there is sudden awakening; riding upon that awakening, all is simultaneously eliminated. As for phenomena, they are gradually removed; through this sequence, they are exhausted.
Tanzhi changed this to: "Principle must be suddenly awakened to; phenomena are cultivated gradually. This is paired with Changsha’s statement: "The work is not yet finished..."
To be equal to all the sages, let me ask Tanji: For what reason does the Buddha say that "principle is realized suddenly," and thus one "simultaneously eliminates all phenomena through awakening"?
I, this old monk, dare to say that it is not necessary to first eliminate phenomena; rather, one must first awaken to principle.
By the power of sudden awakening, all phenomena of both the mundane and supramundane worlds will then naturally be eliminated. Therefore, it is said that [awakening] follows a sequence.
That is all. In the case of the "gradual cultivation" of the events at Tanzhi, what do you call "the event"? And how does one cultivate it?
Because of this, Changsha was asked by the official Haoyue about *nirvāṇa* as the fruit: [Changsha] said, "One's merit has not yet equalled that of the sages.
He was then asked about *nirvāṇa* within the cause: [Changsha] said, "Virtuous One, you are it. Why did Tanzhi not simply say, "Virtuous One, you are it," directly?
Those who take from the lower ranks have their karmic consciousness drifting in a vast void with no foundation to rely upon;

yet they instead rely on seizing cities and plundering territory, advancing gradually according to their merit—this is comparable to the three vehicles and the ten stages, where merit surpasses awakening, and one is directly appointed as a high general.
Those whose rank precedes their merit are comparable to ordinary beings of great resolve, where awakening surpasses merit—is this not so? This old monk relies solely upon the World-Honored One.
Born in a royal palace and being the eldest son, he nevertheless renounced it to become a monk; beholding the morning star, he awakened to the Way.
Is it not, then, truly rare that he directly bestowed [the Dharma] upon an upper general? Linji said: "The person who relies on nothing is the mother of all Buddhas."
If one awakens to the state of non-reliance, even Buddhahood is not attained. Where, then, could the two characters "merit" and "achievement" be placed?

Furthermore, can one who has been directly entrusted as a supreme general be defiled by them? Generally speaking, those who have sudden awakening followed by gradual cultivation have not yet equalled the various sages.
The phrase "until their strength is sufficient" and so forth is most capable of deceiving all people, causing them to give rise to inferior conceptions.
Master Xiushan said: "A bamboo shoot will ultimately become a bamboo; can it still be used as a strip of bamboo now? Master Jinshan said:
"You shall realize this for yourself in the future. If Tanji and the others were to realize it for themselves, they would then know.
In the past, people bit into the words and phrases of the ancients, taking them as their fundamental principles; this is not worth a single laugh.
Once, when a monk had passed away, Changsha stroked him with his hand and said, "Great assembly, this monk has truly held up the essential principles for all of you.
Do you understand this thoroughly?"
Ciming rescued [the argument] by saying: "There is a parable that goes like this: Zang and Gu were two men who together tended sheep, yet both lost their sheep.
When asked what Zang was doing, it was said he was holding a bamboo slip and reading books; when asked what Gu was doing, it was said he was gambling at dice."
The two travelers were engaged in different pursuits, yet their loss of the sheep was one and the same. I have often used this as a metaphor for our Way. Thus, Guishan said:
"When the sentiments of ordinary and sage are exhausted, the essence reveals true permanence; when principle and phenomena are non-dual, that is the Buddha of Suchness.
Ciming came close to this realization. As for those who follow their food with anger, they are like grain [that is consumed]. Yet, to maintain...
The "sagely view" is that which is correct. Although it is as clear as daylight regarding superiority and inferiority, in its failure to achieve full realization, they are one and the same.

The heterodox Chan of recent times takes the indulgence of arbitrary emotions and unrestrained license to be the "unimpededness of all phenomena. This is like abandoning Boyi to take Thievery Foot (Daozhi) as one's teacher.
Is their descent into ruin not even more extreme? Tan Ji criticized the heterodox Chan of recent times for taking emotional indulgence and license as "unimpededness in all things.
But how can emotional indulgence and license possibly be called "unimpededness in all things"?
According to the path of True Purity, "unimpededness in all things" means acting with sovereign mastery and ease; at the crossroads, one simply opens the sack.

Holding a pig's head in his hands while reciting the pure precepts in his mouth—this is precisely the same as Miaoshan’s "When ordinary and sacred emotions are exhausted, the true permanence is revealed;
principle and phenomena are non-dual, and one is the Buddha of Suchness. They breathe through the same nostrils. Why is this so?

The hand that holds the pig's head is the mouth that recites the pure precepts. You might say this is both ordinary and holy; yet it stands forth in its full majesty, untouched by the categories of ordinary or holy.
This is what is called "the true permanence revealed in its essence. When the old monk applies his staff, he does not treat it as a mere staff;
he points directly at all people so that they may realize the true permanence revealed in their essence—thus, ordinary sentiments and holiness [are transcended].
I see it. You wish to seek it, yet you cannot find it; you wish to arise, yet it does not come forth. What need is there to speak of Zang and Gu, Yi and Zhi?

In short, Tanji has studied external scriptures and employs many metaphors; this old monk speaks with a single flavor of directness—striking the head of a stone man until it cracks—to discuss only the actual reality.
▲ Chan Master Chiming (Buchu Yuan) of Shishuang in Tanzhou was a successor of Fenyang. He was born into the Li family of Qingxiang in Quanzhou. In his youth, he was a scholar.
At the age of twenty-two, he received full ordination at Yijing Monastery on Mount Xiang, south of the city.

His mother was a woman of virtuous conduct and encouraged him to travel to study under various masters. The Master had joined eyebrows and prominent eyes; he was tall and of robust build, yet his demeanor remained humble and disciplined.

Wherever Mo went, he was rebuked by elder masters as being too young for the monastic community (*saṃgha*). The Master laughed heartily and said, "The trampling of dragons and elephants is not something a donkey can endure.
He once carried a chest of antiquities in a bag, slung over his shoulder with a bamboo staff, and traveled through the regions of Xiang and Mian.
Together with Shouzhi, he entered Luoyang, where they heard of the spiritual reputation of Chan Master Fenyang Wuye.

He was the foremost in the world. Resolving his will, he sought personal reliance [on the Master]. At that time, the court was inquiring into the offenses of Hedong, and heavy troops were stationed in Lu and Ze;
many urged him not to go. The Master paid no heed; he crossed the Great River, ascended Mount Taihang, changed his clothes to resemble those of a servant, and concealed his name among the fire-teams.
Sleeping in the open and lodging in the grass, he reached Longzhou and subsequently visited the Duke of Fenyang (Li Shaoliang).
He treated him with severity. After two years had passed, he still did not permit him to enter the inner quarters. The Master went to see Zhaoyan;

Zhaoyan, divining his intent, was certain to revile and scold him, and would have his attendants disparage and denigrate the various schools. Whatever instructions he gave were all mundane and vulgar matters. One night, [the Master] complained, saying:
"Since arriving at this Dharma assembly, two summers have passed, yet I have received no instruction; I have only increased my worldly afflictions.

Thinking of how the years and months drift by while my own fundamental task remains unclarified, I have lost the very benefit of leaving the household life. Before he had finished speaking, Master Zhao stared at him intently and scolded, "This is a wicked spiritual friend!
How dare you deceive and exploit me? In a rage, he raised his staff to drive him away. As the Master prepared to intervene and save him, Master Zhao covered [his mouth].
His mouth [was opened]. The Master attained great enlightenment and said, "Now I know that Linji’s Way transcends ordinary sentiment. He served him for seven years before taking his leave.
Jue said, "Linji said, 'Huangbo’s Buddha-dharma is not much,' yet Shishuang said, 'Now I know that Linji’s Way transcends ordinary sentiment.
Consider the lifelong conduct of these two elders; they were like fragrant elephants crossing a river, cutting through it with a single stride."
It flows on and passes by; it does not allow jackals, foxes, or dogs to spy upon its traces of martial prowess. Such is the nature of the Way.
Those who have not yet fully realized the perspective that transcends emotional attachments treat awakening and the fundamental principle as two separate things, muddling them and slandering them.
What is there to marvel at? This old monk does not employ his staff as a mere staff; he points directly to all people so that each may awaken for themselves.
Beyond this, there is no other core teaching. It was not merely because Huangbo struck Linji three times that Linji awakened to himself—there is not much more to the Buddha-dharma than this.
When Fenyang raised his staff to chase Zhiming away, he further covered his mouth, allowing him no room to speak.
Is this not an extension of salvation, causing one to awaken to the Way of deliverance that transcends ordinary sentiment? When a lion roams, does it seek companions?
When a mighty man extends his arm, he relies on no external force. If you say that this old monk’s footsteps follow those of Huangbo and Fenyang, [then you have understood].
This would be to blind your very eyes. As for that "Han Yue," outside of Han Yue itself, he clung to the words and phrases of the ancients as his fundamental principle;
it is thus clear that he treated the fundamental principle and one's own realization as two separate entities.
Addressing the assembly, he struck the meditation seat with his staff once and said, "Does the assembly understand? Have you not heard it said: 'With one blow, all that is known is forgotten;
no further cultivation or refinement is required. Those everywhere who have realized the Way all say this is the highest capacity.
Xiangyan’s awakening in this manner was clearly an awakening to the Buddha-dhyāna (Tathāgata-citta), yet he had not even dreamed of the Patriarchal-dhyāna (Citta of the Patriarchs). Furthermore—"
What long-standing excellence is there in the Chan of the Patriarchal Masters? If you seek it within words, you will mislead future generations.
Even if you were to take it up under the staff, you would betray the former sages. All phenomena are fundamentally at rest; it is only people who create their own clamor.
Therefore, when this mountain monk dwells at Fuyan, I see only the realm of Fuyan: rising late and sleeping early, sometimes clouds arise from the azure peaks. At other times—
At that time, the moon sank into the cold pond; the *śabdika* birds flew and sang before the Prajñā Terrace; and the fragrance of *sāla* flowers wafted beside Mount Zhurong.
Grasping a lean bamboo staff, he sat upon the *pāṇḍava* rock and occasionally discussed the profound and subtle with the monks from the Five Lakes.
With his head and face covered in dust and ash, he resided at Xinghua, seeing only the house style of Xinghua: welcoming and seeing off guests, with the monastery gates connected to the city.

Carriages and horses crowd the streets; fishermen’s songs resound through the Xiao and Xiang rivers; monkeys cry at the foot of Mount Yue; the sounds of stringed and wind instruments, along with folk songs and ballads, enter the ears from time to time.
Furthermore, one converses daily on Chan and the Way with eminent men from all quarters of the world, until years and months have utterly vanished. Now tell me:

does there remain any distinction of superiority or inferiority between dwelling in the deep mountains and residing in the city walls? Try to say something. After a long silence, he said: "In every place is Maitreya; there is no..."

With these words, he was able to point directly to the very place where Linji attained enlightenment. When one has spirit, one adds to that spirit; even in moments lacking elegance, there is still elegance.
Liulü was thus able to point directly to the place where Linji’s total functioning resides; it is exactly the same as the nostrils I have described.
How could it ever be like Tanji, who understood "knowing pain and knowing itch" as the principle of being struck by the staff or touched by the whisk?
When Dongshan Cong answered a monk’s question: "Since you are the Great Sage of Sizhou, why is it that you instead..."
He appeared in Yangzhou and said, "The gentleman loves wealth, but he takes it by the right way.
A monk reported this to Master Xiang'an, who was greatly startled and said, "A descendant of Yunmen still remains!

After Cong took up residence in the world, he showed a monk, saying, "The Patriarch came from the West specifically to sing of this matter; since you, Venerable One, did not realize it, those who enter through the gate..."
It is not a family treasure; to mistake the shadow for the head is surely a great error.
Since the Patriarch came from the West specifically to sing this matter, why must he speak so much to the assembly? According to this, did Master Cong ever place weight on words and phrases?
Xianglin Yuan relied upon Yunmen; Yunmen would often call out to him, "Attendant Yuan! and Yuan would respond, "Yes. Yunmen said, "That is it."
"What is it? After eighteen years in this manner, one day he finally attained realization. Yunmen said, "From now on, I shall no longer call you by name.
One day, Yuan retired to take his leave. Yunmen asked, "How do you express the single phrase 'Light contains the myriad phenomena'?
Yuan hesitated. Yunmen told him to stay for another three years. Considering Yunmen’s majestic bearing, which was like that of a king, his hesitation was understandable.
He did not permit even this much, let alone such redundant phrasing. Thus the ancients said: "It flows forth from the breast and fills heaven and earth;
it is not the fabrication of words to seek something extraordinary that others cannot utter, nor is it a 'brocade heart and embroidered mouth.'"

This refers to the sharp novelty of phrasing and meaning. Tan Ji and others have recklessly applied forced interpretations to the words and phrases of the ancients, passing these down to one another until they became mere vulgar and petty talk.
They have already slandered the ancients to an extreme degree; how much more so could they dare to slander their own ancestors of over two hundred years?
To lack such an eye—how is it that within this world there exist such descendants? [From] *Jiuzhong* (Saving from Within).
Furthermore, the Way has been presented through verses that struck the essential point (*yīngjī*), and Baiyun has already granted his approval. Yet, you have once again exerted great effort;
those of today cannot help but harbor doubts. How difficult this is! Zen must be realized, it must be realized with great awakening;
one must clarify the Great Dharma (*dàfǎ*). What is called the Great Dharma is not merely the speculative calculation of names and characteristics.
That is all. According to the Fifth Patriarch’s words: "Because of this, I broke into a cold sweat and thereby realized that the pure breeze was already on my back.
This served as proof that what he had previously cherished was suddenly cast aside.
How could he have ever said that Chan cannot but be awakened to, that it must be greatly awakened to, or that the Great Dharma cannot but be understood? In short, it is simply a matter of letting go.

He has not yet even dreamed of the Five Patriarchs’ sweat; therefore, he speaks thus in such confusion. The preceding passage emphasized the nature of words and phrases, yet here he claims they are not merely trivial names and forms.
This is a contradiction of his own words. How could it be that names and forms are not words and phrases?
Thus it is said: "One knows where his evasive arguments reach their end."
One day, Yuanwu requested instruction on the "Four Guests and Hosts" of Linji. The Master said, "It is merely a matter of formal procedure;
what idle business is it? He added, "In my place, it is like a wrestling match before a horse: as soon as one falls, it is over."

Jiuyue said: "The words of the Fifth Patriarch here express the very marrow of Linji’s heart. From Fengxue and Shoushan downward, those who have spoken of 'host and guest' have not been as intimate or direct as this.
To cite the two characters 'proscribed period' (*chengxian*) from the *Pibushu* to negate Linji is like seeking a child whose father does not exist;
when there are only many females without a male, how can there even be eggs?"—thus spoke the Old Monk.
Relying solely on what the Fifth Patriarch said—"In my place, it is just like two men wrestling in front of a horse;

as soon as one is thrown down, it is finished"—this is most intimate and direct. Therefore, a single blow does not function as a mere blow; it points directly to all people, who simply fall over themselves.

It is like saying that if there are many hens without a rooster, how could there be any eggs? This is likely not the case; even among many hens there are eggs, yet they cannot produce offspring because they break the shells [without incubation].
Xiangyan said: "The chick pecks from within and the mother pecks from without; the chick awakens and the mother breaks her shell;
both mother and child perish together, yet their response to conditions is never mistaken. Those of the same path sing in harmony; Miaoyun called this the "single-legged" realization—awaken to this!
Thus one knows the place where this old monk pointed out that people fall over themselves; one also knows the place where the Fifth Patriarch collapsed and then simply ceased.
To say that Han Yue has "wiped out" (masheda) the old monk is truly to be a child without a father, yet he conversely claims that it is the old monk who has "wiped out" Linji.
In his "Refutation," he cites the two characters "cheng" and "xian" and immediately treats them as having "wiped out" Linji. That is—
As the Fifth Patriarch said: "What kind of trivial matter is this? And how would you handle it? The Master gave this discourse:
"It is like a water buffalo passing through a window lattice. Its head, horns, and four hooves have all passed through;
why then can its tail not pass?"
Tang Ji said of Pí’s letter: "The 'essential principle' (zongzhi) is the tail; those who speak of the essential principle cannot pass it.
Only this old monk can pass it with a single blow of the staff. The old monk wrote in his letter to Layman Liu:
"As for that which alone cannot be passed—the tail—it is precisely you, Layman, who rely on the words and phrases of the ancients, being entangled and indistinct without end. This is why...
Gao Feng’s Verse: The ox that has been let loose casually—whose horns and head are so distinct? To whom can they be shown?
If you try to understand it at the tip of its tail, the hawks of Silla have already flown past. Tan Ji and others: lean and lean, fine and fine.
If you turn directly toward the tip of the tail, you will hear it. The old monk asks Tanji: "Do you all have tails as well?
If it is like the old monk’s single blow, does it strike Han Yue at his very core, or does it strike Han Yue on the surface?
Or does it strike Han Yue’s tail? If you can understand this clearly, then you will know the essence of the School.
The ultimate point of realization is by no means to be understood through the tail. Whether one succeeds or fails in passing through it, one not only slanders the Old Monk, but also slanders oneself.
The Fifth Patriarch gave this instruction: "It is like a water buffalo passing through a window frame."
"The head, horns, and four hooves have all passed through; why then can the tail not pass?
At that time, had the old monk been present among the assembly, he would have asked the Fifth Patriarch: "The head, horns, and four hooves have all passed through; why then can the tail not pass?
He would certainly have caused him to laugh heartily. Huanglong said: "Those who have already passed the barrier simply wave their arms and walk straight on."
"Go! How could you know there was a gatekeeper? It is I, the old monk. Ask the gatekeeper whether it is permissible;
those who have not yet passed through the gate are all of you here. You take the fundamental principle as a tail; I dare say that your head, horns, and four hooves have all failed to pass."
Jiù said: "The Fifth Patriarch remarked that his predecessor’s words were clumsy; at that time, this was not considered an act of arrogance toward one's superior.
Dàhuì wished to destroy the woodblocks for the *Bīyán jí*; at that time, this was not considered an instance of loftiness or self-display.
Huángbò and Wǎiyǎng did not permit the various venerable masters under Mázǔ; at that time, this was not considered a matter of personal ego or right and wrong. To know this Way..."
This is indeed the public view. Today, among the monastics and laypeople throughout the land, even those who are most virtuous and discerning say:

"The dispute over the ancestral teachings at Sanfeng is indeed correct; however, regarding matters of title and status, it is not permissible. Alas! This shows that the Way has been made lighter than titles and status.
Furthermore, the two elders were not significantly different in their years or virtue; yet they humbled themselves and bowed their wills to honor Linji.

It is simply the Way. If one were to abandon the Way, from what source could names and distinctions arise? Alas! That those who are most brilliant and wise should espouse such a view is merely because they have not yet known the Way. According to Baizhang Yuan, regarding the verse on the occasion of Huichao’s realization: "A single large coin buys a piece of oil-cake; having eaten it into one's belly, one is satisfied. When he said this, [Huichao] attained enlightenment. Thus, even though the cake was purchased for a mere coin, once it had entered the belly, its function was fulfilled. It is the same with the Way: although it is vast and boundless, when it enters the mind, its function is fulfilled. Below, he was no longer hungry. This is the true master of our school; he has revealed the matter of one’s own portion. Seeking cleverness is already impossible—whence could clumsiness come?
Wuzu said that the former master’s words were "clumsy," precisely to provide a discourse that enables people to grasp the meaning beyond the literal phrases.
How could he have ever deceived or oppressed Baiyun? Foguo composed the *Biyanji* (Blue Cliff Record).
The Gate of the School has reached a great turning point here. A true master of the school must receive people according to their fundamental share;
he must strip away their worldly resources all at once, yet further require them to offer up their possessions, leaving them with no way out.
Only then was he willing to relinquish his life to seek the place of death. Had he merely picked up and handled the matter through words and phrases, Huangbo would have left him a path of life.
That Dahui wished to destroy the printing blocks is precisely what is called "knowing gratitude and repaying kindness.
How could he have ever oppressed Foguo? Huangbo said to the assembly, "Do you know that within the Great Tang there is no..."
"Zen Master? At that time, a monk asked, "The venerable elders of all quarters gather assemblies to teach and transform;
why do you instead say there is no Zen master? Baizhang said, "I do not say there is no Zen; I simply say there is no master.
Do you not see that under Great Master Mazu, there were eighty-four people who sat at the site of enlightenment, yet those who attained Mazu’s True Dharma Eye were only..."
There were two or three people; Master Guizong of Mount Lu was one of them.
Those who have left the household life must know the matters of the ancestral lineage before they can succeed. Guishan asked Yangshan about the story of Baizhang’s second visit to Mazu:
"What was the intent of these two venerable masters? Yangshan said, "This was to manifest great capacity and great function. Guishan said, "Mazu..."
The Patriarch produced eighty-four *kalyāṇamitras* (good spiritual friends). How many attained the Great Function (*mahā-vyāpāra*)?
How many attained the Great Capacity (*mahā-śakti*)? Yang said: "Baizhang attained the Great Capacity; Huangbo attained the Great Function;
all the others were merely teachers of exhortation. Muzhou said: "So it is, so it is. For the Great Capacity and Great Function originally issued from the mouth of Huangbo; Baizhang..."
Baizhang addressed the assembly, saying, "The Buddha-Dharma is no small matter. When I was struck by Mazu’s single shout, my ears were deaf for three days.
Upon hearing this recounted, Huangbo involuntarily stuck out his tongue. Baizhang said, "Will you not take up the lineage of Mazu in the future?
Huangbo replied, "Not so. Today, because the Master recounted it, I have come to see the greatness of Mazu."
This is the function of the spiritual capacity. However, you do not yet recognize Mazu. If you were to become his successor, you would cause your future descendants to lose their way.
Baizhang said, "It is so. When one’s insight is equal to the teacher’s, it is a reduction of half the teacher’s virtue;

only when one’s insight surpasses the teacher’s is one fit to receive the transmission. You possess a vision that greatly exceeds your teacher’s. Huangbo then prostrated himself. One day, Baizhang asked Huangbo, "What..."
"Where have you been? Baizhang asked. Baizhang said, "Have you seen a tiger? Huangbo then let out a tiger's roar.
Baizhang raised his axe and made a gesture as if to strike him. Huangbo immediately struck Baizhang with a slap.
Baizhang laughed heartily. Then, ascending the hall, he said: "At the foot of Mount Daxiong, there is a great tiger. All of you—"
One must also observe this closely. This old fellow Baizhang has today personally suffered a blow from his own mouth.

Furthermore, when Baizhang ascended the hall and cited the story of the wild fox, Huangbo asked: "The ancients were wrong for giving but one response; for five hundred lifetimes they fell into the body of a wild fox.
Had they not been wrong at every turn, what would they have become? Baizhang said, "Come forward and I will tell you."
Huangbo stepped forward and gave the Master a slap. The Master clapped his hands and laughed, saying, "I thought the beard was red, but here is a red-bearded barbarian.
This reveals Huangbo’s great capacity and great function; indeed, he achieved a level of realization that surpassed his teacher.
This even extended to Linji, who three times asked about the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma and three times received sixty severe blows from Huangbo. This is the fundamental point.

The Master of Form (Huangbo) only received people with the fodder of his own fundamental share; it was simply like this. If [one speaks of] great capacity and great function, that is not the primary teaching.
Why did Ba say that under Master Ma, eighty-four people sat in the seat of enlightenment?
Those who attained the True Dharma Eye of Master Ma were but two or three people; it is specifically pointed out that Guizong was one of them.
When a monk took his leave of Guizong, Guizong asked, "Where are you going? The monk replied, "I am going to study the 'five flavors' of Chan in various quarters.
Guizong said, "In various quarters there are the five flavors of Chan, but here in my place, there is only the single flavor of Chan. The monk asked, "What is this single flavor?"
In the "Single Flavor Chan," Mazu Daoyi struck him. The monk said, "I understand! I understand! Mazu said, "Speak! Speak!
The monk hesitated, and Mazu struck him again. Later, the monk went to Huangbo and recounted the previous conversation.
Huangbo specifically ascended the hall and said, "Under Master Ma, eighty-four men of great virtue emerged; when questioned, each one was dripping wet. There was only..."
Guizong was "a bit more discerning. Relying on the single flavor of Chan, he would strike immediately upon being questioned; he would strike again if one hesitated.
Thus it is said that Guizong was "a bit more discerning. Relying on a grandmotherly heart, Huangbo would strike three times for every question asked.
Thus it is said that Huangbo attained "great function"—which is precisely what I mean by "the original color and the original portion," with no other dharma given to others.
Thus, when Yangshan and Daowei deferred to Huangbo, and Huangbo deferred to Guizong, they were none other than elucidating the matters of the ancestors.
Furthermore, this was not a matter of bullying the various venerable masters under Mazu; how much less could it have been a matter of bullying Baizhang?

Furthermore, he has bullied Mazu since his youth. Now Han Yueh is arrogant and self-aggrandizing, leading him to treat the Venerable with contempt and bully this old monk by labeling my teaching as "one-piece head hard Chan. He further incites human pride and factionalism, engaging in endless disputes.
This old monk intends to use one most coarse blow to bring Han Yueh to his ultimate end, solely because he has recklessly established a [false doctrine].

He acts as the patriarch of a thousand or ten thousand Buddhas, drilling out the "double-headed single-knot" where the four dharmas intersect, manifesting all manner of strange names and anomalous signs.

Furthermore, he exhaustively searches through the three dharmas of antiquity and the present, mechanically assigning them to the Three Mysteries and Three Essentials to establish them as the core tenets of Linji.
Thus, he buries his own spiritual brilliance and brings shame upon the ancient sages. As the ancients said, Linji was entirely...
The great function of the spiritual capacity: the staff and the shout fly back and forth; one seeks a person upon the edge of a sword; one extends the hand within a flash of lightning.
Han Yue treats everything as a single flavor of erasure, merely pursuing fragments of his own abstract essentials, claiming them to be matters of the inner sanctum.

He has usurped the name of Linji to establish himself as a heterodox outsider, and in doing so, he has instead brought discredit upon this old monk’s true character and fundamental standard. On the contrary—
I have repeatedly exhorted him, yet my exhortations have not been heeded. I have opened my mouth once, and I have opened it again;
that I continue to speak even unto this day without ceasing is for the sake of the Way, not for the sake of fame or status.

Consider the very case where Baizhang personally recounted the circumstances of his second visit to Mazu, and Huangbo personally heard [the Master] spit out his tongue, yet still said: "If you succeed Mazu, hereafter you will lose me, my son."
Grandson! How much more so from the Tang dynasty down to our own Ming—separated by the Five Dynasties, the Song, and the Yuan.
Yet Han Yue looked into the void and offered his petitions, claiming Linji as his true master. I, this old monk, must ask Han Yue: how thick is his face?
An ancient said, "Those who claim self-awakening after the era of King Bhīṣmagarjitasvaranāda are all naturally born heretics."
"Hanyue’s attempt to obliterate this old monk makes him a seed of the heterodox. Therefore, I have exerted every effort to rectify him;
this too is for the sake of the Way, not for the sake of reputation or status. In short, my aim is the fundamental essence and fundamental function, the great capacity and great utility.
Hanyue’s aim is the three strikes on the mortar and the three jars of sauce."
Three times he shook the door-panel; three times he struck him with a heavy staff. He established the Three Mysteries and the Three Essentials as his fundamental tenets.
The world is vast—whom shall we deem right and whom wrong? Surely there must be those who are both worthy and wise enough to arise and discern this.
