Upon repeated reflection, he realized that this was indeed his own original nature. Suddenly, he shattered the doubt regarding "dragging a dead corpse. At that time, he was twenty-four years old.
Previously, when Xueyan had moved to Nanyue, the Master concluded the summer retreat and went immediately to visit him.
As soon as Xueyan saw him, he asked, "Who gave you this dead corpse to carry here? The Master then shouted. Xueyan raised his staff; the Master seized it.
Zhuzhu said, "Today I cannot strike this person. Yun asked, "Why can you not strike him? The Master shook his sleeves and departed.
From then on, his sharp wit was unrivaled. One day, Yun asked him, "In the midst of the vast bustle of the day, are you able to maintain your mastery?"
The Master said, "He maintains mastery. He asked again, "Can one maintain mastery within a dream? The Master said, "One maintains mastery.
He asked again, "When one is fast asleep—without dreams, without thoughts, without seeing, and without hearing—where is the master? The Master was speechless.
Yunyan instructed him, saying, "From this day forward, you need not study the Buddha nor study the Dharma. You need not..."
From antiquity to the present day, it has been nothing more than eating when hungry and sleeping when weary.

As soon as one awakens from sleep, one again rouses one’s spirit and asks: "Where, after all, does this master of a single awakening reside? Where does he establish his dwelling and maintain his life?"
In the winter of the Bingyin year, he resolved to enter Longxu in Lin’an and made a vow to himself: "I shall risk a lifetime of being a foolish and simpleton;

I must by all means attain clarity regarding this one essential point. Five years passed until, upon hearing the sound of a fellow practitioner’s pillow falling to the floor, he attained great enlightenment.
He described it as being like seeing the Great Sage at Sizhou, or like a long-traveling guest returning to his native home.
Originally, it was simply the person of old; they did not change their former way of walking.
[Zhaozhou] said: "The Vajra-king sword leaves nothing behind for Buddhas or Patriarchs. This reached Ying’an of Huqiu, being the twelfth in the lineage.
It is like pouring from one vessel into another. At that time, there were those who appeared before and after Linji;
for instance, Shishuang had a multitude of "withered trees" who took sublime states as the ultimate goal. When the Head Seat passed away, they did not comprehend the fundamental principle.
Had it not been for Jiufeng, who else could have rectified this? Subsequently, it flowed into the heterodox Chan of silent illumination, while the true...
The Five Patriarchs of the Jingzong lineage and various venerable masters of Miaoxi severely censured these errors.
By the time this malady flared up during the succeeding dynasty, even those of vast capacity could not avoid entering through the narrow paths of foxes and rats.

It was thanks to these two elders, who were forged from cast iron, that they ultimately attained correct enlightenment; though after their awakening they bitterly recounted the errors of their past and the detours of their former ways.
This is not so. Yet students become addicted to tranquil stillness and are ultimately unable to relinquish it. How profound is the penetration of false teachings into people!

Consequently, from the beginning of our dynasty until the present, the practice of "sitting in silence" (mozhao chan) has been widespread throughout both the Northern and Southern schools; it is firmly entrenched and impossible to dismantle. —Tiantong.
The Three Peaks stand side by side, emerging forth; for over ten years, they have utterly demolished the dark lairs of the demonic armies.
Yet, the maladies of reckless violence, abusive cursing, and recording names as if marking mud-tracks have arisen before one has even turned a heel.
Such is the difficulty of preaching the Dharma in this degenerate age. One must surely fan it with a pure wind, move others with utmost sincerity, and verify it through the fundamental principle.
I have selected those who represent the fundamental vital energy and root of the lineage from Mazu, Baizhang, Linji, and Xinghua onwards—the total functioning and great utility.

This is not merely a matter of empty clamor and verbal disputes. As for the relationship between Xueyan and his disciples, their handling of the essential principles of the Linji school and their application of the "cutting edge" and "administering medicine" differ significantly from the ancients. Should one assume...
If one were to bestow this today, could it not alone be called an excellent remedy? Therefore it is said: "The Way is the year;

the Sage is the season. This is why Huangbo struck Linji, Dayue struck Xinghua, and Mazu twisted Baizhang’s nose until he cried out in pain—culminating in the practice of striking a monk as soon as he enters the gate. All these great ones...
I, Laozi, provide the basic provisions to receive people; throughout all generations of heaven and earth, there has never been one who pointed at me and called me a madman or a brawler.
Furthermore, those such as the "rice-dregs eaters" and "bed-wetting ghosts"—those evil spiritual friends who dare to peddle my teachings for profit—are of this ilk.
Often, they were subjected to extreme verbal abuse. Thus, an ancient master raised a doubt, saying: "Is reviling truly the Dharma-gift of compassion?

He replied: "Do you understand this as mere abuse? At these words, the student attained realization. Throughout all generations of the world, no one has ever pointed to this as mere "泼骂" (pō-mà—scurrilous abuse). Why is this?
Because it is the total exertion of the great function, not involving the slightest trace of partiality or triviality. It is the Lion’s [Roar].
"Biting people! Standing like a cliff ten thousand fathoms high—this is Linji’s single shout not functioning as a single shout, and this old monk’s single blow not functioning as a single blow.
There are eyes upon the tip of the staff; beneath the shout, one knows the way home.

Who would dare denounce this as madness or falsely accuse it of being mere reckless behavior? To falsely claim that such wild beating and drunken cursing began with Master Tanji was to cause [the decline of] Heaven..."
For ten thousand generations to come, it has been suspected that "beating" is simply madness and "scolding" is merely insolence.
Since Master Han Yue Tanji uttered those words, masters have stood with hands tied and tongues stumped, not daring to receive people with the fodder of their own fundamental division.

As for the corruption of recording names and clinging to traces, this too began precisely with Han Yue Tanji. He caused all under heaven and for ten thousand generations to record the Four Kinds of Provisioning.

To single out the four instances of "shining" (zhào) and "functioning" (yòng), the names of the four guests and hosts, the traces of the three times striking the pestle, the three jars of sauce, and the three times shaking the door panels—their subsequent degeneration is beyond words.
According to Xueyan and Gao Feng, they investigated with bitter diligence and exerted themselves in their practice.
True Suchness is cast from solid iron. As it is said: "Unless one’s bones are thoroughly chilled by the cold, how can one obtain the fragrance of the plum blossoms that strikes the nose?
How could this ever fall into the silent-illumination heresy or the fox-and-mouse paths? Han Yue and others have never attained awakening themselves;
they merely grasp at a single phrase and hold fast to it, taking this to be final liberation. Those who practice with bitter diligence and thorough investigation—[do not do so].
To indiscriminately revile [those who practice] as the dark army of Māra is a grave error, a grave error.

This old monk brandishes a white staff, intending for people to attain awakening on the spot. They undergo bitter study and diligent investigation upon their meditation cushions for twenty or thirty years.
It is permissible to call him a dull-witted fellow, but it is not permissible to call him a practitioner of deviant Chan. It is also like Xueyan’s reception of Gao Feng:

when Feng first came with incense in hand to pay his respects, Xueyan immediately struck him and shut the door in his face. After he had gone back and forth once or twice, he was finally permitted to draw near.
From then on, there was not a single day that he did not seek instruction. Suddenly, Xueyan asked him, "Who gave you this corpse to drag around?"
"Come! Before the words had even faded, he struck him out. In this manner, he did so countless times.

This is truly what is called "the fodder of one's own station," applying the hammer with great severity. I, Tanji, do not know upon what basis [Tanhui] could so recklessly claim that Xueyan and his son were like this.
To grasp and uphold the essential principles of the Jizhou school, and to apply the blade and administer the medicine—there is a real distance between such a person and the ancients.

It would not even be surprising to dismiss Xueyan; however, as for this old man Gao Feng, how can you, Han Yue, dismiss him as well when you claim he was the teacher from whom you received the mind-transmission?
▲ Chan Master Mingben of Tianmu Zhongfeng was a successor of Gaofeng. He was a native of Qiantang in Hangzhou; his secular surname was Sun, and his mother was Lady Li.
She dreamed that the monk Wumen arrived at her home carrying a lantern, and subsequently gave birth to the Master.

His physical presence was exceptionally noble, possessing the marks of a great man (*mahāpuruṣa*). Even before leaving his swaddling clothes, he sat cross-legged; as soon as he could speak, he sang praises and chanted Buddhist hymns. Although he played...

His play was invariably an act of Buddha-work. At nine years of age, he lost his mother; at fifteen, he made a vow to leave the household life. He prostrated before the Buddha and set his arm on fire as an offering, vowing to uphold the five precepts.

By day he recited the *Lotus Sūtra* and other scriptures; by night he constantly practiced walking meditation until he was utterly exhausted. To rouse himself, he would strike his head against a pillar.
Upon reaching adulthood, he read the *Transmission of the Lamp*, arriving at the passage where the girl Āmrapālī asks Mañjuśrī about birth being unborn.

He harbored doubts as to why he was nevertheless still transmigrating within birth and death. One day, while reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, he reached the passage on "shouldering the Tathāgata," whereupon he attained a sudden and profound realization.
He immediately came to understand the underlying meaning and intent of both internal and external classics.

The Master himself, however, considered that his realization was based on intellectual understanding and supernormal powers rather than true awakening. He subsequently went to follow Gao Feng, where he received the tonsure at Shizi Yuan;
he was twenty-four years old at the time. Not long after, while observing a flowing spring, he attained a profound insight and went to Feng to seek verification.
Feng struck him away. At that time, a rumor spread among the common people that the authorities were selecting young boys and girls [for ritual purposes].
The Master therefore asked Feng, "If someone were to come and ask the Master for a young boy or girl, what would you do? Feng replied, "I would simply hand him my bamboo staff.
The Master was unimpeded in his understanding of these words. Thereupon, Feng wrote a portrait eulogy (zhenzan) and gave it to the Master, saying: "My appearance..."
"Inconceivable! Even Buddhas and patriarchs could not behold it; yet he alone granted his unworthy son the sight of half a nose.
Furthermore, he directed his disciples to approach him for instruction, whereupon students flocked to him like spokes converging on a hub, flowing toward him as water seeks its natural descent.

Yet the Master remained profoundly humble and concealed, never once willing to assume the position of a teacher. At that time, the prime ministers and high officials... [the Emperor] ascended [to honor him].

Furthermore, whenever the various great monasteries such as Xuding, Jingshan, and Lingyin received imperial summons from the Son of Heaven, they sent gifts to invite the Master, yet he ultimately could not be brought there.

At times, he would even cross mountains and traverse seas to escape. Consequently, he had no fixed dwelling place; nevertheless, every land he passed through became a precious monastery (*ratnagṛha*).

Monastics and laypeople, men and women alike, regardless of their noble or humble status, all prostrated themselves upon seeing his dust. As for offerings of gold and silk, he regarded them all with equal indifference.
Thus it was. When the Master first attended upon Gaofeng at the Deadman’s Barrier, he performed manual labor by day and practiced silent meditation by night.

He exerted himself with such rigorous austerity that his ribs did not touch the mat for ten years. Through persistent inquiry and exhaustive investigation, he finally received the seal of transmission.
After Gaofeng passed away, the Master traveled by boat or dwelt in huts, naming them "Illusory Abode" (Huànzhù), which he also adopted as his own title.
Zhongfeng cited the story of Dayue striking Xinghua, saying: "Beneath two tigers, no beast can find room for its hooves;

between two blades, no man can find room for his feet. At the moment when Dayue and Xinghua’s staff and shout were exchanged, how could there be any room for thought, mind, or intellectual interpretation?
Nevertheless, it is just as Dayue said: "Take off your patched robe."
Xinghua attained great enlightenment upon hearing the words "Pain and a meal. But what principle did he realize?
If you can see it here, I will grant that you are half a true descendant of Linji. Han Yue said:
"If Xinghua had already realized those two shouts and also said he had studied the 'Guest-Host' phrase, why would he have waited for the soft words within the phrase?"
Wu. Zhongfeng said: "When the Great Awakened Xinghua wielded staff and shout in rapid alternation, how could there be room for conceptual thought?
Thus, since these two elders shared the same nostrils, what further words did Xinghua need to wait for?

Those today who do not recognize the fundamental principle often rely on Zhongfeng’s remarks regarding 'sweeping away the fundamental principle' and 'medicine and disease' as literal doctrine, clinging to them."
He remained at the initial stage of awakening and refused to believe in such matters as the "thoroughly realized guest and host.

If one were to understand it here, one would no longer doubt how the Five Houses each expounded the wondrous seal of the Patriarchs' mind. He further offered this verse: "The shout has already been clarified;
how could you not understand the blow? Meeting twice, why have you awakened only to fall back into intoxication? Having cast off the patched robe..."
"Add a mallet; Huangbo would surely have been reduced to a hundred fragments. It is truly laughable that his descendants pursue the crowd in such numbers;
one might even come to despise Linji as not being worthy of esteem. According to what Old Monk Xinghua himself said: "I was at the place of my elder brother, Master Sansheng..."
You have learned a "guest-host" phrase, yet you have been completely defeated by your senior brother.
Since it is something you have learned, how could it ever be called "awakening"? And how could there ever be a "guest-host" phrase learned apart from the two shouts?
Congzhi’s statement that “the two shouts constitute the guest and host” refers merely to the shouts as a formal exchange.

Therefore, Dajue tested him by saying, “I have a direct doubt regarding those two shouts you made yesterday. When Xinghua proceeded to shout, was it not evident that he was merely learning the shouts as a guest-host exchange?
If even shouting is inadmissible, how much less can it be said that one who has awakened [to the truth] would employ the two shouts?
"Bring it here! Zhongfeng feared that people would rely on intellectual speculation and mental interpretation regarding the interplay of the staff and the shout;
thus he said: "Beneath two tigers, no beast can find room for its hooves; between two blades, no man can find room for his feet.
According to Dajue, he told this blind fellow to take off his patched robe and give him a severe beating; thereupon, Huawen attained great enlightenment beneath these words. Furthermore—
"What principle have you realized? If you can see it here, I will grant that you are half a true descendant of Linji.
Yet Han Yue first embellished Xinghua’s realization of those two shouts, further claiming he had studied the "host and guest" phrase and opened it up into a dualistic discourse.
It is well said of Han Yue: why wait for him to speak within the realm of soft words?
There are two types of those who claim "great enlightenment. The first wishes to falsely accuse Xinghua;

because the one who attained enlightenment earlier [Xinghua] gave two shouts, this person arrogantly assumes the role of master and attempts to misrepresent him as being like an old monk who clings to his initial realization—a kind of rigid, one-sided Zen that refuses to believe in such things as the thoroughgoing guest-host relationship, and instead insists that the Five Houses merely expound the patriarchs' minds through words and phrases.
This is the sublime purport of the Seals (Mudrā). Second, it serves as proof for Han Yue. Previously, it was said that various quarters criticized Wanfeng for having "soft" teachings;
therefore, [Han Yue] remarked, "What need is there to wait? One must attain great enlightenment within the words and phrases of softness. This is based on those words and phrases of softness.
Then, as it says in the verse: "If the patched robe were stripped off and further pounded, Huangbo would surely be reduced to a hundred fragments. Is this not also contradictory?
Han Yue failed to reflect that when he first saw the old monk request him to ascend the seat, [Huangbo] raised his staff and shouted, taking both staff and shout as the direct pointing.

There are those who take staff and shout as the direct pointing, and there are those who take words and phrases as the direct pointing; though words and phrases differ from staff and shouts, they are one in their function.
There is nothing here that does not clarify the direct pointing of the Patriarchs.

For instance, when Dajue first struck Xinghua directly with a single flavor, because Xinghua did not realize it, he instead said: "I learned a phrase regarding guest and host from my elder brother, Master Sansheng;
I have been completely defeated by him. I pray you will grant me a dharma-gate of peace and bliss."
Therefore, Dajue spoke with great urgency, pointing directly at him face-to-face and saying, "You blind fellow! You have come here to suffer defeat.

He stripped off his patched robe and gave him a severe beating, causing him to be transformed beneath the words. Thus he realized the principle of how the late master Linji had received blows from Huangbo.
This was not merely because Dajue and Xinghua provided clear evidence through their words and phrases; it was because... [the text continues].

"Under the staff. Is this not the direct teaching of non-differentiation? If so, how could Huangbo, Dayu, Linji, Daqiao, and Xinghua ever have spoken of a "fundamental tenet" (zongzhi) apart from the principle of receiving a blow of the staff?
Furthermore, to falsely slander Xinghua by saying, "Since his shout was already clear, how could he not understand the strike?"—this reveals the nature of Han Yue.
One merely directs the mind toward the stick and the shout to seek conceptual understanding. Thus it is said: "Meeting twice, having awakened, why return to being drunk?

Since one has already attained awakening and no longer returns to intoxication, does this not contradict Han Yue’s own words in his earlier text, where he clung to his initial realization and refused to believe in such things as the thorough guest and host? Furthermore, there is the ancient saying regarding the arousal of the aspiration...
Ultimately, these two are not distinct. If one’s initial awakening were not thorough, then regarding matters such as guest and host, what would be said?
If one has not yet shed [the skin], how could one see the bone? If the bone possessed the distinction of beginning and end, or the separation of guest and host, [it would not be the bone].
How does this differ from Xinghua’s initial attainment of the "guest and host" phrase?

Since it is said that the patch-robed monk has already cast off his garments and been struck with a mallet, Huangbo would surely have been reduced to fragments; how could one still hold Linji in such high esteem?
Therefore, in my *Seven Letters*, I stated: "A man of true caliber possesses a will that soars toward the heavens;

he does not walk where the Tathāgata has walked—how much less so Linji? And how much less so one who relies on Zhongfeng’s words to sweep away the essential tenets (*zongzhi*)? I have already explained the term "essential tenets" in detail.
But tell me, who is it that relies on Zhongfeng’s words? [Yao] *Note: The final character "藥" (yào) appears to be a scribal error or a fragment from the next section of the text.*

The words of the sick man are taken as the actual Dharma. Han Yue, however, speaks of his own experience and provides his own testimony, clinging to his initial awakening and refusing to believe in such things as the "thoroughly realized guest and host. This is all the more perverse.
If he were given a severe blow, his great awakening would come first, and his study of the guest-host phrases would follow. Yet he likes to make such claims as his evidence. —Xinghua.
At first, he clearly understood the Way; he learned the "guest and host" phrase. Next, he clearly understood the Way; he was struck down by Da Jue’s staff.
Finally, he clearly understood the Way; having cast off his patched robe, he attained awakening at the place where he was struck with a severe blow.
This was the standard fodder for Da Jue; he gave no other dharma to anyone. Xinghua alone attained liberation and independence, awakening to it.
To have attained that which is not learned from others—how could this be compared to Han Yue, who merely pursued the phrases of the Five Houses and took them for the essential teaching?

This is truly what is called "blind donkeys chasing a herd. The concluding line of the verse—"It is laughable how many descendants chase after the herd"—is a manifestation of the clarity of heavenly principle, causing Han Yue to confess his own error without being prompted. At this point, I, the old monk, cannot help but [laugh].
[The Master] laughed. ▲ Chan Master Qianyan Yuanchang of Shengshou Temple at Fulong was a successor of Zhongfeng. He was a native of Xiaoshan County. His secular surname was Dong;
his family had for generations followed the Confucian tradition. His father was Jiuding and his mother was of the He clan. When the Master was born late in their lives, they wished to abandon him.

His paternal aunt, Lady Xie, hurried to his rescue and raised him as her own son. At the age of seven, he began his studies under a tutor; whenever a book came before his eyes, he could recite it from memory.
His deportment was grave and dignified, as if he were already an adult. His father said with delight, "This son shall surely exalt our clan through his literary talent and conduct.
There was a monk named Tanfang, who was the elder brother of [the boy's] paternal uncles; he wished to request the boy to become his successor, but Lady Xie found this difficult to accept.

Before long, the Master fell ill and his condition became critical. The Xie family prayed to the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, and shortly thereafter he indeed recovered. Thereupon, he followed [Master] Fang.
At the age of seventeen, he had thoroughly mastered the teachings of the nine schools and the hundred clans; subsequently, he abandoned them.

At nineteen, he shaved his head and received full ordination, studying the Vinaya at Lingzhi Temple in Wulin. He happened upon an occasion when the Chancellor’s administration was providing meals for monks.
The Master joined the assembly to receive offerings. At that time, Chan Master Zhongfeng Ben was already seated; seeing the Master from afar, he called out, "How do you conduct your daily practice?
The Master replied, "I recite the Buddha's name. Zhongfeng asked, "Where is the Buddha now? The Master hesitated, whereupon Zhongfeng rebuked him with a stern voice.
The Master knelt on his right knee and requested the essential points of the Dharma; Zhongfeng then bestowed upon him the "Mu" (No) koan of Zhaozhou.
"Zan. Thereupon, he bound together thatched grass and built a hut among the mountains of Lingyin. Before long, however, he was moved again due to other affairs, yielding to worldly conditions.
In the blink of an eye, ten years had passed. He sighed and said, "The aspirations of my life have filled the heavens and the earth;

why am I now like a vinegar-gall-insect trapped within a jar? He returned once more to Lingyin and remained there for three years without his side ever touching a mat. Subsequently, he went to Wangting.
Upon hearing the cry of a magpie, he attained a realization. He hurried to see Zhongfeng, who again rebuked him. The Master returned home in indignation.

As the night drew toward stillness, a mouse suddenly ate the cat’s food and fell into its bowl, making a noise. At that moment, he was suddenly awakened to enlightenment. He donned his robes and waited for the dawn.
He went again to consult Zhongfeng. Zhongfeng asked, "For what reason did Zhaozhou say 'no'? The Master replied, "A rat ate the cat’s food. Zhongfeng said, "Not yet.
The Master said, "The vessel for the food has been broken. Zhongfeng asked, "What happens after it is broken? The Master said, "It shatters against the square tiles.
Zhongfeng then smiled and advised the Master, saying, "You should protect and maintain yourself well; seek seclusion in mountain caves until the time is right."
When the time arrived, the principle was naturally revealed. Once the Master had received the entrustment, he retired to the Eastern Hermitage at Tianlong.
Shortly thereafter, Master Xing of Zhongzhu and the Chancellor Xing Dehuang invited the Master to assume the abbacy of a monastery. The Master, together with his disciple Xisheng, [departed].
Carrying his staff and *śikya*, he arrived at Mount Fulong and planned to live in deep seclusion there.
Han Yue said: "At that time, Zhongfeng saw this old man at the place where a cat’s rice bowl had been broken against a square brick;

without even distinguishing whether it was open or closed, [Zhongfeng] immediately instructed him to stay on the mountain to cultivate himself. When it came time for him to appear in the world, he could only say one thing:"
Regarding the word "echo" (xiǎng): if one enters the gate of Sanfeng, one must still undergo further examination before it is acceptable.
According to this, not only does he slander Qianyan—his realization being unreal—but he also slanders Zhongfeng; with his "winter melon seal," he has lost one of his eyes.
Even as for saying the word "echo," what fault would there be? Yunmen, when asked by a monk, "What is..."
Regarding the "sparrow pecking and hen hatching" kōan, the answer was "an echo. I ask: did Han Yue still approve of Yunmen?
Tan Ji cited the epitaph for the Master composed by the Imperial Scholar Song, which, at its conclusion, stated: "Liao once went to Mount Fulong to visit the Master.
The Master asked, 'I have heard that you have read through the entire Tripitaka; is this true? Liao replied, 'Indeed. The Master said, 'As for you...'"
"I have heard this with my ears and observed it with my eyes," he said. "I have observed it with my eyes. But who, according to you, is the one who enables the eyes to observe?
Lian raised his eyebrows toward him; they then looked at each other and laughed, forming a friendship beyond the mundane world.
Judging from this, the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye of Linji had, by the time of this master, already become like the profound *dàgāṅ* (plain soup).
Wine has long been prepared but not used. Subsequently, the patriarch Tianqi (Tianji) instructed people using only the single character "Who" (*shuí*), and so forth.
To claim that the *Zhengfayan zang* (Treasury of the True Dharma Eye) was prepared but not used is already an excessive slander against Qianyan.
For instance, if one asks who it is that is able to see with the eyes, this is precisely why Tianqi raised the cry of the word "Who."
There was still no fault in this. Once, when Baizhang had finished preaching the Dharma and the assembly was descending from the hall, he called out to them.
The assembly turned their heads, and Baizhang said, "What is it? Yeshan later referred to this as "Baizhang’s sentence upon descending from the hall.
I ask you, Tanji: do you approve of Baizhang or not? If Han Yue does not approve of Yunmen, then Tanji—[does not approve of Baizhang].
If you are willing to accept Baizhang, then you may as well refuse to accept Qianyan; otherwise, what enmity does the old man Qianyan have toward you, father and son?
One dismisses him with the word "echo," while the other dismisses him with the word "who.
I ask you all: what kind of mental activity is this?
▲ Chan Master Wansong Shiyu of Sheng’en Temple on Mount Dengwu in Suzhou Prefecture was the dharma heir of Qianyan.

He was the son of the Jin family of Leqing, Wenzhou; his mother was Zheng. She dreamed that two figures, one a Confucian and one a Buddhist, entered her chamber, and upon waking, she gave birth to two sons.
The Master was living at the end [of his life] when a light suddenly illuminated the room. Zheng was terrified and wished not to raise the child, but her sister-in-law took him in and nurtured him.
While still in his swaddling clothes, whenever he saw a monk, he would immediately smile and make the gesture of joining his palms.

His parents, realizing they could not keep him [as a layman], sent him to receive the precepts from Master Sheng, the lecturer at Yongqing Temple in Yue. At that time, he was eleven years old. He once recited the Lotus Sūtra until—
He had a realization that "all dharmas have from the very beginning been characterized by constant quiescence. He subsequently went to Hangzhou, where he received full ordination.
There, he visited Chan Master Zhiyan at Hupao, who showed him the words of Nanquan regarding the "three 'nots'. Consequently, he entered Mount Dapeng.
At the ancient site of Foji Temple, Zhuo’an engaged in intensive investigation day and night, to the point of forgetting both sleep and food.
One day, hearing the Abbot Master Zong of the temple cite the story of Guishan kicking over the water pitcher, he suddenly attained awakening and spoke this verse:
"Toppling and overturning is Nanquan; For half a year, I was burdened by my practice. If one can directly realize it right now, How could there be..."
Not proceeding further, he struck a fist to his chest. He then went to see Jiyuan, but there was no one to be seen;

everyone had already granted him the status of a Dharma vessel and instructed him to reside on the mountain. Thereupon, he returned to Dapeng and lived in solitude for ten years. When Jiyuan passed away, the Master went to sweep the pagoda.
Suddenly, he heard the temple director, Monk Fang, reciting a verse by Master Qianyan that included the line: "I send word to all..."
This refers to the phrase: "Students who have just begun their studies must not let this fine time pass by. The Master then went to Fulong to visit Qianyan.
As soon as he entered the gate, Qianyan asked, "It is not mind, it is not Buddha, it is not a thing—what is it?
The Master took his sitting cloth, drew a perfect circle, stood with his hands folded, and further presented a verse, saying: "Nanquan did not..."
"This vexes the human mind. There is one who intends to take the mind to seize the mind; yet it is not my mind, nor is it the Buddha. Its nature is empty and vast—what is there to seek?
Yanjun agreed. He then appointed the First Seat. Not long after, he resigned from his post and went into seclusion.
Although Master Qianyan repeatedly invited him to return, he did not rise to the call, instead entrusting him with his dharma robe and portrait. Later, he planted his staff in Suzhou.
At Mount Dengwu, monks flocked together and it became a monastic center.
Chan Master Baozang Puchi was the successor of Wanfeng; he resided at Sheng’en as its second patriarch. When Chan Master Wanfeng transmitted the Dharma to him, he gave him this verse:
"The ribs of Dayu ache again from the fist; The Three Essentials and Three Mysteries transcend both the orthodox and the deviant."
A lion cub from the lair of Linji; lamp after lamp, flame following flame, transmitted through ancient and modern times.
▲ Dongming Xubai Hui’an Chan Master Baozang succeeded [to his lineage].

At the age of fourteen, at Miaojue Temple in Danyang, he paid respects to Master Zhanran, shaved his head, and received the precepts. He then visited Songyin in Yunjian to inquire about the seal of the mind, yet he had not yet...
His mind was resolved; he vowed to himself that he would not cease until he had attained thorough realization.

After six days of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), upon emerging from samādhi, he raised his head and beheld a pine tree, whereupon he experienced a sudden and profound awakening. He subsequently traveled to Xuangmu Sheng’en Temple in Suzhou, where he met Master Guolín.
Their minds met like a needle and its eye. Guolín further directed him to see Chan Master Bǎozàngchí, and he related the circumstances of his awakening. Bǎozàng rebuked him, saying:
"The Buddha-dharma is like the great ocean; it becomes deeper as one enters further. How could one find a place to anchor here? The Master then attended closely at the seat of his teacher.
One day, Baizhang asked him, "The mind is not the Buddha, and wisdom is not the Way. How do you understand this?
The Master stepped forward to pay his respects and stood there with his hands joined in *añjali*. Baizhang scolded him, saying, "After all this time you have been here, is this how you practice?"
Regarding this insight: the Master then exerted himself so fervently that he forgot both sleep and food. By the second night, he suddenly penetrated to the very source of the Dharma.
He then presented a verse, saying: "A single punch shatters the vast void; The ten billion Mount Sumerus leave no trace.
If one asks who is the master within this realm, A single red orb surges forth from the Eastern Sea. Cangxiao said, "Even though it is thus, you must still..."
Guard yourself well. When the time arrives, the principle will manifest of itself. [The opponent] says:

"Let us not speak of those Chan practitioners of the末法 (mofa) age who are merely vague and superficial. Even those who have attained a true awakening reach only as far as the point of bowing and joining their palms;
they immediately give rise to 'sacred understanding' (shengjie) and stubbornly assume mastery. Since there are no eyes of wisdom,"
"Master, if you trim and prune it for them, after a long time it will transform the *amṛta* (clarified butter) into poison.
According to this, when Dongming emerged from meditation and raised his head, he attained a realization upon seeing the pine tree; yet originally, he had not achieved a great awakening (*mahābodhi*).

When he later paid his respects with palms joined, he was merely manifesting the meaning of the realization he had previously gained upon raising his head. How could he have ever claimed for himself that he had attained a great awakening? Thus spoke Tanji.
He immediately formed a noble understanding, falsely accusing Dongming and transforming the *amṛta* into poison, thereby slaying Dongming.

This was precisely because you yourself had not yet attained awakening; thus, you claimed that one who has attained true awakening merely reaches the point of bowing with palms joined and arrogantly assumes mastery.
Little do you realize that one who has attained true awakening acts as the master in every situation—how could this be so?
Furthermore, you must firmly exercise mastery. Moreover, there are the entanglements of ordinary sentiment and sage-like understanding, poison and nectar—so many complications!
One can see that Tanji was merely one who parrots the words; even his vague and faint impressions have not yet allowed him to catch a glimpse of the truth.
▲ Chan Master Puci of Dongming Haizhou in Hangzhou was a native of Changshu, Suzhou. His surname was Qian, and his family had followed the Confucian profession for generations.
He left the household life at Poshan [Mountain] and went to Huiri Temple, where he listened to lectures on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.

When he reached the passage stating, "Where there are words, there is no real meaning," he remarked, "Today my verbal explanations have only increased. Thereupon, he returned home and spent day and night reading the scriptures.
As he sought the true meaning [of the Dharma], his countenance grew increasingly haggard. A lay practitioner asked him, "Master, your complexion appears ill.
The Master replied, "It is because I have not yet clarified the Buddha-dharma; it is not illness.

The layman said, "If you have not clarified the Buddha-dharma, why not go to Mount Dengwu in the prefectural seat to inquire with Master Wanfeng? Upon hearing this, the Master was delighted and immediately went to Dengwu to see him.
Wanfeng asked, "Where have you come from, śrāmaṇera? The Master prostrated himself, then rose and said, "From Changshu. Wanfeng asked, "What brings you here?
The Master repeated his previous words and bowed again, requesting instruction. Wanfeng then struck him twice on the head and gave him a kick across the back.
He gave two kicks with his feet and said, "This very thing is the true meaning. The Master attained realization and rose, saying, "Excellent, excellent!

You have truly exhausted the Master's mental and physical efforts. Feng smiled and granted him approval, bestowing upon him a verse that said: "The hair of a tortoise is entrusted to the descendants."
"Bring forth the rabbit's horn to seek its source; a single shout leaves one deaf for three days. Within this, who may be intimate with the message?
He further said, "You should conceal your traces and protect [the Dharma]; do not lightly act as a teacher or model for others. The Master considered himself to have attained it.
He then built a hermitage in a valley of Mount Dongting. Twenty-nine years passed. One day, a monk arrived. The Master asked, "Where have you come from, Elder?
He replied, "Anxi. The Master asked, "Is there anyone in Anxi? He replied, "There is the Venerable Xubai; his preaching of the Dharma is no different from that of Fenggong.
The Master asked, "Whose disciple is he? He replied, "Baozang. The Master asked, "What sayings or phrases does he have? The monk then cited the entire room [of teachings].
The Master tested him by saying, "The mind is not the Buddha; wisdom is not the Way; the Tripiṭaka is not the Dharma. What is it? Those who offered responses failed to accord with the truth.
When the Master had finished speaking, he asked again, "Have you ever studied the Treasure Store? The Master replied, "I have studied the Treasure Store alongside Wanfeng.
The monk asked, "What realization did you have on that day that led you to remain hidden here? The Master then [proceeded to explain].
The monk said, "I will not go to visit other people anymore. The Master said, "In the past, I asked Wanfeng, 'As for all verbal expressions, they possess no real meaning.
Wanfeng then struck me, and from that moment I attained awakening. The monk asked, "Please tell me the reason why you attained it.
The Master said, "One simply needs to know what feels pain and itch; this is the real meaning and the wondrous mind. Verbal expressions belong entirely to the superficial skin. The monk said:
"According to this view," [the Master] thought, "birth and death have not yet been resolved; how can one speak of awakening? It has not yet occurred, it is not yet present. Have you not seen the Way?
Is the mind not the Buddha? Is wisdom not the Way? The Master then became doubtful; he abandoned his hermitage, crossed the lake, and went to Anxi to visit Dongming.
Just then, someone was hosting a vegetarian feast. Upon arriving at the gate, the Master asked Dongming, "Today’s feast..."
"What is its flavor? Ming said, "One knows it only when it reaches the mouth; once described, it is far removed.
The Master asked, "What is the flavor that reaches the mouth? Ming immediately struck him. Meideng said, "If you recognize the light of the lamp, where would the flavor be placed?
Even if it reached the mouth, the Master remained speechless. At dawn the following day, he sent an attendant to invite the Master. When the Master arrived, Ming asked, "Have you seen [it]?"
"Is it a person? the Master asked. Ming laughed and said, "I see only one person; I fear it would startle people if I were to speak of it.
The Master said, "Even if you had personally seen Śākyamuni, he would still have been just an ordinary fellow. Why not simply say so?

Ming said, "Master Wanfeng, do you wish to arrange our chronological order, or do you wish to discuss the Buddha-dharma? If it is to arrange our chronological order, there were a thousand people under Wanfeng's assembly."

"Regarding the discussion of the Buddha-dharma, Old Shili has not even dreamed of it; what is there to be startled by? If you observe the ten thousand peaks, where are those ten thousand peaks right now?
The Master’s face turned red and he was left speechless. The next day, [Zhaozhou] said, "If it is like this, you have never seen the ten thousand peaks.
The Master returned to his guest quarters and for three days and nights forgot both sleep and food. By chance, the cord of the incense lamp snapped and fell.
Dizi suddenly attained great enlightenment. He went before Guanzhi and presented the circumstances of his realization. Guanzhi Ming said, "Old *jiaoli*, you shall inherit the lineage of Wanfeng.
The Master said, "Master Bai has brought me to complete penetration; how could I inherit from Wanfeng? Ming then laughed.
He subsequently gathered the assembly and, stepping out of the cloister, ascended the seat and said: "Gautama had an intention to whom he would transmit it; Kāśyapa needlessly broke into a smile."
"Arriving here, how could even the Seven Buddhas remain long? Mañjuśrī’s face turned red, yet he remained utterly bewildered. Today, the matter of Dongming is truly laughable;
it causes people for a thousand ages to waste their spittle and drool. Fortunately, Master Hai forgot both 'me' and 'self,' so that the single thread of the Jie lineage continues unceasingly.
Thereupon, he cast down his staff and descended from the seat. The Master then entered the abbot's quarters and paid his respects, thanking Dongming, who said, "This old monk..."
He did not leave for more than a month. On the twenty-seventh night, he took his leave of the assembly; on the twenty-ninth day, he manifested parinirvāṇa.
The Master had originally intended to withdraw and return to Lake Dongting, but the fourfold assembly earnestly entreated him to remain, and he consequently succeeded to the seat.

On the anniversary of Wanfeng’s death, the Master offered incense and pointed to the portrait, saying: "I nearly drowned you in a jar. Fortunately, it was Puci; had it been anyone else, there would have been no saving you."
I burn this incense, which is worthy of repaying the guidance [of my teacher]. He lets out a shout and says, "I only laugh at you for protecting your shortcomings and lacking sense;

you treat the Buddha-dharma as a matter of personal favor. He spreads his sitting cloth and prostrates. Again, he takes up the incense and says, "This one portion of incense is offered to the Elder Dongming.
With a single heart of sincerity, he urged me on, enabling me to penetrate far into the source of the lineage. He shouts twice.
He shouted, "In the depths of receiving such profound grace, one immediately feels as if it were one's own home; only then does one know this is one's mother.
He rose from his prostrations and wept bitterly. Returning to the abbot’s quarters, he spoke a verse at the moment of his passing:

"For ninety-six years in the world, For seventy-four years as a monk, How much confusion and error lay within— Upon seeing Dongming, all is extinguished. With his whisk, he struck a circle (○) and said:
"From Śākyamuni until me, there have been incalculable generations," the Old Monk said. He then struck a circle and added, "Most often one establishes oneself here.
Ha! Thereupon he set down his brush and passed away. This was in the first year of the Jingtai era. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa to the left of Dongming.
Twelve people received the Dharma from him.
The *Wujia jiù* (Rescue of the Five Houses) records Chan Master Haizhou Puci, who, based on the lineage transmission, lists him as a Dharma heir of Dongming Xigong.
However, his recorded sayings (*yulu*) have not been seen; he is only listed as a leading disciple in the *Wanfeng lu*.
For now, I have provisionally arranged these according to their source and lineage, awaiting further verification. The *Wanfeng Yinji* (Seal of Myriad Peaks) verse says:
"Entrusting the hair of a tortoise to his descendants; Holding up a rabbit's horn to seek its source. A single shout leaves one deaf for three days."
"Who can intimately receive this inner message? Layman Shen Guan, the District Magistrate of Hai'an, asked the Master:
"The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: 'The teachings of the sūtras are like a finger pointing at the moon; if one sees the moon, one understands what was pointed out.'"
"In the ultimate sense, it is not the moon. How is this so? The Master raised his hand and said, "The sutra, the moon, and the finger.
The scholar was bewildered. The Master struck the table once and said, "The moon falls into the cold pond.

The scholar attained realization and said, "From this point on, I know that the Master’s Way cannot be fathomed by ordinary sentiment. [The Master] replied, "The establishment of the source and its stream is like a family lineage."

This is indeed so. Therefore, one must examine and establish the lineages of one's ancestors and clans, ensuring the proper succession of generations so that descendants may observe their source and follow their current.
They should strive diligently to advance in the Way, ensuring that their conduct does not bring shame upon the virtues of their predecessors;
it is not merely for the purpose of manifesting illustrious titles. If, however, the high and low are confused and the honorable and humble are inverted—like a treasure trove cast to the east...
What use is it to compile a genealogy of the three venerable masters, Ming, Hai, and Zhou?

Since the end of the Yuan dynasty, when warfare was rife, nearly three hundred years have passed until the present day. The conduct of the monastic community has become increasingly mixed, and the Way of our Patriarchs has reached its most profound decline.
Although there are one or two great beings who remain deeply hidden in mountain caves, their fame has not yet spread abroad; thus, their recorded sayings—
There is no transmission record for this. My late master Sanfeng composed a verse on the Linji lineage; having examined it thoroughly from various angles, I have grasped its general outline.
This is because Master Cizong Haizhou was a preeminent disciple who received the Dharma from Chan Master Wanfeng Wei.
Wanfeng had a verse of entrustment [to him], which states... Furthermore, Shen Guan, the District Magistrate of Hai'an, composed an inscription for Wanfeng’s stupa.
In my own preface, I recorded that I received the Dharma from Master Haizhou, a great disciple of Wanfeng.
Thus, Haizhou and Baozang were like brothers, and Master Dongming Cui was indeed Haizhou’s Dharma nephew.
Now, the lineage records treat Haizhou as the successor of Dongming; could there have been two Haizhous? In the winter of the Bingzi year, I rescued...
Regarding the Five Houses, I have recently obtained the *Wencong Chanshi Yulu* (Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Wumen Cong) of my fifth-generation ancestor.

It contains a single piece titled "Night Talks at the Guest Window," which provides a highly authoritative account of the lineage from the beginning down to the present. From Linji to Fengguo, there are eighteen transmissions.
These are no different from what has been recorded in recent times. From High Peak (Gao Feng) downward, it is said that two men emerged:
the first was Zhongfeng Ben; the second was Duanya Yi. Yi is not heard of [in this lineage]. Zhongfeng produced Qianyan Chang;
Chang produced Wanfeng Wei; Wei produced Haizhou Ci; Ci produced Baofeng Xuan. Xuan...
Although the appearance of these celestial wonders is not quite as extensive as that of Baozang and Dongming, it is clear that these two masters appeared in succession.
Furthermore, according to the Fourth Patriarch, Chan Master Xiyuan Yuexin Bao, there are six verses on the "Succession of Fragrance" (Lianfang), the preface to which states:
"I, the unworthy one, inherit from above the primordial ancestor of sixty-three generations since Kāśyapa, and from below..."
As a true descendant of the thirty-first generation of Caoxi, if one now calculates the lineage by its source and flow:
from Kāśyapa down to Xiaoyan, following the current downstream, there are sixty-five generations; from Xiaoyan back up to Caoxi, tracing the current upstream, there are thirty-three transmissions.
Comparing this with the "Preface to the Linked Flowers" (Lianfang), it exceeds that by two generations—namely, those of Master Cong.
It is likely that Baozang Dongming was such a person. Furthermore, Master Cong was the third-generation descendant of Haizhou, and Xiaoyan was the son of Master Cong;
they followed one another’s footsteps with only two generations intervening, much like our own relationship to Longchi.
Had he lived a few years longer, it would still have been possible to behold his countenance—how could this have happened within a span of only several decades?
How could such an error have come to this? It was truly the fault of Longchi (Longqi), not the fault of today.
Yet, how could Longchi have inserted these two names without cause? I once saw the text of the "Memorial for Haizhou" by the late Master Xiangyan Guxi Cheng, which states:
"Continuing the lamp of the seventh generation of Gaofeng; succeeding to the hundred-year legacy of Master Xian."
From Gaofeng to Haizhou, there were indeed seven generations, with Baozang and Dongming included therein.
Thus, it is beyond doubt that a separate line of Haizhou branched out from beneath Dongming.
Otherwise, the oral teachings of Wumen, the handwritten records of Xiaoyan, the verses of Wanfeng, and the inscriptions of Shenzi would all be inconsistent.

This is sufficient to inspire confidence. Whenever there are doubts or difficulties regarding any matter, one should resolve them through careful deliberation and compromise, seeking what is most appropriate before concluding.

Now, by relying on the verses of the lineage masters, examining the records in inscriptions and biographies, harmonizing the numerical correspondences of the ages, and scrutinizing the accounts of our distant ancestors, we find that all four points are in complete agreement. Only the question concerning the memorial inscription for Xiangyan remains unresolved.
This can be resolved with ease. Furthermore, Mazu and Shitou were both active at the same time;
since there were already two paths realized before them, how could one know that there will not be two Hai-zhou following in the footsteps of their descendants, Wan-feng and Dong-ming?
This does not require further debate; it is settled by relying on the previous four propositions. I have heard this from Tian-tong.
My master, the Elder, intended to revise this governance; I have recorded it here for your consideration and selection.

However, the two masters Baozang and Dongming still dare not act unilaterally according to the old ways. As I, this old monk, truly intend to investigate these matters, I have engraved them in small characters.
This seal was placed at the beginning of the *Yulu* (Recorded Sayings), yet for several years it could not be obtained.
Recently, my nephew in the Dharma, Shanzu, has had the karmic encounters between the two patriarchs Haizhou and Baofeng carved and circulated in the world.
This was obtained from Layman Cha Danhe, who preserved it among his family collection of the "Source and Lineage of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. Thus, Wanfeng Wei gave rise to Baozang Chi.
Chichi gave rise to Dongming Xian; Xian gave rise to Haizhou Ci; Ci gave rise to Baofeng Xuan. Furthermore, I obtained the *Recorded Sayings* of Chan Master Jing’an Su.
Su was the second-generation descendant of Haizhou. In the "Chart of Successive Fragrance" (*Lianfang tu*), he wrote:
"Śākyamuni Buddha first transmitted the mind-seal. After twenty-eight generations, it reached Bodhidharma, who [brought it] to the Eastern Land."
The First Patriarch; the Second Patriarch, Master Huìkě; the Third Patriarch, Master Sēngcǎn; the Fourth Patriarch, Master Dàoxìn;
the Fifth Patriarch, Master Hóngrěn; the Sixth Patriarch, Master Huìnéng; Master Shénràng of Nanyuè;
Císhī Mázǔ; Chán Master Bǎizhàng Hǎi; Chán Master Huìyùn of Huángbò; and Chán Master Línjì Xuān.
Chan Master Xinghua Jiang; Chan Master Nanyuan Yongyong; Chan Master Fengxue Yanzhao; Chan Master Shoushan Shengnian;
Chan Master Fenyang Wude; Chan Master Ciming Renyuan; Chan Master Yangqi Fanghui; Chan Master Baiyun Shouduan;
Chan Master Dongshan Daowei; Chan Master Foguo Yuanwu; Chan Master Huqiu Shaolong; and Chan Master Ying’an.
Chan Master Hua; Chan Master Miaoxin Miaman Jie; Chan Master Xian Poyuan Po’an; Chan Master Wenfeng Wuzhun Fayan;
Chan Master Yanchun Xueyan Zhiqin; Chan Master Xuyun Gaofeng Yuanmiao; Chan Master Zhifeng Zhongfeng Mingben; and Chan Master Qianyan Shouchang.
Chan Master Wanfeng Wei, Chan Master Baozang Chi, Chan Master Dongming Chai, Chan Master Haizhou Ci, and Chan Master Yunxi Ying.
Ying and Baofeng Xuan were brothers. Based on this, the lineage and its transmission are further confirmed as being passed down with absolute precision.
It is beyond doubt that Haizhou was the successor of the patriarch Dongming Chai. —Tán.

The *Ji* (Record of Auspiciousness) is said to be the *Wuwen yulu* (Record Without Words). It contains one essay titled "Night Talks at the Guest Window" (*Kechuang yehua*), in which the succession from the preceding masters is extremely precise.
Since it barely mentions Baozang or Dongming, it is evident that these two masters were overlapping figures.
That such errors have reached this state over several decades is truly lamentable; the mistake regarding Longchi merely stems from doubting Xiangyan’s memorial text for Haizhou.
Some say: "He continued the lamp of High Peak for seven generations and followed in the footsteps of Patriarch Xian for a hundred years.
Thus it was said that beneath Dongming, a separate Haizhou emerged; leading Mazu and Shitou, they manifested their transformations simultaneously.

Since there were already two who attained enlightenment before him, and since Wanfeng and Dongming—grandfather and grandson—succeeded one another, how can we know that there was not a second Haizhou?"
Later, Tan Ji could be seen arbitrarily attempting a "compromise," erasing the two patriarchs Baozang and Dongming and refusing to believe in the authentic lineage of our Old Man Longchi.
This single case alone demonstrates that his transgression is already extreme;
what need is there to mention other matters?
▲ Chan Master Baofeng Mingxuan of Nanjing Gaofeng Temple was a dharma successor of Haizhou. He was a native of Wujiang, Gusu, surnamed Fan.
In his lay life, he was a carpenter; while working on a pagoda courtyard for Master Haizhou, he injured his own foot with an axe.
The pain was extreme, and he asked for wine to drink. Guizhou heard of this and went to him, saying, "Just now, Head Carpenter Fan injured his foot; that is still forgivable.
But if you have your head cut off, even if there were a thousand *shí* of wine to give the carpenter to drink, would the carpenter be able to drink it?

The Master had an awakening and immediately stopped drinking. He then requested ordination as a monk. Guizhou immediately shaved his head and gave him the precepts, saying, "Today your head has fallen."
The Master said, "Though the head may fall, it is better; even a man who drinks wine does not have his head fall. He was then appointed as the fire-attendant.

One day, while the Master was carrying firewood, Zhuanzi saw him and asked, "What are you doing with these thorns? The Master replied, "They are firewood. Zhuanzi laughed heartily, "Hehe! The Master was left bewildered.
Zhuanzi said, "If they are firewood, take them away and burn them. The Master gave rise to a doubt and asked, "Master, what exactly are you?"
"What kind of principle is this? That you ask me and yet I cannot answer. That evening, he applied himself with intense resolve to investigate the matter.

Unbeknownst to him, his eyebrows were singed by a fire, and his face felt as if it had been cut with a blade. When he looked into a mirror, he attained a sudden and great awakening. He presented his realization to Zhuan.
Zhaozhou struck him. The Master snatched away the staff and said, "This six-foot pole has not been used for many years;
today you wish to pick it up once more. Zhaozhou laughed heartily. The Master presented a verse, saying:
"Wherever the staff strikes, bloodstains appear; Look closely at the hidden blade within the smile. If you are a truly heroic man, The dead will eat the staff and dance 'nan-nan'. Zhaozhou said:
"This very verse is fit to succeed my school," he said, and then bestowed the verse upon him: "The descendants of Linji are lions;
A single roar brings death to a thousand mountains and a hundred beasts. Today you possess claws and fangs and majesty; Yet you must remain hidden deep within ten thousand ravines."
From this point on, his fame spread far and wide, and students gathered like clouds. Five people attained the Dharma from him.
He passed away on the ninth day of the twelfth month in the eighth year of the Chenghua era. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa to the left of Dongming Temple.
▲ Chan Master Tianqi Bensui was a dharma successor of Baofeng. He was the son of the Jiang family of Zhongling in Nanchang.

At the age of twenty, he accompanied his father on a merchant journey to Yingzhou. Having become weary of worldly phenomena, he set out on foot toward Jingmen, where he paid respects to Master Wushuo Neng and received the tonsure to become a śramaṇa.
He was instructed to contemplate the koan: "All dharmas return to One; where does the One return? The Master then traveled extensively...
He attended upon senior masters and sat in meditation day and night. Upon arriving at Guanyin Temple in Suizhou, he heard that Elder Wenjin was observing the summer retreat there.

Seeing on the wall a copy of "The Exhortation" by Baoning Guangzhong, the Master—who was then observing a vow of silence—would frequently lift his head to look only at the middle two lines, which said: "Who is it that hesitates? Who is the person who raises [the question]? Furthermore...

Look and investigate! As days passed, his realization deepened; he perceived that the mountains, rivers, the great earth, the forests, the ponds, and the six sense faculties and six sense objects were all, in their entirety, nothing but this single word:
"Who? Later, while traveling with the head seat Quan to Xiangyang, they happened to hear a woman calling her pig.
Quan spoke a verse, saying: "Mother calls 'Nan-na' within the wall; The monks on the road understand."
"Ma! Having smashed these few critical pivots, my mother remains as she was before, my grandmother. Having fully manifested this, I shall depart; never again will I look back.
The Master thought to himself, "Yet, one must not simply accept it as it is—'Is this it? After traveling several stages, he remained in a state of lingering confusion.
One day, while ill, he heard a monk cite the story of Chan Master Dahui’s back abscess."
Through these conditions, he suddenly attained a thorough penetration of the meaning of Master Quan’s verse, whereupon he composed a hymn, saying: "To directly accept it, the matter is not mistaken;
It is all because of discrimination that the heavens are separated. If one can turn this light back to shine upon itself, To directly accept it, fundamentally there is no mistake.
Thereafter, he entered Shu to visit the elders such as Chushan and Xuefeng, gradually gaining further awakening and realization. Finally, he went to consult...
Master Baofeng asked, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "From Beijing. Baofeng said, "Are you still only in Beijing, or have you gone elsewhere?
The Master said, "I am carefree wherever I am. Baofeng asked, "Have you ever been to Sichuan? He replied, "I have."
Feng said, "Have you seen Fajian? He replied, "I have. Feng said, "Have you seen Chushan? He replied, "I have.
Feng said, "How many followers does Fajian have? He replied, "Thirty. Feng said, "How many followers does Chushan have? He replied, "Thirty. Feng said, "Yet they are not the same.
He replied, "Fundamentally there is no distinction; how could one differentiate between this and that? Feng said, "Four."
[The monk] said, "Regarding the boundary of the river: how does this boundary of yours compare? Feng said, "Though the mountains and rivers differ, the wind and moon are the same.
He then raised his fist and said, "Is there such a thing as this? The monk said, "No. Feng asked, "Why then is it not there?
The monk said, "It is not my realm. Feng asked, "What, then, is your realm? The monk said, "Even the Buddhas cannot know it; who would dare force it?"
Anming said, "Does this not mean you are clinging to emptiness? He replied, "I will never make my livelihood within a ghost cave.
Feng said, "Among the ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhist paths in India, you are the foremost teacher. With this, he shook out his sleeves and departed.

Jiù said: "Previously, I read a piece of instruction written by the Master; from beginning to end, it consisted of several thousand words, yet it taught people only to contemplate the single character 'Who' (shuí).
Now, reading this account of his life, I realize that the Master had actually applied his finger to that character 'Who' on the wall."
It is simply that their transmission has not yet been fully exhausted. Among the Master’s dharma heirs, there were more than three hundred and forty;
yet within less than a century, they had almost entirely vanished. Only the single branch of Wumen has continued unbroken down to the present day.
It is like a suspended thread. As for the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, it can be known without asking.
I have recorded the accounts of the patriarchs’ awakenings, preserving both the refined and the crude, so that one may see the rise and fall of the times.

Students should not attempt to further analyze or savor the meaning of the single word "Who" (shui). Tan Ji attempts to dismiss the Elder Tianqi based on this single word "Who," harboring a reckless intent.

Regarding the word "Who" (shuí), it is easy to recognize its gateway. Yet you do not realize that as for this very word "Who," whether you recognize the gateway or do not recognize the gateway is up to you.
It is like wishing to pay homage to the Holy Sovereign: whether you go straight into the capital is up to you;
whether you reach the Tongguan Pass is also up to you. Does passing through actually depend on the word "Who"? No, Han.
The Moon [Master] also remains within the current of the discourse. To "wipe it out" regarding Old Man Wumen is unavoidable;
one cannot help but feel a sense of urgency. To "wipe it out" regarding Old Man Xiyuan: when Xiyuan ascended the hall, he held up his staff and said, "Is there anyone?
Is there anyone? At that time, a monk came forward and prostrated. The Master struck him across the back with the staff and said, "Why so talkative? The monk said, "I..."
"Jia has not said a single word. Why do you talk so much? The Master struck him again, saying, "A second offense will not be tolerated.
It was just like when Baoshou opened the hall for teaching; Sansheng pushed forward a monk, and Baoshou immediately struck him.
Sansheng said, "If you act as a teacher in this manner, you will not only blind this monk's eyes, but you will also blind the people of the entire city of Zhenzhou. Baoshou—
He threw down his staff and returned directly to the abbot’s quarters. Fuguo said to Miaoxi, "Behold this authentic style of our school;
it is utterly transcendent and peerless. Miaoxi composed a verse on this occasion, beginning: "Lifting up the first hammer of Mount Sumeru..."
A flash of lightning or a spark from a flint is far too slow. Where the Elephant King treads, the tracks of the fox vanish.
When the Lion roars, the hundred beasts tremble with fear. I ask Master Han Yue: When Baoshou struck in such a manner, was he in a hurry?
When Foguo demonstrated in such a manner, and Miaoxi offered his verse in such a manner—did Han Yue approve of them as well? Could it be that Baoshou simply...?

"If one attains it in such a way," Xixian said, "then one cannot attain it in such a way. I did not expect you, father and son, to bring about the total extinction of our ancestral lineage to this extent.
Chanshi Zhengcong of Guanziling succeeded Tianqi; he was also known as Wumen. He was a native of Shaowu.
His secular surname was Xi, and his mother was of the Wu clan. On the eve of the Master’s birth, a sick monk came seeking lodging; Mrs. Wu declined his request.
At midnight, the Master was born, and that very same night, the sick monk passed away on the road. The villagers all said, "This monk has returned.
When the Master reached the age of three, both his parents died in succession; his maternal grandfather took pity on him and raised him as his own.
Before even a year had passed, his maternal grandfather also died. His uncle, because the Master’s father had been left orphaned and suffering, sent him to Yin’an Monastery to become a monk.

At seventeen, he received the tonsure; at twenty, he received full ordination. He specialized in the Vinaya while concurrently practicing *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, and he conducted a profound study of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and other treatises.
All his fellow students revered him. One day, while traveling to Baiyang Mountain, he encountered an elderly master who questioned him.
He said, "The Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū sat at the site of enlightenment for ten kalpas, yet the Buddha-dharma did not manifest before him, and he could not attain the Way of Buddhahood.

How can this principle be? The Master then lectured on it according to the text. An elder monk reviled and scolded him, then departed. From that point on, the Master’s state of doubt was suddenly aroused;
he pursued it with diligent mindfulness day and night for five or six years. One day, hearing the neighing of a horse, he experienced a sudden, vast awakening.
Wu said, "Such matters as these are clearly seen by the Tathāgata; there is no error or delusion. He then traveled to various regions and received the Dharma from the elder Tianqi.
Tianqi asked, "Suffering and pleasure are both the mind; why do you seek them externally? The Master replied, "It is simply because I have not yet attained full realization.
Tianqi said, "Right and wrong are both phenomena; why do you falsely accept them? The Master replied, "I mistook the zero mark on the scale."
Qi said, "Both delusion and enlightenment are human; why do they not understand? The Master replied, "Had I known early that the lamp was fire, why would I have sought it in the four directions?
[This concludes the record of] Chan Master Xixian Yuexin Debao, a successor of Juexue. He was the son of the Wu family of Jintai. His ancestors were of a noble clan from Jin.

Yi was orphaned at a young age; his character and disposition were naturally inclined toward the Way. When he reached the age of twenty, he entered a monastery and listened to lectures on the Great Commentary on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

Upon reaching the "Ten Stages" chapter, where it describes how the Tathāgata, when he was a wheel-turning monarch, renounced his kingdom, city, wife, and his own head, eyes, hands, and feet, he was profoundly moved.
He then paid homage to the Chan Master Guanghui Neng and left the household life. After his tonsure, he traveled extensively to consult renowned masters, eventually reaching Mount Funiu.

In the "Contemplation Gate of the Pure Land at the Fire Site," there was nothing he had not traversed. One day, while crossing a stream, he lost his footing and fell into the water; both his clothes and shoes became soaked.
Upon arriving at Luyajia (Lüjiadiàn), he changed his clothes and sat in silence. Suddenly, he heard a woman scolding her son and attained a realization.
He then proceeded to Guanling to pay his respects to Master Juexue Cong and presented what he had realized. Cong certified his attainment. The following morning, he entered...
In the room, Chong asked, "Where did all that entanglement of yours go yesterday, Senior?
The Master prepared to answer, but Chong laughed and said, "A hawk flies over Silla. The Master then asked, "The Ten Sages and Three Worthies have already perfected their sage-wisdom."
"Why do you not understand this principle? Cong shouted, "What is this principle? Speak quickly! Speak quickly!

The Master offered several successive turns of phrase, sometimes responding with shouts as soon as he was questioned, yet none were in accord. Later, while washing vegetables by a spring, a single leaf suddenly fell into the water.
The Master followed the water's circular flow, trying to catch it, but could not. Thereupon, he attained realization.
Overjoyed, he returned home. That evening, Cóng questioned him about the saying that Xuánshā had not yet reached full realization.
The Master said, "A thief enters an empty room. Cóng said, "This koan must not be treated lightly. The Master then gave a shout and swept his sleeves out of the room.
A few days later, he took leave of Guānlǐng and joined Shuǎngān as companions to enter Chǔ to visit Dàjué Yuánɡōng. Yuán was advanced in years and possessed a dignified bearing.

His appearance was robust and imposing, and his voice resonated like a bell. He had lived in the mountains for several decades, avoiding all worldly affairs; he was truly a great master of the Chan school.

Upon first seeing him, the Master sought to attend upon him, but Huairang (Jue) declined him. Only after repeated requests did Huairang grant his permission. The Master attended Huairang for several months, questioning and challenging him morning and evening.
Huairang, the elder, would seize and release the situation with shifting winds; his skillful means were unfathomable. One day, while in the meditation hall...
[The Master] cited the story of a non-Buddhist questioning the Buddha: "I do not ask about the word 'existence,' nor do I ask about the word 'non-existence.

After the World-Honored One remained silent for a long while, the non-Buddhist attained awakening. Yuanjue said, "Since he did not involve himself with existence or non-existence, even that 'long silence' is merely an idle name. At such a time, what did the non-Buddhist awaken to?
As the Master was about to respond, Yuanjue covered the Master’s mouth with his hand and said, "Stop, stop! You are still hanging on [to conceptualizations]."
When Shi Zhi was present, the Master suddenly realized and said, "One could say that the monks of this eastern land are not even equal to the non-Buddhists of the western heavens;
they are truly far behind. He then presented a verse, saying: "I laugh at myself for the patterns I drew in years past, How many times it was red, and how many times black.
Now, having thanked my master, I return to my old home; Who cares whether I have attained anything in my life? Jue praised him, saying, "Excellent!"
As Jiǎo Lǎoshùn was about to pass away, his teacher returned from Guānlǐng. Cóng Chánshī held him in high esteem and entrusted him with the seal of the Dharma.
[He] was the successor to Xiàoyán, the Chan Master Zhènghuàn of Jīngxī. His secular surname was Lǚ; he was a native of Lìyáng.
At the age of nineteen, he received the tonsure under Monk Lè’ān. Because he suffered from a chronic illness, Lè’ān instructed him to contemplate "the state before one's parents were born."
Regarding the previous discourse: after a long time, he attained no realization. Thereupon, he applied himself with diligent perseverance for over two weeks.
One night, while walking in meditation (caṅkrama), he sat down; overcome by drowsiness, he was helpless when he suddenly heard the sound of glass lamps bursting into flame.
At that moment, he had a sudden awakening and said: "Only now do I understand what the ancients meant when they said: 'The void is utterly pulverized, and the great earth sinks level. Ten...

"It has no walls or enclosures; on all four sides there are no gates. If a single person gives rise to true realization and returns to the source, the empty space of the ten directions will all vanish away"—such sayings are not empty words. Thereupon, he went directly to the capital of Yan to visit Master Xiangyan and seek his certification.
Before he had finished communicating what he had attained, Xiangyan suddenly kicked out a single sandal and said, "Right here!"
"Speak a single phrase," [Zhaozhou] said. The Master remained silent. He did not sleep throughout the entire night; by the following morning, he was still standing beneath the eaves.
Yanguan came out and called to him. The Master turned his head. Yanguan lifted one foot and assumed the posture of an asura. At this, the Master attained realization.

He served diligently for several years before taking his leave to return south. Yanguan wrote a letter concerning the lineage transmitted from his predecessors and entrusted it to him. As he was departing, Yanguan presented him with a straw rain hat.
[The opponent] says: "Do not expose your sharp edges.
[The respondent] replies: "No; prosperity and adversity give rise to one another; this is the natural order of things.

As for the Huotuo lineage, after several generations, its descendants have spread throughout the world—this may indeed be called a great flourishing. This has continued down to Xueyan and his disciples, and from Qianyan and Wanfeng onwards."
Although the core teachings have gradually declined, there are still many men of heroic stature and upright character whose aspirations transcend the mundane;
yet their decline has perhaps never been as severe as it is today. Alas! While Sanfeng has long since passed away, the Venerable Master Tiantong remains vividly present.
Those who have merely stolen his name from beneath his seat now swarm about the gates of officialdom in a thousand ways and ten thousand guises.
In several years, the resulting corruption will be beyond description. Regarding Tanji’s slander against Xueyan and his disciples:
since Qianyan and Wanfeng, the fundamental teaching has gradually declined. I, this old monk, ask you all: what do you point to as the fundamental teaching?
Yet you say it is gradually vanishing; do you mean to say it is withering away? In the past, Linji said: "This mountain monk..."
Today, having no choice but to comply with human sentiment, I have ascended this seat.
Yet, if we were to discuss the Great Matter according to the tradition of our ancestral patriarchs, it would truly be impossible to open one’s mouth; there would be no place for you to set foot.
This day, because the Attendant has made a firm request, how could I conceal the fundamental principles? Are there any masters or veteran warriors here who can directly display their mettle?
The battle array is opened; look at this as evidence before the assembly. At that time, a monk asked, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma?
Linji then shouted. The monk bowed. Linji said, "This monk is indeed capable of engaging in debate.

Looking at it, it appears that Linji, based on his directness, made it so that one could not open one's mouth and left no place for you to set foot—this was how he established his fundamental tenets. Therefore...

This refers to the hidden thread of the fundamental tenets (*gangzong*). Because Senghui attained [realization] through prostrations rather than through not performing prostrations, Jie said, "This monk is indeed capable of upholding the thread of the fundamental tenets.
Thus, the single school of the Hutuo [Linji] lineage takes only the staff and shout as pointing out people;
this is the great intent of the Buddha-dharma. How could it be like Han Yue, who searched exhaustively through past and present?
Regarding the three dharmas, death, and execution, which are fixedly assigned: the Three Mysteries and Three Essentials are regarded as the guiding principles of the Jingshan lineage.

Danxia, Jiashan, and others followed suit in harmonizing with them, eventually claiming that from the time of Xueyan and his disciples, through Qianyan and Wanfeng, the essential tenets had gradually declined.
This old monk does not employ my staff as a mere staff; it directly points to all people as the Buddha-dharma.
The general gist is this: Han Yue slandered [the lineage] as "one-sided, rigid Chan" and "resembling the drool of wild foxes.
Consequently, Tan Ji established it as a distinct school of the Hutuo tradition; its decline has never been as severe as it is today. Alas!
To erase the old monk [Miaozhuo] might still be excusable, but to erase the lineage from the time of Xueyan and his disciples onward—including all the successive patriarchs—is unforgivable.
It is indeed speakable. Furthermore, the Huatou school has held that using the staff and shouts to point out people constitutes the great purport of the Buddha-dharma;
today, however, it has been annihilated by you all, and can no longer even be spoken of.
