How can they avoid being students themselves, and how can they shatter [the barrier] and break in? I shall ask Master Tanji and his peers: apart from self-awakening, what else can you point to?
This is the True School; it is the Great Dharma. Therefore, when this old monk raises a staff, he does not employ it as a mere staff.
He says: "If you call it a staff, you will enter hell like an arrow shot. Those such as Han Yue, Tan Ji, and their ilk still call it "wild shouts and chaotic blows";
they shall never have the opportunity to emerge from hell. Why? It is simply because they themselves lack realization and entry [into the Way].

To possess but a single eye, yet conversely to take the names and phrases established by the ancients as the True Sect, as the Essential Principle, as our own School, and as the Great Dharma—is this not what is meant by "relying on shrimp for eyes"? This old monk relies upon Linji’s statement:
"Only when you have committed the five deeds of immediate retribution will you attain liberation. [The student] asked: "What are the five deeds of immediate retribution?"

Ji said, "Killing one's father, harming one's mother, shedding the blood of a Buddha, breaking the harmony of the Saṃgha, and burning scriptures and images—these are the five *ānantarya* (uninterrupted) karmas. What, then, is the father? He replied, "Ignorance (*avidyā*) is the father.
When you seek the place of arising and ceasing within a single thought-moment and cannot find it, it is like an echo in a valley; being without affairs wherever you are is called [the state]."
"Kill your father. [The student] asked, "What is meant by 'mother'? He replied, "Craving is the mother.
When you direct a single thought toward the realm of desire, you cannot find that craving; you see only the empty nature of all phenomena. To be unattached everywhere is called 'killing the mother.
[The student] asked, "What is meant by 'shedding the Buddha's blood'? He replied, "Within the pure realm, there is not a single..."
When thoughts arise and one seeks conceptual understanding, one immediately encounters darkness everywhere; this is shedding the blood of the Buddha. One asks:
"What is the breaking up of the harmonious Sangha? He replies: "In a single thought-moment of direct penetration, the fetters and afflictions are like space, having no place to rely upon."
"This is what it means to break the harmony of the Sangha. What is meant by 'incinerating scriptures and images'? He replied:

"To see that causes and conditions are empty, that the mind is empty and phenomena are empty, and to reach a definitive resolution in a single thought—so that one stands utterly free from affairs—this is precisely what it means to incinerate scriptures and images.
Venerable Sir, if you can penetrate this way, you will avoid being obstructed by the names of 'ordinary' or 'sage. Your single thought-moment is merely an empty fist."
This refers to the realization that arises from within. Amidst the phenomena of sense organs and objects, you falsely fabricate strange delusions;
you disparage yourself and become disheartened, saying, "I am an ordinary person; he is a sage. You have been born as a bald-headed monk many times—what is this desperate rush toward death?
You have donned the skin of a lion, yet you still howl like a jackal. A great man does not lack the breath of a great man. [Look at] yourself!
They are unwilling to believe in the things within their own house; they merely seek them outwardly.

They fall under the influence of the ancients' idle phrases and names, leaning on the shadows and seeking the light, unable to achieve direct penetration. Look at Linji saying: "A great man does not act with the breath of a great man.
He is unwilling to believe in the things within his own house, which is just as my late teacher said: "The things..."
To take the path of the Great Man is fundamentally distinct. As soon as one has leaped to the source and grasped it in hand, one simply lifts up and goes;

one does not ask "how" or "what. How could this be the same as those like Han Yue, who merely seek outwardly, relying on the idle phrases and names of the ancients, and—leaning on the shade while seeking the sun—fail to achieve independent penetration? How can one blame them for being of such a kind?
Having attained the "Han-yue" (Chinese Moon), how can you conversely claim he was unfit to serve as a model? Han-yue deceives his own mind and obscures himself;
he does not even realize his own shame, yet falsely claims to be Yangshan, asserting that by the power of his vows he has returned once more to reconnect the severed lineage of Linji.
Why do you not look at what Shoushan said to Fengxue: "I wish to hear its essential point. Fengxue then ascended the hall and cited the World-Honored One...
With eyes like blue lotuses, he looked over the great assembly and said: "At this very moment, tell me, what is being said?
If you say that it is 'speaking without speaking,' you are once again burying the former sages. So tell me, what is being said?"
Shoushan shook his sleeves and went down. Fengxue threw down his staff and returned to his quarters.
The next day, while he was with Zhen the head gardener, they went together to pay their respects. Fengxue asked Zhen, "What is the Buddha’s 'speaking that which is not spoken'?
Zhen replied, "A magpie calling on the tree. Fengxue said, "Why do you accumulate such foolish merit? Why do you not..."
He thoroughly investigated the words and phrases. He then asked Shoushan, "How about you? Shoushan said, "Moving the countenance to reveal the ancient path;
not falling into the silent mechanism. Fengxue said to Zhen, "Why do you not look at the words spoken under the *Lotus Sūtra*? In this way, one may see Fengxue.
Only when he witnessed Shoushan shaking his sleeves and departing did he realize that "moving the countenance to reveal the ancient path" was the total manifestation of the whole body.
This is the Great Function that continues the essential tenets of Linji. This refers to when Yangshan, before Baizhang Weishan, said:
"To offer this profound mind to every dust mote and land is what is called repaying the Buddha's kindness.

He made a vow to come as the head of the lineage to receive the Linji school, yet he encountered a great wind and his line was cut off. However, it is only the act of "sweeping the sleeves and departing" that constitutes the true tradition.

The essential point is this: my late master said that when this monk went straight ahead without looking back, was he not acting in accordance with the principle of "not moving the countenance to reveal the ancient road" and "not falling into the silent mechanism"? This is why I asked Han Yue.
As for the moment after the moon has set, how can they meet? Yet Han-yueh immediately emerged; thus, the old monk alone rejoiced in this.
Furthermore, when Shou-shan received Feng-yang, he simply said, "The dragon’s sleeve is swept aside, and the whole body is revealed. This is self-enjoyment.
He then said, "Where the Elephant King walks, there are no traces of foxes. How could this compare to Han-yueh’s empty boasting that Yang-shan was reborn?

Come! You do not follow the true instructions of Linji, but instead ascend upon his "Four Kinds of Discernment," "Four Types of Guest and Host," "Four Modes of Illumination and Function," and "Three Mysteries and Three Essentials.
Relying on the dark to deceive the light, you claim these are "deeper than deep" and "more secret than secret," ensnaring those who do not recognize them;
thus, in a secluded room where no one is present, you transmit these trivial names.
They take phrases to be the Great Dharma, the True Sect, and the innermost sanctum of the teaching.
They recklessly imagine that this old monk here is also like Han Yue; thus they doubt that I am not dwelling within the Vihāra of the Abbot’s quarters discussing the Buddha-dharma.
Therefore, the Old Monk says: "I thought there was some other substantial dharma transmitted from mouth to ear, but it is truly not the seed of my own house."
"Grass! Is this not the same as Linji’s saying: 'A great man does not act like a great man;

he refuses to trust the things within his own house and instead seeks only outwardly, falling under the influence of the idle phrases and names of the ancients'—is this not identical to the direct pointing of total presentation?
If so, then Han Yue falsely takes Linji as his true teacher, yet conversely..."
Linji’s instructions and admonitions utterly obliterate true awakening and the true Dharma, as well as the authentic lineage and the authentic purport.

That which is brilliantly penetrating and belongs to a great man—his great capacity and great function—is here reduced to a single flavor: relying on the reputation of Yangshan as a "reincarnation" to deceive the world and future generations.
His various mental activities and modes of conduct are fabricated and spurious, such that they can hardly be described in words.
Tán Gǔ (潭吉) conversely claims that Hányuè’s vows are great; yet, look at Shǒushān—when has he ever uttered a single character or word claiming to be the reincarnation of Yǎngshān?

To deceive the world and future generations in this way may indeed be called having "great vows," yet [Shǒushān] did not dare to lightly reveal himself as being superior to all others, lest people lose their self-confidence and become arrogant.
A man seeking it outwardly returns with nothing but an idle reputation. Now, judging by Han Yue, he is a mere fabricator of false views and deluded speech;
he is clearly a wild fox spirit who has infiltrated the Dharma-gate to destroy and erase it.
Thus, he claims to be the reincarnation of Yangshan and to continue the severed lineage of Linji, yet he merely ransacks ancient and modern accounts of the three methods, such as the "three strikes."
The pestle, the three jars of sauce, three days of deafness, the three times shaking the door panels—these and other such matters are fixed by death and execution.

The Three Mysteries and the Three Essentials are taken as the guiding principles of the Linji school. One does not see that Linji said: "O practitioners of the Way, do not seek within words and letters;
the mind becomes weary and exhausted, and inhaling cold air is of no benefit. It is better than [seeking] the non-arising of conditions in a single thought."

He was born as one who transcends the provisional teachings of the three vehicles and the bodhisattvas. Is this not the "patience of non-arising" (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) attained beneath the staff?
It is to see no teacher when facing the critical moment; is it not the direct pointing and singular extraction that surpasses all teachings?
Linji further said: "In years past, I had never attained a place of realization. During those times, everything was pitch black; time and opportunity must not be wasted."
It was past. My belly burned and my mind was frantic; I rushed about seeking the Way. Only after later gaining strength did I reach this present day.

To "discuss the Way with fellow practitioners" in such a manner—is this not the same as seeing the place where Huangbo’s sixty painful blows struck as being like being brushed by a bundle of mugwort? Therefore it is said: "You people everywhere have heard that there is a Linji."
When this old fellow appeared in the world, people intended to pose difficult questions and challenge him, yet they were unable to utter a word;

for the mountain monk had manifested his total functioning, leaving the students with eyes wide open, yet their mouths utterly unable to move. Stunned and bewildered, they did not know how to answer me.
Based on this, Han Yue, Tan Ji, and others did not understand that my single blow was the total functioning of the Great Function (quanti dayong).
They recklessly fabricated all manner of slanders; Zhengkong merely opened his eyes, yet his mouth could not move at all, for he was utterly bewildered and did not know how to answer me.
Is this not what Linji meant when he said: "The treading of dragons and elephants is not for donkeys"?
"Is this not what it means to be capable? For this reason, Linji also said: 'O practitioners of the Way! If you wish to accord with the Dharma, simply do not give rise to obstructions.
When extended, it pervades the entire Dharma-realm; when withdrawn, not even a single hair's breadth remains. It is vividly and individually luminous, never lacking anything.
The eyes do not see it; the ears do not hear it. What thing would you call it? An ancient said: 'To describe it as one thing...'"
This matter is simply not right. You need only look for yourself; what else is there? Linji merely points people toward it:
"You need only look for yourself. How could this compare to Han Yue, who practiced all manner of deceptions to cover up his deeds for all future generations?
On the contrary, you falsely claim Linji to be the true master. Consider what Linji said: "Vividly and radiantly clear, never lacking for a moment;
neither seen by the eye nor heard by the ear—what thing is this? Is this not precisely the "originally there was nothing at all" of the Sixth Patriarch?
Han Yue slanders the Sixth Patriarch, falling into the trap of empty appearances; he is a nihilistic outsider. Because of this, Linji...
It is as the ancients said: "To describe it as a single thing is immediately incorrect. And again: "You need only look within yourself;

what else is there to see? One can clearly perceive Han Yue’s point here. It was simply because he did not know how to look within himself that he failed to understand the Sixth Patriarch’s instruction to "only look within yourself," whereby one finds that "originally there is nothing at all.
Consequently, he slandered this teaching, claiming it fell into the error of the nihilistic heretics. He did not realize...
The former master merely looked within himself and said, "There are no two paths for the holy and the ordinary," yet he slandered [this teaching] by claiming it was unfit to serve as a model.
He did not realize that when this old monk merely looks within himself, he encompasses the entire Dharma-realm;

all things, both sentient and insentient, manifest radiantly and with equal clarity. Therefore, through the functioning of his total being, he points directly to all people, each of whom is a great man.
Consequently, they slanderously claim that "one-stump" hard Zen surpasses what was transmitted by Longchi and constitutes the true lineage of Caoxi;

they falsely imagine that Linji’s *xuan-yao* (profound essentials) transcends this. However, Linji stated that his teachings are inexhaustible and that each person must exert their own effort, while further entrusting them with the instruction to "cherish [this].
How could he have ever taught people to look elsewhere outside of themselves for something else?

"Discriminating wisdom surpasses the depths of one's own house. Since Han Yue has already declared that my late master was unfit to serve as a model, how could there be anything [of value] in this old monk?
Those who come to see me wish to blend themselves into my Dharma gate.
This is the extinction and obliteration of my dharma-gate; it is precisely what Linji meant by "donning the skin of a lion, yet making the cry of a jackal.
Before meeting this old monk, they practiced deception and acted as treacherous go-betweens, hiding in the shadows and lying in wait.
Once they had obtained the lineage seal, they disseminated fragmented and heterodox doctrines openly and publicly. This was not how they were originally instructed; they have altered [the teaching].
How far removed we are from the truth! With such fawning and devious hearts, and such artfully painted faces, the single word "straightforwardness" has no place at all.
This old monk does not resist or speculate; he cannot claim prior realization. His transgressions are indeed real.
What status could one be proud of? What deficiency could one conceal? What slanderous words are being brewed within?

What external influence has been stirring from without? Thus, the fact that today’s opening and re-opening have proceeded directly to their ultimate conclusion is precisely what Han-yueh calls the "True Dharma" (Ch'eng-tsung), not what this old monk calls the True Dharma.
This is not what my late teacher called the "essence" (zongzhi), nor is it what Linji called the "essence. Why is this?
I personally heard from my late teacher that for a great man pursuing the Way, the approach is utterly distinct:
as soon as the root-source is grasped and mastered, one simply seizes the moment and departs. This is what Linji meant by "the thing within your own house"; you need only attend to it yourself.
Those who look at this from the perspective of the household are like Han Yue, who separately established a kind of heterodox path and falsely claimed to be a true son of Linji.
He was a "reincarnation of Yangshan" who, relying on the idle phrases and names of the ancients, used the dark to mask the light; who among them truly possessed the Great Dharma?
What constitutes the True Teaching? What is that which is deeper than the deep and more secret than the secret?
It is precisely what Linji meant when he said that a true man does not act with the breath of a "great man.
Now, when Linji says, "Do not take the Buddha as the ultimate; I see him as nothing more than a latrine hole," this must not be interpreted as a total repudiation of the Tathāgata.
A Letter from the Old Monk to Layman Liu: A man of spirit naturally possesses the ambition to soar toward the heavens;

he does not walk where the Tathāgata has walked—how much less so in the case of Linji? Han Yue has searched exhaustively through ancient and modern texts for the three dharmas, such as the "three strikes on the mortar," the "three jars of sauce," the "three days of deafness," and the "three times shaking the door-panel. He has rigorously classified them into the Three Mysteries and the Three...
It is essential [to consider this]. If one regards him as the true master, then who is it that truly "wiped out" Linji—is it the Old Monk, or is it Han Yue?
How can we rouse Linji himself to ask him for salvation? It is said:
Chan Master Xinghua Jiang was initially a personal attendant to Linji and had already attained realization. Later, at...
The three holy ones were great awakeners who had thoroughly penetrated the source and bottom of the Dharma. Having appeared in the world, Xinghua held up his incense and said:
"This one stick of incense was originally intended for my elder brother, Sansheng; yet Sansheng was too distant from me. It was originally intended for my elder brother, Dayue;
yet Dayue was too remote from me. It is better that I offer it to my late teacher Linji. I say that Xinghua’s offering of the fragrant incense was indeed [profound].
The family tradition of Jibei is presented here in its entirety. In recent times, the Master alone has been the one who understood this method.
Yet, from this very point, polemical treatises have emerged, and from this, rifts have arisen. How difficult it truly is to speak of such matters!
To us, however, it is said that the fundamental tenet is what sustains the life-force of wisdom; our Master continues the lineage of the Buddha.
He is a man of wisdom and life. I do not contend with him; who would dare to contend with him? As for that person at Sanfeng, he says, "I am his disciple.
That a disciple should surpass his master has never occurred in antiquity. I do not suppress him; who could possibly suppress him?
Furthermore, those who believe in Sanfeng have distorted the truth to obtain a semblance of it, while those who favor Tiantong delight in its ease.
Regarding their titles, they scrutinize others with harsh intent and accommodate flatterers to align with themselves; yet each claims to be extensively protecting the Dharma in the Final Age.
This is like people in the same boat crossing perilous waves and treacherous waters, yet brandishing spears against one another.
Even a passerby on the road would feel chilled at heart by such conduct, yet those who do not cease their fighting may truly be called... [the end of the sentence is missing from the source text].
How wise! Tanji merely wishes to rescue Han-yueh by using the "offering of incense" (*niangxiang*) as his justification;
he fails to consider that when Xinghua was first the attendant to Linji, Han-yueh had never served Linji—how could he be compared to Xinghua?
Furthermore, since it is said that Xinghua reached the very bottom of the source of the Dharma under Sansheng and Da-jue, how...
One might say that he attained enlightenment under Linji, yet why would he offer incense at Linji’s site?
This is likely because he does not understand what Xinghua meant by "Sansheng was too distant for me; Dajue was too remote for me.
It seems he has not correctly grasped the principle of how our late teacher Linji received blows from Huangbo. Therefore, it is said: "It is better not to make offerings..."
I have been nurturing the teachings of my late master Linji. Now, Han Yue slanders me for striking people, claiming it is "one-piece head-hard Chan.
This is precisely a slander against the principle by which Linji received blows from Huangbo; he has never even dreamed of the principle behind Xinghua’s offering of incense.
Yet he recklessly treats this as a numerical category and recklessly treats it as a formal method—how bitter!
To die imitating others—does this not make one want to vomit? Thus, my writing as an old monk was prompted by Han-yueh’s chaotic fabrications;
it was certainly not intended to tolerate sycophants who seek to curry favor with me, nor to scrutinize others with harsh intent.
Rather, I have based myself on the principle of Lin-chi receiving blows from Huang-po to correct Han-yueh’s reckless slanders against me as being merely "one-sided."

This is "hard Zen. It is not that I am slandering this old monk; rather, it is precisely Huangbo’s striking with the staff, Linji’s receiving the blows, and Xinghua’s offering of incense that constitute the fundamental tenet (zongzhi) of all those who have come before us.

Since the fundamental tenet is truly what sustains the life of wisdom, and since I, this old monk, am truly one who continues the life of wisdom of the Buddhas—if I am not upright, who can make it so? Sanfeng is indeed my disciple.
To turn one's back on the lineage of the masters and personally propagate a kind of demonic teaching is truly something unprecedented in antiquity.

If I do not refute it, who can? As for Mazu’s majestic single shout that left Baizhang deaf for three days, and Huangbo’s involuntary tongue-flicking upon hearing [the story] being cited—such works that transcend their own teachers have existed in the past. It is a pity, however, regarding Han Yue.
When someone who was not the right person attempted to save the situation, he said, "Lifting one, lifting two. This was the discourse given by Master Qianfeng when he ascended the hall.
At that time, Yunmen stepped forward from the assembly and said, "Yesterday someone came from Tiantai and went on to Jingshan. Qianfeng replied, "The head cook."
"Tomorrow there shall be no communal labor (fusshō). This is what is called the livelihood of the Zen school.
Under the words of the two elders, our late Master uttered a phrase for each; his eye that distinguishes dragons from snakes is clearly visible.

Yet, the *Hibuku* (The Book of Refutation) challenges him, claiming he does not understand "raising one [phrase]" and asserting that the paths of the Way are inherently different. I, this old monk, say: let you all practice as much as you wish.
[This is] merely an ornament. It is not at all to prevent this old monk from throwing down his staff to test Han Yue;

rather, Han Yue mistakenly took the staff to be something else and went forward to seize it, chasing after a mere clod of earth. How could this possibly be the same as when the old monk ascends the hall?
Having thus raised the issue for examination, one who possesses the eye that distinguishes the dragon from the snake offers this rescue:
"That which is said to be 'beyond form and sound' does not definitively refer to the Vīradhvaja of the *Lotus Sūtra* nor to the Dīpaṃkara who conferred the prediction upon Śākyamuni.
Looking upward to our own school, there are three Dīpaṃkaras: the Dīpaṃkara before [the first], the Dīpaṃkara [of the Lotus], and the Dīpaṃkara [who appeared] after.
"After the Lamp" refers to the actual act of lighting the lamp. One forms a large circle (○), which serves as an illustration, much like the Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate (Taiji tu).
This is intended to demonstrate the state prior to the manifestation of heaven, earth, and the myriad things; it does not mean that this specific diagram is itself the Supreme Ultimate.

The *Pibushu* claims that our late master arbitrarily fabricated this circle to "cover over" Dīpaṃkara, asserting that since Śākyamuni appeared after Dīpaṃkara, [the former could not have been his teacher].
Subsequently, this characteristic would not have existed prior to Dīpaṃkara; alas, how could one know that which is referred to above as Dīpaṃkara?
The profound intent within this Dharma is beyond the benefit of mere discourse.
For now, I shall discuss its superficial aspects to clear away the faults of my predecessors. Regarding the realm beyond Vipaśyin, the ancient worthies have indeed spoken repeatedly.
As the Venerable Caoshan had a verse that says: "Before King Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja was awakened, how could Maitreya have been conscious? Furthermore, he drew this [symbol].
Now, one might say that Caoshan falsely fabricated this symbol to cover over King Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja and Maitreya—is this permissible?
I have heard it said: "Those who wear felt and coarse woolen garments find it difficult to discuss the exquisite density of pure silk;
those who eat sorrel soup and parched grain are insufficient to be discussed with regarding the flavors of the great ox sacrifice.

Now, that which was shown by our former masters is the very principle realized and certified by Linji and Deshan. If one practices the Way in Lu, people will already laugh at them; how much more so when practicing the Way of Linji!
"Is the Way of Deshan [still present] in this final five-hundred-year period? This old monk, relying on Tanji, cites the verse of Caoshan:
'Before King Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja, even Maitreya would not be awake. Furthermore, he drew this [mudrā] sign.
Had I seen Caoshan acting in such a manner, I would have given him a blow of my staff, so as to spare the descendants of today from Han Yue’s reckless fabrications."
[He] is the progenitor of the thousand Buddhas and ten thousand Buddhas. This means that each of the five schools emerges from but one aspect of [him], thereby eclipsing the five schools.
Furthermore, Danji fails to consider that Cao Shan cited both Weiyin and Maitreya as examples of those who surpassed Śākyamuni;
yet the Weiyin in question is not the Weiyin recorded in the *Lotus Sūtra*, nor is the Maitreya the same as the one in the *Lotus Sūtra*.
Regarding the verses on the Five Ranks of Bias and Rectitude by Miliye of Dongshan, which are included herein:

"Simultaneously reaching the center—'Who dares to harmonize with that which does not fall into existence or non-existence? Everyone wishes to taste the flowing stream; yet when all is settled, one returns to sitting in the charcoal.
Thus, Caoshan painted this [symbol] to represent "sitting in the charcoal. Now, I ask Han Yue Tanji: When has anyone ever...?
When someone came who did not sit on the charcoal, Caoshan spoke in verse: "The principle and phenomena are entirely concealed; their first signs are ultimately difficult to clarify.
Even King Bhīṣmagarjitasvaranāda did not understand them; how could Maitreya be so alert? Furthermore, how could there ever have been no King Bhīṣmagarjitasvaranāda or Maitreya?
He further questioned Tanji: "Is there still a Caoshan? If there is a Caoshan, is he also alert in this way?"
How can you speak thus? Do you speak thus without being clearly awake? If you are not clearly awake, then how could you have seen that even King Weyin was unawakened?
Is Maitreya not clearly awake? If this is so, then you may see the old monk: his single blow is not used as a single blow;
stroke after stroke, he points directly at people, so that they may awaken for themselves and realize for themselves. Even if you were to reach a final conclusion...
To one who sits amidst the charcoal embers, I give a blow; before the lamp is lit, I give a blow;
after the lamp is lit, I give a blow; while the lamp is being lit, I give a blow. Why is this?
You perceive phenomena as having distinctions of shallow and deep, thereby contradicting Cao Shan’s principle of non-alteration. I, the old monk, however, see these very phenomena as they are.
Because of equality. If, outside of the burning lamp, one recognizes this single circle (○), it is precisely like Hanlu the hound chasing after a clod of earth.
Therefore, the ancient masters said: "If we speak of battle, each and every one stands at the point of turning; taking back the objects is superior, while chasing after the objects is inferior.
How could this compare to Han Yue’s reckless fabrication of a single circle as the ancestor of the thousand Buddhas and ten thousand Buddhas? Five.
Each school puts forth one aspect of the circle (○) and attempts to ensnare all under heaven and future generations, unaware that there is the matter of one's own fundamental share.
By taking your single circle as the patriarch, do you wish to establish yourselves as a separate kind of outsider?
Han Yue, Tan Ji, and others falsely assume the names of Linji and Deshan, yet they instead slander the Way of Linji and Deshan. How [can this be]?
Deishan did not look at the monks; as soon as they entered the gate, he would strike them with his staff. Linji, upon seeing a monk enter the gate, would immediately shout.
Furthermore, Linji said in a formal lecture: "All of you, within this mass of red flesh, there is a true person of no station."
He used to enter and exit through the face-gate; let those who have not yet attained realization look closely! Then he descended from the seat.
At that time, a monk came forward and asked, "What is the true person of no station? Linji seized him and said, "Speak! Speak!
As the monk hesitated, Linji pushed him away and said, "The true person of no station—what a dried-up shit-stick! This is so even for one who merely hesitates.

This is impossible. How much less could it accommodate Han Yue raising his intention or raising his hand to form the symbol of a circle (○)? Furthermore, he falsely interprets and falsely explains, saying:
"Wei" refers to that which is beyond form; "Yin" refers to that which is beyond sound; thus, "King Wei-Yin" refers to that which is beyond both form and sound.
There has been no record of it being transmitted; there is nothing to rely upon as evidence. Is this the most supreme matter prior to written words? Deshan said:
"If one discusses this matter, even the Buddhas of the three periods find their mouths hanging on the wall. Yet there is another person who laughs heartily.
If you recognize this person, your studies are complete. Furthermore, in ascending to the hall, he said: "If you wish to gather [the essence]..."

To harbor phrases and sentences within one's breast, to employ clever rhetoric and manage matters with the tongue, and to wear a high-placed cloth skirt solely to ensure others know one is a Chan master—this is merely seeking a place to show one's head. If you hold such a view, [you have missed the point].
"Striking that ghost’s bony buttocks—there will surely come a day when you enter the Hell of the Plucked Tongue! Old Hanshan Deshan’s perspective is not like this:
here there is no Buddha, and there is no Dharma. What is there to speak of as the beginning of the Seven Buddhas? It began with Vipaśyin Buddha (Viyinwang).
Simply make a great circle (the *yuanxiang*), and after that, each of the Seven Buddhas had their own words."
